A user auditor using a type 1 or type 2 report must therefore determine whether the complementary user entity controls identified by the service organisation are relevant to the user entity and, where they are, obtain an understanding of whether the user entity has designed and implemented them and test their operating effectiveness at the user entity. Two further things are evaluated before a type 2 report supports reliance: whether the period it covers is appropriate for the user auditor's purposes, and the adequacy of the time period covered by the tests of controls together with the time elapsed since those tests were performed.

citation.ref: para 8(a) defining a complementary user entity control, with the requirement, when a type 1 or type 2 report is used, to determine whether those controls are relevant and to test them at the user entity

concepts.subsection: SA 330 — The Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks
concepts.statement: Audit evidence about the operating effectiveness of controls obtained in a previous audit may be carried forward, on conditions. The auditor first establishes the continuing relevance of that evidence by obtaining audit evidence about whether significant changes in those controls have occurred since, through inquiry combined with observation or inspection. Where the controls have changed, they are tested in the current audit. Where they have not changed, they are tested at least once in every third audit, and some controls from the rotating population are tested in each audit so that no year passes with none of them tested. The concession stops at a significant risk: where the auditor plans to rely on controls over a risk he has determined to be a significant risk, those controls are tested in the current period, every period he relies on them.

citation.ref: para 14 and para 15, with the continuing-relevance test in para 13

concepts.subsection: SA 330 — The Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks
concepts.statement: Substantive procedures performed at an interim date leave a gap between that date and the period end, and SA 330 does not let it stay open. The auditor covers the remaining period by performing substantive procedures combined with tests of controls for the intervening period, or, where he determines that is sufficient, further substantive procedures only — either route having to provide a reasonable basis for extending the audit conclusions from the interim date to the period end. And where misstatements that the auditor did not expect are detected at the interim date, the auditor evaluates whether the related assessment of risk and the planned nature, timing and extent of the substantive procedures covering the remaining period need to be modified. Interim work is a way of spreading the audit, not a conclusion that survives contrary evidence found while doing it.

concepts.subsection: SA 450 — Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
concepts.statement: Before the evaluation of uncorrected misstatements begins, SA 450 sends the auditor back to materiality. The auditor communicates on a timely basis all misstatements accumulated during the audit with the appropriate level of management, unless prohibited by law or regulation, and requests management to correct them. Where management refuses to correct some or all of them, the auditor obtains an understanding of management's reasons for not making the corrections and takes that understanding into account when evaluating whether the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement. And prior to evaluating the effect of uncorrected misstatements, the auditor reassesses materiality determined in accordance with SA 320 to confirm whether it remains appropriate in the context of the entity's actual financial results. The planning figure was built on an expectation; by the end of the audit the year has actually happened.

concepts.subsection: SA 701 — Communicating Key Audit Matters
concepts.statement: SA 701 states its own limits. Communicating key audit matters in the auditor's report is not a substitute for disclosures in the financial statements that the applicable financial reporting framework requires management to make; not a substitute for the auditor expressing a modified opinion when the circumstances of the engagement require it under SA 705 (Revised); not a substitute for reporting in accordance with SA 570 (Revised) where a material uncertainty relating to going concern exists; and not a separate opinion on individual matters. It follows that a matter giving rise to a modified opinion, and a material uncertainty related to going concern, are by their nature key audit matters — and that neither is described in the Key Audit Matters section. Each is reported under its own standard, and the Key Audit Matters section carries a reference to the Basis for Qualified (Adverse) Opinion section or to the Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section.

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: A limitation imposed by management after the auditor has accepted the engagement has its own path, and the path does not begin with the opinion. The auditor requests management to remove the limitation. If management refuses, the auditor communicates the matter to those charged with governance and determines whether it is possible to perform alternative procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. If he remains unable to obtain that evidence, the consequence is graded. Where the possible effects on the financial statements of undetected misstatements, if any, could be material but not pervasive, the opinion is qualified. Where they could be both material and pervasive, the auditor withdraws from the audit where withdrawal is practicable and possible under applicable law or regulation, and disclaims an opinion only where withdrawal before issuing the report is not practicable or possible. Where he withdraws, he first communicates to those charged with governance any matters regarding misstatements identified during the audit that would have given rise to a modification of the opinion.

concepts.subsection: SA 570 (Revised) — Going Concern
concepts.statement: SA 570 has three reporting outcomes and they are not interchangeable. Where the financial statements have been prepared using the going concern basis of accounting but, in the auditor's judgement, management's use of that basis is inappropriate, the auditor expresses an adverse opinion — and a full and accurate note does not rescue it, because the basis of preparation runs through every figure rather than through one disclosure. Where the use of the going concern basis is appropriate but a material uncertainty exists and is adequately disclosed, the opinion is unmodified with a separate Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section; where that disclosure is not adequate, the opinion is qualified or adverse as appropriate. And where management is unwilling to make or extend its assessment when the auditor requests it, the auditor considers the implications for the auditor's report, the question being an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the appropriateness of the basis itself.

concepts.subsection: SA 805 — Special Considerations: Single Financial Statements and Specific Elements
concepts.statement: SA 805 draws a line between a single financial statement and a specific element of a financial statement once the opinion on the complete set has gone wrong. Where the opinion on the entity's complete set of financial statements is adverse, or the auditor disclaimed an opinion on it, the auditor shall not express an unmodified opinion in the same auditor's report on a single financial statement that forms part of those financial statements, or on a specific element that forms part of them, because the unmodified opinion would contradict the adverse opinion or disclaimer. A specific element may still carry an unmodified opinion in a separate audit, on three conditions that must all hold: the auditor is not prohibited by law or regulation from doing so, that opinion is expressed in an auditor's report that is not published together with the report containing the adverse opinion or disclaimer of opinion, and the specific element does not constitute a major portion of the entity's complete set of financial statements. A single financial statement never can, because the standard deems it to constitute a major portion of those financial statements.

concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 10
concepts.statement: A member in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he charges or offers to charge, accepts or offers to accept, in respect of any professional employment, fees which are based on a percentage of profits or which are contingent upon the findings or results of such employment, except as permitted under any regulation made under the Chartered Accountants Act. The exception is Regulation 192, which names the permitted cases: a receiver or a liquidator may charge on a percentage of the realisation or disbursement of the assets; the auditor of a co-operative society may charge on a percentage of the paid-up capital, the working capital, the gross or net income or the profits; a valuer for the purposes of direct taxes and duties may charge on a percentage of the value of the property valued; and the Council has permitted a percentage or contingent basis for certain management consultancy services, fund raising services, debt recovery services and cost optimisation services. Anything outside that list is misconduct however the engagement letter dresses it, and the clause reaches every kind of professional employment, not audit alone.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 10, read with Regulation 192 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xix)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(xix) makes the auditor state, on the basis of the financial ratios, the ageing and expected dates of realisation of financial assets and payment of financial liabilities, other information accompanying the financial statements, and his knowledge of the Board of Directors' and management's plans, whether he is of the opinion that no material uncertainty exists as on the date of the audit report that the company is not capable of meeting its liabilities existing at the date of the balance sheet as and when they fall due within a period of one year from the balance sheet date. The clause also makes him state that his reporting is based on the facts up to the date of the audit report, and that he neither gives any guarantee nor any assurance that all liabilities falling due within a period of one year from the balance sheet date will get discharged by the company as and when they fall due. It is anchored twice to the balance sheet date — the liabilities are those existing then, and the one-year window runs from then — and it is not the going concern conclusion under SA 570.

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xiv)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(xiv) has two limbs and each is answered on its own. The first asks whether the company has an internal audit system commensurate with the size and nature of its business. That is a question about fit, not about section 138 — a company outside the classes section 138 covers still attracts a negative answer if the function it does run is inadequate, and a company inside those classes still fails the limb if the coverage does not match the size and nature of its business. The second limb asks whether the reports of the Internal Auditors for the period under audit were considered by the statutory auditor, which is a statement about what the statutory auditor did. Considering those reports is not the same as adopting them: SA 610 (Revised) governs whether and how the internal audit function's work may be used at all.

concepts.subsection: Section 143(1) — Right of access and the duty of inquiry
concepts.statement: Section 143(1) gives every auditor a right of access at all times to the books of account and vouchers of the company, kept at the registered office or elsewhere, and entitles him to require from the officers of the company such information and explanation as he may consider necessary for the performance of his duties. Its proviso then names six matters he shall inquire into: whether loans and advances made on the basis of security have been properly secured and whether the terms on which they have been made are prejudicial to the interests of the company or its members; whether transactions of the company which are represented merely by book entries are prejudicial to the interests of the company; whether so much of the assets of the company as consist of shares, debentures and other securities have been sold at a price less than that at which they were purchased, the company not being an investment company or a banking company; whether loans and advances made by the company have been shown as deposits; whether personal expenses have been charged to revenue account; and, where the books state that shares have been allotted for cash, whether cash has actually been received and, if not, whether the position as stated in the account books and the balance sheet is correct, regular and not misleading. The inquiry is a duty. The reporting is not: nothing is stated on these matters unless the inquiry produces an adverse finding.

citation.ref: Section 143(1) and its proviso, clauses (a) to (f)

concepts.subsection: Section 140(1) — Removal of an auditor before expiry of term
concepts.statement: An auditor appointed under section 139 may be removed from his office before the expiry of his term only by a special resolution of the company, after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government, and the auditor concerned must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before any action is taken. Rule 7 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 fixes the sequence: the Board passes a resolution; the application to the Central Government goes in Form ADT-2 with the prescribed fee within thirty days of that Board resolution; and the company holds the general meeting to pass the special resolution within sixty days of receiving the Central Government's approval. Approval first, special resolution second — the word in the section is previous approval. None of this is the resignation route under section 140(2), where the auditor leaves of his own motion and files a statement in Form ADT-3 with the company and the Registrar within thirty days.

citation.ref: Section 140(1) with its proviso, read with Rule 7(1), Rule 7(2) and Rule 7(3) of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014

concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part I — Clauses 5, 6, 8 and 9
concepts.statement: Four clauses of Part I of the Second Schedule punish the auditor for what his report does not say. A member in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he fails to disclose a material fact known to him which is not disclosed in a financial statement, but disclosure of which is necessary in making such financial statement where he is concerned with that financial statement in a professional capacity (Clause 5); if he fails to report a material misstatement known to him to appear in a financial statement with which he is concerned in a professional capacity (Clause 6); if he fails to obtain sufficient information which is necessary for expression of an opinion, or its exceptions are sufficiently material to negate the expression of an opinion (Clause 8); and if he fails to invite attention to any material departure from the generally accepted procedure of audit applicable to the circumstances (Clause 9). Clause 5 is about a fact absent from the statements, Clause 6 about a wrong figure present in them, Clause 8 about the evidence behind the opinion, and Clause 9 about the audit's own method. All four sit in the Second Schedule, which routes the case to the Disciplinary Committee.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part I, Clauses 5, 6, 8 and 9

concepts.subsection: Income recognition and asset classification
concepts.statement: A term loan turns non-performing when interest or principal stays overdue for more than ninety days; a cash credit when the account stays out of order. Once non-performing, the asset walks a ladder — substandard for its first twelve months as an NPA, doubtful once it stays substandard beyond twelve months, loss when identified as such — and income on it is recognised only on realisation, not accrual.

citation.ref: Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning

concepts.subsection: Long form audit report
concepts.statement: The LFAR is the RBI-prescribed questionnaire the bank auditor answers alongside the main report — advances, credit appraisal, NPA identification, internal controls, frauds — branch LFARs feeding the central auditor's consolidated one. It supplements the statutory report and does not dilute it: a matter grave enough to affect the true and fair view belongs in the main report, qualified, not parked in the LFAR.

concepts.subsection: Section 141 — Auditor disqualifications
concepts.statement: Section 141(3)(d) with Rule 10 draws money lines around the auditor's independence: a relative may hold securities of the company up to one lakh rupees face value; indebtedness to the company beyond five lakh rupees disqualifies; a guarantee for a third party's debt to the company beyond one lakh rupees disqualifies. The disqualification reaches the member, the firm and its partners, and one incurred during the term vacates the office.

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xi)
concepts.statement: CARO's fraud clause asks three things: whether any fraud by the company or on the company was noticed or reported during the year, with nature and amount; whether any section 143(12) report was filed in Form ADT-4; and whether the auditor considered whistle-blower complaints received by the company. The clause covers fraud on the company by anyone, not only by its officers and employees.

concepts.subsection: SQC 1 — Engagement quality control review
concepts.statement: SQC 1 requires an engagement quality control review — an objective evaluation of the significant judgments and the conclusions reached — for audits of financial statements of listed entities, completed before the report is dated. The reviewer stands outside the engagement team, and the report cannot be signed past an unresolved difference with the reviewer.

concepts.subsection: Due diligence, investigation and audit
concepts.statement: An audit expresses an opinion on financial statements against a framework; due diligence is a purchaser-side examination of a target's whole position — financial, legal, operational — to price a deal and surface hidden liabilities; an investigation is a deep, targeted probe into a suspected specific matter, going wherever the suspicion leads. Scope, purpose and the reporting audience differ across all three; assurance levels are not interchangeable.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting

concepts.subsection: Government audit — propriety
concepts.statement: Propriety audit asks questions regularity audit cannot: not only was the expenditure sanctioned and lawful, but was it wise, economical, and free of personal advantage — would a person of ordinary prudence have spent his own money so? The C&AG's audit of public undertakings runs on both rails, and a transaction can pass every rule yet fail propriety.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings

concepts.subsection: Peer review
concepts.statement: Peer review examines a practice unit's systems — whether its quality controls, documentation and compliance with technical standards for attestation services are adequate and were followed — through sample engagements. The reviewer evaluates the unit, not the clients: a review is not a second audit of any auditee, and its report speaks to the unit's systems, leading to a peer review certificate.

concepts.subsection: Section 139(6) — First auditor
concepts.statement: A company's first auditor (other than a government company) is appointed by the board within thirty days of registration; if the board fails, the members appoint within ninety days at an extraordinary general meeting. The first auditor holds office until the conclusion of the first annual general meeting — and needs no ratification meanwhile.

concepts.subsection: Forensic accounting and investigation
concepts.statement: Forensic engagements run under ICAI's Forensic Accounting and Investigation Standards and differ from audit at the root: the mindset presumes the possibility of fraud rather than neutrality, procedures chase evidence that will stand in legal proceedings — chain of custody, corroboration, documentation to litigation grade — and the outcome states findings of fact, not an opinion or an assurance conclusion. Materiality thresholds do not excuse small frauds from a forensic scope.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting

concepts.subsection: NBFC audit — scale-based regulation
concepts.statement: RBI regulates NBFCs in layers by size and risk — base, middle, upper and a normally empty top layer — with regulatory intensity rising through the stack: the upper layer carries bank-like requirements. The auditor's concerns scale accordingly: income recognition and asset classification norms, the layer's specific prudential requirements, and the statutory auditor's own direct reporting duties to RBI on matters such as non-compliance with the RBI Act.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies

concepts.subsection: Section 143(3) — The auditor's report
concepts.statement: Section 143(3) prescribes what every company audit report states: whether information and explanations sought were obtained, whether proper books were kept, whether the accounts agree with the books, whether the statements comply with the accounting standards, the section 164(2) director disqualification status, internal financial controls where applicable, and the rule-prescribed matters. Each is answered — a negative or qualified answer comes with reasons under 143(4).

concepts.subsection: Audit in an IT environment
concepts.statement: General IT controls govern the environment — access, change management, operations, backup — while application controls live inside each system, checking individual transactions: input validations, exception reports, interface reconciliations. Weak general controls undermine every application control running on that system, so the auditor tests the foundation before relying on what stands on it; automated controls tested once can be relied on across the period only if change management held.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit in an Automated Environment

concepts.subsection: Section 144 — Services an auditor may not render
concepts.statement: A company's auditor may not render, directly or indirectly, to the company, its holding or its subsidiary: accounting and book keeping, internal audit, design and implementation of financial information systems, actuarial services, investment advisory and investment banking, outsourced financial services, and management services. "Directly or indirectly" reaches the auditor's relatives, connected persons and entities using the firm's brand or network. Permitted other services need audit committee or board approval.

concepts.subsection: Insurance audit — claims provisions
concepts.statement: In a general insurer's audit the claims liability has two layers: outstanding claims — reported but unsettled, verified against surveyor reports and case estimates — and claims incurred but not reported (IBNR), an actuarial estimate the appointed actuary certifies and the auditor evaluates as an accounting estimate using an expert's work. Premium deficiency and unexpired risk reserves sit beside them; the auditor tests data integrity feeding the actuary as hard as the outputs.

concepts.subsection: Review engagements and agreed-upon procedures
concepts.statement: A review gives limited assurance in negative form — "nothing has come to our attention" — built mainly on inquiry and analytical procedures; an agreed-upon procedures engagement gives no assurance at all, reporting factual findings of the exact procedures the parties specified, for those parties alone to judge. An audit's reasonable assurance sits above both. Naming the engagement wrongly misleads every reader about what stands behind the numbers.

citation.ref: Ch. Review and Related Services (SRE 2400, SRS 4400)

concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part II — Members in service
concepts.statement: A member in employment commits professional misconduct by paying any person a share of the emoluments of his employment, or by accepting any part of the fees, profits or gains of a lawyer, chartered accountant, broker or agent engaged by his employer. The profession's fee-sharing discipline follows the member into service — kickbacks on either side of an employer's engagements are the mischief.

concepts.subsection: Tax audit — Forms 3CA, 3CB and 3CD
concepts.statement: Every tax audit report carries Form 3CD, the statement of particulars; what varies is its cover. Form 3CA is used where the accounts are already audited under any other law — a company under the Companies Act — and it references that statutory audit; Form 3CB is used where no other audit exists, and there the tax auditor himself expresses the true and fair opinion on the accounts. Picking 3CB for a company duplicates an opinion someone else owns.

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(ii)
concepts.statement: CARO's second clause covers inventory and borrowings against it: whether physical verification of inventory was conducted at reasonable intervals with material discrepancies dealt with in the books — and, where working capital limits above five crore rupees are sanctioned against current assets, whether the quarterly returns filed with the banks agree with the books of account, with disagreements detailed. Statements to bankers and statements to shareholders must be the same statements.

concepts.subsection: Government audit — performance audit
concepts.statement: Performance audit examines the three Es — economy (spending less for the same inputs), efficiency (getting more output per input), and effectiveness (achieving the intended outcome) — of a programme or entity, against criteria agreed or derived, reporting findings and recommendations rather than an opinion. It differs from propriety audit's transaction-level prudence test: performance audit judges the scheme, not the voucher.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings

concepts.subsection: Interim reviews — SRE 2410
concepts.statement: The statutory auditor's review of a listed company's quarterly results runs under SRE 2410: inquiry of finance personnel and analytical procedures, sized for limited assurance, concluding in negative form. It is not a small audit — no control testing, no third-party confirmations by default — but the auditor who becomes aware of a possible material misstatement must extend procedures until the doubt resolves; the lighter vehicle carries no licence to drive past red flags.

concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — Responding to NOCLAR
concepts.statement: On becoming aware of non-compliance or suspected non-compliance with laws and regulations at a client, the member's response runs in sequence: understand the matter, raise it with the appropriate level of management and those charged with governance, urge rectification and disclosure, then judge whether further action — up to withdrawal or disclosure to an authority — is needed in the public interest. Confidentiality does not bar a disclosure the framework calls for; walking away silently is the response the framework rejects.

citation.ref: Responding to Non-Compliance with Laws and Regulations

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(iii)
concepts.statement: Where a company has made investments in, given guarantees or security for, or granted loans or advances in the nature of loans to any parties, CARO asks: the amounts involved (with related-party loans separately shown), whether the terms are prejudicial to the company's interests, whether repayment schedules exist and repayments are regular, overdue amounts beyond ninety days and the steps taken, whether loans were renewed or fresh loans settled old ones, and loans repayable on demand or without terms — again with the related-party share disclosed.

concepts.subsection: Sections 45(4) and 9B — Reconstitution of a firm
concepts.statement: On reconstitution of a specified entity (firm, AOP, BOI), section 9B first deems the entity to have transferred to a partner or member any capital asset or stock-in-trade received by that person, taxable as the entity's own income in the year of receipt, at fair market value. Section 45(4) then separately taxes any excess of the money and the fair market value of capital assets received by the partner over the balance standing in that partner's capital account, as capital gains in the entity's hands — never in the retiring partner's hands.

concepts.subsection: Section 47 — Transactions not regarded as transfer
concepts.statement: Section 47 lists transactions that section 45 does not reach at all — no capital gains arise even though an asset changes hands. Distribution of assets on total partition of a HUF, transfer under a gift or an irrevocable trust (other than of ESOP shares), and transfer of a capital asset by a wholly-owned subsidiary to its Indian holding company (or the reverse) sit among them; the cost to the previous owner carries over to whoever holds the asset next, ready to be taxed when that person eventually transfers it.

concepts.subsection: Section 54B — Capital gains on transfer of agricultural land
concepts.statement: Section 54B exempts capital gains, short-term or long-term, on the transfer of land that the assessee or the assessee's parent used for agricultural purposes in the two years immediately before the transfer — available only to an individual or a HUF. The exemption needs another agricultural land purchased within two years of the transfer; unlike section 54EC, there is no monetary cap on the amount that can be invested.

concepts.subsection: Section 54D — Capital gains on compulsory acquisition of land or building for an industrial undertaking
concepts.statement: Section 54D exempts capital gains where land or a building forming part of an industrial undertaking, and used for the undertaking's business in the two years before the transfer, is compulsorily acquired. Any assessee, not only an individual or HUF, qualifies. The exemption needs the compensation reinvested, within three years of receipt, in land or a building to shift, re-establish or set up another industrial undertaking.

concepts.subsection: Section 80AC with Chapter VI-A — Structure of deductions from gross total income
concepts.statement: Chapter VI-A deductions reduce gross total income and can never exceed it — a loss cannot be manufactured by claiming more deduction than there is income to absorb. Section 80AC additionally denies specified deductions (profit-linked deductions such as those under sections 80-IA and 80JJAA, among others it names) altogether, not merely delays them, unless the return of income is furnished on or before the due date under section 139(1) — a belated return filed after that date does not save the claim.

citation.ref: Section 80AC read with Chapter VI-A (Sections 80C to 80U)

concepts.subsection: Section 40A(2) — Disallowance of excessive payments to related persons
concepts.statement: Where an assessee pays for goods, services or facilities to a person having a substantial interest in the business, or a relative of such a person, and the Assessing Officer forms an opinion that the expenditure is excessive or unreasonable having regard to its fair market value or the business's legitimate needs, the excess is disallowed. The disallowance reaches only the excess over what is reasonable — not the entire payment — and rests on the officer's opinion, formed on evidence, not on the relationship alone.

concepts.subsection: Section 40A(3) — Disallowance of cash expenditure
concepts.statement: An expenditure otherwise deductible is disallowed in full if the payment, or aggregate of payments to one person in a day, exceeds the prescribed limit and is made otherwise than by an account payee cheque, account payee bank draft, or a prescribed electronic mode — genuineness of the expense or identity of the payee does not save it. Section 40A(3A) extends the same disallowance to a later year: an expense allowed on accrual in an earlier year, if actually paid in cash beyond the limit, is deemed profit of the payment year.

concepts.subsection: Section 32 — Block of assets and additional depreciation
concepts.statement: Depreciation under section 32 is computed on the written down value of a block of assets — similar assets carrying the same rate — not asset by asset; an asset put to use for less than 180 days in the year of acquisition draws only half the normal rate for that year. Additional depreciation, over and above normal depreciation, is available on new plant and machinery acquired and installed by an assessee engaged in manufacturing or generation of power, but not on office appliances, road transport vehicles, second-hand plant and machinery, or assets on which the entire cost is otherwise allowed as a deduction.

concepts.subsection: Section 72A — Carry forward of losses in amalgamation
concepts.statement: Section 72A lets the accumulated business loss and unabsorbed depreciation of an amalgamating company be treated as the amalgamated company's own loss and depreciation for the year of amalgamation, opening a fresh period of carry forward — but only where the amalgamating company is an industrial undertaking, a ship, a hotel, a banking company, or another class the section names, and specified continuity conditions on the business and its fixed assets are met before and after the amalgamation. Failing those conditions after the set-off has been claimed reverses it: the set-off amount becomes the amalgamated company's taxable income in the year the conditions fail.

concepts.subsection: Section 92E — Transfer pricing accountant's report
concepts.statement: Every person who has entered into an international transaction or a specified domestic transaction during the previous year must obtain a report from an accountant in the prescribed form, and furnish it on or before the specified date — the same extended due date section 139(1) gives a person required to furnish a transfer pricing report. The obligation attaches to the existence of the transaction itself, not to whether it actually shifted profit, and for an international transaction it carries no minimum value threshold.

concepts.subsection: Section 195 — TDS on payments to non-residents
concepts.statement: Section 195 requires tax deduction at source on any sum chargeable to tax under the Act paid or credited to a non-resident — chargeability itself is the trigger, not a named list of payments — at the time of credit or payment, whichever is earlier, at the rates in force under the Finance Act or the applicable DTAA, whichever is more beneficial to the payee. A payer unsure how much of a composite sum is chargeable may apply under section 195(2) for the Assessing Officer to determine the taxable proportion, while the recipient may separately seek a nil or lower deduction certificate under section 197.

concepts.subsection: Section 253 — Appeal to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal
concepts.statement: An assessee aggrieved by an order of the Commissioner (Appeals), among other specified orders, may appeal to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal; the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may likewise direct an appeal against such an order. Once an appeal is filed, the other side may file a memorandum of cross-objections without needing to file a separate appeal of its own. The Tribunal is the final fact-finding authority in the appeal hierarchy — a further appeal to the High Court under section 260A lies only on a substantial question of law, not a fresh look at facts the Tribunal has settled.

concepts.subsection: Section 92BA — Specified domestic transaction
concepts.statement: A specified domestic transaction is a transaction between related domestic parties that the transfer pricing machinery reaches even though no foreign party is involved — but only where the aggregate of all such transactions in the previous year exceeds twenty crore rupees. What remains inside the definition are transactions of an undertaking claiming a profit-linked deduction, such as inter-unit transfers to which section 80-IA(8) or 80-IA(10) applies, and similar transactions under section 10AA. Payments to related persons covered by section 40A(2)(b) were dropped from the definition when clause (i) of section 92BA was omitted with effect from 1 April 2017, so those payments are tested for reasonableness under section 40A(2) alone and never counted towards the twenty crore aggregate.

citation.ref: Section 92BA (clause (i) omitted w.e.f. 1-4-2017) read with Section 80-IA(8) and (10)

concepts.subsection: Sections 92CA and 92C(4) — Reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer
concepts.statement: The Assessing Officer may, with the approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, refer the computation of the arm's length price to a Transfer Pricing Officer under section 92CA; the TPO's order determining the arm's length price binds the Assessing Officer, who then computes total income in conformity with it. Where the arm's length price so determined increases the assessee's income, the proviso to section 92C(4) denies any deduction under section 10AA or under Chapter VI-A on the amount of that enhancement — a tax-holiday unit therefore gains nothing by understating its transfer price, because the adjustment lands as fully taxable income.

citation.ref: Section 92CA read with the proviso to Section 92C(4)

concepts.subsection: Sections 92CC and 92CD — Advance pricing agreement
concepts.statement: An advance pricing agreement fixes the arm's length price, or the manner of determining it, in advance for an international transaction, and binds both the assessee and the tax authorities for the previous years the agreement covers — not exceeding five consecutive previous years. A rollback may be sought so that the same agreed position applies to as many as four previous years preceding the first year of the agreement, and the applicant must seek the rollback for every one of those years in which the transaction was undertaken; picking only the favourable years is not open to it. Section 92CD then requires a modified return within three months of the month in which the agreement is entered into, for each earlier year the agreement covers.

citation.ref: Sections 92CC and 92CD read with Rules 10MA and 10RA

concepts.subsection: Sections 115JC and 115JD — Alternate minimum tax
concepts.statement: Alternate minimum tax applies to a person other than a company that has claimed a deduction under Chapter VI-A heading "C" (deductions in respect of certain incomes, such as section 80-IA), or under section 10AA, or under section 35AD. It is charged on adjusted total income, which is total income with those deductions added back. The twenty lakh rupee floor in section 115JC(4) is not a general exemption: it protects only an individual, a Hindu undivided family, an association of persons, a body of individuals or an artificial juridical person. A firm or a limited liability partnership gets no such floor and is inside the AMT net whatever its adjusted total income. Tax paid in excess of the regular liability becomes AMT credit under section 115JD, carried forward for fifteen assessment years and set off only in a year when regular tax exceeds AMT; no interest is payable on the credit.

concepts.subsection: Section 2(19AA) — Demerger
concepts.statement: A transfer of an undertaking is a demerger for tax purposes only if it satisfies every condition in section 2(19AA) together. Two do most of the work in an examination. First, all the property and all the liabilities of the undertaking must be transferred at values appearing in the books of account immediately before the demerger — any increase on revaluation is ignored, so recording the assets in the resulting company at fair value breaks the definition. Second, shareholders holding not less than three-fourths in value of the shares of the demerged company must become shareholders of the resulting company. Fail any condition and the transaction is not a demerger at all, which means the exemptions in section 47 and the loss carry-forward in section 72A(4) are simply unavailable.

concepts.subsection: Section 12AB — Registration of a charitable trust and its validity
concepts.statement: Registration under section 12AB is never permanent, unlike the old section 12AA registration it replaced. Provisional registration runs for three years. On renewal, the period depends on the size of the trust: ten years where the trust's total income, computed without giving effect to sections 11 and 12, did not exceed five crore rupees in each of the two previous years immediately preceding the previous year in which the application is made, and five years otherwise. The ten-year period comes from the proviso to section 12AB(1), inserted with effect from 1 April 2025. In every case the trust must apply for renewal at least six months before the registration expires, and the registration lapses if it does not.

citation.ref: Section 12AB(1) with its proviso (inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2025), read with Section 12A(1)(ac)

concepts.subsection: Section 115TD — Tax on accreted income of a trust
concepts.statement: Section 115TD is an exit charge on a registered trust or institution that leaves the charitable régime — where its registration is cancelled, where it converts into a form not eligible for registration, where it merges with an entity not having similar objects and registration, or where on dissolution it fails to transfer its assets to another registered trust within twelve months. Accreted income is the fair market value of the total assets on the specified date reduced by the liabilities on that date, and it bears additional income-tax at the maximum marginal rate. The charge is on accreted net worth, not on income, so it is payable whether or not the trust earned anything that year, and it is in addition to any income-tax otherwise payable.

concepts.subsection: Section 206C(1H) omitted — TCS on sale of goods and its overlap with Section 194Q
concepts.statement: Section 206C(1H), which made a seller with turnover above ten crore rupees collect tax at source on sale consideration beyond fifty lakh rupees from a buyer, stands omitted with effect from 1 April 2025. For previous year 2025-26 it does not operate at all, and the old tie-break rule — where both provisions applied to one transaction, section 194Q prevailed and the seller was relieved — has nothing left to resolve. What survives is section 194Q: a buyer whose total sales, turnover or gross receipts exceeded ten crore rupees in the immediately preceding financial year deducts tax at 0.1 per cent on the value of goods purchased from a resident seller in excess of fifty lakh rupees in the year. The obligation now sits on the buyer alone.

concepts.subsection: Sections 201(1) and 201(1A) — Assessee in default for a TDS failure
concepts.statement: A payer who fails to deduct tax at source is deemed an assessee in default under section 201(1) and can be recovered from as though the tax were his own. The first proviso rescues him where the resident payee has furnished a return under section 139, has taken the sum into account in computing income in that return, has paid the tax due on the income declared, and the payer furnishes an accountant's certificate in the prescribed form. That relief is from the tax alone. Interest under section 201(1A) still runs at one per cent for every month or part of a month from the date on which the tax was deductible to the date on which the payee furnished his return of income — the compensation for the delay survives the payee's compliance.

citation.ref: Section 201(1) with its first proviso, and Section 201(1A)

concepts.subsection: Section 149 — Time limit for a notice of reassessment
concepts.statement: For a notice under section 148 issued on or after 1 September 2024, section 149 allows three years and three months from the end of the relevant assessment year in the ordinary case. That stretches to five years and three months, but only where the Assessing Officer has books, documents or evidence revealing that income chargeable to tax which has escaped assessment amounts to, or is likely to amount to, fifty lakh rupees or more for that year. The extended limb is not confined to search cases, and the ten-year outer limit that existed before this amendment is gone. The period runs from the end of the assessment year, never from the end of the financial year in which the income was earned.

citation.ref: Section 149(1) as substituted with effect from 1 September 2024, read with Section 148A

concepts.subsection: Section 144C — Draft order and the Dispute Resolution Panel
concepts.statement: Where the Assessing Officer proposes a variation prejudicial to an eligible assessee — a person in whose case a transfer pricing adjustment has been made under section 92CA(3), or a non-resident, or a foreign company — he must first forward a draft of the proposed assessment order. The assessee then has thirty days from receipt of the draft order to either accept the variation or file objections with the Dispute Resolution Panel and the Assessing Officer. Miss those thirty days and the Assessing Officer may complete the assessment on the basis of the draft. Where objections are filed, the Panel's directions bind the Assessing Officer and must issue within nine months from the end of the month in which the draft order was forwarded.

concepts.subsection: Equalisation levy — both levies withdrawn
concepts.statement: Neither equalisation levy operates in previous year 2025-26. The two per cent levy on the consideration of an e-commerce operator for e-commerce supply or services ceased to apply to consideration received or receivable on or after 1 August 2024, and the six per cent levy on consideration for online advertisement and related services ceased on or after 1 April 2025. The exemption in section 10(50), which kept income already bearing the levy outside the Income-tax Act, falls away with the levy it was tied to. The consequence is that these payments are now tested for chargeability in the ordinary way — under section 9 for a business connection or significant economic presence, under section 195 for withholding, and against the applicable double taxation avoidance agreement.

citation.ref: Chapter VIII, Sections 165 and 165A of the Finance Act, 2016 (levies withdrawn w.e.f. 1-8-2024 and 1-4-2025), read with Section 10(50) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Section 9(1)(vii) — Fees for technical services deemed to accrue in India
concepts.statement: Fees for technical services payable by a resident are deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(vii), except where the services are utilised for a business carried on outside India or for earning income from a source outside India. The Explanation to section 9(2) settles the argument that once succeeded before the courts: such income is deemed to accrue in India whether or not the non-resident has a residence, a place of business or a business connection in India, and whether or not the services were rendered in India. Physical presence is therefore irrelevant to the source rule. What is not irrelevant is the treaty — section 90(2) lets the non-resident take the double taxation avoidance agreement where it is more beneficial, and many treaties tax fees for technical services only if the services make available technical knowledge or skill to the recipient.

citation.ref: Section 9(1)(vii) with the Explanation to Section 9(2), read with Section 90(2)

concepts.subsection: Section 44B — Presumptive profits of a non-resident shipping business
concepts.statement: For a non-resident carrying on the business of operating ships, other than cruise shipping, section 44B deems seven and a half per cent of a specified aggregate to be the profits chargeable under the head profits and gains of business or profession. The aggregate has two limbs. The first takes the amount paid or payable, whether in India or outside India, for the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at any port in India — so a freight collected abroad still counts if the cargo loaded in India. The second takes the amount received or deemed to be received in India for carriage from a port outside India. Compare the neighbouring presumptive rates before answering: section 44BB, for services connected with the extraction of mineral oils, deems ten per cent, and section 44BBA, for the operation of aircraft, deems five per cent.

citation.ref: Section 44B(1) and (2), read with Sections 44BB and 44BBA

concepts.subsection: Section 194A — TDS on interest and the thresholds from 1 April 2025
concepts.statement: Section 194A requires tax at ten per cent to be deducted from interest other than interest on securities paid to a resident, and the threshold below which nothing is deducted was raised on 1 April 2025. Where the payer is a banking company, a co-operative society engaged in the business of banking or a post office, the threshold is one lakh rupees for a resident senior citizen and fifty thousand rupees for anyone else. In any other case — a company, a firm or a non-banking finance company paying interest on a loan or a deposit — the threshold is ten thousand rupees. Two traps sit in the section. The threshold is tested on the aggregate for the financial year, not on each payment, and once it is crossed the deduction is on the whole sum and not merely on the excess over the threshold.

citation.ref: Section 194A(1) and Section 194A(3)(i) with its provisos, as amended with effect from 1 April 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 194-I — TDS on rent and the threshold from 1 April 2025
concepts.statement: Section 194-I makes a payer other than an individual or Hindu undivided family not liable to tax audit deduct tax from rent paid to a resident, at two per cent where the rent is for the use of plant, machinery or equipment and at ten per cent where it is for the use of land, a building, furniture or fittings. From 1 April 2025 the threshold is fifty thousand rupees for a month or part of a month, replacing the old figure of two lakh forty thousand rupees for the financial year; on an even rent that works out at six lakh rupees for the year. The two rates are the examinable half of the section, because the equipment limb is often given the ten per cent rate by reflex. As everywhere in Chapter XVII-B, once the threshold is crossed the deduction is on the whole rent and not on the excess.

citation.ref: Section 194-I(a) and (b) with its second proviso, as amended with effect from 1 April 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 194J — TDS on professional and technical fees and the category-wise threshold
concepts.statement: Section 194J covers four different payments to a resident — fees for professional services, fees for technical services, royalty, and a sum for not carrying out any activity or not sharing any know-how. The rate is ten per cent, except that it is two per cent for fees for technical services other than professional services, for royalty in the nature of consideration for the sale, distribution or exhibition of cinematographic films, and for a payee engaged only in the business of operating a call centre. From 1 April 2025 the threshold is fifty thousand rupees, raised from thirty thousand rupees, and the proviso applies that figure separately to each of the four categories rather than to their aggregate. A payee can therefore take forty-nine thousand rupees of professional fees and forty-nine thousand rupees of technical fees from the same payer in a year with nothing deducted from either.

citation.ref: Section 194J(1) with its first proviso, as amended with effect from 1 April 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 194H — TDS on commission or brokerage after the rate and threshold changes
concepts.statement: Section 194H requires deduction from commission or brokerage paid to a resident, and both its numbers moved recently. The rate fell from five per cent to two per cent for sums credited or paid on or after 1 October 2024, and the threshold rose from fifteen thousand rupees to twenty thousand rupees on 1 April 2025. The threshold is on the aggregate credited or paid during the financial year, so a series of small payments that individually fall below it still triggers deduction once they add up past twenty thousand rupees, and the deduction is then on the whole aggregate including the earlier payments from which nothing was taken. Insurance commission is outside this section and falls under section 194D.

citation.ref: Section 194H with its first proviso, rate amended with effect from 1 October 2024 and threshold with effect from 1 April 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 206C(1G) — TCS on remittance under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme
concepts.statement: An authorised dealer remitting money abroad under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme collects tax at source under section 206C(1G). From 1 April 2025 the threshold is ten lakh rupees, raised from seven lakh rupees, and the collection is on the amount in excess of that figure and not on the whole remittance — which makes this section behave differently from the deduction provisions in Chapter XVII-B. The rate is five per cent on the excess where the remittance is for education or for medical treatment and twenty per cent on the excess for any other purpose. Also from 1 April 2025, where the remittance for education is made out of a loan obtained from a financial institution as defined in section 80E(3)(b), no tax is collected at all, whatever the amount.

citation.ref: Section 206C(1G) with its provisos, as amended with effect from 1 April 2025, read with Section 80E(3)(b)

concepts.subsection: Section 286 and Rule 10DA — Country-by-Country report and the master file
concepts.statement: Two separate documentation duties sit on an Indian member of a multinational group and they have different triggers. The master file under Rule 10DA is required where the consolidated group revenue of the international group for the preceding accounting year exceeds five hundred crore rupees and, in addition, either the aggregate value of the entity's international transactions exceeds fifty crore rupees or its international transactions in intangible property exceed ten crore rupees; it is furnished in Form 3CEAA, and Form 3CEAB designates which of several Indian entities will file. The Country-by-Country report under section 286 is required only where the consolidated group revenue exceeds six thousand four hundred crore rupees, the figure aligned with the OECD's 750 million euro standard; it is filed in Form 3CEAD by the parent entity or the alternate reporting entity, with the intimation in Form 3CEAC. A group can therefore owe a master file and owe no Country-by-Country report at all.

citation.ref: Rule 10DA and Rule 10DB read with Section 286 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and Notification No. 31/2021

concepts.subsection: Rule 128 — Foreign tax credit and Form 67
concepts.statement: A resident who has paid tax in a foreign country on income also taxed in India takes credit under Rule 128. Two limits define the credit. It is available against tax, surcharge and cess payable under the Income-tax Act, 1961 and never against interest, fee or penalty; and it cannot exceed the amount of tax arrived at by applying the Indian rate of tax to that same doubly taxed income, so where the foreign rate is the higher one the excess is simply lost, being neither refunded nor carried forward. The procedure changed in 2022: the statement in Form 67 may now be furnished at any time on or before the end of the relevant assessment year, where it previously had to accompany a return filed by the due date under section 139(1).

citation.ref: Rule 128(1), 128(2) and 128(9) as amended by Notification No. 100/2022, read with Section 90(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Sections 115A and 44DA — Royalty and fees for technical services of a non-resident
concepts.statement: Whether a non-resident's royalty or fees for technical services is taxed gross or net turns on one fact: whether the right, property or contract is effectively connected with a permanent establishment or fixed place of profession in India. Where it is not, section 115A charges the gross amount at twenty per cent — raised from ten per cent with effect from assessment year 2024-25 — with no deduction for any expenditure and no allowance under sections 28 to 44C. Where it is, section 115A steps aside and section 44DA taxes the income as business profits on a net basis at the ordinary rate, which for a foreign company is thirty-five per cent from assessment year 2025-26; the non-resident must then keep books under section 44AA and furnish an audit report in Form 3CE, and section 44DA disallows head-office reimbursements and any expenditure not wholly and exclusively for the permanent establishment. Section 90(2) still lets the non-resident take a lower treaty rate.

citation.ref: Section 115A(1)(b) and Section 44DA(1) with its provisos, read with Section 90(2) and Rule 6GA (Form 3CE)

concepts.subsection: Article 4(2) of a treaty — Tie-breaker for a dual resident individual
concepts.statement: An individual can be a resident of India under section 6 and a resident of the other country under its own law at the same time. Section 90(2) then lets him take the treaty, and Article 4(2) breaks the tie by a strict order that must be worked in sequence and abandoned the moment one test decides. He is treated as a resident of the state in which he has a permanent home available to him; if a permanent home is available in both, of the state with which his personal and economic relations are closer, that is his centre of vital interests; if that cannot be determined, of the state in which he has an habitual abode; if he has an habitual abode in both or in neither, of the state of which he is a national; and if he is a national of both or of neither, the two competent authorities settle it by mutual agreement. Winning the tie-breaker does not change his residential status under section 6 for the Act's own purposes; it decides which state may tax what under the treaty.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital
citation.ref: Article 4(2), as adopted in India's double taxation avoidance agreements, read with Section 90(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Sections 158B and 113 — Block assessment in search cases
concepts.statement: Block assessment came back with the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 and applies where a search under section 132 is initiated, or a requisition under section 132A is made, on or after 1 September 2024. Section 158B(b) defines the block period in these words — the period comprising previous years relevant to six assessment years preceding the previous year in which the search was initiated or the requisition was made, and also including the period starting from the first day of April of the previous year in which the search was initiated or the requisition was made and ending on the date of execution of the last of the authorisations. All of it is assessed as one under section 158BC rather than year by year, and any assessment for a year inside the block period that is pending on the date of the search abates under section 158BA. Section 113 then charges the total undisclosed income of the block period at a flat sixty per cent, whatever the status of the assessee, increased by the surcharge levied by the Central Act applicable in the assessment year relevant to the previous year in which the search was initiated, and by cess.

citation.ref: Sections 158B(b), 158BA and 158BC read with Section 113, as inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 September 2024

concepts.subsection: Sections 143(2) and 153(1) — Time limits for the scrutiny notice and the assessment order
concepts.statement: Two different clocks govern a scrutiny assessment and they start from different events. The notice under section 143(2) must be served within three months from the end of the financial year in which the return is furnished — a period cut from six months to three by the Finance Act, 2021 — so it runs from the end of that financial year and never from the date of filing. The order under section 143(3) or section 144 must then be passed within twelve months from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable, which is the limit for assessment year 2022-23 and every year after it. Where a reference is made to the Transfer Pricing Officer under section 92CA the twelve months is extended by a further twelve months.

citation.ref: Section 143(2) proviso as amended by the Finance Act, 2021, and Section 153(1) with Section 153(4)

concepts.subsection: Section 245MA — Dispute Resolution Committee and the e-Dispute Resolution Scheme, 2022
concepts.statement: Section 245MA gives a small taxpayer a route that is neither an appeal nor a revision. The committee may be approached only against a specified order, defined in the Explanation to the section as one where the aggregate of the variations proposed or made does not exceed ten lakh rupees and the returned income for the relevant assessment year does not exceed fifty lakh rupees. Both tests must hold. An order founded on a search or survey, or on information received under an agreement referred to in section 90 or section 90A, is excluded whatever the figures. What the committee can do that an appellate authority cannot is grant a reduction or waiver of penalty and immunity from prosecution, under Rule 44DAC, and it must pass its order within six months from the end of the month in which the application is admitted.

citation.ref: Section 245MA with the Explanation defining a specified order, read with Rule 44DAC and the e-Dispute Resolution Scheme, 2022

concepts.subsection: Section 56(2)(viib) omitted — share premium of a closely held company
concepts.statement: Section 56(2)(viib), the provision known as angel tax, charged a company in which the public are not substantially interested on the amount by which consideration received for shares exceeded their fair market value. It was omitted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from assessment year 2025-26, so for previous year 2025-26 no charge arises on share premium at all, and the extension of the charge to non-resident subscribers made only a year earlier goes with it. Two things survive the omission and are the examinable half of the topic. Section 68 still lets the Assessing Officer treat the share application money as an unexplained cash credit where the identity, creditworthiness and genuineness of the subscriber are not established, and section 56(2)(x) still taxes a person who receives shares for less than their fair market value — a charge on the recipient, which section 56(2)(viib) never was.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(viib) omitted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 April 2025 (A.Y. 2025-26), read with Sections 68 and 56(2)(x)

concepts.subsection: Section 115BBI — Tax on the specified income of a trust
concepts.statement: Section 115BBI charges specified income of a registered trust or institution at a flat thirty per cent, plus surcharge and cess. Specified income is defined by the section and includes income accumulated or set apart in excess of fifteen per cent where it is not applied as required, income deemed under section 11(1B) or 11(3), income applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of a person referred to in section 13(3), income not invested in a mode specified in section 11(5), and income applied outside India without approval. Sub-section (2) is where the marks sit: no deduction is allowed for any expenditure, allowance or set-off of loss against specified income, so the charge falls on the gross figure. Only the specified income is taken out; the rest of the trust's income continues to be governed by sections 11 to 13 in the ordinary way.

citation.ref: Sections 115BBI(1) and 115BBI(2) with the Explanation, read with Sections 11(5) and 13(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 32(2) — Unabsorbed depreciation and the order of set-off
concepts.statement: Unabsorbed depreciation is not a loss and is not governed by the rules that govern one. Section 32(2) deems it to be part of the depreciation allowance of the following year, which gives it three privileges a business loss does not have: it may be set off against income under any head except salaries, it is carried forward indefinitely with no eight-year limit, and it survives even where the return was not filed within the time allowed by section 139(1), because section 80 does not reach it. Nor does it need the same business to continue. The price of those privileges is that it goes last. The settled order of set-off is current year depreciation first, then brought forward business loss under section 72, and only then brought forward unabsorbed depreciation — which matters, because a business loss can only meet business income and would otherwise be stranded.

concepts.subsection: Section 14A and Rule 8D — Disallowance of expenditure relating to exempt income
concepts.statement: Section 14A disallows expenditure incurred in relation to income that does not form part of total income. The Finance Act, 2022 settled the long-running argument by inserting a non-obstante clause and an Explanation saying that the section applies, and the disallowance is made, whether or not such exempt income has accrued or arisen or been received during the previous year — so a year with no dividend is no defence. Where the Assessing Officer is not satisfied with the assessee's own working, Rule 8D fixes the amount as the sum of the expenditure directly relating to the exempt income and one per cent of the annual average of the monthly averages of the opening and closing balances of the investments the income from which does not or shall not form part of total income. The rule carries its own ceiling: the total disallowed can never exceed the total expenditure claimed by the assessee.

citation.ref: Section 14A(1) with its Explanation inserted by the Finance Act, 2022, read with Rule 8D(2) and 8D(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

concepts.subsection: Section 54 — Capital gains on residential property
concepts.statement: Section 54 exempts long-term capital gains on the transfer of a residential house only when the gain is reinvested in a residential house in India — purchased within one year before or two years after the transfer, or constructed within three years. Reinvestment in commercial property earns no exemption.

concepts.subsection: Section 44AB — Tax audit
concepts.statement: Tax audit applies to a business at turnover above ₹1 crore, but the limit rises to ₹10 crore where cash receipts and cash payments each stay within 5 per cent of the respective totals. For a profession the limit is gross receipts above ₹50 lakh.

concepts.subsection: Section 115BAA — Concessional company rate
concepts.statement: A domestic company that opts for section 115BAA pays tax at the concessional rate, must give up the specified deductions and incentives, and is outside MAT entirely — book profit tax does not apply to it at all.

concepts.subsection: Section 139 — Return filing
concepts.statement: A company files its return by 31 October of the assessment year. Where it must furnish a transfer pricing report under section 92E, the due date extends to 30 November. The 31 July date belongs to persons with no audit requirement.

concepts.subsection: Section 112A — Listed equity gains
concepts.statement: Long-term capital gains on listed equity shares where STT is paid are taxed under section 112A above an annual exemption threshold, without indexation. The rate and threshold are Finance Act figures and move; the structure — exemption slab, no indexation, STT condition — is the stable part.

concepts.subsection: Section 44AD — Presumptive business taxation
concepts.statement: An eligible resident individual, HUF or firm with business turnover within the limit may declare profit at 8 per cent of turnover — 6 per cent for amounts received through banking channels — and skip books and tax audit. Companies and LLPs are outside the scheme, as are commission, agency and section 44AE transport businesses.

concepts.subsection: Sections 72 and 80 — Carry forward of losses
concepts.statement: A business loss carries forward for eight assessment years, but only if the return of the loss year was filed by its due date — section 80 makes the timely return the price of the carry forward. Unabsorbed depreciation lives under section 32(2) instead, needs no timely return, and has no eight-year limit.

concepts.subsection: Section 56(2)(x) — Taxation of gifts
concepts.statement: Money received without consideration is taxable as other-sources income if the aggregate from all persons in the year exceeds fifty thousand rupees — and then the whole amount is taxed, not the excess. Gifts from relatives as defined, and on the occasion of the individual's marriage, stay outside regardless of size.

concepts.subsection: Section 44ADA — Presumptive taxation for professionals
concepts.statement: A resident individual or firm in a specified profession with gross receipts within the limit may declare 50 per cent of receipts as income. The enhanced limit applies where cash receipts stay within 5 per cent. Declaring less than 50 per cent while over the basic exemption brings books and audit.

concepts.subsection: Section 194-IA — TDS on purchase of property
concepts.statement: A buyer of immovable property, other than rural agricultural land, deducts tax at 1 per cent of the consideration where consideration or stamp duty value is fifty lakh rupees or more — and then on the whole amount, not the excess. The buyer needs no TAN; the deduction rides on the buyer's PAN.

concepts.subsection: Section 6 — Residence
concepts.statement: An individual is resident if present in India for 182 days in the year, or 60 days in the year plus 365 across the four preceding years. The 60-day limb stretches to 182 for a citizen leaving for employment or as crew, and to 120 for a visiting citizen or person of Indian origin whose Indian income exceeds fifteen lakh rupees.

concepts.subsection: Section 64(1A) — Clubbing of minor's income
concepts.statement: A minor child's income is clubbed with the income of the parent whose total income is higher, with an exemption of fifteen hundred rupees per child. Income from the minor's own manual work or from activity involving the minor's skill and talent stays with the minor.

concepts.subsection: Section 71(3A) — House property loss set-off
concepts.statement: Loss under house property can be set off against other heads only up to two lakh rupees in a year; the balance carries forward for eight years, and then only against house property income. The interest deduction itself may be larger — the cap bites at set-off, not at computation.

concepts.subsection: Section 43B(h) — Payments to micro and small enterprises
concepts.statement: Sums payable to micro and small enterprises are deductible only in the year of actual payment when paid beyond the time section 15 of the MSMED Act allows — and the usual escape of paying before the return's due date does not apply to this clause. Medium enterprises are outside it.

concepts.subsection: Section 50C — Stamp duty value on transfer of land or building
concepts.statement: Where land or a building sells below its stamp duty value, the stamp value is deemed the consideration for capital gains — but only when it exceeds one hundred and ten per cent of the actual consideration; within that tolerance the actual price stands. The seller can also ask for a valuation officer's reference where the stamp value is contested.

concepts.subsection: Section 40(a)(ia) — Disallowance for TDS default
concepts.statement: Where tax deductible on a payment to a resident is not deducted, or not deposited by the return's due date, thirty per cent of the expense is disallowed — not the whole of it — and the thirty per cent comes back as a deduction in the year the tax is finally paid.

concepts.subsection: Section 54EC — Capital gains bonds
concepts.statement: The 54EC exemption is only for long-term capital gains from land or a building or both, only up to fifty lakh rupees in a financial year, and only where the specified bonds are bought within six months of transfer. The bonds lock in for five years, and taking a loan against them counts as cashing out.

concepts.subsection: Section 79 — Carry forward on change in shareholding
concepts.statement: A closely held company loses its carried-forward losses if, on the last day of the year the loss is set off, shares carrying at least fifty-one per cent of voting power are not held by the persons who held them on the last day of the loss year. Eligible start-ups get a softer test — continuity of all original shareholders, or the seven-year window. Unabsorbed depreciation is outside section 79 entirely.

concepts.subsection: Section 90(4) — Treaty relief and the TRC
concepts.statement: A non-resident claiming treaty benefit must hold a tax residency certificate from its home government; without it the treaty door does not open. The Act also lets the taxpayer choose whichever is more beneficial — treaty or domestic law — provision by provision, and a treaty can never be used to make the position worse than the Act.

concepts.subsection: Section 68 — Cash credits
concepts.statement: An unexplained credit in the books is taxed as income unless the taxpayer explains its nature and source to the officer's satisfaction; for share capital in a closely held company, the source of the source — the resident investor's own funds — must be explained too. Income taxed this way falls under section 115BBE: a sixty per cent rate plus surcharge, with no deductions, allowances, or set-off of losses against it.

concepts.subsection: Section 64(1)(iv) — Income from assets transferred to spouse
concepts.statement: Income from an asset transferred to a spouse without adequate consideration is clubbed with the transferor's income. The clubbing follows the transferred asset's income, not income earned on that income — reinvested earnings belong to the spouse. A transfer before the marriage, or for adequate consideration, or under an agreement to live apart, escapes.

concepts.subsection: Section 44AE — Presumptive income for transporters
concepts.statement: An assessee owning not more than ten goods carriages at any time in the year may declare presumptive income: for a heavy goods vehicle (over 12MT gross weight), one thousand rupees per ton of gross vehicle weight per month or part; for others, seven thousand five hundred per vehicle per month or part. Ownership months count, idle or running; declaring lower than the presumption invites books and audit.

concepts.subsection: GAAR — Impermissible avoidance arrangement
concepts.statement: GAAR strikes an arrangement whose main purpose is a tax benefit and which carries a tainted element — non-arm's-length dealings, misuse of the Act, lack of commercial substance, or means not ordinarily employed for bona fide purposes. Both limbs must be satisfied; a tax benefit alone is legitimate planning. The rules spare arrangements whose aggregate tax benefit is within three crore rupees.

concepts.subsection: Transfer pricing — Arm's length price methods
concepts.statement: The arm's length price of an international transaction between associated enterprises is determined by the most appropriate of the prescribed methods — comparable uncontrolled price, resale price, cost plus, profit split, transactional net margin, or other prescribed method. No hierarchy ranks them; suitability to the transaction, functions and available data picks the method, and CUP prevails only when true comparables exist.

concepts.subsection: Section 115JB — Minimum alternate tax
concepts.statement: A company not under the concessional regimes pays the higher of tax on total income and fifteen per cent of book profit — the audited profit adjusted by the section's own list of additions and deletions. Excess MAT paid becomes credit, carried forward to set against regular tax for up to fifteen years. Companies opting into section 115BAA leave MAT, and MAT credit, behind.

concepts.subsection: Section 270A — Under-reporting and misreporting
concepts.statement: Under-reported income draws a penalty of fifty per cent of the tax on it; where the under-reporting flows from misreporting — misrepresentation of facts, false entries, unrecorded investments, claims without evidence — the penalty is two hundred per cent. A bona fide explanation with disclosed material facts takes an addition out of under-reporting altogether; immunity under section 270AA needs tax and interest paid and no appeal, and never covers misreporting.

concepts.subsection: Section 263 — Revision of orders prejudicial to revenue
concepts.statement: The Commissioner may revise an assessment only where it is both erroneous and prejudicial to the revenue's interests — two conditions, cumulative. An officer's view that is a possible view after real enquiry is not erroneous merely because the Commissioner prefers another; no enquiry where enquiry was called for is the classic error. The window is two years from the end of the financial year of the order.

concepts.subsection: Section 94B — Limitation on interest deduction
concepts.statement: Interest paid to a non-resident associated enterprise beyond one crore rupees is deductible only up to thirty per cent of EBITDA; the excess carries forward up to eight years. The section reaches loans guaranteed by the associated enterprise too, and spares banks and insurers. It caps deduction, not the interest's character — TDS and the lender's taxation run unaffected.

concepts.subsection: Section 9 — Business connection and significant economic presence
concepts.statement: A non-resident's income is deemed to accrue in India through a business connection — which since 2018 includes an agent habitually playing the principal role in concluding contracts, and since the SEP amendment, a significant economic presence built on transactions or user engagement in India without any physical presence. Treaty definitions of permanent establishment still override for treaty residents, which keeps SEP's bite mainly on non-treaty cases.

concepts.subsection: Sections 11-12 — Charitable trusts
concepts.statement: A registered trust's income is exempt to the extent applied to charitable purposes in India, with at least eighty-five per cent to be applied in the year — fifteen per cent may be accumulated freely.
