concepts.statement: Regulation 3(1) of the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011 triggers an open offer the moment an acquirer with persons acting in concert crosses twenty-five per cent of the voting rights of a target company for the first time. Regulation 3(2) is the creeping acquisition route and is available only to someone already holding twenty-five per cent or more but below the maximum permissible non-public shareholding: he may add up to five per cent of voting rights in a financial year without an offer, and an open offer is due the moment he acquires more than that. Regulation 4 triggers an offer on the acquisition of control however few shares change hands. The offer must be for at least twenty-six per cent of the target's voting capital under Regulation 7(1). The public announcement is made on the date of agreeing to acquire under Regulation 13(1), the detailed public statement follows within five working days under Regulation 13(4), and Regulation 29(1) separately makes any person crossing five per cent disclose to the company and the exchanges within two working days.

citation.source: SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011

concepts.subsection: Related party transactions of a listed entity — LODR Regulation 23
concepts.statement: A listed entity answers to three regimes on the same related party transaction and they do not line up. Section 188 of the Companies Act exempts a transaction in the ordinary course of business and on an arm's length basis from its board and shareholder approvals. Regulation 23(2) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 grants no such exemption — every related party transaction needs the prior approval of the audit committee, and only the independent directors on that committee may give it. Regulation 23(4) sends a material related party transaction to the shareholders, and Regulation 23(7) makes every related party abstain from voting on the resolution whether or not it is a party to that particular transaction. Regulation 23(5) exempts a transaction between a holding company and its wholly-owned subsidiary whose accounts are consolidated, and transactions between two such wholly-owned subsidiaries. Materiality under Regulation 23(1) is the lower of a rupee ceiling SEBI prescribes and ten per cent of annual consolidated turnover per the last audited financial statements — SEBI replaced the flat rupee cap with a turnover-scaled ceiling with effect from 19 December 2025, so confirm the figure applicable to your attempt before quoting one. Over and above all of it, Ind AS 24 requires the relationship and the transaction to be disclosed in the financial statements whether or not any approval was needed.

citation.ref: Regulations 23(1), 23(2), 23(4), 23(5) and 23(7), read with section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Ind AS 24

concepts.subsection: Significant beneficial owner — section 90 and the SBO Rules
concepts.statement: Section 90(1) speaks of an individual holding a beneficial interest of not less than twenty-five per cent "or such other percentage as may be prescribed", and Rule 2(1)(h) of the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018 prescribes ten per cent — so ten is the working line and twenty-five is a figure the Rules have overtaken. The test is not the size of a shareholding but its route: a significant beneficial owner holds indirectly, or indirectly together with any direct holding, not less than ten per cent of the shares, or of the voting rights, or of the distributable dividend, or exercises significant influence or control. A purely direct holding, however large, makes a person a registered member and not a significant beneficial owner. He declares in Form BEN-1 within thirty days; the company files Form BEN-2 within thirty days of that declaration and keeps the register in Form BEN-3. Section 90(4A) puts the company under a duty to go and identify its significant beneficial owners, section 90(5) lets it serve notice in Form BEN-4, section 90(6) gives the recipient thirty days to answer, and on no answer or an unsatisfactory one section 90(7) sends the company to the Tribunal within fifteen days for an order restricting the shares, which the Tribunal passes within sixty days under section 90(8).

citation.ref: Sections 90(1), 90(4A), 90(5), 90(6), 90(7) and 90(8), read with Rules 2(1)(h), 3 and 4 of the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018

concepts.subsection: Scheme of compromise or arrangement — section 230
concepts.statement: A scheme under section 230 clears three separate gates. The meeting gate is section 230(6): a majority of the persons voting, representing three-fourths in value of the creditors or class of creditors or members or class of members voting in person, by proxy or by postal ballot — a majority in number and three-fourths in value, both, of those who actually vote. The objection gate is the proviso to section 230(4): only a person holding not less than ten per cent of the shareholding, or having outstanding debt of not less than five per cent of the total outstanding debt as per the latest audited financial statement, may object at all. The accounting gate is the proviso to section 230(7): the Tribunal cannot sanction the scheme unless a certificate from the company's auditor has been filed with it stating that the accounting treatment proposed in the scheme conforms to the accounting standards prescribed under section 133. That last one is where company law reaches into the audit file — an accounting treatment engineered inside a scheme does not escape the standards by being carried in a court-sanctioned document.

citation.ref: Sections 230(4) proviso, 230(6) and the proviso to section 230(7)

concepts.subsection: Re-opening and revising filed accounts — sections 130 and 131
concepts.statement: Financial statements once adopted and filed cannot be pulled back by the board on its own. Section 130 allows a re-opening and recasting only on an order of a court or the Tribunal, and only on an application by the Central Government, the income-tax authorities, the Securities and Exchange Board, any other statutory regulatory body or authority, or any person concerned — never on the company's own motion — and no order may reach a period earlier than eight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year. Accounts so revised are final. Section 131 is the directors' own route: with the Tribunal's approval they may prepare a revised financial statement or a revised Board's report for any of the three preceding financial years, only where the original does not comply with section 129 or section 134, confined to that non-compliance, and not more than once in a financial year. Neither section is engaged by an Ind AS 8 prior period error — restating the comparative figures in the current year's financial statements is ordinary accounting and needs nobody's approval. The Tribunal enters the picture only when the earlier year's own filed statements are to be replaced.

citation.ref: Sections 130(1), 130(3) and 131(1), read with Ind AS 8

concepts.subsection: Preferential transactions — section 43 and the two look-back periods
concepts.statement: Section 43(2) makes a transaction preferential where the corporate debtor transfers property or an interest in it for the benefit of a creditor, surety or guarantor on account of an antecedent debt, and the transfer puts that person in a better position than he would have been in on a distribution under section 53. Section 43(4) then fixes two different windows measured back from the insolvency commencement date — two years for a related party, one year for anybody else — and a transfer outside the applicable window cannot be a preference however unfair it looks. Section 43(3) carves out transfers made in the ordinary course of the business or financial affairs of the corporate debtor or the transferee, and transfers creating a security interest for new value; the Supreme Court in Anuj Jain (Jaypee Infratech) read that "or" as "and", so the transaction must be ordinary for both sides. Section 44 lists the orders the Tribunal may pass, chiefly restoring the property to the corporate debtor. Section 26 is the sting for the timetable: filing an avoidance application does not affect the corporate insolvency resolution process, so the plan is neither held up by the application nor discharged by the plan's approval.

concepts.subsection: Fraudulent and wrongful trading — sections 66 and 67 of the IBC
concepts.statement: Section 66(1) is fraudulent trading. It applies in a corporate insolvency resolution process or a liquidation, it reaches any persons who were knowingly parties to carrying on the business with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, and it requires that intent to be proved. Section 66(2) is wrongful trading and is a much lower bar: on an application by the resolution professional the Tribunal may direct a director or partner to contribute to the assets where, before the insolvency commencement date, he knew or ought to have known that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding the commencement of a corporate insolvency resolution process, and he did not exercise due diligence in minimising the potential loss to creditors. No dishonesty is needed. The Explanation measures due diligence against a reasonably diligent person having the knowledge, skill and experience reasonably expected of a person carrying out the same functions. Section 67 lets the Tribunal make the liability a charge on the person's assets. This is where the audit file becomes evidence: a going-concern paragraph written under SA 570, and the board minutes that answered it, are the record of what the directors knew and when. Contrast section 339 of the Companies Act, 2013, whose fraudulent-conduct liability still needs the intent section 66(2) does without.

citation.ref: Sections 66(1), 66(2) with its Explanation, and 67, read with SA 570 and section 339 of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Insolvency of a personal guarantor — sections 60(2) and 94 to 100
concepts.statement: A personal guarantor to a corporate debtor is dealt with under Part III of the Code, but he is not sent to the Debt Recovery Tribunal whenever the company is already in front of the National Company Law Tribunal. Section 60(2) requires an application relating to the insolvency resolution or bankruptcy of a personal guarantor to be filed before, or stand transferred to, the same National Company Law Tribunal where a corporate insolvency resolution process or liquidation of the corporate debtor is pending, and section 60(4) arms that Tribunal with all the powers of the Debt Recovery Tribunal for the purpose. The debtor applies under section 94 and a creditor under section 95, in either case through a resolution professional. Section 96 then starts an interim moratorium from the date of the application itself — not from admission — staying pending legal proceedings in respect of any debt and barring fresh ones. Section 97 confirms or appoints the resolution professional, section 99 gives him ten days from his appointment to examine the application and report recommending admission or rejection, and section 100 gives the Tribunal fourteen days from that report to admit or reject. On admission the interim moratorium ends and the section 101 moratorium of one hundred and eighty days begins.

concepts.subsection: Voluntary liquidation of a solvent company — section 59
concepts.statement: Section 59(1) opens voluntary liquidation only to a corporate person that has not committed any default — it is an exit for the solvent, not a route out of debt. Section 59(3) sets the order of steps and each has its own clock. A declaration of solvency is made by a majority of the directors, verified by affidavit, saying the company has no debt or will be able to pay its debts in full from the proceeds of the assets, and that it is not being liquidated to defraud any person; it is accompanied by the audited financial statements and a record of the business operations for the previous two years or since incorporation, whichever is later, and a valuation report of the assets where there are assets. Within four weeks of that declaration the members pass a special resolution to wind up voluntarily and appoint an insolvency professional as liquidator. Where the company owes any debt, creditors representing two-thirds in value of the debt must approve that resolution within seven days of it. Section 59(5) makes the liquidation commence on the date of the resolution — or the creditors' approval where one was needed. Section 59(6) then applies sections 35 to 53 to the process, so the section 53 waterfall governs the order of payment even here; the difference is that in a solvent liquidation the water reaches the bottom and the surplus goes to the members.

concepts.subsection: The clean slate for a rescued company — section 32A of the IBC
concepts.statement: Section 32A(1) stops the corporate debtor being prosecuted for an offence committed before the commencement of the corporate insolvency resolution process, from the date the Tribunal approves a resolution plan under section 31, but only where the plan results in a change in the management or control of the corporate debtor to a person who was not a promoter, was not in the management or control of the corporate debtor, is not a related party of such a person, and against whom no investigating authority has reported or complained of having abetted or conspired in the offence. Section 32A(2) carries the same protection to the property of the corporate debtor, which then ceases to be liable to attachment, seizure, retention or confiscation for that offence — this is the provision on which attachments made under the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act have been ordered released. What the section does not do is clear anybody else. The proviso to section 32A(1) says every person who was a designated partner, officer in default or in any manner in charge of or responsible to the corporate debtor for the conduct of its business shall continue to be liable to prosecution and punishment, and section 32A(3) obliges the corporate debtor and such persons to extend all assistance and co-operation to the investigating authority. The company walks away; the people who ran it do not.

citation.ref: Sections 32A(1) with its proviso, 32A(2) and 32A(3), read with section 31

concepts.subsection: Delisting under an approved resolution plan — Delisting Regulation 3(2)
concepts.statement: A listed company that comes out of insolvency is usually delisted, and the ordinary delisting machinery is impossible there — reverse book building assumes a promoter with money and a market with a discovered price, and an insolvent company has neither. Regulation 3(2)(b) of the SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021 therefore takes the whole of the Regulations off a delisting made pursuant to a resolution plan approved under section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, where the plan either provides for the delisting of the shares or gives the existing public shareholders an exit at a specified price. Two conditions ride on the exemption. The first proviso fixes a floor on fairness rather than on value: the exit price for the public shareholders shall not be less than the price at which a promoter, any entity of the promoter group, or any other shareholder is given an exit under that plan. The second proviso requires the details of the delisting, together with the justification for the exit price, to be disclosed to the recognised stock exchanges within one day of the approval of the resolution plan. The Bombay High Court upheld the validity of the carve-out in December 2024.

citation.ref: Regulation 3(2)(b) and its two provisos, read with section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

concepts.subsection: Preferential issue by a listed company — ICDR pricing and lock-in
concepts.statement: A preferential allotment by a listed company answers to company law and to SEBI at the same time, and SEBI's conditions are the ones company law never imposes. Section 62(1)(c) with section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013 supplies the special resolution, the valuation and the private placement machinery. Chapter V of the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018 then adds a floor price and a lock-in. Regulation 164 fixes the floor for frequently traded shares at the higher of the volume weighted average price of the ninety trading days preceding the relevant date and the volume weighted average price of the ten trading days preceding it — the amendment of 2022 replaced the old twenty-six weeks and two weeks with those trading-day windows. Regulation 167 locks the allotted shares in: eighteen months for an allotment to promoters or the promoter group up to twenty per cent of the post-issue paid-up capital, six months for the part above that twenty per cent, and six months for an allottee who is not a promoter, all reduced from three years and one year by the 2022 amendment. Regulation 160 separately shuts out an allottee who has sold or transferred any equity shares of the issuer in the ninety trading days preceding the relevant date.

citation.source: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
citation.ref: Regulations 160, 164 and 167 of Chapter V, read with sections 42 and 62(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Material events — LODR Regulation 30 and its three clocks
concepts.statement: Regulation 30 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 splits events into two lists in Schedule III Part A. Para A events are disclosed on their own, with no materiality test applied at all. Para B events are disclosed only where the listed entity's own materiality policy or the quantitative test bites. That quantitative test, in Regulation 30(4)(i)(c), is the lower of three numbers, computed on the last audited consolidated financial statements: two per cent of turnover, two per cent of net worth except where net worth is negative, and five per cent of the average of the absolute value of profit or loss after tax for the last three financial years. Taking the lower makes the trigger easier to cross, not harder, which is the opposite of what most readers assume. Regulation 30(6) then supplies three clocks: thirty minutes from the closure of the board meeting in which the decision was taken; twelve hours where the event emanates from within the listed entity; and twenty-four hours where it does not. None of this answers the accounting question. An event after the reporting date is separately tested under Ind AS 10 for whether it gives evidence of a condition that existed at the reporting date, and the auditor tests the same facts under SA 560 — a twenty-four-hour exchange filing and a non-adjusting event disclosure can be, and often are, the correct answer to the same fact together.

citation.ref: Regulations 30(4)(i) and 30(6), read with Schedule III Part A, Ind AS 10 and SA 560

concepts.subsection: NFRA's reach and the boundary with the Institute — section 132
concepts.statement: The National Financial Reporting Authority does not oversee every auditor. Rule 3(1) of the NFRA Rules, 2018 fixes the classes: companies whose securities are listed on any stock exchange in India or outside India; unlisted public companies having paid-up capital of not less than five hundred crore rupees, or annual turnover of not less than one thousand crore rupees, or outstanding loans, debentures and deposits of not less than five hundred crore rupees in aggregate as on the thirty-first of March of the immediately preceding financial year; insurance companies, banking companies and companies engaged in generation or supply of electricity; and any body corporate referred by the Central Government in the public interest. Those three unlisted-public-company tests are alternatives — crossing any one is enough. Section 132(4) gives NFRA the power to investigate professional or other misconduct of a member or firm auditing such a company, and its proviso shuts the door on everyone else: no other institute or body shall initiate or continue any proceedings in such matters of misconduct where NFRA has initiated an investigation. Section 132(4)(c) sets the penalty at not less than one lakh rupees extending to five times the fees received for an individual, and not less than five lakh rupees extending to ten times the fees received for a firm, with debarment from audit or valuation work for a minimum of six months and a maximum of ten years. Outside those classes, the disciplinary route under sections 21A and 21B of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 continues to be the only one.

citation.ref: Sections 132(2), 132(4) with its proviso and 132(4)(c), read with Rule 3(1) of the NFRA Rules, 2018

concepts.subsection: CSR set-off under Rule 7(3) and what the Income-tax Act does with the spend
concepts.statement: Overspending on corporate social responsibility is not lost. Rule 7(3) of the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014 lets a company set the excess off against the requirement of up to the immediately succeeding three financial years, on two conditions — the excess must not include any surplus arising out of the CSR activities themselves, and the Board must pass a resolution to that effect. Section 135(9) removes the need for a CSR Committee altogether where the amount required to be spent does not exceed fifty lakh rupees, the Board doing its work instead. Section 135(6) sends an unspent amount relating to an ongoing project to a separate Unspent CSR Account within thirty days of the end of the financial year, to be spent within three financial years; anything not relating to an ongoing project goes to a Schedule VII fund within six months of the end of the year. Now the tax side, which pulls the other way. Explanation 2 to section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 says expenditure incurred on activities relating to corporate social responsibility referred to in section 135 shall not be deemed to be expenditure incurred for the purposes of the business, so it is not deductible under section 37(1) at all. Section 80G still allows a deduction for a qualifying donation made as CSR, except that it expressly denies it for a CSR sum paid to the Swachh Bharat Kosh and to the Clean Ganga Fund. Deductions that stand on their own feet, such as section 35, are unaffected by the label.

citation.ref: Sections 135(6) and 135(9) with Rule 7(3) of the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014, read with Explanation 2 to section 37(1) and section 80G of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Producer companies — Chapter XXIA of the Companies Act
concepts.statement: Chapter XXIA, sections 378A to 378ZU, was inserted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2020 with effect from 11 February 2021, carrying Part IXA of the 1956 Act into the present one. Section 378C admits exactly three ways of forming a producer company — ten or more individuals, each of them a producer; or two or more producer institutions; or a combination of ten or more individuals and producer institutions. On registration it becomes a body corporate as if it were a private limited company, but with two departures written into the section itself: the limit on the number of members does not apply to it, and it can never become or be deemed to be a public company. Section 378D(1)(a) gives every member a single vote irrespective of his shareholding or patronage where the membership is all individuals, which is the co-operative principle sitting inside a company. Section 378O requires at least five and not more than fifteen directors. Section 378ZG is where audit meets the chapter: the auditor reports, over and above everything section 143 already requires, on the amount of debts due along with particulars of bad debts, the verification of cash balance and securities, the details of assets and liabilities, all transactions that appear contrary to the provisions of the chapter, loans given to directors, and donations or subscriptions given by the producer company.

citation.ref: Sections 378C, 378D(1), 378O and 378ZG of Chapter XXIA, read with section 143

concepts.subsection: Land-border investment and downstream investment under the NDI Rules
concepts.statement: Two rules of the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 decide more structuring questions than any sectoral cap. The proviso to Rule 6(a), which carries Press Note 3 of 2020 into law, says an entity of a country which shares a land border with India, or an investment whose beneficial owner is situated in or is a citizen of such a country, may invest only with Government approval — and that applies whatever the sector's own entry route, so a hundred per cent automatic sector gives such an investor nothing. Rule 23 governs what happens one level down. Where an Indian company that is owned or controlled by a person resident outside India invests in another Indian company, that investment is a downstream investment and counts as indirect foreign investment in the second company; it must comply with the entry route, the sectoral caps, the pricing guidelines and the other attendant conditions that would have applied had the money come directly from abroad. Rule 23 also requires the funds for a downstream investment to be brought in from abroad and forbids leveraging funds borrowed in the domestic market for it, and the investment is reported to the Reserve Bank in Form DI. An Indian company that is neither owned nor controlled by a non-resident makes no downstream investment at all — its investment is domestic, however much foreign money sits on its share register.

citation.ref: Proviso to Rule 6(a) and Rule 23 of the FEM (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019, read with Press Note 3 (2020 Series) dated 17 April 2020

concepts.subsection: Branch and liaison offices — FEMA 22(R) and the tax that follows
concepts.statement: The Foreign Exchange Management (Establishment in India of a Branch Office or a Liaison Office or a Project Office or any other place of business) Regulations, 2016, notified as FEMA 22(R), set two different entry tests. A branch office needs a profit-making track record during the immediately preceding five financial years in the home country and a net worth of not less than USD 100,000 or its equivalent, certified by the applicant's auditor. A liaison office needs a profit-making track record during the immediately preceding three financial years and a net worth of not less than USD 50,000 or its equivalent. What the two may do differs even more than what they must show. A branch office may carry on the permitted activities and earn income in India. A liaison office may act only as a communication channel between the head office and parties in India — it may not undertake any commercial, trading or industrial activity, it may not earn any income in India, and it must meet its expenses wholly through inward remittances of foreign exchange from the head office. Both file an Annual Activity Certificate from a chartered accountant with the authorised dealer bank and the Director General of Income-tax (International Taxation) on or before 30 September each year. That certificate is where the tax exposure is usually discovered: an office that negotiates prices, concludes contracts or secures orders is doing more than preparatory or auxiliary work, and it creates a business connection under section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and a permanent establishment under the relevant treaty, making the foreign enterprise taxable in India on the profits attributable to it.

citation.ref: Regulation 4 and the Annex to the FEM (Establishment in India of a Branch Office or a Liaison Office or a Project Office or any other place of business) Regulations, 2016 (FEMA 22(R)), read with section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Liberalised Remittance Scheme and the tax collected at source on it
concepts.statement: The Liberalised Remittance Scheme lets a resident individual, including a minor, remit up to USD 250,000 or its equivalent in a financial year for any permissible current or capital account transaction or a combination of both — one aggregate ceiling for the year across all purposes and all authorised dealers, not a limit per remittance. It runs under Schedule III to the Foreign Exchange Management (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000 read with the Reserve Bank's Master Direction on the Scheme, requires a PAN, and is the route through which a resident individual makes overseas direct or portfolio investment under the FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022. It cannot be used at all for margins or margin calls to overseas exchanges, for trading in foreign exchange abroad, for lottery and banned publications, or for remittances to countries identified by the Financial Action Task Force as non-co-operative. The same remittance is a tax event. Section 206C(1G) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 makes the authorised dealer collect tax at source, and the Finance Act, 2025 moved the figures with effect from 1 April 2025: the threshold rose from seven lakh rupees to ten lakh rupees of aggregate remittance in a financial year, the rate is five per cent for education and medical purposes and twenty per cent for everything else on the amount exceeding that threshold, and no tax at all is collected where the remittance for education is made out of a loan obtained from a financial institution referred to in section 80E. Tax collected is not a cost — section 206C(4) credits it against the individual's own tax liability.

citation.ref: Schedule III to the FEM (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000 and the RBI Master Direction on the Liberalised Remittance Scheme, read with section 206C(1G) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 as amended by the Finance Act, 2025

concepts.subsection: Combinations — the deal value threshold and the standstill obligation
concepts.statement: Section 5 of the Competition Act, 2002 tells you when an acquisition, merger or amalgamation is a combination that must be notified to the Competition Commission of India. Clauses (a) to (c) do it on the assets and turnover of the enterprises and their group, on figures the Central Government revises by notification. Clause (d), inserted by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 and brought into force in September 2024, added a wholly different gate: any transaction whose value exceeds two thousand crore rupees is a combination if the enterprise being acquired, merged or amalgamated has substantial business operations in India. That clause was written for the deal that buys a large user base holding almost no assets and earning almost no revenue here, and it means an asset and turnover analysis showing nothing is only half the answer. Section 6(2) requires notice of a combination to the Commission, and section 6(2A) supplies the standstill: no combination shall come into effect until one hundred and fifty days have passed from the day the notice was given, or the Commission has passed an order under section 31, whichever is earlier. Closing before that is gun-jumping, and section 43A lets the Commission impose a penalty which may extend to one per cent of the total turnover or assets or the value of the transaction referred to in clause (d) of section 5, whichever is higher.

citation.ref: Sections 5(d), 6(2), 6(2A) and 43A, as amended by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023

concepts.subsection: Investment advice by a chartered accountant — SEBI registration and Council permission
concepts.statement: Regulation 3(1) of the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013 forbids any person acting as an investment adviser or holding himself out as one without obtaining a certificate of registration from the Board. Regulation 4 lists who is outside that requirement, and one of the exemptions covers a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India who provides investment advice to his clients incidental to his professional service. The word doing the work is incidental. SEBI's own frequently asked questions give the example that passes — a chartered accountant acting as a tax consultant who, in the course of tax planning, advises a client to invest in an equity linked savings scheme — and state the condition that fails it: where a member provides investment advisory services in securities as an activity or business to clients or investors, not incidental to his main activity, registration is required. A separately marketed, separately charged advisory service is not incidental to anything. Company law and SEBI are not the whole answer either. Clause 11 of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 makes a member in practice guilty of professional misconduct if he engages in any business or occupation other than the profession of accountancy without the general or specific permission of the Council, so a registration granted by SEBI does not by itself make the activity permissible for him.

citation.ref: Regulations 3(1) and 4, read with Clause 11 of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

concepts.subsection: Going concern across FR and audit
concepts.statement: Material uncertainties about going concern are disclosed in the financial statements themselves — Ind AS 1 requires it of management when it is aware of them. A mention in the board's report or a covering letter is not a substitute, and the auditor's going concern section points to the note, so the note must exist.

concepts.subsection: Related party transactions under company law
concepts.statement: A contract with a related party of the kinds listed in section 188 — sale or purchase of goods, property, services, agency — needs board approval by resolution when it is not in the ordinary course of business or not at arm's length, and shareholder approval past the prescribed thresholds. An interested director does not participate.

concepts.subsection: Professional ethics on fees
concepts.statement: A chartered accountant in practice cannot charge professional fees as a percentage of profits or contingent on results, outside the specific exceptions the Council has carved out — an auditor paid a share of what he certifies has bought a stake in the number.

concepts.subsection: Fraud reporting under the Companies Act
concepts.statement: An auditor who has reason to believe a fraud of one crore rupees or more is being or has been committed against the company by its officers or employees reports it to the Central Government, routed first through the board or audit committee for their reply within the prescribed time. Frauds below that threshold go to the board or audit committee, and are disclosed in the board's report.

concepts.subsection: Corporate social responsibility under section 135
concepts.statement: A company crossing any one threshold — net worth ₹500 crore, turnover ₹1000 crore, or net profit ₹5 crore in the immediately preceding year — must constitute a CSR committee and spend 2 per cent of its average net profits of the three preceding years. Unspent amounts follow the ongoing-project rules or move to a specified fund; mere disclosure no longer discharges it.

concepts.subsection: Internal financial controls in the auditor's report
concepts.statement: The auditor of a company reports on whether the company has an adequate internal financial controls system with reference to financial statements and whether it operated effectively — a separate opinion under section 143(3)(i), distinct from the opinion on the statements themselves. Smaller private companies are exempted by notification.

concepts.subsection: Professional ethics on solicitation
concepts.statement: A chartered accountant in practice may not solicit clients or professional work directly or indirectly — by circular, advertisement, personal communication or interview. Responding to tenders, applying for empanelment that has been announced, and seeking work from another chartered accountant in practice sit outside the bar.

concepts.subsection: Audit committee under section 177
concepts.statement: The audit committee of a listed public company needs a minimum of three directors, with independent directors forming a majority, and a majority of members — the chairperson included — able to read and understand financial statements. It recommends auditor appointment and remuneration, reviews independence, and runs the vigil mechanism.

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 applicability
concepts.statement: CARO 2020 applies to companies generally but not to banking companies, insurance companies, section 8 companies, one person companies, small companies, and private companies within all the prescribed size limits — paid-up capital and reserves up to one crore, borrowings up to one crore, and revenue up to ten crore. Cross any one limit and the order applies.

concepts.subsection: Declaration of dividend under section 123
concepts.statement: Dividend is declared out of profits after providing for depreciation, or out of free reserves under the prescribed conditions. Losses and depreciation of earlier years are set off first, and the securities premium and revaluation surplus are not distributable — a dividend needs earned, realised profit behind it.

concepts.subsection: Auditor rotation under section 139
concepts.statement: Listed companies and the prescribed classes cannot appoint an individual auditor for more than one term of five consecutive years, or an audit firm for more than two such terms, followed in each case by a five-year cooling-off. A firm sharing common partners with the retiring firm is caught by the same bar.

concepts.subsection: Internal audit under section 138
concepts.statement: Internal audit is compulsory for every listed company, and for unlisted public companies and private companies crossing the prescribed size lines — for a private company, turnover of two hundred crore rupees or outstanding borrowings of one hundred crore during the preceding year. The internal auditor may be a chartered accountant, cost accountant, or other professional the board decides, and may be an employee.

concepts.subsection: Independent directors under section 149
concepts.statement: A listed public company needs at least one-third of its board as independent directors. An independent director holds office for up to five years a term, at most two consecutive terms, then a three-year cooling-off during which no association with the company is permitted. Independence is defined by negatives — no pecuniary relationship with the company beyond permitted limits, no promoter linkage, and the director must declare independence at first appointment and annually.

concepts.subsection: Loans and investments under section 186
concepts.statement: A company's loans, guarantees, securities and investments beyond sixty per cent of paid-up capital plus free reserves and securities premium — or one hundred per cent of free reserves plus securities premium, whichever is more — need a special resolution. Every such loan needs prior approval of all directors present at the board meeting, carries interest at no less than the prevailing government-security yield, and is barred entirely while the company is in default on public deposits.

concepts.subsection: Loans to directors under section 185
concepts.statement: A company may not lend to, or guarantee or secure the debts of, its directors or their partners and firms — that circle is absolute. One ring out — a private company in which a director is interested, or a body corporate under a director's control — the loan is possible, but only with a special resolution and the borrower using it for its principal business. Loans to managing or whole-time directors ride narrow exceptions such as a scheme for all employees.

concepts.subsection: IBC — Operational creditor's route
concepts.statement: An operational creditor must serve a demand notice under section 8 before filing; the corporate debtor has ten days to point to a pre-existing dispute or proof of payment, and a genuine pre-existing dispute kills the section 9 application — insolvency is not a debt recovery forum. A financial creditor under section 7 faces no such dispute defence; default alone carries the application.

concepts.subsection: Key managerial personnel under section 203
concepts.statement: Prescribed companies must have whole-time key managerial personnel — a managing director or CEO or manager (or in their absence a whole-time director), a company secretary, and a chief financial officer. A whole-time KMP holds office in only one company at a time (a subsidiary excepted), and a vacancy must be filled by the board within six months.

concepts.subsection: Oppression and mismanagement — who may apply
concepts.statement: A petition under section 241 needs standing under section 244: for a company with share capital, either the member count — one hundred members or one-tenth of the total members, whichever of those two is less — or, as a separate alternative, any member or members holding one-tenth of the issued share capital. "Whichever is less" governs only the two member-count figures; the capital route stands on its own beside them. All calls and other sums due on the applicants' shares must be paid. The Tribunal may waive the requirement for a deserving case, and consenting members can combine to make up the numbers.

concepts.subsection: Buy-back of shares under section 68
concepts.statement: A buy-back may not exceed twenty-five per cent of paid-up capital plus free reserves, with the board alone able to approve up to ten per cent of paid-up equity plus free reserves and a special resolution needed beyond; post buy-back debt may not exceed twice the capital and free reserves; shares must be fully paid; and a year must pass between buy-backs. Funding comes from free reserves, securities premium or fresh issue proceeds of other securities.

concepts.subsection: Private placement under section 42
concepts.statement: A private placement offer goes to identified persons only — at most two hundred in a financial year, excluding qualified institutional buyers and employee stock options — with no public advertisement, application money through banking channels into a separate account, allotment within sixty days or refund, and no use of the money before allotment and filing. Breach of the public-solicitation bar converts the issue into a deemed public offer with all its consequences.

concepts.subsection: Registration of charges
concepts.statement: A charge on company property must be registered within thirty days of creation, with the Registrar able to allow late filing on payment of ad valorem fees within the extended statutory window. An unregistered charge is void against the liquidator and other creditors — the debt survives and becomes immediately payable, but the lender queues as unsecured when it mattered most. Registration is the charge-holder's protection and may be filed by the lender itself if the company defaults on filing.

concepts.subsection: Secretarial audit under section 204
concepts.statement: Every listed company — and public companies above the prescribed size lines of paid-up capital or turnover — annexes a secretarial audit report from a practising company secretary to the board's report, covering compliance with the Companies Act, securities laws and other laws applicable to the company. The board must respond to every qualification in the report; the auditor here is a company secretary in practice, not a chartered accountant.

concepts.subsection: Annual general meeting — section 96
concepts.statement: The first AGM is held within nine months of the first financial year's close; every later AGM within six months of the financial year's end, with no more than fifteen months between two AGMs. The Registrar may extend a later AGM by up to three months for special reasons — never the first. Business hours, a non-national-holiday day, and the registered office's city frame where and when it happens.

concepts.subsection: Strike off and restoration — sections 248 and 252
concepts.statement: The Registrar may strike off a company that never commenced business or has not operated for two financial years without dormant status — after notice and a chance to respond — and a company may apply for strike off itself after clearing its liabilities. Restoration runs through the Tribunal: an aggrieved person appeals within three years, and the company, a member, creditor or workman may apply within twenty. Liability of directors and members survives the striking off as if the company continued.

concepts.subsection: Additional directors — section 161
concepts.statement: The board, if the articles authorise, may appoint an additional director who holds office only up to the next annual general meeting — or the date by which that AGM should have been held, so delaying the meeting cannot extend the seat. A person who fails to get appointed as a director in a general meeting cannot come in as an additional director. Regularisation at the AGM converts the seat into an ordinary directorship.

concepts.subsection: Small companies — thresholds and privileges
concepts.statement: A small company is a non-public company with paid-up capital up to four crore rupees and turnover up to forty crore — never a holding or subsidiary company, a section 8 company, or one governed by a special Act. The status buys lighter compliance: no cash flow statement, an abridged annual return signable by a director alone, two board meetings a year in place of four, no auditor rotation, and lighter penalties under the Act's small-company provisions.

concepts.subsection: Fast track mergers — section 233
concepts.statement: Small companies, a holding company with its wholly owned subsidiary, and other prescribed classes may merge without the Tribunal: notice to the Registrar and Official Liquidator for objections, member approval by ninety per cent of total shares and creditor approval by ninety per cent in value, then registration of the scheme by the Central Government (the Regional Director). If objections raise substance, the Regional Director may refer the scheme to the Tribunal — the fast track can slow down, but it starts without a court.

concepts.subsection: SFIO investigation — section 212
concepts.statement: Once the Central Government assigns a company's affairs to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office, no other investigating agency under the Companies Act proceeds with the same matter, and pending investigations transfer to SFIO. SFIO officers hold arrest powers for the fraud offence under section 447, which is cognizable for that purpose, with bail conditioned on the twin tests. Its report can found prosecution as if it were a police report.

concepts.subsection: Deposits — sections 73 to 76
concepts.statement: A company may accept deposits from its members by resolution with the prescribed conditions; accepting deposits from the public is reserved to eligible companies — public companies with net worth of at least one hundred crore rupees or turnover of at least five hundred crore — with credit rating, deposit repayment reserve and the rest. Amounts from directors (declared as own funds) and many commercial receipts are excluded from "deposit"; on default, depositors reach the Tribunal, and fraudulent acceptance attracts personal liability.

concepts.subsection: Nomination and remuneration committee
concepts.statement: Listed and prescribed public companies constitute a nomination and remuneration committee of three or more non-executive directors, at least half independent; the chairperson of the company may sit on it but may not chair it. The committee identifies candidates, evaluates performance, and frames the remuneration policy the board discloses. Its recommendations discipline board appointments the way the audit committee disciplines the accounts.

concepts.subsection: Vigil mechanism
concepts.statement: Every listed company — and companies that accept public deposits or have borrowed more than fifty crore rupees from banks and financial institutions — must operate a vigil mechanism for directors and employees to report genuine concerns, with safeguards against victimisation and direct access to the audit committee's chairperson in appropriate or exceptional cases. Its existence is disclosed on the website and in the board's report.

concepts.subsection: Managerial remuneration — section 197
concepts.statement: A public company's total managerial remuneration caps at eleven per cent of net profits — within it, five per cent for one managing or whole-time director, ten per cent for all of them together, and one per cent (or three where no managing director exists) for other directors. Exceeding a limit needs a special resolution — Central Government approval was abolished in 2018 — and in a no-profit year, Schedule V's slabs by effective capital govern instead. Excess drawn without authority is held in trust and recovered, unless the company waives it by special resolution.

concepts.subsection: Section 20 — Input Service Distributor
concepts.statement: An Input Service Distributor is an office of the supplier that receives tax invoices for input services and distributes the credit to its other registered units — distinct persons of the same legal entity — by issuing an ISD invoice. Distribution runs pro rata to the turnover of each recipient unit in the relevant period, eligible and ineligible credit are kept apart, and the distributor can never distribute more credit than is available for the period.

concepts.subsection: Rule 42 — Reversal of ITC on inputs and input services
concepts.statement: Where inputs and input services are used partly for taxable or business supplies and partly for exempt supplies or non-business purposes, credit attributable exclusively to the exempt or non-business use is reversed in full at the outset. The remaining common credit — used for both — is reversed monthly by a formula keyed to the ratio of exempt turnover to total turnover, and the reversal is trued up once a year against the actual annual figures.

concepts.subsection: Section 18(6) — ITC on capital goods, disposal before useful life
concepts.statement: Credit on capital goods is available in full at the time of receipt, without the staggering that the earlier VAT regime used. If capital goods on which credit was taken are later supplied outward, the registered person must pay an amount equal to the credit taken reduced by the prescribed percentage points for each quarter of use, or the tax on the transaction value of that supply — whichever of the two is higher. Disposal claws back whatever share of the credit the period of use has not yet earned.

concepts.subsection: QRMP scheme — quarterly return, monthly payment
concepts.statement: A registered person whose aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year is up to ₹5 crore, and who files GSTR-3B, may opt to file that return quarterly while still paying tax in each of the first two months of the quarter in Form GST PMT-06 by the 25th of the following month — either a fixed sum (35 per cent of the tax paid in cash in the preceding quarter, where that return was quarterly) or a self-assessed amount. Crossing ₹5 crore during any quarter of the current year puts the person out of the scheme from the next quarter. Invoices for the first two months can be uploaded through the Invoice Furnishing Facility, up to ₹50 lakh a month, between the 1st and the 13th of the succeeding month, so recipients see credit without waiting for the quarterly return.

citation.ref: Rule 61A (manner of opting) and Rule 59(2) (Invoice Furnishing Facility), read with Notification No. 84/2020-Central Tax dated 10.11.2020 issued under the proviso to section 39(1), and CBIC Circular No. 143/13/2020-GST dated 10.11.2020

concepts.subsection: Section 44 — Annual return
concepts.statement: Every registered person, other than the specified exceptions such as a casual taxable person, a non-resident taxable person, an Input Service Distributor and persons subject to TDS or TCS, must furnish an annual return for the financial year on or before the thirty-first of December following its end. The annual return reconciles the year's periodic returns; it is a summary instrument, not a fresh assessment.

concepts.subsection: Sections 73, 74 and 74A — Demands, and the FY 2024-25 dividing line
concepts.statement: Which section governs a GST demand now turns first on the period, and only then on honesty. For tax pertaining to periods up to FY 2023-24, section 73 covers shortfalls arising for reasons other than fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression, and section 74 covers the identical shortfalls where one of those is present, with a longer limitation and a heavier penalty. Sub-section (12) of each, inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, stops both at that year. From FY 2024-25 onwards section 74A governs instead, whether or not there was fraud, and its heading says so. It gives one common limitation — notice within forty-two months of the due date for the annual return, order within twelve months of the notice, extendable by six — and pushes the fraud line into the penalty alone: under section 74A(5), ten per cent of the tax or ₹10,000 whichever is higher without fraud, and the whole of the tax with it. No notice issues at all where the amount for the financial year is under ₹1,000.

citation.ref: Section 74A (inserted by section 138 of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, brought into force 01.11.2024 by Notification No. 17/2024-Central Tax dated 27.09.2024), read with sections 73(12) and 74(12)

concepts.subsection: Section 107 — Appeal to the Appellate Authority, pre-deposit
concepts.statement: An appeal to the first Appellate Authority is not entertained unless the appellant has paid the full amount admitted as due, plus ten per cent of the remaining disputed tax. That ten per cent is capped: at twenty crore rupees of CGST, a figure the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 brought down from twenty-five crore. Where the order demands a penalty without demanding any tax, a proviso inserted with effect from 1 October 2025 sets the pre-deposit at ten per cent of that penalty instead. This pre-deposit is what buys a stay on recovery of the balance disputed amount while the appeal is pending — it is a precondition to the appeal being heard at all, not a discretionary figure an officer can vary.

citation.ref: Section 107(6) and its proviso — the maximum reduced from twenty-five to twenty crore rupees by section 141 of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, and the penalty-only proviso inserted with effect from 1 October 2025 by section 129 of the Finance (No. 7) Act, 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 60 — Provisional assessment
concepts.statement: A taxable person unable to determine the value of a supply or the applicable rate of tax may request provisional assessment, executing a bond with security for the differential tax. The proper officer must finalise the assessment ordinarily within six months, extendable, and interest on any additional tax found due at finalisation runs from the original due date for payment of that tax, not from the date of the final order.

concepts.subsection: Section 36 — Period of retention of accounts
concepts.statement: Every registered person must retain the accounts and records section 35 requires for seventy-two months from the due date of furnishing the annual return for the year they relate to. A registered person who is party to an appeal, revision or any other proceeding, or under investigation, must keep the relevant records for a further year after the proceeding's final disposal, or to the seventy-two-month mark, whichever is later.

concepts.subsection: Customs — Warehousing, the two clocks under section 61
concepts.statement: Goods deposited in a licensed customs warehouse under a warehousing bond remain there without payment of duty until an ex-bond bill of entry is filed for home consumption or the goods are re-exported. Two separate clocks then run, and confusing them is the usual mistake. For ordinary imported goods — clause (c) of section 61(1) — the warehousing period is one year from the date of the proper officer's order under section 60(1) permitting the deposit, extendable by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner by not more than a year at a time. Interest under section 61(2) starts much sooner: once those goods sit beyond ninety days from that same section 60(1) order, interest at the section 47 rate runs on the duty payable at clearance, from the ninety-first day until the duty is paid. On clearance, the rate of duty and tariff value are those on the date the ex-bond bill of entry is presented under section 68, while the value of the goods stays as assessed on the into-bond bill of entry.

citation.ref: Sections 61(1)(c) and 61(2) (ninety days from the order under section 60(1)), read with sections 68 and 15(1)(b)

concepts.subsection: Baggage Rules, 2026 — personal effects and the General Free Allowance
concepts.statement: The Baggage Rules, 2026 replaced the Baggage Rules, 2016 with effect from 2 February 2026, and the old test of which country the passenger flew back from is gone. Rule 3 clears used personal effects required for satisfying daily necessities of life, and travel souvenirs, free of duty with no value ceiling at all — other than the articles listed in Annexure-I, which is firearms, cartridges over 50, cigarettes over 100 sticks or cigars over 25 or tobacco over 125 grams, alcohol over two litres, gold or silver in any form other than ornaments, and television. Rule 5 then gives a General Free Allowance, for articles outside Annexure-I, of ₹75,000 to a resident, a tourist of Indian origin or a foreigner on a valid visa other than a tourist visa, not being an infant, arriving in India other than by land; ₹25,000 to a tourist of foreign origin on the same terms. A passenger arriving by land gets used personal effects only, whatever his category. Rule 5 also clears one new laptop or notepad free of duty for a passenger of eighteen or above who is not a crew member, and no passenger may pool his allowance with another's.

citation.ref: Rules 3 and 5 of the Baggage Rules, 2026 (Notification No. 14/2026-Customs (N.T.) dated 01.02.2026, in force 02.02.2026), read with CBIC Master Circular No. 4/2026-Customs dated 01.02.2026

concepts.subsection: Section 27 — Casual taxable person, registration validity
concepts.statement: A casual taxable person must apply for registration at least five days before commencing business and deposit an amount equal to the estimated tax liability for the period of registration, as advance tax. The certificate of registration is valid for the period specified in the application or ninety days from the effective date of registration, whichever is earlier, and it may be extended by a further period not exceeding ninety days.

concepts.subsection: Section 12(2) — Place of supply of services, general rule
concepts.statement: Where supplier and recipient are both in India, and the service is not one of the special cases in sub-sections (3) to (14), the place of supply is the location of the recipient if he is registered. If the recipient is unregistered, it is the address on record with the supplier, and only where no address is on record does it fall back to the supplier's own location. Where the service is physically performed has nothing to do with it.

concepts.subsection: Section 12(6) and 12(7) — Place of supply for events
concepts.statement: Admission to a cultural, artistic, sporting, scientific, educational or entertainment event, or to an amusement park, is supplied where the event is actually held or the park is located — whoever buys the ticket, registered or not. Organising such an event, services ancillary to organising it, and assigning of sponsorship, follow a different rule — the place of supply is the location of the recipient where he is registered, and only where the recipient is unregistered does it become the place the event is held. Admission looks at the venue; organisation looks at the customer.

concepts.subsection: Section 13(3)(a) — Place of supply where goods are made physically available
concepts.statement: Where either the supplier or the recipient is outside India, and the service needs goods to be made physically available by the recipient to the supplier, the place of supply is where the service is actually performed. Two provisos cut that back. Where the service is rendered from a remote location by electronic means, the place of supply is where the goods are at the time of supply. And where goods are temporarily imported into India for repairs or for any other treatment or process and are exported after it without being put to any use in India beyond what the work itself required, this clause does not apply at all — the general rule in section 13(2), the location of the recipient, takes over. The second proviso once covered repairs alone and was later widened to any other treatment or process.

concepts.subsection: Sections 12(3) and 13(3) — Time of supply under reverse charge
concepts.statement: Under reverse charge the clock is the recipient's, not the supplier's. For goods, the time of supply is the earliest of the date the goods are received, the date payment is entered in the recipient's books or debited from his bank account, and the day immediately following thirty days from the supplier's invoice. For services the list drops the receipt limb and stretches the outer limit — the earlier of the date of payment and the day immediately following sixty days from the invoice. Where none of these can be determined it is the date the entry is made in the recipient's books. Thirty days for goods, sixty for services, is the whole distinction.

concepts.subsection: Section 9(4) — Reverse charge on supplies from unregistered persons
concepts.statement: As first enacted, section 9(4) put every registered person on reverse charge for anything bought from an unregistered supplier. That version was suspended and then replaced with effect from 1 February 2019. What stands now is narrow — tax under reverse charge falls on a notified class of registered persons, on notified supplies, and on nobody else. The live notification covers promoters in real estate, who must pay under reverse charge on the shortfall where less than eighty per cent of the inputs and input services for a project are bought from registered suppliers. An ordinary trader buying from an unregistered supplier owes nothing under this sub-section.

citation.ref: Section 9(4), as substituted with effect from 1 February 2019, with Notification 07/2019-Central Tax (Rate)

concepts.subsection: Section 17(5)(c) and (d) — Blocked credit on construction
concepts.statement: Clause (c) blocks credit on works contract services for construction of immovable property, unless they are an input service for further supplying works contract service. Clause (d) blocks credit on goods or services received for construction of immovable property on the taxpayer's own account, and says so even where the property is used in the course or furtherance of business — business use is no answer to this block. Construction here takes in reconstruction, renovation, addition, alteration and repairs, to the extent the spending is capitalised. Plant and machinery is carved out of both clauses, and that carve-out expressly excludes land, buildings and other civil structures.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(c) and (d), with the explanation to section 17

concepts.subsection: Section 17(4) — Banking company option, fifty per cent credit
concepts.statement: A banking company, a financial institution or a non-banking financial company supplying services by way of accepting deposits or extending loans may either do the ordinary proportionate reversal under section 17(2), or take a flat fifty per cent of the eligible input tax credit each month on inputs, capital goods and input services. The choice is made for the year and cannot be withdrawn during the rest of that financial year, and the half not taken simply lapses. One proviso matters more than the rule — the fifty per cent restriction does not touch tax paid on supplies received from another registered person holding the same PAN, so credit on inward supplies from the taxpayer's own other registrations comes in full.

concepts.subsection: Section 19 — Input tax credit on inputs sent for job work
concepts.statement: The principal keeps his input tax credit on inputs sent to a job worker, and section 19(2) says so even where the inputs go straight from the supplier to the job worker's premises without ever reaching the principal. If the inputs are not received back, or supplied out from the job worker's premises, within one year — three years for capital goods — the despatch is deemed a supply on the day the inputs went out. Where the goods were sent directly to the job worker, that one year is counted from the date the job worker received them, not from any earlier date. Moulds, dies, jigs, fixtures and tools sit outside the time limit altogether.

concepts.subsection: Rule 138(10) — Validity period of an e-way bill
concepts.statement: An e-way bill is valid for one day for the first 200 kilometres, and one further day for every 200 kilometres or part thereof after that. Over dimensional cargo, and a multimodal shipment with at least one leg by ship, run on the tighter scale — one day for the first 20 kilometres and one more for every 20 kilometres or part. The period runs from the date and time the transporter first enters vehicle details in Part B, and a part of a stretch counts as a whole one. The 200-kilometre figure replaced an earlier 100-kilometre one, so a validity worked out on the old scale comes out roughly twice as long as the law now allows.

concepts.subsection: Section 54(6) — Provisional refund of ninety per cent
concepts.statement: On a refund claim arising from zero-rated supplies, the proper officer sanctions ninety per cent of the amount claimed on a provisional basis, ahead of the detailed verification that precedes final sanction, and rule 91 gives him seven days from the acknowledgement to do it. Rule 91(2), as amended with effect from 1 October 2025, ties that provisional sanction to the system's own identification and evaluation of risk, and lets the officer decline the provisional route in a given case for reasons recorded in writing. From the same date the ninety per cent route was extended to refund claims arising from the inverted duty structure.

citation.ref: Section 54(6) with Rule 91(2), as amended by Notification 13/2025-Central Tax

concepts.subsection: Rule 28 — Value of supply between distinct or related persons
concepts.statement: A supply between distinct persons under section 25, or between related persons, is valued at open market value; failing that, at the value of goods or services of like kind and quality; failing both, by rule 30 or rule 31. Two provisos do most of the work in practice. Where the goods are meant for onward supply as such by the recipient, the supplier may opt for ninety per cent of the price the recipient charges his unrelated customer. And where the recipient is eligible for full input tax credit, whatever value is declared in the invoice is deemed to be the open market value. Separately, rule 28(2) deems the value of a corporate guarantee given to a bank or financial institution on behalf of a related person at one per cent per annum of the amount guaranteed, or the actual consideration, whichever is higher.

citation.ref: Rule 28, with its second proviso and rule 28(2)

concepts.subsection: Section 31(2) — Time limit for issuing a tax invoice
concepts.statement: For goods, the tax invoice goes out before or at the time of removal where the supply involves movement, and otherwise on delivery or on making the goods available. For services, rule 47 allows thirty days from the date of supply, stretched to forty-five days for an insurer, a banking company, a financial institution or a non-banking financial company. Rule 47A, in force from 1 November 2024, fixes the other invoice people forget — the self-invoice a recipient paying under reverse charge must raise under section 31(3)(f) where his supplier is unregistered — at thirty days from the date he receives the supply.

citation.ref: Section 31(2) and 31(3)(f), with Rules 47 and 47A of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Rule 10(2) — Transport and insurance in the customs value
concepts.statement: To the price paid or payable are added the cost of transport, loading, unloading and handling associated with delivering the imported goods to the place of importation, and the cost of insurance. Where the cost of transport cannot be ascertained it is taken at twenty per cent of the free on board value; where insurance cannot be ascertained it is taken at 1.125 per cent of the free on board value. Both are fallbacks — an actual, documented figure is used as it stands. The flat one per cent landing charge that the older rules loaded on top of the CIF value was removed with effect from 26 September 2017 and is no longer added to anything.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(2), as amended by Notification 91/2017-Customs (N.T.) dated 26 September 2017

concepts.subsection: Section 75 — All Industry Rate and brand rate of drawback
concepts.statement: Section 75 gives back the duty suffered on inputs used in making goods that are then exported. The Central Government fixes All Industry Rates for classes of goods. Where no All Industry Rate has been determined for the exporter's product, he applies for a brand rate under rule 6 of the Drawback Rules. Where an All Industry Rate does exist but recovers less than eighty per cent of the duties actually paid on his materials, he applies under rule 7 for a special brand rate. Both applications run to three months from the relevant date, extendable on payment of the prescribed fee, and rule 9 caps any amount or rate at one third of the market price of the export product.

citation.ref: Section 75, with Rules 3, 6, 7 and 9 of the Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Circular 254/11/2025 — Monetary limits for a section 74A notice and order
concepts.statement: Section 74A says what may be demanded; it does not say who may demand it. Circular No. 254/11/2025-GST dated 27 October 2025 does, extending to section 74A the scheme Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST had set for sections 73 and 74. Taking central tax alone: a Superintendent of Central Tax issues the show cause notice and passes the order up to ₹10 lakh, a Deputy or Assistant Commissioner above that and up to ₹1 crore, and an Additional or Joint Commissioner above ₹1 crore with no ceiling. For integrated tax both steps double, to ₹20 lakh and ₹2 crore. Where one notice covers central tax, integrated tax and cess together, the officer is fixed on the combined amount tested against the doubled steps, never on any single tax read on its own. The same three-tier structure governs a penalty-only notice under section 122, and where the demand grows past an officer's limit during adjudication the case moves up by corrigendum.

citation.ref: Section 74A, read with Tables II and III of Circular No. 254/11/2025-GST dated 27 October 2025, which extends to section 74A the scheme of Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST dated 9 February 2018

concepts.subsection: Rules 9A and 14A — Three-day registration and the simplified scheme
concepts.statement: The Central Goods and Services Tax (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2025 — Notification No. 18/2025-Central Tax dated 31 October 2025, in force from 1 November 2025 — opened two new routes into registration. Rule 9A lets the system grant registration electronically within three working days of the application, on its own data analysis and risk parameters, with an officer stepping in only where a risk parameter is flagged. Rule 14A is an optional simplified scheme a small supplier may choose: he qualifies where his total output tax liability — central tax, State or Union territory tax, integrated tax and cess together — on supplies made to registered persons does not exceed ₹2,50,000 in a month, and where Aadhaar is authenticated for the primary authorised signatory and at least one promoter or partner. That ₹2,50,000 is a monthly output tax figure on business-to-business supplies; it is neither a turnover limit nor the section 22 registration threshold. A person registered under rule 14A in one State cannot take a second rule 14A registration on the same PAN in another State.

citation.ref: Rules 9A and 14A, inserted by the Central Goods and Services Tax (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2025, Notification No. 18/2025-Central Tax dated 31 October 2025, with effect from 1 November 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 109(8) and rule 110A — When a single Member hears a GST appeal
concepts.statement: An appeal before the Appellate Tribunal is normally heard by two Members, one Judicial and one Technical. Section 109(8) carves out an exception: where the tax or input tax credit involved, or the fine, fee or penalty determined by the order appealed against, does not exceed ₹50 lakh, and the appeal involves no question of law, it may be heard by a single Member with the President's approval. Rule 110A, in force from 22 September 2025, supplies the machinery — the President, or a Vice-President authorised for a State Bench, may on his own motion or on a party's application scrutinise an appeal and transfer it to a single Member Bench in that State; and a single Member who later concludes that a question of law is involved must record his reasons in writing and send the appeal back for reconsideration. The ₹50 lakh is read cumulatively across every issue and every tax period the order covers, not issue by issue.

citation.ref: Sections 109(8) and 109(9), read with Rule 110A of the CGST Rules, 2017, inserted by Notification No. 13/2025-Central Tax dated 17 September 2025 with effect from 22 September 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 18(1B) — Time limit for finalising a provisional customs assessment
concepts.statement: A provisional assessment under section 18(1) of the Customs Act once had no outer date; the Finance Act, 2025 gave it one. Section 18(1B) requires the proper officer to finalise within two years from the date of the provisional assessment, and its first proviso lets the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs extend that by one further year on sufficient cause recorded in writing. The Customs (Finalisation of Provisional Assessment) Regulations, 2025 — Notification No. 55/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 12 September 2025 — work the detail: the proper officer calls for the documents and information he needs within fifteen days of the provisional assessment, the importer or exporter has two months to supply them with extensions possible, and the assessment is finalised within three months of the documents arriving or the enquiry ending. Certain periods stand outside the two years and the clock restarts when the reason ends — a stay by a court or tribunal, a direction of the Board, a pending request to a foreign authority, a matter before the Settlement Commission. Where a provisional assessment was already pending on 29 March 2025, the two years run from that date, not from the original assessment.

citation.ref: Section 18(1B) with its first proviso, inserted by the Finance Act, 2025, read with the Customs (Finalisation of Provisional Assessment) Regulations, 2025, Notification No. 55/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 12 September 2025

concepts.subsection: RoDTEP and section 51B — The electronic duty credit ledger
concepts.statement: Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products gives an exporter back the embedded central, State and local taxes no other scheme refunds — value added tax and excise on the fuel his transport burns, mandi tax, electricity duty, stamp duty on export documents. It is a remission of taxes actually borne, not a bounty, and that is what keeps it inside India's obligations at the World Trade Organization; it replaced the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme for the same reason. The claim is made in the shipping bill at the time of export and the benefit arrives as duty credit in the electronic duty credit ledger that section 51B of the Customs Act, 1962 creates, issued as an e-scrip under the Electronic Duty Credit Ledger Regulations, 2021. Three limits carry the marks. The credit pays only the duties of customs specified in the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 — basic customs duty — and never the integrated tax or compensation cess collected at import. The e-scrip is valid for two years from its creation in the ledger, a period the 2022 amendment raised from one year, and anything unused at the end lapses and is not regenerated. And an e-scrip transfers to another Importer-Exporter Code holder only whole: part transfer is not permitted, and the transfer leaves the two years running as they were.

citation.ref: Section 51B, read with regulations 6 and 7 of the Electronic Duty Credit Ledger Regulations, 2021, as amended by the Electronic Duty Credit Ledger (Amendment) Regulations, 2022, Notification No. 79/2022-Customs (N.T.) dated 15 September 2022

concepts.subsection: Entries 36C to 36E — Individual life and health insurance exempted
concepts.statement: Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 put three entries into the exemption notification, Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), with effect from 22 September 2025. Entry 36C exempts services of life insurance business provided by an insurer to the insured where the insured is not a group — a contract covering an individual, or an individual and his family. Entry 36D does the same for health insurance business on the same terms. Entry 36E exempts reinsurance of the services covered by 36C and 36D. What sits outside stays taxable at eighteen per cent: a group term policy, a group credit life policy, a group health policy an employer takes for his staff. The exemption follows the description of the service and the identity of the insured, not the size of the premium — and because it is an exemption rather than zero rating, it breaks the insurer's input tax credit chain on those supplies instead of preserving it.

citation.ref: Serial numbers 36C, 36D and 36E, inserted by Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 with effect from 22 September 2025

concepts.subsection: Rule 7 — The composition rate, and the turnover it applies to
concepts.statement: Section 10 settles who may compound; rule 7 settles at what rate, and on what. A manufacturer, other than of goods the Government has kept out of the scheme, pays one per cent — half central tax, half State tax — of the turnover in State or turnover in Union territory. A restaurant not serving alcohol pays five per cent of that same turnover in State. Any other supplier eligible under section 10(1) and 10(2), which in practice means a trader, also pays one per cent, but of the turnover of taxable supplies of goods and services in State — and that difference is the whole point of the rule.
