A trader dealing partly in exempt goods leaves the exempt turnover out of his base; the manufacturer's one per cent runs on the entire turnover in State, exempt supplies included. A supplier of services under the section 10(2A) scheme pays six per cent of turnover in State. In every case the amount comes out of the supplier's own pocket: section 10(4) forbids him to collect it from his customer, and he takes no input tax credit.

citation.ref: Rule 7, read with sections 10(1), 10(2A) and 10(4) of the CGST Act, 2017

concepts.subsection: Section 148A — Track and trace, and the section 122B penalty
concepts.statement: The Finance Act, 2025 built an enabling frame for marking goods that are easy to evade tax on. Section 148A lets the Government notify goods, and the persons or classes of persons in possession of or dealing with them, and require a unique identification marking to be affixed and the prescribed information about it to be stored and shared electronically. Section 2(116A) defines that marking — a digital stamp, digital mark or similar marking that is unique, secure and non-removable. Section 148A by itself carries no punishment; section 122B, in force from 1 October 2025, supplies it. A person covered by clause (b) of section 148A(1) who acts in contravention pays a penalty of ₹1,00,000 or ten per cent of the tax payable on those goods, whichever is higher, and that amount is in addition to any penalty under Chapter XV or under the penalty chapter itself, not a substitute for it.

citation.ref: Sections 148A and 122B with the definition in section 2(116A), inserted by the Finance Act (No. 7) of 2025, section 122B in force from 1 October 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 18A — Voluntary revision of an entry after clearance
concepts.statement: Before the Finance Act, 2025 an importer who found his own mistake after clearance had no clean way to correct it: section 149 amended a document, and anything touching the assessment waited for the department to issue a notice under section 28. Section 18A now lets the importer, the exporter or an authorised person voluntarily revise an entry already made in a bill of entry, shipping bill or bill of export after the goods are cleared, and the revised entry is treated as a self-assessment. Where the revision shows duty short paid, he pays it with interest, no penalty attaches and no notice under section 28 issues. Where it shows duty paid in excess, the application is itself treated as a claim for refund under section 27, so no separate refund application is needed. The route is closed in defined cases — where an audit, search, seizure or investigation has already been started and intimated, and where the entry has already been reassessed under section 17, 18 or 84. The Customs (Voluntary Revision of Entries Post Clearance) Regulations, 2025, Notification No. 70/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 30 October 2025 and in force from 1 November 2025, prescribe an electronic application filed at the port where the duty was paid, with a fee of ₹1,000.

citation.ref: Section 18A, inserted by the Finance Act, 2025, read with the Customs (Voluntary Revision of Entries Post Clearance) Regulations, 2025, Notification No. 70/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 30 October 2025, and Circular No. 26/2025-Customs dated 31 October 2025

concepts.subsection: Sections 37(4), 39(11), 44(2) and 52(15) — Three years and the return is barred
concepts.statement: A late GST return was once late for ever and could still be filed, with late fee and interest. The Finance Act, 2023 shut that door by inserting a sub-section into each of the four return provisions — section 37(4) for the statement of outward supplies, section 39(11) for the return, section 44(2) for the annual return and section 52(15) for the electronic commerce operator's statement — barring the furnishing of any of them after three years from the due date. Those sub-sections came into force on 1 October 2023 under Notification No. 28/2023-Central Tax dated 31 July 2023, and the portal began enforcing the bar from 1 October 2025. The three years runs from the due date of that return itself, not from the end of the financial year and not from the annual return's due date. Each of the four sub-sections carries a proviso letting the Government, on the recommendations of the Council, notify conditions on which a barred return may still be furnished — so the bar is hard, not absolute.

citation.ref: Sections 37(4), 39(11), 44(2) and 52(15) with their provisos, inserted by the Finance Act, 2023 and brought into force with effect from 1 October 2023 by Notification No. 28/2023-Central Tax dated 31 July 2023

concepts.subsection: Second proviso to section 16(2) and rule 37 — Paying the supplier within 180 days
concepts.statement: Credit taken on an invoice the recipient has not paid does not stay taken. The second proviso to section 16(2) says that where the recipient fails to pay the supplier the value of the supply together with the tax within 180 days from the date of the invoice, an amount equal to the credit availed is added to his output tax liability, with interest. Rule 37, as substituted with effect from 1 October 2022, works out how much and when: the reversal is proportionate to the amount left unpaid, it goes into the return for the tax period immediately following the 180 days, and interest runs on it under section 50. When the recipient later pays, rule 37(4) lets him take the credit back, and that re-availment is expressly outside the section 16(4) time limit. Supplies on which tax is payable under reverse charge sit outside the proviso altogether, because there is no supplier's tax to hand across.

citation.ref: Second proviso to section 16(2), read with rule 37 of the CGST Rules, 2017 as substituted by Notification No. 26/2022-Central Tax dated 26 December 2022 with effect from 1 October 2022

concepts.subsection: Sections 100 and 101 — Appeal against an advance ruling
concepts.statement: An advance ruling under section 98 is not the end of the road. Section 100 gives an appeal to the Appellate Authority for Advance Ruling — to the applicant, or to the concerned officer or the jurisdictional officer who disagrees with the ruling — within thirty days from the date the ruling is communicated, and the proviso lets the Appellate Authority allow a further thirty days where it is satisfied the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause. Section 101(2) requires the Appellate Authority to pass its order within ninety days of the appeal being filed. Section 101(3) holds the trap: where the two members of the Appellate Authority differ on any point, it is deemed that no advance ruling can be issued on that point. There is no casting vote and no further appeal — the applicant is left exactly where he began. The Advance Ruling Authority below must itself pronounce within ninety days of receiving the application.

citation.ref: Sections 100(2) with its proviso, 101(2) and 101(3), read with section 98(6)

concepts.subsection: Section 25(4A) — Two-year sunset on a conditional customs exemption
concepts.statement: Section 25(1) lets the Central Government exempt goods from customs duty by notification in the public interest — a general exemption, open to anyone importing those goods. Section 25(2) is a different power: it exempts goods of a strategic or secret nature, or goods for a charitable purpose, by special order made in each individual case, and needs no notification. Section 25(4A), inserted by the Finance Act, 2021, puts a clock on the first kind wherever it carries conditions. A conditional exemption granted under section 25(1) ceases to have effect on the 31st day of March falling immediately after two years from the date it was granted, unless the notification itself specifies otherwise or the Government varies or rescinds it sooner. For conditional exemptions already in force when the provision came in, the two years count from 1 February 2021. Section 25(4B) keeps whole classes outside the sunset, among them exemptions flowing from a multilateral or bilateral trade agreement and from obligations under international agreements, treaties or conventions. An unconditional exemption is not touched by the sunset at all.

citation.ref: Sections 25(4A) and 25(4B), inserted by the Finance Act, 2021, read with sections 25(1) and 25(2)

concepts.subsection: Rule 96A — Export under bond or LUT, and the two clocks
concepts.statement: An exporter who chooses to export without payment of integrated tax furnishes a bond or a Letter of Undertaking under rule 96A, undertaking to pay the tax with interest if the export does not in fact happen. Two different clocks then run, and they measure different things. For goods, the tax falls due within fifteen days after three months from the date the export invoice was issued, if the goods have not left India by then — or such further period as the Commissioner allows. For services the test is money, not movement: the tax falls due within fifteen days after one year from the invoice date if payment has not been received in convertible foreign exchange, again subject to extension by the Commissioner. Missing either date costs more than tax and interest — the facility of exporting under bond or Letter of Undertaking is withdrawn until the amount is paid, and restored once it is. Non-receipt of payment does not by itself set off the goods clock; for goods the only question is whether they were exported.

citation.ref: Rule 96A(1)(a) and 96A(1)(b), read with section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017 and Circular No. 37/11/2018-GST dated 15 March 2018

concepts.subsection: IGCR Rules, 2022 — One year for the end use, and a quarterly statement
concepts.statement: An importer claiming a concessional rate of duty that depends on what he does with the goods runs on the Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty or for Specified End Use) Rules, 2022. He files a one-time prior intimation estimating quantity and value, obtains an identification number, executes a continuity bond, and accounts for the goods in a prescribed record. Notification No. 07/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 1 February 2025, in force from 2 February 2025, loosened two periods. The time within which the imported goods must be put to the intended purpose, and the time within which unutilised or defective goods may be re-exported or cleared on payment of the differential duty, both became one year in place of six months. And the statement in Form IGCR-3 became quarterly — a quarter being three consecutive calendar months ending in March, June, September or December — in place of the monthly statement the rules first demanded. Failing the end use does not undo the import: it makes the differential duty payable, with interest.

citation.ref: Rules 6, 7 and 10 of the Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty or for Specified End Use) Rules, 2022, as amended by Notification No. 07/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 1 February 2025 with effect from 2 February 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 20 as substituted — Input Service Distributor becomes compulsory
concepts.statement: Until 31 March 2025 the Input Service Distributor route was a choice: a head office receiving common input services for its branches could distribute the credit through an ISD registration or cross-charge the service to them as a distinct person. From 1 April 2025 the choice is gone. Section 2(61) and section 20, as substituted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, say that an office receiving tax invoices for input services for or on behalf of distinct persons shall distribute the credit through the ISD mechanism, and section 24(viii) makes a separate ISD registration compulsory for that office. Two things widened with the substitution. The definition now expressly takes in invoices for services on which tax is payable by the recipient under section 9(3) or section 9(4), so a reverse-charge input service received on a branch's behalf goes through the ISD as well — the office pays that tax under its ordinary registration and then distributes the credit through its ISD registration. And distribution now covers central tax, State or Union territory tax and integrated tax, with rule 39 saying which head goes out as which. The word that changed is one syllable and decides everything: may became shall.

citation.ref: Sections 2(61) and 20, as substituted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 April 2025, read with section 24(viii) and rule 39 of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Section 16 — Input tax credit conditions
concepts.statement: Input tax credit needs every section 16(2) condition together — a tax invoice, receipt of the goods or services, the detail appearing in GSTR-2B, the tax actually paid to the Government by the supplier, and the return filed. Holding a valid invoice while the supplier has not paid the tax defeats the credit.

concepts.subsection: Section 9(3) — Reverse charge
concepts.statement: For notified supplies — legal services from an advocate to a business entity among them — the recipient, not the supplier, is liable to pay the tax, and pays it in cash rather than through input tax credit.

concepts.subsection: Section 22 — Registration
concepts.statement: Registration becomes compulsory when aggregate turnover crosses ₹20 lakh for a supplier of services. The ₹40 lakh limit is for suppliers exclusively of goods in eligible States, and special category States carry lower limits.

concepts.subsection: Section 10 — Composition levy
concepts.statement: A composition taxpayer cannot make inter-State outward supplies of goods. The scheme trades a small turnover-based levy for staying local; crossing the State line with outward supplies forfeits eligibility.

concepts.subsection: Customs valuation
concepts.statement: Additions to the transaction value of imported goods include selling commissions, and cost of transport and insurance to the place of importation — but buying commission, paid to the importer's own agent for representing him abroad, is not added.

concepts.subsection: Section 16(4) — Time limit for input tax credit
concepts.statement: Input tax credit for an invoice cannot be taken after the thirtieth of November following the end of the financial year the invoice belongs to, or the filing of the relevant annual return, whichever is earlier. A valid, eligible credit dies purely of lateness.

concepts.subsection: IGST Act — Place of supply of goods
concepts.statement: Where a supply involves movement of goods, the place of supply is the location where the movement terminates for delivery to the recipient. Who arranges the transport does not decide it; where the goods end up does.

concepts.subsection: Time of supply — advances
concepts.statement: An advance received for a supply of services is taxable when received. For goods, suppliers other than composition taxpayers pay tax only on issue of the invoice — advances for goods were taken out of the tax net by notification. The same rupee of advance is taxed on one side of the goods-services line and not the other.

concepts.subsection: Section 15 — Value of supply
concepts.statement: A discount given after the supply reduces the taxable value only if it was agreed before or at the time of supply and can be linked to the specific invoices, and the recipient reverses the proportionate input tax credit. A goodwill discount invented after the event changes the price, not the tax.

concepts.subsection: Section 50 — Interest on delayed payment
concepts.statement: Interest on delayed payment of tax runs at 18 per cent, and on the portion paid through the electronic cash ledger it is charged only on that net cash amount where the return is filed late — the credit-covered portion carries no interest. Wrongly availed and utilised credit draws its own interest.

concepts.subsection: Section 143 — Job work
concepts.statement: Inputs sent for job work must return, or be supplied from the job worker's premises, within one year; capital goods within three years. Miss the window and the original despatch is deemed a supply from the day the goods went out, with tax and interest reaching back to it.

concepts.subsection: IGST Act — Zero-rated supply
concepts.statement: Exports and supplies to SEZ units are zero-rated, not exempt: the output carries no tax, yet input tax credit survives. The exporter either supplies under a letter of undertaking without paying tax and claims refund of unutilised credit, or pays IGST and claims refund of the tax paid.

concepts.subsection: Rule 138 — E-way bill
concepts.statement: An e-way bill is generated before movement of goods worth more than fifty thousand rupees in a consignment. The obligation attaches to the movement, not the sale — stock transfers, job work despatches and sales returns all need one, and some States set higher intra-State limits.

concepts.subsection: Section 129 — Detention of goods in transit
concepts.statement: Goods moved in contravention — typically without a valid e-way bill or invoice — are detained, and release requires a penalty of two hundred per cent of the tax payable where the owner comes forward. Detention is a transit consequence and runs independently of whether the tax on the supply itself was ever evaded.

concepts.subsection: Schedule I — Supply without consideration
concepts.statement: Four transactions are supplies even without consideration — permanent transfer of business assets on which credit was taken, supplies between related or distinct persons in business, goods moved through agents who undertake to supply or receive on the principal's behalf, and imported services from a related person for business. Employer gifts to an employee stay out up to fifty thousand rupees a year.

concepts.subsection: Schedule III — Neither goods nor services
concepts.statement: Schedule III lists what GST cannot touch at all — an employee's services to the employer in the course of employment, sale of land and of completed buildings, actionable claims other than specified ones, funeral services, and duties of courts and MPs. These are not exempt supplies; they are not supplies, so they never enter aggregate turnover.

concepts.subsection: Section 54 — Refunds
concepts.statement: A refund claim is filed within two years from the relevant date, and the relevant date moves with the ground of the claim — export shipment dates for goods exported, the date payment lands for export of services, the judgment's date where tax was paid under a later-reversed demand. Miss the window and the money stays with the Government however good the ground was.

concepts.subsection: Section 10(2A) — Composition for service providers
concepts.statement: A supplier of services outside the restaurant category, ineligible for the ordinary composition scheme, may opt for the special scheme where aggregate turnover in the preceding year stayed within fifty lakh rupees, paying six per cent. The ordinary scheme's goods-centred gates do not decide this one.

concepts.subsection: Section 17(5) — Blocked credits
concepts.statement: Input tax credit on motor vehicles for transporting persons with seating capacity up to thirteen (including the driver) is blocked — unless the vehicle is used for further supply of such vehicles, transporting passengers, or driving training. Vehicles above thirteen seats and goods-transport vehicles are outside the block, and services of insurance, repair and maintenance follow the vehicle they attach to.

concepts.subsection: Section 13 — Time of supply of services
concepts.statement: For services, time of supply is the earlier of invoice and payment where the invoice issues within the thirty-day limit; where it does not, the earlier of the date the service is provided and the payment. The clock decides which tax period the liability lands in — issuing the invoice late does not push the liability later.

concepts.subsection: Customs — Duty drawback on re-export
concepts.statement: Section 74 refunds up to ninety-eight per cent of import duty when the imported goods themselves are re-exported within two years, identified as the same goods. Goods that were used before re-export get tapering rates by period of use. Section 75 is the other drawback — for duty on inputs consumed in manufacturing exported goods — and the two never apply to the same claim.

concepts.subsection: IGST — Place of supply for immovable property services
concepts.statement: Services directly relating to immovable property — architects, surveyors, engineers, hotel accommodation, letting, construction-linked services — are supplied where the property sits, whatever the locations of supplier and recipient. The property anchors the tax, and if it lies outside India the default recipient-location rule takes over.

concepts.subsection: Schedule II — Works contract as a service
concepts.statement: A works contract — a contract for building, construction, fabrication or similar work on immovable property involving transfer of property in goods — is deemed wholly a supply of services by Schedule II. One levy, one classification: the old VAT-plus-service-tax split of a single contract is gone, and works contract input credit has its own restrictions in section 17(5).

concepts.subsection: Customs valuation — Transaction value
concepts.statement: Customs duty is assessed on transaction value — the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to India — plus prescribed additions, at the time and place of importation. A relationship between buyer and seller displaces that price only where it influenced it; a related-party price the importer shows to be at arm's length stands.

concepts.subsection: Section 15(2) — Inclusions in value
concepts.statement: The value of supply includes taxes other than GST itself, amounts the supplier was liable to pay but the recipient paid, incidental expenses like packing and commission charged by the supplier, interest or penalty for delayed payment of consideration, and subsidies directly linked to price from anyone other than the Government. Each inclusion widens the base beyond the bare price.

concepts.subsection: IGST — Export of services definition
concepts.statement: A service is exported only when all five conditions hold: supplier in India, recipient outside India, place of supply outside India, payment received in convertible foreign exchange (or INR where RBI permits), and supplier and recipient not merely two establishments of one person. Failing any one, the supply is not an export and zero-rating is lost.

concepts.subsection: Section 34 — Credit and debit notes
concepts.statement: A supplier who has charged too much tax — goods returned, deficient supply, price revised down — issues a credit note and reduces output liability, but only up to the thirtieth of November following the financial year of supply (or the annual return, if earlier), and only if the incidence of tax has not been passed to someone who bears it. A commercial credit note without GST can issue any time, adjusting price but not tax.

concepts.subsection: IGST on imported goods
concepts.statement: Import of goods is taxed as inter-State supply, but the IGST is levied and collected as customs duty — under the Customs Tariff Act, on the value determined under the Customs Act at the point of importation, together with basic customs duty. The importer generally takes credit of the IGST so paid; basic customs duty is never creditable.

concepts.subsection: Section 25 — Distinct persons
concepts.statement: Registrations of one entity in different States are distinct persons, and supplies between them — stock transfers, services of one office to another — are taxable supplies even without consideration, valued under the rules with full input credit typically flowing. One legal person, several taxable persons: the design keeps each State's revenue whole.

concepts.subsection: Customs — Pilferage and remission
concepts.statement: Goods pilfered after unloading but before clearance attract no duty from the importer — unless restored — and the custodian pays instead; goods lost or destroyed before clearance earn remission on the Assistant Commissioner's satisfaction, and goods relinquished before clearance drop the duty too. Pilferage is automatic by the section's operation; remission must be sought and shown.

concepts.subsection: E-commerce — TCS and section 9(5)
concepts.statement: An e-commerce operator collects tax at source on the net value of supplies made through it by others — a collection mechanism, not a levy. For the notified services — passenger transport, accommodation, restaurants, housekeeping — section 9(5) goes further: the operator is liable to pay the tax as if it were the supplier, and the actual supplier's registration position changes accordingly. TCS and 9(5) never apply to the same supply.

concepts.subsection: Exempt, nil-rated, non-taxable and zero-rated
concepts.statement: Four different fates: a nil-rated supply is taxable at zero in the tariff; an exempt supply is freed by notification and includes nil-rated and non-taxable supplies for definition purposes; a non-taxable supply is outside the levy itself, like alcohol for human consumption; zero-rated means exports and SEZ supplies — taxable in principle, taxed at zero, with input credit preserved. Only zero-rating keeps the credit; exemption breaks the credit chain.

concepts.subsection: Advance ruling — binding scope
concepts.statement: An advance ruling binds only the applicant who sought it and the jurisdictional officers in respect of that applicant — not other taxpayers, however identical their facts, and not other States' authorities. It holds unless law, facts or circumstances change, and a ruling obtained by fraud or suppression is void from the start. Other taxpayers may read it as persuasive weather, never as shelter.

concepts.subsection: Section 51 — Tax deduction at source
concepts.statement: Government departments, local authorities and notified entities deduct tax at source at two per cent from payments to suppliers where a contract's taxable value exceeds two and a half lakh rupees — the deduction tested contract-wise, on value excluding GST. No deduction where the supplier's State and the place of supply differ from the recipient's State. The deductee takes the amount as cash ledger credit, not as input tax.

concepts.subsection: Section 54(3) — Refund of unutilised input tax credit
concepts.statement: Accumulated input tax credit is refundable in exactly two cases: zero-rated supplies made without payment of tax, and the inverted duty structure — input tax rates exceeding output rates. Credit piling up because sales are slow, or because outputs are exempt, earns no refund; the inverted-structure refund runs on the rule's formula and excludes input services from the computation.

concepts.subsection: Customs — Date for rate of duty
concepts.statement: The rate of duty and tariff valuation for imports is taken on the date of filing the bill of entry for home consumption — or, for warehoused goods, the date of the ex-bond bill of entry when the goods leave the warehouse for home consumption. A rate change while goods sit in bond therefore lands on the importer; the vessel's arrival date matters only where the bill was filed in advance.

concepts.subsection: Section 24 — Compulsory registration
concepts.statement: Certain persons register regardless of turnover: inter-State taxable suppliers of goods, persons liable under reverse charge, casual taxable persons with no fixed place in the State, non-resident taxable persons, e-commerce operators, TDS deductors, and agents supplying for others. The threshold exemption belongs to section 22; section 24's list overrides it — though inter-State suppliers of services enjoy a notified threshold relaxation the goods side never got.

concepts.subsection: Foreign trade policy — EPCG
concepts.statement: The Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme imports capital goods at zero customs duty against an export obligation of six times the duty saved, to be discharged over six years from authorisation — with the goods installed and put to use, and the obligation over and above the average of past exports. Default surrenders proportionate duty with interest; the scheme buys machinery cheap with a promise, and the promise is enforced.

citation.ref: EPCG scheme (export obligation 6x duty saved in 6 years)

concepts.subsection: IGST — Bill-to-ship-to supplies
concepts.statement: Where goods are delivered to one person on the instruction of another, the law sees two supplies: supplier to the instructing buyer, and instructing buyer to the actual recipient — with the first leg's place of supply deemed to be the instructing buyer's principal place of business, wherever the goods physically went. Tax type on each leg follows its own deemed geography, and each leg carries its own invoice.

concepts.subsection: Customs — General rules of interpretation
concepts.statement: Tariff classification walks the General Interpretative Rules in order: headings and their notes first; incomplete articles classify as complete if they have the essential character; mixtures and composites classify by the material giving essential character; and only when goods remain equally classifiable under two headings does the later heading win. The specific description always beats the general one before any tie-breaker is reached.

concepts.subsection: Rule 32(5) — Margin scheme for second-hand goods
concepts.statement: A dealer in second-hand goods, selling them as such after at most minor processing that does not change their nature, may pay GST only on the margin — selling price less purchase price, with a negative margin ignored — provided no input tax credit was taken on the purchase. Buying from unregistered consumers is the scheme's habitat; take credit on the inward side and the whole selling price becomes taxable.

concepts.subsection: Rule 33 — Pure agent
concepts.statement: Costs a supplier incurs as a pure agent of the recipient stay out of the value of supply when every condition holds: the supplier contracts as the recipient's authorised agent for that payment, the recipient alone uses what was procured, the actual amount is separately indicated on the invoice and recovered without markup, and it is in addition to the supplier's own services. Mark it up, or bundle it, and the exclusion is gone.

concepts.subsection: Section 8 — Composite and mixed supplies
concepts.statement: A composite supply bundles naturally — two or more taxable supplies ordinarily supplied together with one principal supply — and takes the principal supply's rate. A mixed supply is an artificial bundle for a single price whose parts could be sold separately, and it takes the highest rate among them. Natural bundling is tested by trade practice: what buyers expect to come together.

concepts.subsection: Actionable claims and specified activities
concepts.statement: Actionable claims are goods by definition, yet Schedule III keeps them outside GST — except the specified ones: lottery, betting, gambling, and since the 2023 amendments, online money gaming, which are taxable, valued on their own rules. An unsecured debt assigned, an insurance claim transferred — outside the levy; a lottery ticket sold — squarely inside it.

concepts.subsection: Section 50(3) — Interest on wrongly availed credit
concepts.statement: Interest on wrongly availed input tax credit runs only where the credit is also utilised — credit that sat unused in the electronic credit ledger until reversal costs nothing. The same mercy governs delayed payment interest under section 50(1): where the return is late but the tax was paid by balance in the cash ledger, interest applies on the portion paid through cash late, computed on the net cash liability. Both rules arrived as retrospective corrections of harsher readings.

concepts.subsection: Customs refunds — unjust enrichment
concepts.statement: A customs duty refund is paid to the claimant only on proof that the duty's incidence was not passed on to any other person; otherwise the refund is sanctioned but credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund. The presumption runs against the claimant — passing on is assumed until displaced by evidence such as a chartered accountant's certificate and unchanged prices. Captive consumption and duty paid under protest walk the same test.

concepts.subsection: Import of services — reverse charge
concepts.statement: Services imported for business bear IGST in the recipient's hands under reverse charge — the foreign supplier is beyond the levy's practical reach, so the Indian recipient self-assesses, pays in cash, and takes credit where eligible. Import by an individual for personal purposes stays outside as not being in the course of business — except OIDAR services, which are taxed even to consumers with the foreign supplier itself required to register.

concepts.subsection: OIDAR services
concepts.statement: Online information and database access or retrieval services — streaming, cloud storage, e-books, online advertising, essentially automated digital delivery with minimal human intervention — are taxed in India even when supplied to unregistered consumers. The foreign supplier (or its appointed person) registers under the simplified scheme and pays; for registered business recipients, ordinary reverse charge applies instead. The 2023 amendments deleted the minimal-human-intervention escape arguments by tightening the definition.

concepts.subsection: E-invoicing
concepts.statement: Registered persons with aggregate annual turnover above five crore rupees (in any year from 2017-18) must report B2B invoices to the Invoice Registration Portal, which returns an IRN and QR code — without which the invoice is not a valid invoice at all. B2C supplies, and notified exclusions like banks, insurers, GTAs and passenger transporters, stay outside. The e-invoice auto-populates GSTR-1 and travels with the e-way bill system.

concepts.subsection: FTP — Advance authorisation
concepts.statement: Advance authorisation imports inputs duty-free for physical incorporation in export products, on actual user condition — the inputs and the resulting goods cannot be sold domestically until the export obligation is discharged. The scheme demands minimum value addition (generally fifteen per cent) and export within the specified period, with inputs quantified by standard input-output norms or self-declaration. It frees inputs; EPCG frees capital goods — parallel schemes, different subject matter.

concepts.subsection: Goods transport agencies — the two routes
concepts.statement: A GTA's services are taxed one of two ways: reverse charge at five per cent paid by the specified recipient with the GTA taking no input credit, or forward charge by the GTA's own annual declared option — at five per cent without credit or eighteen per cent with full credit. The credit-preserving rate was twelve per cent until 21 September 2025 and became eighteen per cent on 22 September 2025, when the twelve per cent slab went. Services to unregistered persons largely ride exemptions. The declaration binds for the financial year; recipients must know which regime their transporter elected, since the liability moves with it.

citation.ref: Section 9(3) with the notified GTA options, the forward-charge rate with credit raised to eighteen per cent by Notification No. 15/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 with effect from 22 September 2025

concepts.subsection: SA 200 — Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor
concepts.statement: An audit conducted under the Standards on Auditing obtains reasonable assurance, which is a high level of assurance but not absolute assurance.

concepts.subsection: SA 200 — Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor
concepts.statement: The audit is planned and performed with professional skepticism — a questioning mind alert to conditions indicating possible misstatement, and a critical assessment of evidence. It neither assumes management dishonest nor assumes it honest; records are accepted as genuine absent reason to believe otherwise, and doubted the moment there is one.

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: The preconditions for an audit are an acceptable financial reporting framework and management's agreement to the premise on which an audit is conducted — its responsibility for the financial statements, for internal control, and for giving the auditor access and information. Where the preconditions are not present, the auditor does not accept the engagement.

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: Where management imposes a limitation on scope before the engagement is accepted, and the auditor expects that limitation will result in a disclaimer of opinion, the auditor does not accept the engagement unless law or regulation requires it.

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: On recurring audits the auditor assesses whether circumstances require the engagement terms to be revised and whether the entity needs reminding of the existing terms. A fresh letter every year is not demanded; a changed situation — new management, changed ownership, a changed framework, misunderstood scope — is what calls for one.

concepts.subsection: SA 220 (Revised) — Quality Management for an Audit
concepts.statement: The engagement partner takes overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality on the engagement. Work may be delegated across the engagement team, but the responsibility for quality is not delegated with it.

concepts.subsection: SA 230 — Audit Documentation
concepts.statement: The final audit file is assembled ordinarily within not more than 60 days after the date of the auditor's report.

concepts.subsection: SA 230 — Audit Documentation
concepts.statement: Audit documentation must be sufficient for an experienced auditor with no previous connection to the audit to understand the procedures performed, the results and evidence obtained, and the significant matters and conclusions. The file must speak for itself; the auditor's memory is not part of the record.

concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: Management override of controls is a significant risk presumed to be present in every audit, and it is not rebuttable.

concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: There is a presumed risk of fraud in revenue recognition, and unlike management override that presumption may be rebutted with documented reasons.

concepts.subsection: Auditor resignation under the Companies Act
concepts.statement: An auditor who resigns files a statement in the prescribed form with the company and the Registrar within thirty days of resignation, stating the reasons and any relevant facts. For specified companies the statement also goes to the Comptroller and Auditor-General. Failure invites a penalty on the auditor personally.

concepts.subsection: SA 250 — Consideration of Laws and Regulations
concepts.statement: SA 250 splits laws into two categories, and the auditor's responsibility differs between them. For laws with a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures, the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about compliance. For other laws that are fundamental to the operating aspects of the business, the auditor only performs specified procedures to help identify non-compliance.

concepts.subsection: SA 260 (Revised) — Communication with Those Charged with Governance
concepts.statement: The auditor communicates the planned scope and timing of the audit to those charged with governance, not only the findings.

concepts.subsection: SA 265 — Communicating Deficiencies in Internal Control
concepts.statement: Significant deficiencies in internal control are communicated in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis.

concepts.subsection: SA 299 (Revised) — Joint Audit of Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Each joint auditor is responsible for the work divided to that auditor, and all joint auditors are jointly and severally responsible for the work not divided.

concepts.subsection: SA 315 (Revised) — Identifying and Assessing the Risks of Material Misstatement
concepts.statement: A significant risk is one requiring special audit consideration, and for such risks the auditor must obtain an understanding of the entity's related controls.

concepts.subsection: SA 320 — Materiality in Planning and Performing an Audit
concepts.statement: Performance materiality is set below materiality for the financial statements as a whole, to reduce to an appropriately low level the probability that uncorrected and undetected misstatements aggregate above materiality.

concepts.subsection: SA 330 — The Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks
concepts.statement: When the auditor has determined that an assessed risk of material misstatement at the assertion level is a significant risk, substantive procedures specifically responsive to that risk must be performed.

concepts.subsection: SA 330 — The Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks
concepts.statement: Irrespective of the assessed risks, the auditor designs and performs substantive procedures for each material class of transactions, account balance and disclosure. Excellent controls reduce substantive work; they never reduce it to zero for anything material.

concepts.subsection: SA 402 — Audit Considerations Relating to an Entity Using a Service Organisation
concepts.statement: A Type 1 report describes the service organisation's system and the design of its controls at a point in time. A Type 2 report also reports on their operating effectiveness over a period. Only a Type 2 report can give evidence about operating effectiveness.

concepts.subsection: SA 450 — Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
concepts.statement: Uncorrected misstatements are communicated to those charged with governance and the auditor evaluates whether they are material individually or in aggregate.

concepts.subsection: SA 500 — Audit Evidence
concepts.statement: Sufficiency is the measure of the quantity of audit evidence; appropriateness is the measure of its quality, being its relevance and its reliability.

concepts.subsection: SA 501 — Audit Evidence: Specific Considerations for Selected Items
concepts.statement: When inventory is material to the financial statements, the auditor must attend the physical inventory counting unless it is impracticable.

concepts.subsection: SA 501 — Audit Evidence: Specific Considerations
concepts.statement: Where inventory held by a third party is material, the auditor obtains evidence of its existence and condition by requesting confirmation from the custodian, or by inspection, or both — and considers whether more is needed where the custodian's integrity or independence is in doubt.

concepts.subsection: SA 505 — External Confirmations
concepts.statement: Negative confirmations may be used as the sole substantive procedure only when the assessed risk is low, the population is large and homogeneous, a very low exception rate is expected, and the auditor is not aware of circumstances that would cause recipients to disregard them.

concepts.subsection: SA 510 — Initial Audit Engagements: Opening Balances
concepts.statement: In an initial audit engagement the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about whether opening balances contain misstatements that materially affect the current period's financial statements, and whether accounting policies reflected in the opening balances have been consistently applied.

concepts.subsection: SA 520 — Analytical Procedures
concepts.statement: Analytical procedures are mandatory at two points in an audit — as risk assessment procedures during planning, and near the end of the audit to form an overall conclusion. Using them as substantive procedures is optional, a choice the auditor makes about how to respond to an assessed risk.

concepts.subsection: SA 530 — Audit Sampling
concepts.statement: Misstatements found in a sample are projected to the population the sample was drawn from. The sample is a means of reaching a conclusion about the whole population, so the error found in it is evidence about the whole population, not only about the items examined.

concepts.subsection: SA 540 — Auditing Accounting Estimates
concepts.statement: The auditor reviews the outcome, or subsequent re-estimation, of the prior period's accounting estimates — not to second-guess last year's audit, but to learn how management estimates: where its judgments proved biased, where uncertainty was understated, and where this year's risk therefore sits. Estimates resolved far from their booked amounts are risk assessment gold, not automatic prior-period errors.

concepts.subsection: SA 550 — Related Parties
concepts.statement: A significant related party transaction outside the entity's normal course of business gives rise to a significant risk. The auditor inspects the underlying contracts and evaluates whether the business rationale suggests the transaction was entered into to engage in fraudulent financial reporting or to conceal misappropriation of assets.

concepts.subsection: SA 560 — Subsequent Events
concepts.statement: Where the report is amended for a subsequent event, dual dating confines the auditor's responsibility for events after the original date to that amendment alone.

concepts.subsection: SA 560 — Subsequent Events
concepts.statement: Between the financial statements' date and the auditor's report date, the auditor actively performs procedures to catch events needing adjustment or disclosure. After the report's date the duty to search ends — but a fact coming to the auditor's knowledge before the statements are issued, which would have changed the report, must be pursued: discuss, determine amendment, and act on the outcome.

concepts.subsection: SA 570 (Revised) — Going Concern
concepts.statement: Where a material uncertainty about going concern exists and is adequately disclosed, the opinion is unmodified and a separate section headed "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern" is included.

concepts.subsection: SA 580 — Written Representations
concepts.statement: Written representations are audit evidence, but they are not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about any of the matters they deal with. Obtaining them does not affect the nature or extent of the other evidence the auditor obtains.

concepts.subsection: SA 600 — Using the Work of Another Auditor
concepts.statement: Where a principal auditor uses the work of another auditor for a component, the principal auditor states the division of responsibility in the audit report, indicating the extent of the financial information audited by the other auditor. The principal auditor is not responsible for the work entrusted to the other auditor, except where circumstances should have aroused suspicion about its reliability.

concepts.subsection: SA 610 (Revised) — Using the Work of Internal Auditors
concepts.statement: SA 610 (Revised) permits internal auditors to provide direct assistance under the external auditor's direction, supervision and review — but never for procedures that involve significant judgments, relate to higher assessed risks where more than limited judgment is required, or cover work the internal audit function has itself reported on. Written agreements from the entity and the internal auditors come first.

concepts.subsection: SA 620 — Using the Work of an Auditor's Expert
concepts.statement: The auditor has sole responsibility for the audit opinion, and that responsibility is not reduced by using the work of an auditor's expert. The auditor's report does not refer to the expert unless the reference is required by law or regulation, and where it is, the report must state that the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility.

concepts.subsection: SA 700 (Revised) — Forming an Opinion and Reporting
concepts.statement: The auditor's report presents the Opinion as its first section, and the Basis for Opinion comes directly after it. The conclusion is stated before the reasons for it, so a reader who stops after the first paragraph has still read the opinion.

concepts.subsection: SA 701 — Communicating Key Audit Matters
concepts.statement: Key audit matters are required for audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities, and where otherwise required by law or voluntarily undertaken.

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: A material misstatement that is not pervasive gives a qualified opinion; a material misstatement that is pervasive gives an adverse opinion.

concepts.subsection: SA 706 (Revised) — Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter Paragraphs
concepts.statement: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph refers to a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements; an Other Matter paragraph refers to a matter not so disclosed but relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the report.

concepts.subsection: SA 710 — Comparative Information: Corresponding Figures and Comparative Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Where comparatives are presented as corresponding figures, the auditor's opinion refers to the current period only and does not refer to the corresponding figures. Where they are presented as comparative financial statements, the opinion refers to each period for which financial statements are presented.

concepts.subsection: SA 720 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Other Information
concepts.statement: The auditor reads the other information in the annual report and considers whether it is materially inconsistent with the financial statements or with the auditor's knowledge obtained in the audit. The auditor does not audit the other information and expresses no opinion or conclusion on it.

concepts.subsection: SA 800 — Special Considerations, Special Purpose Frameworks
concepts.statement: Financial statements prepared for specific users under a special purpose framework — a tax basis, a regulator's format, a contract's accounting clauses — are audited with the SAs applied to that framework, and the report carries an Emphasis of Matter alerting readers that the statements follow a special purpose framework and may be unsuitable for any other purpose; the auditor may also restrict distribution. The opinion itself is not modified by the framework being special.

citation.ref: special purpose framework reporting — Emphasis of Matter alert

items.stem: What is the company's WACC for discounting project cash flows?

options.text: 12.0 per cent, using the book-value weights of 625:375 with the after-tax cost of debt
options.misconception: weights the sources of capital by book value instead of the market value the firm actually raises money at
options.why: The book split is 500:300, or weights of 0.625 and 0.375. Applying those to 15% and 7% gives 9.375% + 2.625% = 12.0% — the after-tax cost of debt is right here, but market value, not book value, is what WACC must weight.

options.text: 14.0 per cent, using market-value weights but the pre-tax cost of debt of 10 per cent
options.misconception: omits the tax shield on interest, using debt's quoted rate instead of its after-tax cost
options.why: Interest is tax-deductible, so debt's true cost to the firm is 10% × (1 − 0.3) = 7%, not 10%. Using the pre-tax figure gives 0.8 × 15% + 0.2 × 10% = 14.0%, overstating the discount rate.

options.text: 13.4 per cent, using market-value weights of 80:20 and an after-tax cost of debt of 7 per cent
options.why: Weights come from market value: 800/1000 = 0.8 for equity, 200/1000 = 0.2 for debt. Debt's after-tax cost is 10% × (1 − 0.3) = 7%. WACC = 0.8 × 15% + 0.2 × 7% = 12% + 1.4% = 13.4%.

options.text: 8.6 per cent, using the market-value weights but assigning equity's weight to debt and debt's weight to equity
options.misconception: swaps the equity and debt weights before applying them to their respective costs
options.why: Swapping the weights gives 0.2 × 15% + 0.8 × 7% = 3% + 5.6% = 8.6%, understating WACC by crediting the cheaper source with the larger share it does not actually have.

items.scenario: A company's equity has a market value of ₹800 crore and a cost of equity of 15 per cent. Its debt has a market value of ₹200 crore and a pre-tax cost of 10 per cent. The tax rate is 30 per cent. The same company's books show equity at ₹500 crore and debt at ₹300 crore.

items.stem: Under real options reasoning, what should the firm do and why?

options.text: Reject — total value is −5 − 9 = −₹14 crore, since the option adds another cost on top of the shortfall
options.misconception: subtracts the option value instead of adding it, treating flexibility as a further cost rather than a source of value
options.why: An option the firm holds, not one it owes, only ever adds to value — it is the right, not the obligation, to expand. It is added to static NPV, giving +4 crore, not subtracted.

options.text: Reject — the static NPV is −5 crore and real options do not change accept-or-reject decisions
options.misconception: treats real options as inapplicable and evaluates the project on static NPV alone
options.why: The whole point of real options is that flexibility has value discounting misses. A project rejected on static NPV alone can still be strategically positive once its embedded options are priced in, as here.

options.text: Accept — total strategic value is −5 + 9 = ₹4 crore, since the expansion option is worth more than the pilot's shortfall
options.why: Real options add the option's value to the static NPV rather than ignoring it: −5 + 9 = +4 crore. Discounting alone prices the pilot as if the expansion choice did not exist, which is exactly what real options corrects.

options.text: Accept, with total value of ₹9 crore, since only the option matters once one exists
options.misconception: credits the option value alone and drops the underlying project's own negative static NPV
options.why: The option sits on top of the base project, not instead of it. Both figures belong in the total: −5 crore from the pilot itself, +9 crore from the option to expand, netting to +4 crore.

items.scenario: A pilot plant has a static NPV of −₹5 crore on its own cash flows. It also carries the option to expand into a full plant in three years if the pilot succeeds; that option, valued separately, is worth ₹9 crore.

items.stem: Which technique is this, and what does it give that changing one variable at a time cannot?

options.text: Scenario analysis — because it uses a set of named cases such as best, base and worst
options.misconception: mistakes the description of scenario analysis's few discrete bundles for a method that draws thousands of random combinations
options.why: Scenario analysis bundles a handful of internally consistent cases by name. Ten thousand random draws from each variable's own distribution is a different exercise entirely — simulation, not a short list of scenarios.

options.text: Sensitivity analysis — because several variables are varied at the same time
options.misconception: defines sensitivity analysis by the number of variables moved, when its defining trait is moving exactly one at a time
options.why: Sensitivity analysis isolates one variable, holding the rest fixed, precisely so each variable's own break-even point is visible. Moving several together, randomly, is what simulation does.

options.text: Simulation — a full probability distribution of NPV, including the chance of a negative outcome, not just a handful of break-even points
options.why: Drawing many random combinations from probability distributions and building the full outcome spread is Monte Carlo simulation. Sensitivity analysis only ever answers "what if this one variable moves," never the chance of any particular result.

options.text: The certainty equivalent approach — because it converts risky flows into a single risk-adjusted figure
options.misconception: confuses simulation's output, a distribution of outcomes, with the certainty equivalent method's output, a single deflated cash flow
options.why: Certainty equivalents shrink each risky flow to one certain-equivalent number and discount it at the risk-free rate. That produces one adjusted NPV, not the spread of ten thousand outcomes described here.

items.scenario: An analyst reruns a project's NPV model ten thousand times, each run drawing sales volume, selling price and unit cost independently from their own probability distributions, and plots the resulting spread of ten thousand NPV outcomes.

items.stem: What is the one-step binomial value of the call?

options.text: ₹12.00, the expected payoff at the correct risk-neutral probability, left undiscounted
options.misconception: computes the correct expected payoff but forgets to discount it back to the present at the risk-free rate
options.why: 0.6 × 20 = ₹12 is the expected payoff one period from now, not its value today. The option's price is that payoff discounted at 1.08, giving ₹11.11, not ₹12.00.

options.text: ₹9.26, taking the up and down moves as equally likely instead of computing the risk-neutral probability
options.misconception: substitutes a naive 50-50 probability for the no-arbitrage risk-neutral probability the model requires
options.why: At p = 0.5 the expected payoff would be 0.5 × 20 = ₹10, discounting to 10/1.08 ≈ ₹9.26. But 0.5 is not the probability that removes arbitrage here — 0.6 is, from the risk-free rate and the up and down factors.

options.text: ₹11.11: risk-neutral probability 0.6, expected payoff ₹12, discounted at 1.08
options.why: p = (1.08 − 0.9) / (1.2 − 0.9) = 0.18/0.3 = 0.6, using u = 1.2 and d = 0.9. Payoffs are ₹20 up and ₹0 down, so expected payoff = 0.6 × 20 = ₹12, discounted at 1.08 gives 12/1.08 ≈ ₹11.11.

options.text: ₹7.41, swapping u and d in the risk-neutral probability formula
options.misconception: swaps the up and down factors inside the probability formula, inverting which state is which
options.why: Swapping gives p = (1.08 − 1.2)/(0.9 − 1.2) = 0.4, not 0.6. Expected payoff falls to 0.4 × 20 = ₹8, discounting to 8/1.08 ≈ ₹7.41 — a probability drawn from the wrong pairing of factor to state.

items.scenario: A share trading at ₹100 will move in one period to either ₹120 or ₹90. The risk-free growth factor for the period is 1.08. A call option on the share has a strike of ₹100.

items.stem: What happens to the two premiums?

options.text: The call rises and the put falls by the same amount, to keep put-call parity satisfied
options.misconception: misapplies put-call parity, which fixes call-minus-put, to mean the two must move in opposite directions
options.why: Parity fixes C − P at a value independent of volatility, which both premiums rising together, by the same amount, still satisfies exactly. Parity requires them to move together, not apart.

options.text: Only the call premium rises, since higher volatility only helps a bet on the price going up
options.misconception: assumes volatility only benefits upside bets, when a put profits just as much from a large favourable (downward) move
options.why: A put gains from a big fall the same way a call gains from a big rise; both are bets on movement, not direction. Volatility raises the value of optionality on both sides at once.

options.text: Both premiums fall, since higher volatility is priced as a risk cost the way it would depress a bond's price
options.misconception: treats volatility like a bond's default or duration risk, which lowers value, instead of like optionality, which volatility raises
options.why: Unlike a bond holder, an option holder's downside is fixed at the premium already paid while the upside is open-ended, so more volatility can only help, never hurt, the option's value.

options.text: Both the call and the put premium rise
options.why: Higher volatility raises the chance of a large favourable move for either option, while the loss on each stays capped at its premium — so both gain value together, and by the same amount, since put-call parity's right-hand side does not depend on volatility.

items.scenario: A dealer revises only her volatility estimate for an underlying share upward, holding spot, strike, time to expiry and the risk-free rate unchanged, and reprices both a call and a put on that share with Black-Scholes.

items.stem: What price does the convexity-adjusted estimate give, and how does it compare with the duration-only estimate?

options.text: ₹880 — the duration-only fall of 12 per cent, with convexity ignored entirely
options.misconception: uses the linear duration estimate alone and skips the convexity correction altogether
options.why: −6 × 0.02 = −12% gives ₹880, but that straight-line estimate overstates the loss for a positive-convexity bond — the true fall is smaller once the 1.6% convexity add-back is included.

options.text: ₹896 — a 10.4 per cent fall, softer than the 12 per cent duration-only fall because convexity adds back 1.6 per cent
options.why: Duration-only: −6 × 0.02 = −12%. Convexity term: 0.5 × 80 × 0.02² = 0.5 × 80 × 0.0004 = 1.6%. Combined: −12% + 1.6% = −10.4%, so price = 1,000 × 0.896 = ₹896 — less severe than the straight-line estimate, as positive convexity always is on a yield rise.

options.text: ₹912 — omitting the one-half factor in the convexity term
options.misconception: drops the standard one-half multiplier on the convexity term, overstating the correction
options.why: The convexity adjustment is 0.5 × C × (Δy)², not C × (Δy)²  — the one-half comes from the second-derivative term in the Taylor expansion the estimate is built on. Skipping it gives 3.2% instead of 1.6%, and an overstated ₹912.

options.text: ₹864 — subtracting the convexity term from the duration estimate instead of adding it
options.misconception: subtracts the convexity term from the duration-only estimate, doubling the mis-estimate of the loss instead of correcting it
options.why: The convexity term is always added, not subtracted: −12% + 1.6% = −10.4%, not −12% − 1.6% = −13.6%. Positive convexity works in the bondholder's favour on both a rise and a fall in yield, so it can only soften a loss, never worsen it.

items.scenario: A bond priced at ₹1,000 has a modified duration of 6 years and a convexity of 80. Its yield rises by 200 basis points.

items.stem: What is the bond's current yield, and how does it sit against the coupon rate and the yield to maturity?

options.text: 8.33 per cent, dividing the coupon by the average of price and face value
options.misconception: applies the approximate-YTM shortcut, which averages price and face value in its denominator, to a plain current-yield question
options.why: Current yield only ever divides by the market price: 80/920 ≈ 8.70%. Averaging price and face value, 80/960 ≈ 8.33%, belongs to an approximation of YTM, a different figure answering a different question.

options.text: 8.70 per cent — above the 8.00 per cent coupon, with YTM higher again, since a discount bond also gains from the pull to par
options.why: Current yield = 80/920 ≈ 8.70%, above the 8.00% coupon because the price sits below face value. YTM adds the capital gain to par at redemption on top of that, so the order is coupon rate < current yield < YTM for any discount bond.

options.text: 8.70 per cent, but with YTM the lowest of the three since the discounted price marks the bond as cheap
options.misconception: reverses the ordering, reading a discount price as depressing the yield instead of raising it further still through the pull to par
options.why: A price below par is exactly what makes YTM the highest of the three, not the lowest — the buyer collects both the coupon stream and the gain to par at maturity. The current yield figure of 8.70% is right; the ordering claimed after it is not.

options.text: 8.00 per cent, dividing the coupon by the face value rather than the market price
options.misconception: computes current yield on face value instead of the bond's actual market price
options.why: Current yield is defined against what the bond actually costs today, ₹920, not its ₹1,000 face value. 80/1,000 = 8.00% is just the coupon rate restated, not the yield an investor buying at ₹920 earns.

items.scenario: An 8 per cent coupon bond with face value ₹1,000 is trading at ₹920.

items.stem: Ignoring time value of money, what is the bank's net cash flow across the premiums paid and the default payout?

options.text: Net gain of ₹6 crore, the payout alone, with the premiums paid left out of the reckoning
options.misconception: reports the default payout as the net benefit and forgets to deduct the premiums paid over the life of the position
options.why: The premiums are a real cost the buyer paid every year the contract ran, ₹0.45 crore in total here, and belong in the net figure alongside the ₹6 crore payout: 6 − 0.45 = ₹5.55 crore.

options.text: Net gain of ₹9.55 crore, with the payout set at the full ₹10 crore face value
options.misconception: pays out the full face value instead of the loss given default, ignoring the stated 40 per cent recovery rate
options.why: The seller's obligation is the loss given default, ₹10 crore × (1 − 0.4) = ₹6 crore, not the whole face value. Paying the full ₹10 crore ignores the recovery the bond still returns.

options.text: Net gain of ₹5.55 crore — a ₹6 crore payout on the 60 per cent loss given default, less ₹0.45 crore of premiums paid over three years
options.why: Premiums: ₹10 crore × 1.5% × 3 years = ₹0.45 crore. Payout: (1 − 0.4) × ₹10 crore = ₹6 crore, since the seller covers only the loss given default, not the whole face value. Net: 6 − 0.45 = ₹5.55 crore.

options.text: Net gain of ₹5.25 crore, continuing to count premiums for the full five-year tenor even though default ended the contract in year 3
options.misconception: keeps paying CDS premiums out to the original five-year tenor instead of stopping at the default that ends the contract
options.why: Protection ends when the reference entity defaults; only the premiums actually paid up to that point, two years' worth here, count. Charging five years of premium against a contract that ended in year 3 overstates the cost and understates the net gain.

items.scenario: A bank holds a ₹10 crore bond and buys five-year CDS protection on it at a spread of 150 basis points a year, paid annually. The reference entity defaults at the start of year 3, after two full annual premiums have been paid, and the recovery rate is 40 per cent.

items.stem: What is the theoretical ex-rights price, and what is the value of the right attached to one existing share?

options.text: TERP ₹130; value of the right ₹5 per existing share, taking a simple average of the cum-rights and issue prices
options.misconception: averages the cum-rights and subscription prices equally instead of weighting them by the number of shares outstanding at each price
options.why: A simple average, (150 + 110)/2 = ₹130, ignores that four times as many shares trade at ₹150 as are issued at ₹110. The weighted figure, ₹142, reflects that four-to-one mix; a plain average does not.

options.text: TERP unchanged at ₹150; value of the right ₹40, the gap between the cum-rights price and the subscription price
options.misconception: ignores the dilution the new shares cause, comparing the subscription price to the undiluted cum-rights price instead of the ex-rights price
options.why: Once the new shares are issued, the price settles at the blended ex-rights figure, ₹142, not the pre-issue ₹150. The right's value is 142 − 110 = ₹32, spread over four shares — ₹150 − 110 = ₹40 skips the dilution the rights issue itself causes.

options.text: TERP ₹142; value of the right ₹8 per existing share
options.why: TERP = (4cr × 150 + 1cr × 110) / 5cr = (600 + 110)/5 = ₹142. The right to buy one new share is worth 142 − 110 = ₹32; spread over the four old shares needed to earn it, that is ₹8 per existing share.

options.text: TERP ₹142; value of the right ₹6.40 per existing share, dividing by the post-issue share count of five instead of four
options.misconception: divides the right's value by the total post-issue share count instead of the subscription ratio of old shares needed for one new share
options.why: The right's ₹32 value belongs to the four old shares that earn one new share under a 1-for-4 issue, so 32/4 = ₹8. Dividing by five, the post-issue total, answers a different question and understates the figure.

items.scenario: A company with 4 crore shares outstanding, trading cum-rights at ₹150, offers a 1-for-4 rights issue — one new share for every four held — at a subscription price of ₹110.

items.stem: What does Walter's model give as the share price at this payout, and what does it say the firm should do?

options.text: About ₹73.33, inverting the ratio to Ke/r instead of r/Ke
options.misconception: inverts the r/Ke multiplier in Walter's formula, understating what retained earnings contribute for a growth firm
options.why: Using Ke/r = 0.12/0.15 = 0.8 gives [4 + 0.8 × 6]/0.12 = 8.8/0.12 ≈ ₹73.33. The formula's multiplier is r/Ke = 1.25, which rewards a firm earning above its cost of equity — the inverted ratio does the opposite.

options.text: About ₹95.83; since r (15%) exceeds Ke (12%), the firm should retain more and cut its payout further to raise the price above this
options.why: P = [4 + (0.15/0.12)(10 − 4)]/0.12 = [4 + 1.25 × 6]/0.12 = 11.5/0.12 ≈ ₹95.83. Because the firm earns more on retained cash than shareholders' own opportunity cost, Walter's rule says push retention toward 100%, not hold it at 40%.

options.text: About ₹95.83, but since r exceeds Ke the firm should raise its payout toward 100 per cent to maximise price
options.misconception: reverses Walter's decision rule, recommending higher payout for a growth firm when full retention is what maximises price
options.why: The price figure is right, but the direction is backwards. When r > Ke the firm compounds shareholders' money better than the market does, so the rule calls for retaining more, not distributing more.

options.text: ₹11.50, stopping at the formula's numerator and forgetting the final division by Ke
options.misconception: computes the numerator of Walter's formula correctly but omits the final division by the cost of equity
options.why: 4 + 1.25 × 6 = 11.5 is only the bracketed numerator; Walter's price is that figure divided by Ke, 11.5/0.12 ≈ ₹95.83, not the undiscounted 11.5 itself.

items.scenario: A company has EPS of ₹10, pays a dividend of ₹4 per share, earns an internal return of 15 per cent on retained earnings, and has a cost of equity of 12 per cent.

items.stem: What money multiple (MOIC) does the sponsor earn on exit, and what drove it?

options.text: 2.5x — exit equity of 500 − 250 = ₹250 crore against ₹100 crore of sponsor equity, driven purely by debt paydown
options.why: Exit equity value is enterprise value less the debt still outstanding: 500 − 250 = ₹250 crore. Against the ₹100 crore the sponsor put in, that is a 2.5x return, and since EBITDA and the multiple never moved, debt paydown alone explains it.

options.text: 1.5x — treating the ₹150 crore of debt paid down as if it were itself the exit equity value
options.misconception: equates the amount of debt paid down with the exit equity value, instead of computing exit enterprise value less remaining debt
options.why: Debt paid down (400 − 250 = 150) measures how much less is owed, not what the equity is worth. Equity value is what is left after debt: 500 − 250 = ₹250 crore, not the ₹150 crore paydown itself.

options.text: 5.0x — treating the full ₹500 crore exit enterprise value as belonging to the sponsor, with no debt netted off
options.misconception: forgets that debt still outstanding at exit belongs to the lenders, not the sponsor, and credits the whole enterprise value to equity
options.why: ₹250 crore of debt is still owed at exit and comes off the top before anything belongs to the sponsor. 500/100 = 5.0x skips that deduction entirely.

options.text: 1.0x — measuring the return on the unchanged ₹500 crore enterprise value rather than on the sponsor's equity slice
options.misconception: measures the return on the whole, unchanged enterprise value instead of the sponsor's leveraged equity slice, which is where the paydown accrues
options.why: The enterprise value did stay flat, but the sponsor never owned the whole enterprise — only the ₹100 crore equity slice beneath ₹400 crore of debt. That slice grew to ₹250 crore precisely because the debt above it shrank.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A sponsor buys a company for ₹500 crore, funded with ₹400 crore of debt and ₹100 crore of sponsor equity. Over five years the debt is paid down to ₹250 crore from the company's own cash flow; EBITDA and the exit multiple are unchanged, so the exit enterprise value is again ₹500 crore.

items.stem: What is the portfolio's standard deviation?

options.text: 24.0 per cent, the simple weighted average of the two standard deviations
options.misconception: takes the weighted average of the two standard deviations, which is only correct at perfect positive correlation, ignoring the actual 0.2 correlation's diversification benefit
options.why: 0.6 × 20% + 0.4 × 30% = 24% is what the formula gives only when correlation is +1. At 0.2 the assets do not move together nearly that closely, and the true portfolio risk, 18.6%, sits well below the weighted average.

options.text: About 35.3 per cent, plugging the 0.2 correlation directly into the covariance term without multiplying by the two standard deviations
options.misconception: uses the correlation coefficient as if it were the covariance itself, skipping the multiplication by each asset's standard deviation
options.why: The cross term is 2 × wA × wB × ρ × σA × σB, not 2 × wA × wB × ρ alone. Leaving out the two standard deviations inflates the cross term to 0.096 and the standard deviation to ≈35.3%, far above the correctly weighted 18.6%.

options.text: About 18.6 per cent, using the full variance formula with the covariance term at correlation 0.2
About 17.0 per cent, dropping the covariance term as if the assets were uncorrelated
options.misconception: sets the cross term to zero as though correlation were 0, when the stated correlation of 0.2 still contributes a small positive covariance term
options.why: At zero correlation, variance would be just 0.0144 + 0.0144 = 0.0288, giving ≈17.0%. But 0.2 correlation is not zero — it adds a further 0.00576 to variance, lifting the true figure to 18.6%.

items.scenario: A portfolio holds 60 per cent in Asset A, with a standard deviation of 20 per cent, and 40 per cent in Asset B, with a standard deviation of 30 per cent. The correlation between the two assets is 0.2.

items.stem: Which machine should the plant buy, and on what comparison?

options.text: Machine A, because its capital outlay of ₹9 lakh is lower than Machine B's ₹12 lakh
options.misconception: decides on the purchase price alone, ignoring both the running costs and the number of years each machine serves
options.why: The ₹3 lakh saved on purchase is repaid several times over by ₹30,000 a year of extra running cost and by having to buy again after three years instead of five. Both belong in the comparison, and once they are in, B wins.

options.text: Machine B, at about ₹3.31 lakh a year against Machine A's ₹4.24 lakh, dividing each total present value of cost by the number of years
options.misconception: divides the present value by the plain count of years instead of by the annuity factor, dropping the time value that the annuity factor carries
options.why: 12,73,050 / 3 = ₹4,24,350 and 16,54,920 / 5 = ₹3,30,984 both understate the annual charge, because a rupee due in year 5 is not the same rupee as one due in year 1. Dividing by the annuity factor — 2.487 and 3.791 — is what converts a present value back into a level annual amount, giving ₹5.12 lakh and ₹4.37 lakh.

options.text: Machine B, at an equivalent annual cost of about ₹4.37 lakh against Machine A's ₹5.12 lakh
options.why: Machine A's total PV of cost is 9,00,000 + 1,50,000 × 2.487 = ₹12,73,050, and dividing by its own annuity factor gives 12,73,050 / 2.487 ≈ ₹5,11,881 a year. Machine B's is 12,00,000 + 1,20,000 × 3.791 = ₹16,54,920, and 16,54,920 / 3.791 ≈ ₹4,36,539 a year. Because the machine will be replaced indefinitely, the annual charge is the only fair comparison, and B's is about ₹75,000 lower.

options.text: Machine A, because its total present value of cost is ₹12.73 lakh against Machine B's ₹16.55 lakh
options.misconception: compares total present values of assets with unequal lives, which credits the shorter-lived machine for simply carrying fewer years of cost
options.why: Machine A's total is smaller only because it covers three years while B's covers five. Put on the same footing — cost per year of service — A is the dearer of the two at ₹5.12 lakh against ₹4.37 lakh. Totals over different spans are not comparable at all.

items.scenario: A plant needs one packing machine and will need one indefinitely. Machine A costs ₹9,00,000, lasts 3 years and runs at ₹1,50,000 a year. Machine B costs ₹12,00,000, lasts 5 years and runs at ₹1,20,000 a year. Neither has any salvage value. The cost of capital is 10 per cent; the annuity factors are 2.487 for 3 years and 3.791 for 5 years.

items.stem: What is the project's adjusted present value, and what does the firm do?

options.text: ₹6 crore, so accept — the ₹12 crore tax shield less ₹1 crore of issue costs outweighs the ₹5 crore base-case shortfall
options.why: The annual tax shield is 40 × 10% × 30% = ₹1.2 crore, and in perpetuity at the 10 per cent cost of debt that is 1.2 / 0.10 = ₹12 crore, which is the same as debt times the tax rate, 40 × 0.30. APV = −5 + 12 − 1 = +₹6 crore, so the financing side effects turn a reject into an accept.

options.text: ₹7 crore, so accept — base-case NPV of −₹5 crore plus the ₹12 crore tax shield
options.misconception: counts the tax shield but omits the issue costs, taking only the financing side effect that helps
options.why: Issue costs are a financing side effect exactly as the tax shield is, and APV requires every one of them, favourable or not. −5 + 12 − 1 = ₹6 crore, not ₹7 crore.

options.text: −₹5 crore, so reject — the base-case NPV is the project's value and financing is a separate matter
options.misconception: stops at the all-equity base case and treats financing side effects as irrelevant to the accept-or-reject decision, which is the one thing APV exists to prevent
options.why: Separating the two halves is not the same as discarding one of them. APV values the project ungeared precisely so the financing benefit can be added explicitly rather than buried in a discount rate — and here that benefit, +₹11 crore net, is what decides the case.

options.text: ₹34 crore, so accept — the debt supports ₹40 crore of interest payments in present value terms, less ₹1 crore of issue costs
options.misconception: treats the whole interest payment as the financing benefit instead of only the tax saved on it, valuing a cost as though it were a gain
