options.why: Needing the stock to rise means carrying market risk. The arbitrage earns the gap with both legs locked, indifferent to direction — that indifference is what makes it arbitrage.

options.text: Buy the stock with borrowed money and sell the futures against it
options.misconception: runs the cash-and-carry in the wrong direction
options.why: That trade profits when futures are rich. Here it locks in buying at ₹500 plus ₹15 of interest to deliver at ₹508 — a guaranteed loss of the same ₹7.

options.text: Nothing — ₹508 for a ₹500 stock already includes a fair carrying charge
options.misconception: eyeballs the premium instead of computing it
options.why: The question is never whether futures exceed spot but whether the gap equals the carry. Three months of 12 per cent on ₹500 is about ₹15; a ₹8 premium is ₹7 short.

items.scenario: A stock trades at ₹500 and pays no dividend. Money costs 12 per cent a year. The three-month futures contract on the stock trades at ₹508, while the cost-of-carry fair value works out to about ₹515.

items.stem: What does the EPS rise actually prove?

options.text: Only that T's earnings were bought at a lower multiple than A's — the market may still mark the deal down
options.why: Shares worth ₹400 crore at A's price bought ₹25 crore of earnings — a multiple of 16 against A's own 20, so the arithmetic guarantees accretion. Whether value was created depends on what T's earnings deserve; if their quality merits only a low multiple, the higher EPS can price at a lower P/E and shareholders gain nothing.

options.text: That A overpaid, since issuing 2 crore shares diluted control
options.misconception: confuses ownership dilution with earnings dilution
options.why: Existing holders do own a smaller fraction of a bigger company — that is every share-funded deal. Overpayment is measured against T's value, and a 16-times price for earnings A's own market rates at 20 is not overpayment on its face.

options.text: That the merger created value for A's shareholders
options.misconception: reads bootstrap arithmetic as wealth creation
options.why: EPS accretion follows mechanically from buying low-multiple earnings with high-multiple paper. Value creation needs synergies or underpricing — neither is shown by the ₹0.42.

options.text: Nothing — EPS should fall whenever new shares are issued
options.misconception: sees only the denominator of the fraction
options.why: The new shares arrive carrying T's ₹25 crore of earnings. Whether EPS rises or falls is the race between the two, settled by the relative multiples.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: Acquirer A earns ₹100 crore on 10 crore shares (EPS ₹10) and trades at a P/E of 20. Target T earns ₹25 crore and A buys it by issuing 2 crore new shares. The CFO announces the merger is a success because combined EPS rises to about ₹10.42.

items.stem: How does the money market hedge run, and roughly what does it lock in?

options.text: The hedge fails because rupee interest is higher than dollar interest
options.misconception: reads the rate differential as a barrier instead of the price
options.why: The differential is exactly what sets the locked rate above spot. Higher home interest is why the exporter's manufactured forward is favourable, not why the hedge breaks.

options.text: Borrow about $0.98 million now, convert at ₹84, invest in rupees — locking roughly ₹85.6 per dollar
options.why: Borrowing $1m ÷ 1.02 today means the $1 million receivable exactly repays the loan in six months. The ₹82.35 crore-odd raised at spot grows at 4 per cent for the half year, and the effective rate works out near 84 × 1.04/1.02 ≈ ₹85.6 — the same figure interest rate parity would quote as the forward.

options.text: Borrow rupees now, convert to dollars, and invest the dollars for six months
options.misconception: runs the importer's hedge on an exporter's exposure
options.why: That trade builds a dollar asset — useful when dollars must be paid later. The exporter already has dollars coming; the hedge must create the offsetting dollar liability.

options.text: Invest $1 million abroad now and convert whatever it grows to at the spot rate then
options.misconception: hedges nothing and postpones the conversion risk
options.why: The exporter has no dollars today to invest — they arrive in six months — and converting at an unknown future spot is the exposure itself, prolonged rather than removed.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: An exporter will receive $1 million in six months. Dollar interest is 4 per cent a year, rupee interest 8 per cent, spot ₹84. The exporter wants the rupee amount fixed today without using the forward market.

items.stem: What has the board misunderstood?

options.text: Nothing — a 99 per cent VaR is designed to state the maximum loss
options.misconception: reads a quantile as a bound
options.why: A quantile marks where the worst 1 per cent begins, not where losses end. Maximum loss on a leveraged book may have no finite bound at all.

options.text: The error is the horizon — one-day VaR must be annualised before boards may read it
options.misconception: converts a comprehension problem into a units problem
options.why: The horizon was stated and matched the daily question. Stretching it changes the number, not the board's mistake of treating any VaR as a worst case.

options.text: The board should double the VaR to be safe, making the true ceiling ₹1 crore
options.misconception: patches a conceptual gap with an arbitrary multiplier
options.why: Scaling a quantile still yields a quantile. What the board wants is a tail measure — expected shortfall reports the average loss on the breaching days — not a bigger copy of the same blind spot.

options.text: VaR is a threshold crossed about one day in a hundred, and is silent about how bad those days get
options.why: Ninety-nine per cent confidence means roughly two or three trading days a year should breach the number in the ordinary course. Beyond the threshold, VaR offers no ceiling — the ₹2 crore day lives precisely in the tail the measure does not describe.

items.scenario: A treasury reports a one-day 99 per cent VaR of ₹50 lakh. The board takes comfort that the worst possible loss on any day is ₹50 lakh, and that a ₹2 crore loss is therefore impossible.

items.stem: What does the stock's position actually show?

options.text: Overpricing — a correctly priced asset must plot on both lines
options.misconception: treats the two lines as one test administered twice
options.why: Only perfectly diversified holdings can sit on the CML. Demanding it of a single stock condemns every individual security in the market as overpriced at once.

options.text: The analyst mixed up the axes, since both lines chart the same risk
options.misconception: misses that the lines are drawn against different risk measures
options.why: The CML's horizontal axis is standard deviation; the SML's is beta. The stock's two positions differ precisely because its total risk exceeds its systematic risk.

options.text: A buying opportunity — below a line means cheap
options.misconception: applies the SML's alpha reading to the CML
options.why: Above or below has that meaning on the SML, where the line is the fair price of beta. Distance below the CML measures inefficiency of diversification, not a bargain.

options.text: Normal pricing — single stocks carry diversifiable risk, so they sit on the SML and below the CML
options.why: The SML is the pricing line for all assets: on it means fairly priced for beta. The CML is reserved for efficient portfolios, whose only risk is market risk. A lone stock's extra, diversifiable volatility pushes it rightward off the CML without any mispricing — both lines are saying exactly what they should.

items.scenario: An analyst finds that a single pharmaceutical stock, correctly priced by CAPM, plots exactly on the security market line but well below the capital market line. He concludes the stock must be overpriced, since it fails one of the two lines.

items.stem: Who is misusing the theorem?

options.text: Neither — they are debating taste, on which finance is silent
options.misconception: files a structured disagreement under preference
options.why: Both positions make testable claims about wealth effects. The frictions that separate them — taxes, signalling, clienteles — are the syllabus of dividend policy, not matters of taste.

options.text: Only the director — market reactions are noise around a proven identity
options.misconception: defends the proof by dismissing the evidence
options.why: The reaction is real and repeatable; it documents signalling. A theorem holding under assumptions is not a description of markets that breach them.

options.text: Only the CFO — MM was refuted the day dividends started moving prices
options.misconception: reads a conditional proof as an empirical claim
options.why: MM never predicted real prices would ignore dividends; it proved they would under stated conditions. The interesting question is which condition fails, and here it is symmetric information.

options.text: Both — MM's irrelevance assumes perfect markets, and the price fall shows a signalling friction, not a refuted proof
options.why: The CFO transplants a frictionless-market result into a world of taxes and information gaps — in that world a cut can carry a message. The director errs the mirror way: the 4 per cent fall is investors reading the cut as bad news about earnings, which is a violated assumption, not a disproof. The theorem's value is telling you exactly where to look — at the frictions.

items.scenario: A CFO cites MM to the board: "dividend policy is irrelevant, so scrapping our dividend to fund the new plant changes nothing for shareholders." A director counters that the share price fell 4 per cent the last time a dividend was cut, so MM must simply be wrong.

items.stem: What changes hands, and what does the debt now cost?

options.text: Net differences only, but the cost floats at MIBOR + 2 as before, plus 7 fixed
options.misconception: adds the legs without netting the received one
options.why: The received MIBOR leg exists precisely to cancel the loan's MIBOR. Adding all three without the cancellation double-counts the floating rate.

options.text: Nothing until maturity, when one lump sum settles the whole swap
options.misconception: confuses a running swap with a single forward settlement
options.why: A vanilla swap is a strip of periodic settlements aligned to the loan's interest dates. Deferring everything to maturity would leave the interim cash flows unhedged.

options.text: Only periodic net interest differences; the all-in cost is fixed at 9 per cent
options.why: Notional principal is a measuring rod, never a payment. Each period the company pays 7 fixed, receives MIBOR, and pays MIBOR + 2 on the loan — the MIBOR legs cancel, leaving 7 + 2 = 9 per cent whatever rates do. That cancellation is the synthetic fixing.

options.text: The ₹100 crore principals are exchanged at the start and returned at the end
options.misconception: imports currency-swap mechanics into an interest rate swap
options.why: Exchanging identical rupee principals would be handing money to yourself through a counterparty. Same-currency swaps settle interest differences only.

items.scenario: A company has ₹100 crore of floating-rate debt at MIBOR + 2 per cent and fears rates will rise. It enters a swap on ₹100 crore notional: pay 7 per cent fixed, receive MIBOR. The treasurer's junior worries the company must now find ₹100 crore to hand over, and cannot say what the debt effectively costs.

items.stem: Which circle makes the riskless profit, and roughly how much?

options.text: Rupees to euros at ₹90, euros to dollars at 1.10, dollars to rupees at 84 — about ₹2.2 lakh on ₹84 lakh
options.why: The euro is cheap in the cross market, so buy it there: ₹84,00,000 ÷ 90 ≈ €93,333, which becomes about $102,667, which becomes about ₹86.24 lakh — a gain near ₹2.24 lakh with no open position at any moment. Buy where the quote is below the implied rate, and the circle does the rest.

options.text: No profit exists — ₹90 against ₹92.40 is within normal quoting variation
options.misconception: waves away a 2.6 per cent gap as noise
options.why: Transaction costs in liquid currency markets are hundredths of a per cent. A gap this size funds the round trip many times over, which is exactly why real quotes are never left this far apart.

options.text: Hold euros and wait for the quoted rate to rise to ₹92.40
options.misconception: converts an arbitrage into a directional bet
options.why: Waiting bears currency risk the arbitrage does not. The three simultaneous legs collect the discrepancy whatever rates do next — that simultaneity is the whole trick.

options.text: Rupees to dollars, dollars to euros, euros to rupees at ₹90 — the same profit the other way
options.misconception: assumes any direction around a mispriced triangle pays
options.why: Run that way, ₹84 lakh becomes $1,00,000, then about €90,909, then ₹81.8 lakh — a loss of the same order. The mispricing has one profitable direction; the reverse circle pays the market instead.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: Quotes: one dollar buys ₹84; one euro buys $1.10; one euro is quoted at ₹90 in the cross market. A dealer holds ₹84 lakh and spots that the implied euro-rupee rate is 84 × 1.10 = ₹92.40, above the quoted ₹90.

items.stem: What two errors sit in this valuation?

options.text: Nothing — a higher discount rate is conservative, and conservative valuations protect users
options.misconception: confuses bias with prudence
options.why: A valuation is useful when unbiased; deliberate understatement misleads a seller as surely as overstatement misleads a buyer. Conservatism is not a licence to mismatch flows and rates.

options.text: Only the discount rate — FCFF valuations do produce equity value directly
options.misconception: forgets whose cash the firm-level flow is
options.why: FCFF includes the cash that services debt. Handing its full present value to shareholders values the lenders' claim at zero — the bondholders would object.

options.text: Only the missing debt deduction — any defensible discount rate is acceptable
options.misconception: treats rate selection as taste rather than matching
options.why: The rate must price the risk of the specific flow being discounted. WACC and cost of equity differ by five points here; the mismatch alone misstates value materially.

options.text: FCFF discounted at the equity rate, and enterprise value passed off as equity value without deducting net debt
options.why: FCFF pairs with WACC because the flow belongs to debt and equity together; discounting it at 16 per cent punishes lenders' cash flows with shareholders' risk premium and calls the resulting understatement caution. And whatever the rate, an FCFF valuation yields enterprise value — the shares are worth that less net debt, a subtraction the analyst skipped.

items.scenario: An analyst projects a company's free cash flow to the firm, discounts it at the cost of equity of 16 per cent "to be conservative" (WACC is 11 per cent), and presents the result as the value of the company's shares without further adjustment.

items.stem: What does the constant risk-adjusted rate do to the year-eight flow?

options.text: It understates risk, since 18 per cent is too low for an eight-year horizon
options.misconception: doubles down on the compounding in the wrong direction
options.why: The complaint runs the other way: the year-eight flow is over-penalised. Raising the rate further would widen the very distortion at issue.

options.text: It compounds an eleven-point risk premium for eight years, punishing a flow whose risk did not grow with time
options.why: A constant premium in the discount rate charges for risk exponentially with distance, so the year-eight flow is treated as vastly riskier than year one's despite bearing the identical uncertainty. Certainty equivalents — ₹9 crore in each year, discounted at 7 per cent — price the risk once, where it actually lives.

options.text: Nothing wrong — later cash flows are always riskier, and compounding reflects that
options.misconception: assumes risk always accumulates with time
options.why: Often true, not here: the scenario's risk resolves at year one. When risk's time profile is flat or front-loaded, the compounding premium misprices by construction.

options.text: The two methods always agree, so nothing turns on the choice
options.misconception: assumes equivalence that holds only under a specific risk pattern
options.why: They coincide only when certainty equivalent factors decay geometrically to match the compounding premium. Any other risk profile — like this one-time risk — splits their answers.

items.scenario: A project's ₹10 crore expected inflow in year one is judged worth ₹9 crore for certain; the identical ₹10 crore expected in year eight is also judged worth ₹9 crore for certain — the risk in both years is the same one-time regulatory approval, already resolved by year one. An analyst instead applies a constant 18 per cent risk-adjusted rate (risk-free is 7 per cent) to both flows.

items.stem: What went wrong in the analyst's valuation?

options.text: Dollar flows met a rupee rate — the five-point currency differential was charged without ever crediting the expected dollar appreciation
options.why: The 14 per cent rupee rate embeds rupee inflation and depreciation expectations; the dollar flows do not. Consistency demands either dollar flows at 9 per cent with spot conversion of the NPV, or flows converted at forward rates — which build in the rupee's expected slide — discounted at 14. The analyst charged the premium and denied the compensation, manufacturing the negative NPV.

options.text: Both approaches are flawed — currency risk should instead be handled by adding 2-3 points to any rate
options.misconception: replaces consistency with an arbitrary loading
options.why: An ad hoc premium double-counts risk the forward rates already price, and its size is folklore. The framework needs no patch — only matching.

options.text: Nothing — Indian shareholders make the rupee rate the only defensible one
options.misconception: right investor, wrong pairing
options.why: The home rate is fine — against home currency flows. Shareholder nationality decides the reporting currency, not the licence to mismatch flows and rates.

options.text: The error is treasury's — foreign projects must always use the foreign rate
options.misconception: crowns the other route as the only one
options.why: Both routes are valid and, with parity-consistent forwards, agree to the rupee. The only sin is crossing them.

items.scenario: An Indian company appraises a US project with dollar cash flows. Rupee discount rate: 14 per cent. Dollar discount rate: 9 per cent. An analyst discounts the dollar flows at 14 per cent "because our shareholders are Indian", converts the result at spot, and reports a barely negative NPV where the treasury's model showed a healthy positive one.

items.stem: How does the immunised portfolio behave, and is "no further trades" sound?

options.text: Nothing can move — an immunised portfolio's value is fixed against any rate change
options.misconception: reads immunisation as freezing market value
options.why: Value swings immediately with rates; what is protected is the terminal amount at the horizon, where price and reinvestment effects meet. Interim statements will show the turbulence.

options.text: The portfolio loses outright — duration six with maturity nine means rate risk was never hedged
options.misconception: hedges by maturity instead of duration
options.why: Duration, not maturity, measures rate sensitivity. Maturity nine with duration six is exactly how coupon bonds achieve the match; the offset works at the horizon regardless.

options.text: The jump's price loss is offset by higher reinvestment income by year six — but the match drifts, so rebalancing remains necessary
options.why: At duration six, a rate rise costs market value and simultaneously raises the return on every reinvested coupon; the horizon is the point where the two cancel. The protection is not permanent: as time passes, the portfolio's duration falls more slowly than the horizon shortens, and each rate move shifts durations again — set-and- forget lets the mismatch reopen.

options.text: The strategy is sound and permanent — duration matching is a one-time construction
options.misconception: grants the trustee's question no force
options.why: Duration drift is arithmetic, not misfortune: a six-duration portfolio a year later is not a five-duration portfolio. Without rebalancing the fund gradually returns to the exposure it paid to remove.

items.scenario: A pension fund must pay ₹500 crore in exactly six years. Its manager buys bonds maturing in six years is one option; instead he buys a portfolio with duration six but average maturity nine, and declares the liability immunised for good, planning no further trades. A trustee asks what happens if rates jump 2 per cent next month.

items.stem: Which position actually protects against the crash, and what does the friend's trade really do?

options.text: Neither helps — only selling the stock removes the risk
options.misconception: sees exits where hedges exist
options.why: Selling removes upside along with downside. The protective put is precisely the instrument for keeping the position while renting away the crash — for a stated, visible price.

options.text: Both are equivalent since both combine stock with one option
options.misconception: counts legs instead of reading payoffs
options.why: One position's payoff flattens on the downside, the other flattens on the upside. Put-call parity links their prices, not their protections — the equivalent of a protective put is not a covered call but a bought call plus lending.

options.text: The friend is right — premium received is protection received
options.misconception: prices comfort as coverage
options.why: The premium is compensation for taking on an obligation, not a shield. In the feared scenario — a deep fall — the sold call pays once and the stock keeps falling.

options.text: The put floors the loss near ₹480 minus ₹18; the sold call only cushions a fall by its premium and caps the recovery
options.why: With the put, a crash to ₹350 still lets the investor sell at ₹480 — worst case about ₹462 net, upside intact above that. The covered call collects perhaps ₹15 and then rides the crash all the way down, softer by only that premium — while a rebound past ₹520 belongs to the call buyer. Income and insurance are different products.

items.scenario: An investor holds shares at ₹500 and fears a crash over the next quarter but wants to keep the position. A friend advises: "sell the ₹520 call — the premium is free money and it protects you." The investor instead considers buying the ₹480 put for ₹18.

items.stem: What has the junior analyst misunderstood?

options.text: Nothing — the swap should indeed re-exchange at the year-five spot rate
options.misconception: builds the risk back into the hedge
options.why: A spot-rate re-exchange makes the final flows unknowable — a position, not a hedge. The certainty of the locked rate is what each treasurer is buying.

options.text: The fixed re-exchange rate is the hedge itself — each party's currency exposure is eliminated precisely because year five's market rate will not apply
options.why: If maturity re-exchange happened at the future spot rate, both parties would carry five years of currency risk — the exact thing they swapped to remove. Locking the original rate means the Indian firm knows its rupee outflow today; the interest differential across the two legs prices the expected currency movement, the way forward premiums do.

options.text: The parties should each have borrowed directly in the foreign currency instead
options.misconception: ignores the comparative advantage the structure exploits
options.why: Each firm borrows cheaper at home than abroad; the swap converts the cheap home borrowing into the foreign exposure needed. Borrowing directly abroad pays the foreigner's premium and forgoes the gain the swap splits.

options.text: The principals should never move — swaps exchange only interest differences
options.misconception: carries the interest rate swap's same-currency logic across currencies
options.why: In one currency, exchanging identical principals is pointless. Across currencies the principals are the point — each party needs the other's currency in hand.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: An Indian company needs dollars for five years; a US company needs rupees. The Indian firm borrows rupees at 8 per cent (its home advantage) and the US firm borrows dollars at 5 per cent, and they swap: principals exchanged today at ₹84, interest streams serviced across, principals re-exchanged at maturity at the same ₹84. A junior analyst objects that re-exchanging at today's rate in year five ignores where the currency will actually be.

items.stem: What does the APT reading say about the 2 per cent?

options.text: The colleague found an arbitrage — short the low returner, buy the high one
options.misconception: calls a risk premium an arbitrage
options.why: Arbitrage needs identical exposures with different returns. These portfolios differ in interest rate exposure, so the long-short position is a bet on rates, paid for bearing that risk.

options.text: APT and CAPM cannot disagree, since both price only systematic risk
options.misconception: assumes one systematic risk instead of several
options.why: They agree that diversifiable risk earns nothing; they part on how many systematic dimensions exist. Two portfolios can match on the market dimension and differ on the others — this pair does.

options.text: The analyst is right — equal betas earning unequal returns proves inefficiency
options.misconception: treats CAPM residuals as market failures
options.why: A model's unexplained return is evidence about the model before it is evidence about the market. Multi-factor pricing absorbs exactly this pattern.

options.text: It is compensation for a priced factor CAPM's single beta cannot see — reward for risk, not free money or inefficiency
options.why: Identical market betas conceal different factor loadings; the extra 2 per cent pays the holder for bearing interest rate risk the other portfolio avoids. Under APT the returns are consistent with equilibrium once all priced exposures are counted — the anomaly was in the one-factor lens, not the market.

items.scenario: Two portfolios have the same CAPM beta of 1.2, yet one persistently returns 2 per cent more. An analyst concludes CAPM is broken and markets are inefficient. An APT-minded colleague measures the portfolios against inflation and interest rate factors and finds the higher-returning one carries much larger exposure to interest rate risk.

items.stem: What is wrong with the 15 per cent discount rate here?

options.text: Lease-vs-buy flows are debt-like and near-certain, so they discount at the 6 per cent after-tax cost of debt — 15 per cent distorts the comparison
options.why: Rentals, tax shields and depreciation shields are contractual or highly predictable — the risk of debt service, not of the project. Discounting them at 15 per cent shrinks the distant costs of leasing far more than the near ones of buying, flattering the lease by rate choice alone. WACC prices the machine's business risk in the separate investment decision, already made.

options.text: Nothing — one corporate hurdle rate keeps all decisions comparable
options.misconception: uses one rate for two different risks
options.why: Comparability comes from matching each flow to its risk. A single rate misprices every flow whose risk differs from the average — and financing flows differ by design.

options.text: The rate should be even higher, since leases carry default consequences
options.misconception: adds a premium to flows whose burden is fixed
options.why: Default risk belongs to the lessor pricing the rentals, and it is already in them. The lessee's evaluation discounts committed outflows, which are as certain as its debt service.

options.text: The pre-tax cost of debt of about 8.5 per cent is the correct rate
options.misconception: right family of rate, missing the tax adjustment
options.why: The cash flows are computed after tax, so the rate must be too. Mixing after-tax flows with a pre-tax rate misstates every present value by the tax wedge.

items.scenario: A company evaluating whether to lease or buy a machine discounts the lease-versus-buy cash flows at its 15 per cent weighted average cost of capital, reasoning that all company decisions should clear the same hurdle. Its after-tax cost of debt is 6 per cent. The analysis makes the lease look far cheaper than buying.

items.stem: What actually supports the senior tranche's higher rating?

options.text: Nothing — paper can never be rated above the company that created the assets
options.misconception: chains the securities to the originator the structure exists to break
options.why: Severing that chain is the whole engineering: bankruptcy-remoteness plus subordination make the senior slice safer than the whole. Rating the parts differently from the whole is the design working.

options.text: The rating agencies' guarantee — a AAA is a promise of payment
options.misconception: mistakes an opinion for insurance
options.why: Ratings are opinions on default probability, not undertakings. The support under the senior notes is cash-flow subordination and enhancement, not the agency's balance sheet.

options.text: The NBFC's obligation to top up any shortfall in the pool
options.misconception: reads recourse into a true sale
options.why: A general top-up obligation would defeat the true sale and drag the assets back on balance sheet. Enhancement is sized and capped precisely so the transfer stays a sale.

options.text: The structure — losses hit the equity and mezzanine first, and the senior notes look to the ring-fenced pool, not to the NBFC's credit
options.why: The SPV's true-sale purchase puts the receivables beyond the NBFC's creditors, so senior investors face the pool's behaviour, not the originator's rating. ₹75 crore of subordination means collections can fall 15 per cent before the senior notes lose a rupee. The 2008 lesson is real but different: the structure fails when pool quality was misjudged or correlations understated — not because tranching itself is a trick.

items.scenario: An NBFC rated BBB securitises ₹500 crore of loan receivables through an SPV that issues ₹425 crore of senior notes rated AAA, ₹50 crore of mezzanine paper, and retains a ₹25 crore equity tranche with the NBFC. An investor asks how paper backed by a BBB company's loans can be AAA, and suspects the rating agencies of the same blindness as 2008.

items.stem: What has the founder's celebration missed?

options.text: He now holds 75 per cent, and in any modest exit the fund's ₹20 crore comes off the top first — his ₹60 crore is a paper number, not a floor
options.why: Post-money arithmetic gives the fund 20/80 = 25 per cent. The liquidation preference is the substance the founder called paperwork: if the company sells for ₹30 crore, the fund takes its ₹20 crore first and the founder shares what remains — nothing like 75 per cent of the price. The headline valuation prices the best case; the preference stack owns the downside.

options.text: The founder should have taken the same money as a bank loan to avoid dilution
options.misconception: prices only the equity given, not the risk transferred
options.why: A pre-revenue startup rarely gets bank debt, and debt's covenants and personal guarantees would put the founder's downside where the fund's preference now sits. Dilution is the fee for risk capital.

options.text: The valuation is fake since no cash changed hands at ₹80 crore
options.misconception: dismisses round pricing altogether
options.why: ₹20 crore of real cash bought exactly 25 per cent — the valuation is as real as the round. What it is not is a guarantee that applies to every exit price.

options.text: Nothing — 75 per cent of ₹80 crore is ₹60 crore in every scenario
options.misconception: multiplies ownership by headline value across all outcomes
options.why: The percentage divides the upside; the preference reorders the downside. Founder wealth in venture deals is scenario-dependent by construction.

items.scenario: A founder owns 100 per cent of a startup. A venture fund invests ₹20 crore at a pre-money valuation of ₹60 crore, taking convertible preference shares with a 1x liquidation preference. The founder celebrates that at the implied ₹80 crore post-money value his stake is worth ₹60 crore, and treats the preference structure as paperwork.

items.stem: Which exposure did the CFO miss, and why did no hedge exist for it?

options.text: Transaction exposure hidden in the timber purchases
options.misconception: hunts for an invoice where the risk needs none
options.why: The timber is bought in rupees from Indian suppliers. The company's exposure arrived through its customers' alternatives, not through its own payables.

options.text: Translation exposure from the competitor's accounts
options.misconception: assigns a consolidation effect to a company with nothing to consolidate
options.why: Translation exposure is the parent's arithmetic over foreign subsidiaries. The furniture maker consolidates nothing foreign; its wound is in sales, not restatement.

options.text: Economic exposure — competitiveness moved with the rupee though no transaction did, and its remedy is operational, not a forward contract
options.why: With no foreign invoices there was no transaction exposure, and no subsidiaries meant no translation exposure — the CFO's checklist was clean and incomplete. The strengthening rupee cheapened the competing import, which is economic exposure acting through market position. Forwards need a notional and a date; a competitiveness drift has neither, so the defences are operational — sourcing, product differentiation, cost structure.

options.text: None — the lost sales are competition risk, unrelated to currency
options.misconception: separates the competitor from what priced the competitor
options.why: The import's new price advantage is the exchange rate wearing a competitor's face. Calling it mere competition hides the driver and forestalls the operational response.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: A purely domestic furniture maker sells only in India, buys only Indian timber, and holds no foreign currency. Its CFO declares the company free of currency risk. That year the rupee strengthens sharply, and imported Malaysian furniture undercuts the company's prices in every showroom, taking a third of its sales.

items.stem: What does the pair of statistics say about the investor's choice?

options.text: Neither — tracking error means index funds fail and active funds are safer
options.misconception: reads a fidelity statistic as an indictment of indexing
options.why: A 0.3 per cent tracking error is high fidelity, and active funds carry both higher fees and deliberate, larger deviations. The statistic argues for the tighter fund, not for abandoning the category.

options.text: Fund B — demonstrated outperformance is worth the higher fee
options.misconception: reads noise as skill in a product that promises neither
options.why: A fund holding the index outperforms it only by not holding it faithfully — cash drag, sampling, timing. Chance governs the sign of that gap; the fee governs its centre, and B's centre is lower.

options.text: The funds are equivalent since both track the same index
options.misconception: treats the benchmark as the product
options.why: The benchmark is the target; costs and fidelity are the product. On both measures the funds differ by multiples.

options.text: Fund A is the better index fund — B's outperformance is the same looseness that will underperform next time, bought at five times the fee
options.why: An index fund's job is delivering the index, and tracking error measures how loosely it does that in either direction: the 1.8 per cent that produced last year's lucky beat is equally capable of a matching miss. Meanwhile the 1.1 per cent ratio is a certain, permanent drag. Paying more for less fidelity is the reverse of the passive proposition.

items.scenario: Two index funds track the same index. Fund A: expense ratio 0.2 per cent, tracking error 0.3 per cent. Fund B: expense ratio 1.1 per cent, tracking error 1.8 per cent — but last year Fund B beat the index by 2 per cent through cash-timing luck, and an investor prefers it for that reason.

items.stem: What actually happens to the margin account over the three days?

options.text: Losses accumulate as book entries, with cash needed only if the position is closed at a loss
options.misconception: treats variation margin as notional
options.why: Variation margin is cash, moved daily. A trader who cannot fund a losing day is closed out on day two of a position meant for months.

options.text: The exchange absorbs daily swings; margin exists only for default at expiry
options.misconception: inverts who bears the daily move
options.why: The margin system exists so the exchange absorbs nothing: each trader funds his own losses nightly, keeping the clearing house whole at all times.

options.text: Day one debits ₹15,000; day two's further ₹25,000 drops the account below maintenance, calling ₹40,000 back to the initial level; day three credits ₹20,000
options.why: Marking to market settles each day's move in cash: 300 points × 50 = ₹15,000 out on day one, leaving ₹1,35,000, still above maintenance. Day two's 500-point fall takes ₹25,000 more, and at ₹1,10,000 the account is under the ₹1,12,500 maintenance line — the call restores the full initial ₹1,50,000, not merely the shortfall. Day three's 400-point rally credits ₹20,000. Expiry settles nothing the evenings have not already settled.

options.text: Nothing until expiry — profits and losses crystallise only on closing out
options.misconception: applies forward-contract settlement to futures
options.why: Deferred settlement is the forward's design and its counterparty risk. The futures clearing house collects every day's loss that evening, which is why defaults are rare and margin calls common.

items.scenario: A trader buys one index futures contract at 24,000 (lot 50), posting initial margin of ₹1,50,000 with maintenance margin at ₹1,12,500. Over three days the index settles at 23,700, 23,200 and 23,600. The trader believes nothing is payable until expiry, since no position was closed.

items.stem: What does the zero-cost collar commit the borrower to?

options.text: The borrower now profits when rates fall below 6 per cent, holding both options
options.misconception: forgets which side of the floor the borrower sits
options.why: The floor was sold, not bought. Below 6 per cent the borrower is the payer — that obligation is exactly what funded the cap.

options.text: An obligation to convert the loan to 7.5 per cent fixed if either strike is hit
options.misconception: mistakes a collar for a knock-in swap
options.why: Nothing converts. The loan stays floating, and the two options simply pay or collect at their strikes, fencing the effective rate into the band.

options.text: Nothing — the premiums cancel, so the protection is genuinely free
options.misconception: prices the collar at its premium instead of its payoff
options.why: Premium-neutral means the market values what was bought and sold equally. The floor obligation is real money in low-rate years; free at inception is not free in outcome.

options.text: A rate confined between 6 and 9 per cent — above 9 the cap pays, below 6 the borrower pays the floor buyer, surrendering the benefit of cheap money
options.why: The sold floor is the price: whenever MIBOR fixes below 6 per cent, the borrower compensates the floor's buyer, so its effective cost never falls below 6. In exchange the bought cap tops the cost at 9. Zero premium is not zero cost — the collar trades away the low-rate upside the borrower might otherwise have enjoyed.

items.scenario: A borrower paying MIBOR on ₹200 crore fears rising rates but finds the 9 per cent cap's premium too dear. A banker proposes: buy the 9 per cent cap and simultaneously sell a 6 per cent floor whose premium fully funds the cap. The borrower asks what, exactly, has been given up for the free protection.

items.stem: What does EVA say about the record year and the proposed bonus?

options.text: EVA and NOPAT must agree, so the computation is mistaken
options.misconception: expects a capital charge to leave rankings unchanged
options.why: Diverging is EVA's purpose: it disagrees with profit precisely when growth is bought below the cost of capital, which is when the disagreement matters.

options.text: EVA fell from ₹24 crore to nil — the new capital earned less than it cost, and a NOPAT bonus pays managers to keep doing that
options.why: Last year: 120 − 12% × 800 = ₹24 crore of value created. This year: 150 − 12% × 1,250 = 0. The extra ₹450 crore of capital generated ₹30 crore of profit — a 6.7 per cent return against a 12 per cent cost. NOPAT growth rewarded alone invites exactly this: buying profit with underpriced capital. An EVA-linked bonus charges managers for the capital they demand.

options.text: The division destroyed ₹150 crore of value, since EVA is nil
options.misconception: reads zero EVA as total loss
options.why: Zero EVA means the capital earned exactly its cost — shareholders got a fair return and nothing more. Disappointing after last year, but far from losing the profit itself.

options.text: The record stands — ₹150 crore is more profit than ₹120 crore by any measure
options.misconception: reads profit without its capital charge
options.why: By the measure that prices capital, the division went from creating ₹24 crore to creating nothing. Shareholders supplied ₹450 crore for that journey.

items.scenario: A division reports NOPAT rising from ₹120 crore to ₹150 crore and claims a record year. Its capital employed grew from ₹800 crore to ₹1,250 crore over the same period; the group's WACC is 12 per cent. The CEO proposes a bonus scheme rewarding NOPAT growth.

items.stem: What is wrong with this sequence?

options.text: The plan is the formality here; only the overall strategy is a substantive audit document
options.misconception: reverses which document sets direction and which converts it into procedures
options.why: The plan is the substantive working document that translates the strategy into the specific procedures the team performs; SA 300 requires both, and dismissing the plan drops the actual programme of work.

options.text: The order does not matter, since both documents serve the same audit and can be prepared in either sequence
options.misconception: treats the strategy as filler paperwork rather than the input the plan is drawn from
options.why: The plan's content — nature, timing and extent of risk assessment and further procedures — only makes sense once the strategy's scope and resourcing decisions exist; reversing the order plans for a strategy not yet chosen.

options.text: The strategy sets scope, timing and direction and guides the plan's development, so it comes first — and even once set, discoveries made while planning can send the auditor back to revise it
options.why: SA 300 has the strategy establish scope, timing and direction and guide development of the plan; the two stay interrelated afterward, since changes identified while developing the detailed plan may in turn lead to changes in the strategy already decided.

options.text: Neither document is required once the engagement partner already knows the client well from prior years
options.misconception: substitutes familiarity for the documented planning SA 300 requires every year
options.why: SA 300 requires the strategy and the plan to be established and documented for every audit; a recurring engagement changes how much new work each takes, not whether either is required.

citation.ref: Overall audit strategy and the audit plan

items.scenario: A first-year audit senior drafts the detailed audit plan before the engagement partner has settled the overall audit strategy, reasoning the plan is the "real" working document that the team actually follows, while the strategy is a formality that can be signed off afterward to complete the file.

items.stem: Is this sentence appropriate in the auditor's report?

options.text: Yes — disclosing the reliance is transparent and protects the user auditor if the service organisation's controls later fail
options.misconception: treats disclosure of reliance as a shield that dilutes the auditor's own responsibility
options.why: Transparency about methodology is not the concern SA 402 addresses; the standard removes the option because the sentence, however honestly meant, reads as passing part of the opinion's weight to someone else.

options.text: No — the report should not refer to the service auditor's report at all unless law or regulation requires it, and reliance never divides the user auditor's own responsibility for the opinion
options.why: SA 402 bars the reference precisely because a reader could take it as splitting responsibility between the two auditors; the user auditor's opinion covers the whole of the financial statements, service organisation transactions included, and remains the user auditor's own.

options.text: Yes, provided the service auditor consents in writing to being named in the report
options.misconception: invents a consent route around a bar the standard states without a consent exception
options.why: The standard's only exception is a reference required by law or regulation, not the named party's consent; consent does nothing to remove the risk of readers dividing responsibility.

options.text: No, and the auditor's report should instead qualify the opinion for the outsourced payroll function
options.misconception: escalates a drafting bar into an opinion modification with no evidential basis for one
options.why: Nothing in the facts shows insufficient evidence or a misstatement; the fix is removing the reference sentence, not modifying an opinion the type 2 report otherwise supports.

citation.ref: Reference to a service auditor in the auditor's report

items.scenario: A company's payroll processing is outsourced to a service organisation. The audit team obtains and relies on a type 2 report on the service organisation's controls, and drafts the auditor's report on the user entity adding a sentence: "We have relied on the report of [Service Auditor], and the balances processed through the payroll service are covered by that firm's opinion, not ours."

items.stem: Is the team's threshold for accumulating misstatements correct?

options.text: No — every misstatement found, however small, must be corrected in the financial statements
options.misconception: confuses accumulation with mandatory correction
options.why: SA 450 requires accumulating and evaluating misstatements, then communicating them; correcting immaterial items is invited, not compelled — the aggregate assessment is what actually bears on the opinion.

options.text: Yes — performance materiality already builds in a safety margin below overall materiality, so items under it are safe to drop
options.misconception: collapses the clearly trivial threshold into performance materiality
options.why: Performance materiality is set to reduce the risk that aggregate uncorrected misstatements exceed materiality; it is not the line for what gets logged during fieldwork. SA 450 needs a much finer sieve than that.

options.text: No — SA 450 sets the accumulation threshold at clearly trivial, not at performance materiality, and clearly trivial is a much smaller figure; unrecorded small misstatements can add up past materiality in aggregate
options.why: SA 450 requires accumulation of all misstatements other than clearly trivial ones, and clearly trivial means inconsequential in amount and nature, individually and in aggregate — a threshold well below performance materiality, not synonymous with it. Dropping everything under performance materiality risks an unnoticed aggregate that crosses it.

options.text: Yes, provided the sum of the dropped items stays under materiality by the year end
options.misconception: turns a per-item screen applied as work proceeds into a running-total check instead
options.why: Items are screened against clearly trivial as they are found, not reconciled against a year-end total; logging them individually is exactly what lets the aggregate be evaluated at the end.

items.scenario: Performance materiality for an audit is set at ₹20 lakh. During fieldwork the team notes several individually small misstatements — ₹4,000, ₹9,000 and ₹15,000 — and does not record any of them in the summary of misstatements, reasoning that anything comfortably below performance materiality need not be tracked.

items.stem: What has the senior skipped in evaluating this evidence?

options.text: The senior should independently re-perform the valuation using the auditor's own model
options.misconception: replaces evaluation of the expert's work with re-performance of it
options.why: SA 500 asks the auditor to evaluate the expert's work as evidence, not to become the valuer; re-performance is one possible response to an inadequate evaluation, not the baseline requirement.

options.text: Evaluating the appropriateness of the expert's work itself — the source data, methods and assumptions used — not only the expert's credentials
options.why: SA 500's evaluation of a management's expert covers competence and objectivity, an understanding of the expert's field, and the appropriateness of the work as evidence, including its underlying data and assumptions. A membership certificate answers only the first limb; the valuation's inputs and logic remain untested.

options.text: The senior should reject the valuation and insist on cost, since fair value estimates by outside experts are inherently unreliable
options.misconception: dismisses an entire category of evidence instead of evaluating it
options.why: Expert-based estimates are routine audit evidence when properly evaluated; blanket rejection has no basis in SA 500 and ignores the accounting framework's own requirement to test for impairment.

options.text: Nothing — a qualified expert's certificate is itself sufficient appropriate evidence for an impairment provision
options.misconception: substitutes a credential check for the full evaluation SA 500 requires
options.why: Competence is necessary but not sufficient; even a well-qualified expert can be given wrong asset data or apply assumptions the auditor has not evaluated for reasonableness.

citation.ref: Using the work of a management's expert

items.scenario: A company recognises an impairment provision on plant based on a valuation report from an external valuer engaged by management. The audit senior takes the valuer's professional membership certificate as sufficient and moves on, without reviewing the valuation's assumptions or the asset data supplied to the valuer.

items.stem: What does SA 540 (Revised) say about this approach?

options.text: The approach is wrong, but only because the warranty provision needed more work, not the credit loss model
options.misconception: scales the response in the wrong direction
options.why: Estimation uncertainty and complexity run higher for the model built on scenarios and overlays; that is the estimate needing the deeper procedures, not the formula-driven provision.

options.text: The approach is wrong because expected credit loss models fall outside SA 540's scope entirely
options.misconception: exempts a textbook accounting estimate from the standard that governs it
options.why: An expected credit loss allowance is a measurement subject to estimation uncertainty — precisely SA 540's subject matter, and one of the standard's own examples of a high-uncertainty estimate.

options.text: The approach is correct — SA 540 (Revised) defines a single set of procedures applicable to every accounting estimate without differentiation
options.misconception: flattens the spectrum concept the revised standard was built around
options.why: The revision's central idea is scaling the response to risk; a uniform programme for every estimate is exactly the practice the revised standard replaced.

options.text: Estimates sit on a spectrum of inherent risk, and audit effort scales with where an estimate falls on it — the warranty formula and the credit loss model do not warrant the same rigour
options.why: The revised standard organises estimates by their estimation uncertainty, complexity, subjectivity and susceptibility to bias; a model built on scenarios and management overlays sits far higher on that spectrum than a fixed-percentage formula, and the standard expects deeper testing of methods, data, assumptions and bias indicators as complexity rises.

items.scenario: An audit manager applies the identical testing programme to a straightforward warranty provision computed as a fixed percentage of sales and to a complex expected credit loss model built on macroeconomic scenarios and management overlays, reasoning that both are "accounting estimates" and SA 540 treats them as one category.

items.stem: What must clause 3(i) actually report here?

options.text: Only the title deed issue — a revaluation is a management estimate outside CARO's scope
options.misconception: excludes revaluation from a clause that names it expressly
options.why: Clause 3(i)(d) is written for exactly this fact — a revaluation during the year and whether it rests on a registered valuer. It sits inside the clause by its own terms, not beside it.

options.text: Neither — both are commercial matters the accounts already reflect correctly
options.misconception: treats CARO's rule-based disclosures as satisfied once the accounting outcome looks fine
options.why: Clause 3(i) asks specific questions independent of whether the resulting numbers are otherwise acceptable; both facts trigger their own sub-clause regardless of the balance sheet's overall health.

options.text: Only the revaluation — title deeds registered in a promoter's name are a legal matter for the company secretary, not for CARO
options.misconception: assigns a named CARO reporting duty to a different function
options.why: Clause 3(i)(c) is the auditor's own reporting duty on title deeds; that the underlying issue is also a legal one does not remove it from the CARO report.

options.text: Both facts — the title deed not held in the company's own name, with the required particulars, and the revaluation, flagged because it rests on an internal certificate rather than a registered valuer's valuation
options.why: Clause 3(i)(c) requires disclosure whenever title deeds are not held in the company's name, in the prescribed format, whatever the reason for the gap; clause 3(i)(d) asks specifically whether a revaluation was based on a registered valuer, and a 20 per cent increase here is well past the 10 per cent disclosure trigger. Assets existing and being used answers a different question than either of these.

items.scenario: A company's factory land, carried at ₹8 crore, is still registered in the name of the promoter who transferred it to the company nine years ago through an unregistered family arrangement; the company's other property records are in order. Separately, the company revalued its plant this year, raising net carrying value from ₹10 crore to ₹12 crore based on an internal engineer's certificate rather than a registered valuer. The audit team plans to report clause 3(i) clean since the assets otherwise exist and are used in operations.

items.stem: What does clause 3(vii) actually require here?

options.text: Report all three items together as undisputed arrears
options.misconception: merges the disputed-dues limb into the undisputed-dues limb
options.why: The income tax demand is under appeal, placing it in the separate disputed-dues limb with its own disclosure of amount and forum, not in a six-month arrears list built for undisputed amounts.

options.text: Report nothing — a company otherwise regular in payments, and a matter still sub judice, sit outside the statutory dues clause
options.misconception: reads both trigger conditions the clause was drafted around as exclusions instead
options.why: A six-month arrear and a pending dispute are exactly the conditions clause 3(vii) exists to catch, not reasons to stay silent.

options.text: Report only the income tax demand, since disputed matters are the clause's real concern and short arrears are routine
options.misconception: drops a clearly triggered undisputed arrear because a larger disputed item is also present
options.why: The two limbs operate independently; an eight-month-old TDS arrear crosses its own six-month line and is reportable whether or not a separate dispute also exists.

options.text: Report only the TDS arrears under the undisputed-dues limb, since four months is inside the six-month trigger — and separately report the income tax demand under the disputed-dues limb, since a pending appeal is exactly what that limb asks for
options.why: The undisputed-dues sub-clause triggers only past six months of non-payment, so the four-month GST balance is not yet reportable there while the eight-month TDS balance is; the disputed-dues sub-clause exists precisely to capture demands under appeal, with amount and forum. The team gets both halves wrong: reporting an item not yet due while skipping the one squarely disputed and disclosable.

items.scenario: At year end a company has GST of ₹6 lakh outstanding for four months and TDS of ₹2 lakh outstanding for eight months, neither disputed. It also has an income tax demand of ₹50 lakh raised two years ago, unpaid, under appeal before the Commissioner. The audit team plans to report only the TDS arrears, reasoning the GST amount falls within a normal payment cycle and the income tax demand is sub judice and so not yet "due".

items.stem: Is the finance team right that there is nothing to report?

options.text: Right — clause 3(ix) is built around default, and no default occurred here
options.misconception: reads the whole clause through its default limb only
options.why: The clause's repayment focus is broad, but its sub-parts separately test wilful-defaulter status, term-loan application and short-term-to-long-term fund diversion — each independent of whether repayments stayed timely.

options.text: No — clause 3(ix) separately asks whether term loans were applied for their stated purpose, and this diversion is reportable there even with a clean repayment record
options.why: The clause bundles several distinct questions: default in repayment is one, but application of term-loan proceeds for their stated purpose is a separate limb entirely, triggered by the diversion itself and not by any missed instalment. A company can be current on every payment and still have a reportable clause 3(ix) finding.

options.text: Wrong, but only because the diverted amount should have been reclassified as a fresh short-term borrowing in the accounts
options.misconception: turns a CARO disclosure question into an accounting reclassification issue
options.why: How the loan is accounted for is separate from CARO's factual question of whether term-loan proceeds were applied to their stated purpose; the diversion is disclosable as a fact regardless of the accounting entries made.

options.text: Wrong, and the auditor must also declare the company a wilful defaulter in the CARO report
options.misconception: lets the auditor make a determination that belongs to lenders and credit information authorities
options.why: The clause asks whether the company has been declared a wilful defaulter by a bank or lender; the auditor reports that status if it exists, and does not make the declaration himself.

items.scenario: A company took a five-year term loan for a new plant but diverted ₹3 crore of it to clear an unrelated short-term working capital overdraft, while staying current on every instalment and interest payment to the lender all year. The finance team argues clause 3(ix) has nothing to report since there is no default.

items.stem: Does Clause 3 of Part I of the First Schedule catch this arrangement?

options.text: Yes, but only above a fee-sharing threshold the Council has prescribed
options.misconception: invents a materiality threshold the clause does not contain
options.why: Clause 3 sets no minimum percentage or amount; sharing any part of professional profits with a non-member outside the Council's prescribed exceptions is misconduct in terms.

options.text: No, because the consultant performs no audit work and so cannot be said to share in professional profits
options.misconception: reads "profits of professional work" as requiring the recipient to have done the work
options.why: The clause addresses the member's payment out of his own professional profits to a non-member; the non-member's role in the underlying engagement is not the test — the CA's payment out of fees earned is.

options.text: No — Clause 3 restricts only partnerships, and a referral fee is a separate commercial arrangement
options.misconception: confuses the profit-sharing clause with the neighbouring partnership clause
options.why: Partnership with a non-member is addressed by Clause 4; Clause 3 stands on its own and targets profit-sharing specifically, which is exactly what a percentage-of-fees referral payment is.

options.text: Yes — paying a share of professional profits to a person who is not a member is the misconduct Clause 3 names, whatever the payment is called and however the referral relationship is framed
options.why: Clause 3 reaches accepting or agreeing to accept part of the profits of professional work by a person who is not a member; a percentage-of-fees referral payment to an unqualified consultant is precisely that, and relabelling it a marketing expense does not change its substance.
keywords: part of the profits of professional work
person who is not a member

items.scenario: A practising chartered accountant regularly receives audit referrals from a well-regarded but unqualified accounts-writing consultant. In appreciation, the CA pays the consultant 15 per cent of the fees earned on every referred engagement. He reasons this is a marketing expense, not misconduct, since the consultant is not a competitor and does none of the audit work himself.

items.stem: Which of the three proposed partnerships does Clause 4 of Part I of the First Schedule permit?

options.text: All three — the clause only restricts partnerships with rival chartered accountancy firms
options.misconception: narrows a general non-CA restriction into a competitor-only rule
options.why: Clause 4's bar runs against any person other than a CA in practice, with only the notified professional bodies as exceptions; it says nothing about rival firms and everything about the partner's own qualification.

options.text: Only the company secretary — cost accountants sit outside the Council's notified list
options.misconception: drops a professional body that is in fact on the Council's permitted list
options.why: Cost accountants in practice are among the bodies the Council has notified for this purpose, on the same footing as company secretaries.

options.text: The cost accountant and the company secretary — both belong to professional bodies the Council has notified as permitted partners; the brother-in-law, holding no such qualification, is squarely barred
options.why: Clause 4 bars partnership with anyone other than a CA in practice unless that person belongs to a Council-notified professional body — cost accountants and company secretaries in practice are among them. An unqualified relative in an unrelated business falls outside every permitted category, however close the relationship.

options.text: None of the three — Clause 4 bars all partnerships outright, permitting only sole proprietorship
options.misconception: erases the Council's notified-body exception entirely
options.why: The clause's own structure carves out professional bodies the Council permits; treating it as an absolute bar ignores the exception that makes multidisciplinary practice possible at all.

items.scenario: A practising CA wants to widen his firm's offering and considers three partnership proposals: with a cost accountant holding a valid certificate of practice, with his brother-in-law who runs an unrelated trading business and holds no professional qualification, and with a company secretary in practice. He assumes all three are equally fine since partnership rules concern only rival chartered accountancy firms.

items.stem: Was including the internal financial controls opinion required here?

options.text: Yes — section 143(3)(i) applies uniformly to every company regardless of size or structure
options.misconception: ignores the notified exemption that qualifies the section's reach
options.why: The section's own wording is broad, and that is exactly what notification G.S.R. 583(E) narrowed, using the power in section 462 to exempt classes of private company. Reporting is not universal despite the section's phrasing.

options.text: No, because internal financial controls reporting was withdrawn entirely for all companies
options.misconception: overreads a partial exemption as a full repeal
options.why: The notification exempts named categories of private company only. Listed companies, larger private companies and public companies remain squarely inside section 143(3)(i), and even an exempt company must still maintain the controls — only the auditor's reporting on them falls away.

options.text: No — the company is under ₹50 crore of turnover, and meeting either the turnover test or the borrowing test is enough on its own
options.misconception: reads the two figures as alternatives, as the notification first published them, missing the corrigendum that made them cumulative
options.why: The right answer for the wrong reason. As published on 13 June 2017 the entry read "statement or", so either test would have done; the corrigendum of 13 July 2017 substituted "and", so a private company must be under ₹50 crore of turnover and under ₹25 crore of borrowings. This company happens to satisfy both, which is why the exemption still holds.

options.text: No — notification G.S.R. 583(E) lifts the requirement for a private company under ₹50 crore turnover and under ₹25 crore of borrowings, and this company is under both and has no filing default
options.why: Entry 9A of the notification exempts a private company that is a one person company or a small company, or whose turnover is under ₹50 crore as per the latest audited financial statement and whose aggregate borrowings from banks, financial institutions or any body corporate at any point in the year are under ₹25 crore. ₹30 crore of turnover and nil borrowings clear both figures. Paragraph 2A adds the catch that matters here — the exemption is available only to a private company with no default in filing under section 137 or section 92 — and this company has none.

citation.ref: Section 143(3)(i), read with entry 9A and paragraph 2A of MCA Notification G.S.R. 583(E) dated 13.06.2017 (amending G.S.R. 464(E) dated 05.06.2015, issued under section 462) and the corrigendum thereto dated 13.07.2017

items.scenario: A private company with turnover of ₹30 crore and no borrowings from any bank, financial institution or body corporate at any point in the year is audited. It has filed every annual return and set of financial statements with the Registrar on time. The audit senior includes a full internal financial controls opinion in the report, reasoning that section 143(3)(i) applies to every company audit without exception.

items.stem: What must the auditor's report say about the audit trail requirement?

options.text: That the financial statements must be qualified, since the books lack audit trail evidence for part of the year
options.misconception: escalates an audit-trail reporting gap into an opinion modification without evidence of misstatement
options.why: The audit trail finding is reported through its own prescribed statement; it bears on the opinion only if it leaves the auditor unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence on the figures themselves, which the facts here do not show.

options.text: That the audit trail feature was not operated throughout the year — the four-month gap is reportable regardless of whether the underlying books are otherwise accurate
options.why: The reporting requirement asks specifically whether the audit trail feature operated throughout the year for all transactions and was not tampered with; a period where the feature was switched off answers that in the negative, independent of whether the books themselves ended up correct. Accuracy of the books is a different question from whether the trail of how they got there was preserved.

options.text: That the requirement is satisfied, since the feature exists in the software and was active for eight of twelve months
options.misconception: treats partial-year operation as substantial compliance
options.why: The requirement's own wording asks for operation throughout the year; a four-month disabled window is a gap the report must state, not a majority-compliance figure that rounds up to a clean answer.

options.text: Nothing — audit trail is an IT control matter for the company's internal audit function, not the statutory auditor's report
options.misconception: places a named statutory reporting duty outside the statutory auditor's scope
options.why: The reporting requirement runs to the statutory auditor by rule; internal audit's interest in the same control does not remove the auditor's own duty to state a position on it.

items.scenario: For the year ended 31 March 2024, a company's accounting software has the audit trail feature available, but the IT team disabled it for the first four months to speed up month-end closing, re-enabling it from August. Management tells the auditor the books for the full year are otherwise accurate and complete.

items.stem: What is wrong with the manager's proposal?

options.text: Group materiality is computed by the principal auditor for the group as a whole, and it is the principal auditor who determines the materiality for each component and communicates it to the component auditor — a figure set for a different, standalone opinion cannot be inherited
options.why: The Guidance Note has the auditor compute materiality for the group as a whole, use it to test the consolidation adjustments and to decide which components are scoped in, and separately compute and communicate materiality for each component where that is needed for a true and fair view on the consolidated financial statements. The component auditor's ₹40 lakh was set to support his own standalone opinion, not the group's.
keywords: materiality for the group as a whole

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because ₹40 lakh sits well below group materiality and a lower threshold can only make the work more thorough
options.misconception: treats a smaller number as automatically safe and lets the component auditor decide the group's threshold
options.why: Lower is not the test; who sets it is. Adopting the component auditor's figure leaves the principal auditor with no threshold of his own for the consolidation adjustments, and no communication to the component auditor about what the group needs.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because SA 600 makes the principal auditor not responsible for the work entrusted to the other auditor
options.misconception: stretches the SA 600 division of responsibility into an excuse for setting no group materiality at all
options.why: SA 600 divides responsibility for performing the component's audit; it does not divide the opinion on the consolidated financial statements, which stays the principal auditor's. Determining group materiality is part of forming that opinion.

options.text: The proposal fails because the parent auditor must re-audit the subsidiary himself wherever the component auditor's materiality differs from the group's
options.misconception: escalates a duty to set and communicate materiality into a duty to re-perform the component audit
options.why: Different materiality figures are the normal state of affairs, not a trigger to redo the work. What is required is that the principal auditor set the group figure, communicate a component figure, and obtain the confirmations he needs from the component auditor.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements (Revised 2016)
citation.ref: Materiality in the audit of consolidated financial statements

items.scenario: You are the parent auditor of a group. One subsidiary contributing 12 per cent of consolidated revenue is statutorily audited by another firm, which set materiality of ₹40 lakh for its own standalone opinion on that subsidiary. Your materiality for the group as a whole is ₹1.5 crore. The engagement manager proposes to adopt the other firm's ₹40 lakh as the component materiality for group purposes, on the ground that it is lower and therefore safer, and to send that firm no instruction of your own.

items.stem: How should these be classified?

options.text: The unrealised profit in inventory and the intra-group interest are current period consolidation adjustments; goodwill and the non-controlling interests' share of net assets at the acquisition date are permanent adjustments, revisited only when the shareholding changes
options.why: Permanent adjustments are made on the first occasion of consolidation and again only where the shareholding in a consolidated entity changes — the determination of goodwill or capital reserve, and of the equity attributable to the minority. Elimination of intra-group transactions and balances, including unrealised intra-group profit and intra-group interest, is exactly what current period adjustments consist of.

options.text: All three are current period adjustments, because every one of them is posted in this year's consolidation working
options.misconception: classifies by the period the journal is posted in rather than by whether the adjustment recurs or is fixed at acquisition
options.why: Every consolidation entry is posted in the current working; that is not what makes an adjustment "current period". The dividing line is whether the adjustment is fixed at the acquisition date and left alone until the shareholding moves.

options.text: Only the unrealised profit is a consolidation adjustment; intra-group interest is a related party disclosure matter under SA 550 and is not eliminated
options.misconception: confuses disclosing a related party transaction with eliminating it on consolidation
options.why: Both things happen. The transaction is disclosed as a related party transaction in the standalone statements and eliminated in full on consolidation, because from the group's point of view no interest left the group.

options.text: The unrealised profit and the intra-group interest are permanent adjustments, because the parent-subsidiary relationship they arise from is itself permanent
options.misconception: reads "permanent" as describing the group relationship rather than the adjustment
options.why: The word describes the adjustment, not the relationship. An elimination that must be recomputed on fresh figures every year is by definition not fixed once and carried forward.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements (Revised 2016)
citation.ref: Permanent consolidation adjustments and current period consolidation adjustments

items.scenario: A parent acquired 80 per cent of a subsidiary four years ago and its shareholding has not changed since. This year the subsidiary sold goods to the parent, and ₹60 lakh of them at a mark-up are still in the parent's closing inventory; the subsidiary also paid the parent ₹15 lakh of interest on an intra-group loan. The audit senior's working paper classifies both of these as permanent consolidation adjustments, and proposes to recompute goodwill and the non-controlling interests' share of net assets at acquisition afresh this year as a current period adjustment.

items.stem: What has the parent auditor missed?

options.text: Nothing — SA 600 permits the principal auditor to use the work of another auditor whatever accounting or auditing standards that auditor applied
options.misconception: treats SA 600 reliance as blind to the framework the other auditor worked under
options.why: SA 600 governs how the principal auditor evaluates and uses that work; it does not make the underlying framework irrelevant. Figures on another GAAP are not consolidatable, and a report issued under standards that do not correspond to Indian GAAS is not one to lean on.

options.text: The principal auditor must himself convert the component's financial statements to the parent's framework before consolidating them
options.misconception: moves a management preparation responsibility onto the auditor
options.why: Preparing the consolidated financial statements, conversion included, is the parent management's responsibility. The auditor audits the conversion adjustments; performing them would put him in the position of preparing what he then reports on.

options.text: The subsidiary must be excluded from the consolidated financial statements because its accounting framework differs from the parent's
options.misconception: turns a framework difference into an exemption from consolidation
options.why: The exceptions to consolidating a component come from the applicable accounting standards, not from a difference in GAAP. A different framework is a conversion problem, and conversion is the answer to it.

options.text: Two things — the parent's management must convert the component's audited financial statements to the framework used for the consolidated financial statements, and the principal auditor must audit those conversion adjustments; and reliance on the local auditor's report requires the component to have been audited under a framework corresponding to Indian GAAS
options.why: Consolidation needs the component's information to be on the group's accounting framework, and the conversion is management's work which the principal auditor audits. Separately, to rely on and refer to the other auditor's report, the audit behind it has to have been performed under a framework corresponding to Indian GAAS.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements (Revised 2016)
citation.ref: Component auditor reporting under an accounting or auditing framework different from the parent's

items.scenario: A parent listed in India consolidates a wholly-owned subsidiary in Vietnam. The subsidiary's financial statements are prepared under Vietnamese local GAAP and audited by a local firm under that jurisdiction's own auditing standards.
