options.misconception: denies the rotation SA 330 permits and turns every audit into a full test of every control relied on
options.why: SA 330 expressly allows audit evidence obtained in previous audits to be used once the auditor has established its continuing relevance. Testing everything every year is not what the standard asks for and is not what the file has to show.

items.scenario: Two controls are in question. The first is a three-way bank reconciliation over cash. The second is a management review control over revenue cut-off; you have assessed revenue recognition as a significant risk under the SA 240 presumption. Both were tested two years ago and found effective, and inquiry combined with observation shows that neither has changed since. The senior plans to rely on both this year without testing either, since neither has reached its third audit.

items.stem: What does SA 330 require?

options.text: Cover the remaining period with procedures that give a reasonable basis for extending the interim conclusion to the year end, and — the December error being one you did not expect — reassess the risk and reconsider the remaining-period work before performing it
options.why: SA 330 gives two routes across the remaining period: substantive procedures combined with tests of controls for the intervening period, or further substantive procedures only where the auditor determines that is sufficient. Either has to provide a reasonable basis for extending the audit conclusions from the interim date to the period end. And where misstatements that the auditor did not expect are detected at an interim date, the auditor evaluates whether the related assessment of risk and the planned nature, timing and extent of the substantive procedures covering the remaining period need to be modified — a scan for unusual items is not that evaluation.
keywords: reasonable basis for extending the audit conclusions
misstatements that the auditor did not expect

options.text: Re-circularise the whole population at 31 March, since interim substantive testing may not be relied on once an unexpected misstatement has been found
options.misconception: converts a requirement to reassess into a bar on interim testing that SA 330 does not contain
options.why: SA 330 requires the auditor to evaluate whether the risk assessment and the remaining-period procedures need to be modified. It does not throw the interim work away, and redoing everything substitutes effort for the judgement the standard asks for.

options.text: Treat the ₹70 lakh as an anomaly, its cause being known and confined to September despatches, and carry on with the planned scan
options.misconception: reaches for the anomaly label to make an unexpected misstatement stop counting, when nothing here supplies the certainty that label needs
options.why: An anomaly under SA 530 needs a high degree of certainty, obtained by performing additional audit procedures, that the misstatement is not representative of the population — and even then the label removes it only from the projection, never from the evaluation. Nothing here has established any of that.

options.text: Nothing more — 92 per cent of the balance was confirmed, and external confirmation is the strongest evidence available for receivables
options.misconception: treats the strength of the interim evidence as covering a period it never touched
options.why: A confirmation dated 31 December says nothing about a balance at 31 March. The strength of a procedure does not extend its date, and the three months it does not reach are where the year's cut-off risk has just been shown to sit.

items.scenario: Trade receivables were circularised at 31 December for a 31 March year end and 92 per cent by value was confirmed. During that same interim work you found ₹70 lakh of credit notes issued in December against September despatches, never accrued — an error nobody expected. Performance materiality is ₹60 lakh. The manager proposes to roll the December conclusion forward by scanning the January to March receivables ledger for unusual items.

items.stem: What has the manager skipped?

options.text: Reassessing materiality against the entity's actual results before evaluating the uncorrected misstatements, and obtaining an understanding of management's reasons for refusing to correct them
options.why: SA 450 requires the auditor, prior to evaluating the effect of uncorrected misstatements, to reassess materiality determined in accordance with SA 320 to confirm whether it remains appropriate in the context of the entity's actual financial results. At the same 5 per cent of an actual profit before tax of ₹7 crore the figure is ₹35 lakh, not ₹1.2 crore, and ₹65 lakh is then material. The standard separately requires the auditor to obtain an understanding of management's reasons for not making the corrections and to take that understanding into account.

options.text: Nothing — materiality is set at planning, and revising it once the results are known would be designing the audit around its own answer
options.misconception: treats planning materiality as fixed, when SA 320 requires revision as the audit progresses and SA 450 requires a reassessment before the final evaluation
options.why: Both standards say the opposite. SA 320 requires materiality to be revised where the auditor becomes aware of information that would have caused a different figure to be set initially, and SA 450 makes the reassessment a step before the evaluation. A figure built on a forecast that missed by ₹17 crore is not a figure to measure anything against.

options.text: Obtaining a written representation that management believes the effects of the uncorrected misstatements are immaterial, which would have settled the point
options.misconception: treats the representation about uncorrected misstatements as evidence that they are immaterial, when it records management's belief and nothing more
options.why: SA 450 does require that representation, with a summary of the items included in or attached to it, but a written representation is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own. Management's belief that ₹65 lakh does not matter is the very belief the auditor is testing.

options.text: Communicating the uncorrected misstatements to those charged with governance, which would have taken the decision out of the auditor's hands
options.misconception: treats the communication to those charged with governance as discharging the auditor's own evaluation
options.why: That communication is required, and it is not what was skipped — it accompanies the evaluation rather than replacing it. SA 450 leaves the determination of whether uncorrected misstatements are material, individually or in aggregate, with the auditor.

items.scenario: At planning you set materiality for the financial statements as a whole at ₹1.2 crore, being 5 per cent of a forecast profit before tax of ₹24 crore. The audited profit before tax comes out at ₹7 crore after a bad year. Uncorrected misstatements total ₹65 lakh. Management declines to correct any of them, saying each is small and the effort is not worth it. The manager proposes an unmodified opinion because ₹65 lakh sits comfortably below ₹1.2 crore.

items.stem: How does SA 701 have the report set out?

options.text: Replace the qualification with a full key audit matter describing the ₹28 crore, which tells the reader everything a qualification would
options.misconception: treats a description in the auditor's report as an alternative to modifying the opinion, which is the substitution SA 701 names first
options.why: A key audit matter is not a substitute for the auditor expressing a modified opinion when the circumstances require it. The ₹28 crore is a material misstatement in the financial statements, and a misstatement that is material but not pervasive is answered by a qualified opinion.

options.text: Describe both in the Key Audit Matters section, saying why each was of most significance and how each was addressed, and drop the separate going concern section as duplicative
options.misconception: uses the Key Audit Matters section to carry matters the reporting standards give their own sections, so a description stands where a modification is required
options.why: That is the substitution SA 701 forbids in terms. A reader who finds the ₹28 crore discussed among the key audit matters and nowhere else has been handed a description in place of a qualification.

options.text: Both are by their nature key audit matters, but neither is described in the Key Audit Matters section — the impairment goes in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section, the uncertainty in a Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section, and the Key Audit Matters section carries a reference to each
options.why: SA 701 says that communicating a key audit matter is not a substitute for the auditor expressing a modified opinion under SA 705 (Revised), and not a substitute for reporting under SA 570 (Revised) where a material uncertainty related to going concern exists. Such matters are by their nature key audit matters, but the standard directs that they shall not be described in the Key Audit Matters section, and that a reference to the relevant section is included there instead.
keywords: material uncertainty related to going concern

options.text: Put the impairment in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section and say nothing about it in the Key Audit Matters section, since one matter cannot sit in two places
options.misconception: drops the cross-reference SA 701 requires, leaving the Key Audit Matters section reading as though the qualification was not among the significant matters
options.why: The standard's answer is not silence but a reference. The Key Audit Matters section includes a reference to the Basis for Qualified Opinion section so that the reader is sent to where the most significant matter actually went.

items.scenario: A listed company. You are qualifying the opinion because ₹28 crore of capital work in progress on an abandoned project is carried without impairment — material but not pervasive. Separately, a material uncertainty related to going concern exists and is adequately disclosed. The engagement partner wants both written up as key audit matters, "because they are plainly the two most significant matters in this audit", and wants no separate going concern section on the ground that the key audit matter description covers it.

items.stem: What does SA 705 require?

options.text: Express an unmodified opinion on the Indian operations alone, with an Other Matter paragraph stating that the overseas branches were not audited
options.misconception: carves the audited part out of the financial statements the opinion covers, and uses an Other Matter paragraph to record a limitation
options.why: The opinion covers the financial statements as a whole, and there is no separate set for the Indian operations. An Other Matter paragraph never signals that the auditor was blocked — an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence goes into the opinion.

options.text: Request management to remove the limitation, communicate the refusal to those charged with governance, attempt alternative procedures — and then withdraw from the audit, first telling those charged with governance about the misstatements you identified that would have given rise to a modification
options.why: SA 705 (Revised) routes a management-imposed limitation through the request, the communication to those charged with governance and the alternative procedures before any opinion is reached. Where the auditor is still unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence and the possible effects of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive, the standard asks first whether withdrawal is practicable and possible under applicable law or regulation.

options.text: Disclaim an opinion at once, the possible effects of the inability to obtain evidence being both material and pervasive
options.misconception: reaches the disclaimer without taking the withdrawal step SA 705 puts ahead of it where withdrawal is practicable and possible
options.why: A disclaimer of opinion is what happens where withdrawal is not practicable or not possible under applicable law or regulation. Here it is both, and the standard puts withdrawal first — a disclaimer would leave a report in the world on 71 per cent of revenue nobody audited, in place of a refusal to give one.

options.text: Qualify the opinion, describing the three branches you were unable to audit in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section
options.misconception: grades a limitation covering most of the entity as material but not pervasive
options.why: Pervasiveness asks whether the possible effects are confined to specific elements of the financial statements. Branches carrying 71 per cent of revenue and 64 per cent of assets are not a specific element — the possible effects represent a substantial proportion of the financial statements, so this is material and pervasive, not material but not pervasive.

items.scenario: Two months into the audit of a listed company the managing director instructs you in writing not to visit the three overseas branches, not to correspond with their bankers and not to obtain their trial balances. Those branches carry 71 per cent of revenue and 64 per cent of assets. Your alternative procedures produce nothing you can rely on. The engagement letter signed in April gave you full access, and withdrawal is both practicable and possible under your terms of appointment and under the Act.

items.stem: What opinion does SA 570 require?

options.text: An adverse opinion, the going concern basis of accounting being inappropriate
options.why: SA 570 (Revised) is unconditional here: where the financial statements have been prepared using the going concern basis of accounting but in the auditor's judgement management's use of that basis is inappropriate, the auditor expresses an adverse opinion. Adequate disclosure answers a material uncertainty; it cannot answer a wrong basis of preparation, because every figure in the statements is measured on it.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph drawing attention to the note
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter where a modification is required, and where the standard gives going concern its own named section in any event
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter refers to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed and never carries a going concern conclusion. SA 570 (Revised) gives going concern its own section where the basis is appropriate, and an adverse opinion where it is not.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with a Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section, the position being fully and accurately disclosed
options.misconception: applies the adequately-disclosed material uncertainty rule to a case where the going concern basis itself is inappropriate
options.why: That section belongs to a case where the going concern basis of accounting is still appropriate and a material uncertainty about it is adequately disclosed. Here there is no uncertainty left to disclose — the plant is gone, the licences are surrendered and the board has resolved to liquidate.

options.text: A qualified opinion, the misstatement being confined to the basis of preparation and the note telling the reader everything
options.misconception: treats a wrong basis of preparation as a matter confined to one element, when it runs through every figure in the statements
options.why: The basis of preparation is not one element. Assets carried at values that assume continued operations, liabilities classified as non-current and the absence of closure costs all follow from it, so the effects are pervasive to the financial statements — and a pervasive misstatement takes an adverse opinion.

items.scenario: A manufacturer's only plant was sold in February under a court-monitored order, its manufacturing licences have been surrendered, and the board resolved in March to apply for voluntary liquidation. The financial statements are nevertheless drawn up on a going concern basis, with a note describing the sale, the surrender and the resolution, and stating that management is exploring alternatives. You are satisfied the note is complete and accurate.

items.stem: On which, if either, may you express an unmodified opinion?

options.text: On both, each engagement being separate, the work complete, and neither report published with the disclaimer
options.misconception: applies the specific-element concession to a single financial statement, which SA 805 excludes by deeming it a major portion
options.why: Separate publication is one of three conditions and it is available only for a specific element. A single financial statement is deemed to constitute a major portion of the complete set, so the bar holds even where the two reports never travel together.

options.text: On both, provided each report carries an Other Matter paragraph stating that the opinion on the complete set was disclaimed
options.misconception: uses an Other Matter paragraph to license an opinion the standard prohibits
options.why: Disclosure does not create permission. SA 805 offers no Other Matter paragraph as an alternative to its three conditions, and a single financial statement stays barred however the report is worded.

options.text: On neither, since an unmodified opinion on any part of financial statements you have disclaimed an opinion on would contradict the disclaimer
options.misconception: reads the contradiction rule as absolute, when SA 805 opens a narrow route for a specific element audited separately
options.why: The contradiction bites where both opinions appear in the same auditor's report, or where the element is a major portion of the complete set. SA 805 sets out the conditions on which a specific element may still be reported on, and the secured borrowings schedule meets them.

options.text: On the schedule of secured borrowings only
options.why: SA 805 allows an unmodified opinion on a specific element after a disclaimer of opinion on the complete set only where three conditions all hold — the auditor is not prohibited by law or regulation, the report is not published together with the report containing the disclaimer, and the specific element does not constitute a major portion of the complete set. ₹60 crore of a ₹1,400 crore balance sheet is not a major portion. The statement of profit and loss is a single financial statement, which the standard deems to constitute a major portion, so it is barred.

items.scenario: You disclaimed an opinion on a company's complete set of financial statements, having been unable to obtain evidence over an ₹800 crore related party receivable. A lender now engages you separately to audit and report on the company's schedule of secured borrowings — ₹60 crore against a balance sheet of ₹1,400 crore — and, on a second separate engagement, on the company's statement of profit and loss. Your work on both is complete and finds nothing wrong, and neither report would be published together with the disclaimer.

items.stem: Which of these amount to professional misconduct?

options.text: The second and the third
options.why: Clause 10 of Part I of the First Schedule bars fees based on a percentage of profits or contingent upon the findings or results of the employment, except as permitted by regulation. Regulation 192 permits a receiver or a liquidator to charge on a percentage of the realisation of the assets, which saves the first engagement. It permits a percentage of profits only for the auditor of a co-operative society, so an audit fee at 1 per cent of profit before tax in a private company is misconduct, and it nowhere permits a fee that rises with a tax demand being deleted.

options.text: The third only — a fee contingent on a result is misconduct, but a percentage of profits is merely a way of measuring a fee and falls outside the clause
options.misconception: separates a percentage-of-profits fee from a contingent fee, when Clause 10 names both
options.why: Clause 10 names two things: fees based on a percentage of profits, and fees contingent upon the findings or results of the employment. The first limb catches an audit fee set at 1 per cent of profit before tax whatever the second limb does.

options.text: All three, Clause 10 admitting no exception once a fee moves with an outcome
options.misconception: reads Clause 10 without the words "except as permitted under any regulations made under this Act", which sit in the clause itself
options.why: The exception is written into the clause. Regulation 192 names the permitted cases, and a liquidator's percentage of the realisation of the assets is the first of them.

options.text: The second only — a tax representation is advocacy rather than professional employment, so Clause 10 does not reach the third
options.misconception: reads "professional employment" as confined to audit and assurance, when it covers the whole of a member's practice
options.why: Clause 10 applies in respect of any professional employment. Appearing before an appellate authority is professional work of a member in practice, and a fee of 15 per cent of the demand deleted is contingent upon the results of that employment.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 10, read with Regulation 192 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988

items.scenario: A chartered accountant in practice accepts three engagements. First, as liquidator of a company in members' voluntary liquidation, at 2 per cent of the assets realised. Second, as statutory auditor of a private limited company, at a fee of 1 per cent of its profit before tax for the year. Third, representing a client before the Commissioner (Appeals) in an income tax matter, at 15 per cent of whatever demand is ultimately deleted.

items.stem: What is the position under clause 3(xix)?

options.text: Yes to both — a clean going concern conclusion under SA 570 answers clause 3(xix), and the two together tell the committee the company will meet its liabilities
options.misconception: collapses a CARO clause with its own named inputs into the SA 570 conclusion, and reads either as an assurance about the future
options.why: The two questions overlap but are not the same, and the clause makes the auditor state in terms that he neither gives any guarantee nor any assurance that all liabilities falling due within a period of one year from the balance sheet date will get discharged.
keywords: neither gives any guarantee nor any assurance
one year from the balance sheet date

options.text: The clause is answered on its own named inputs, and the report must also say that the reporting is based on facts up to the date of the audit report and carries no guarantee about the liabilities being discharged
options.why: Clause 3(xix) does not import the SA 570 conclusion. It asks whether the auditor is of the opinion that no material uncertainty exists as on the date of the audit report that the company is not capable of meeting its liabilities existing at the date of the balance sheet as and when they fall due within a period of one year from the balance sheet date, and it names the inputs — the financial ratios, the ageing and expected dates of realisation of financial assets and payment of financial liabilities, other information accompanying the financial statements, and the auditor's knowledge of the Board of Directors' and management's plans. The clause itself answers the committee's second question: the auditor neither gives any guarantee nor any assurance.
keywords: ageing and expected dates of realisation
neither gives any guarantee nor any assurance

options.text: The clause looks one year forward from the date of the audit report and covers every liability the company will incur in that period
options.misconception: shifts both the window and the population, when the clause fixes them at liabilities existing at the balance sheet date and falling due within one year of it
options.why: The clause is anchored twice to the balance sheet date. It reaches only the liabilities existing at the date of the balance sheet, and the one-year period runs from the balance sheet date. Only the auditor's opinion is dated as on the date of the audit report.
keywords: liabilities existing at the date of the balance sheet

options.text: The clause cannot be reported clean where the current ratio is below one, a ratio below one being a material uncertainty in itself
options.misconception: turns one of the named inputs into the conclusion, skipping the plans and the expected dates of realisation the clause names alongside it
options.why: The financial ratios are one of four things the clause puts in front of the auditor. The ageing and expected dates of realisation of financial assets and payment of financial liabilities, the other information accompanying the financial statements and the auditor's knowledge of the Board of Directors' and management's plans — the enforceable support letter among them — go in beside the ratios.

items.scenario: You are satisfied the going concern basis is appropriate and that no Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section is needed, a promoter having given a binding and enforceable letter of support and having the means to honour it. The current ratio is 0.6 and ₹90 crore of borrowings fall due within eleven months of the balance sheet date. The audit committee asks whether clause 3(xix) can therefore be reported clean, and whether a clean answer means the company will survive the year.

items.stem: Is that right?

options.text: No — the first limb asks whether the internal audit system fits this company's size and nature whether or not section 138 applies, and the second limb separately asks whether the internal auditors' reports for the period were considered by you
options.why: The clause is not keyed to section 138. It asks whether the company has an internal audit system commensurate with the size and nature of its business, and a one-person function leaving eleven branches and the whole of procurement uncovered is not that. The second limb stands on its own: the reports of the Internal Auditors for the period under audit have to be considered by the statutory auditor, and these ones name repeated irregularities.
keywords: internal audit system commensurate with the size and nature

options.text: No, and you must therefore adopt the internal auditor's procurement findings as audit evidence, he being inside the company and closer to the facts
options.misconception: treats internal audit findings as evidence the statutory auditor may take over, skipping the evaluation SA 610 requires before any of that work is used
options.why: SA 610 (Revised) has the auditor evaluate the internal audit function's objectivity, its level of competence, and whether it applies a systematic and disciplined approach, before using its work at all — and then evaluate the adequacy of the particular work used. Considering the reports under clause 3(xiv)(b) is not adopting their conclusions.

options.text: Yes — clause 3(xiv) reports on the internal audit that section 138 requires, so a company outside those classes reports the clause as not applicable
options.misconception: reads a CARO clause about the adequacy of a system as a compliance check on section 138
options.why: Section 138, read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014, decides who must appoint an internal auditor. Clause 3(xiv) asks a different question — whether the system this company actually has fits this company — and it is answered wherever CARO applies.

options.text: No, but only the first limb fails — the second is answered by the company having an internal auditor at all
options.misconception: reads the second limb as another applicability test rather than as a question about what the statutory auditor did
options.why: Clause 3(xiv)(b) asks whether the reports of the Internal Auditors for the period under audit were considered by the statutory auditor. It is a statement about the audit, and an appointment whose reports nobody read does not answer it.

items.scenario: An unlisted public company has paid-up share capital of ₹4 crore and turnover of ₹60 crore, and is outside the classes section 138 covers. Its internal audit function is one person, who covers head office cash and payroll and nothing else, leaving eleven branches and the whole of procurement untouched. His four quarterly reports name repeated procurement irregularities at two branches. The audit senior drafts clause 3(xiv) as "not applicable, the company not being covered by section 138".

items.stem: Is the manager right?

options.text: Half right — the inquiry is a duty and not a right, and nothing is reported where the inquiry is satisfied, but an adverse finding on the book-entry adjustments and on the family travel is stated in your report
options.why: The proviso to section 143(1) says the auditor shall inquire, so the six matters are a duty. What is not required is a positive statement in the auditor's report where the answers are satisfactory, which is why the first advance goes unreported. Where the inquiry produces an adverse finding — here on transactions represented merely by book entries, and on personal expenses charged to revenue account — the auditor states it.
keywords: personal expenses charged to revenue account

options.text: No — all six matters in the proviso must be positively answered in the auditor's report every year, whether the answers are satisfactory or adverse
options.misconception: turns a duty of inquiry into a standing reporting format, which section 143(1) does not create
options.why: Nothing in section 143(1) prescribes a form of words for the report. The auditor inquires into all six and reports only what is adverse, which is why a clean report is silent about them.

options.text: No, and the ₹40 lakh of family travel goes into the CARO report as a fraud on the company by its officers
options.misconception: routes a personal expense charged to revenue straight to the fraud clause without the reason to believe an offence of fraud that fraud reporting needs
options.why: Personal expenses charged to revenue account is a named matter of inquiry under the proviso to section 143(1), and an adverse finding is stated in the report. CARO 2020 clause 3(xi) reports a fraud by the company or on the company noticed or reported during the year, which is a different finding needing its own basis — as does a report under section 143(12).
keywords: personal expenses charged to revenue account

options.text: Yes — section 143(1) confers a right of access and a right to inquire, and everything the auditor must report is listed in section 143(3)
options.misconception: reads the proviso's "shall inquire" as an option, and treats section 143(3) as the whole of the auditor's reporting
options.why: The proviso is cast as a duty in the same words as the rest of the section. And section 143(3) is not exhaustive of the report — an adverse finding under section 143(1) belongs in it, as do the matters the Central Government orders under section 143(11).

items.scenario: An unlisted company's books show ₹14 crore of advances against supplies to three parties, unsecured, on which no goods have moved in two years; ₹2.6 crore of inter-company adjustments passed entirely by journal entry with no cash movement either way; and ₹40 lakh of the managing director's family travel charged to sales promotion. Your inquiries satisfy you on the first. On the second and third they do not. The manager plans to report nothing under section 143(1), saying it creates a right of inquiry rather than a reporting obligation.

items.stem: What is wrong with what the company has done?

options.text: Only the hearing — the sequence is a matter of form, and the Central Government's approval cures the special resolution once it arrives
options.misconception: treats "previous approval" as an approval that may follow, when the word fixes the order
options.why: The section says previous approval, and Rule 7 counts the sixty days for the general meeting from receipt of that approval. An approval arriving afterwards approves nothing that had not already been done without it.

options.text: The company should have proceeded under section 140(2) instead, filing Form ADT-3 within thirty days
options.misconception: confuses removal by the company with resignation by the auditor, and hands the company a filing that belongs to the auditor
options.why: Section 140(2) is the auditor's own route out — he resigns and files a statement in Form ADT-3 with the company and the Registrar within thirty days. A company cannot resign on its auditor's behalf, and nothing about that route is available where the auditor has not resigned.

options.text: Nothing — an auditor holds office at the pleasure of the members, and a special resolution is the highest authority in the company
options.misconception: treats the members' resolution as sufficient, when section 140(1) deliberately puts a government approval and a hearing between the members and the auditor
options.why: The point of section 140(1) is that the auditor is not removable at will. The previous approval of the Central Government and the reasonable opportunity of being heard exist to protect an auditor who has qualified a report from the board he qualified it against.
keywords: previous approval of the Central Government

options.text: The order is reversed and a step is missing — the previous approval of the Central Government must come before the special resolution, with the general meeting held within sixty days of that approval, and the auditor must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before any action is taken
options.why: Section 140(1) permits removal before the expiry of the term only by a special resolution of the company after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government, and its proviso requires that the auditor concerned be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Rule 7 puts the application in Form ADT-2 within thirty days of the Board resolution and the general meeting within sixty days of receipt of the approval, so a resolution passed on 8 July, before any application was even made, removes nobody.
keywords: previous approval of the Central Government

citation.ref: Section 140(1) with its proviso, read with Rule 7(2) and Rule 7(3) of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: A company's board falls out with its auditor, appointed for five years at the 2024 annual general meeting, over a qualification. On 10 June the board resolves to remove him. On 8 July the company convenes an extraordinary general meeting, passes a special resolution removing him, and posts him the resolution that evening. On 20 July it applies to the Central Government in Form ADT-2, enclosing the special resolution as evidence of the members' wishes. The auditor was never asked for his views.

items.stem: Which clauses of Part I of the Second Schedule are engaged?

options.text: Clause 5 for the undisclosed guarantee, Clause 8 for the inventory, and Clause 6 for the understated payables
options.why: Clause 5 catches a member who fails to disclose a material fact known to him which is not disclosed in a financial statement but whose disclosure is necessary — the guarantee. Clause 8 catches a member who fails to obtain sufficient information which is necessary for expression of an opinion — an inventory balance taken on management's schedule with no count and no alternative procedures. Clause 6 catches a member who fails to report a material misstatement known to him to appear in a financial statement — the ₹3 crore of unrecorded invoices sitting in his own working papers.
keywords: fails to disclose a material fact
fails to report a material misstatement

options.text: Clause 7 alone — the three failures together are gross negligence in the conduct of his professional duties, which covers all of them
options.misconception: collapses several specific clauses into the general negligence clause, when the Schedule names each failure in its own words
options.why: Clause 7 covers a member who does not exercise due diligence, or is grossly negligent in the conduct of his professional duties, and it may well be charged alongside. It does not displace the specific clauses, and a complaint resting on it alone leaves out the disclosure, evidence and reporting failures the Schedule describes separately.
keywords: grossly negligent in the conduct of his professional duties

options.text: Clause 5 and Clause 6 only — the inventory is a matter of audit quality answered by SA 501 rather than by the Schedule
options.misconception: treats a failure to obtain evidence as a standards matter outside the disciplinary Schedules, when Clause 8 names it in terms
options.why: Clause 8 names the failure to obtain sufficient information which is necessary for expression of an opinion as professional misconduct in its own right. SA 501 says what should have been done about the inventory; the Second Schedule says what follows from not doing it.
keywords: sufficient information which is necessary for expression of an opinion

options.text: None — the member expressed his opinion in good faith, and Part I of the Second Schedule requires an intention to mislead before misconduct is made out
options.misconception: reads an intention requirement into clauses that turn on knowledge and on failure rather than on motive
options.why: The clauses are worded on what the member knew and what he failed to do. Clause 5 and Clause 6 both turn on a fact or a misstatement known to him, and Clause 8 does not ask about his state of mind at all.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part I, Clauses 5, 6 and 8

items.scenario: A member issues an unmodified opinion on a company's financial statements. Three things are later established. He knew of a ₹9 crore guarantee given to a promoter entity that appears nowhere in the notes. He accepted management's schedule for a ₹6 crore inventory balance without attending any count and without any alternative procedures, and said nothing about it. And he knew trade payables were understated by ₹3 crore through unrecorded purchase invoices that he had himself listed in his working papers.

items.stem: How should the account stand in the year-end financial statements?

options.text: Standard, because the post-year-end instalment cured the overdue position
options.misconception: uses a later receipt to rewrite the balance sheet date
options.why: Classification is tested as at the reporting date. The week-later payment is next year's recovery — evidence for upgrade in due course, not an eraser for the year-end position.

options.text: Doubtful, since any default this size shows the loan is unlikely to be repaid
options.misconception: skips the ladder's first rung
options.why: Doubtful status is earned by remaining substandard for twelve months, not by the auditor's pessimism on day one. Over-classifying misstates provisions exactly as under-classifying does.

options.text: Standard — the security cover means the bank will lose nothing
options.misconception: lets collateral answer a question asked about repayment
options.why: Security affects how much is provided, not whether the asset performs. An account can be fully secured and fully non-performing at once; the ninety-day clock reads payments, not valuations.

options.text: Substandard NPA, with the accrued interest reversed — record of recovery decides, not security or reputation
options.why: Past ninety days overdue at the balance sheet date, the classification is automatic and borrower-wise reputation, group standing and security value have no vote — the norms look at the record of recovery alone. A fresh NPA starts as substandard, and unrealised interest on it comes out of income.

citation.ref: Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning

items.scenario: As branch auditor you find a term loan whose last instalment was received 100 days before year-end, shown as standard with interest accrued to income. The branch manager explains the borrower is a reputed group, the security comfortably covers the loan, and one further instalment arrived a week after year-end.

items.stem: Has the auditor discharged his reporting duty?

options.text: Yes — the LFAR is the designated channel for advances-related findings
options.misconception: routes by subject matter instead of by severity
options.why: The LFAR is where advances findings go when they inform rather than distort. Once the numbers themselves are materially wrong, the opinion on those numbers must say so.

options.text: No, but the fix is a longer LFAR with quantified impact
options.misconception: cures the wrong document
options.why: Quantification helps, in the report that carries the opinion. An unqualified opinion sitting beside a devastating LFAR is exactly the contradiction the rule against substitution prevents.

options.text: Yes, since NPA classification is RBI's supervisory concern, not the auditor's opinion
options.misconception: hands the true and fair view to the regulator
options.why: Provisioning driven by classification lands in the profit and loss the auditor opines on. RBI's interest adds a reader; it subtracts nothing from the opinion.

options.text: No — a matter affecting the true and fair view must qualify the audit report itself; the LFAR is a supplement, not a substitute
options.why: The two documents answer different questions to different readers. Shareholders and the public read the audit report's opinion on the true and fair view; a material misclassification of advances falsifies that opinion however fully the LFAR describes it. The finding belongs in both places — described in the LFAR, and qualifying the opinion.

items.scenario: A branch auditor finds systemic failure in the branch's NPA identification — dozens of accounts past ninety days still standard, with material impact on the branch's results. He writes it up thoroughly in the LFAR's advances section and issues an unqualified branch audit report, satisfied the matter is on record for RBI and the central auditors.

items.stem: Which facts block the appointment?

options.text: All three — any financial connection with an audit client disqualifies
options.misconception: replaces the statutory thresholds with a zero-tolerance rule
options.why: Parliament drew money lines precisely so trivial connections would not bar appointment. Reading them as zero makes the limits in the rule meaningless.

options.text: B's loan and C's guarantee — only the relative's shareholding is tolerated
options.misconception: forgets the guarantee has its own threshold
options.why: The guarantee disqualifies only beyond one lakh rupees. At ₹90,000 it is inside the line; the only fact past its ceiling is the ₹6 lakh debt.

options.text: None — the interests belong to a spouse, a borrower on market terms, and a guarantor, not the auditors themselves
options.misconception: shrinks the provision to the signing partner's own name
options.why: The section speaks of the person, the relative and the partner, and the rule prices each connection. B's own debt crosses its line regardless of the loan's fairness.

options.text: Only B's loan — the spouse's holding and C's guarantee sit within their limits
options.why: A relative's securities are permitted up to one lakh rupees face value, so ₹80,000 passes. The guarantee limit is one lakh, so ₹90,000 passes. Indebtedness has a five-lakh ceiling and B's ₹6 lakh crosses it — market terms do not matter — and one disqualified partner disqualifies the firm.

items.scenario: A firm is proposed as auditor of a company. Partner A's spouse holds shares of the company of face value ₹80,000. Partner B owes the company ₹6 lakh on a car loan taken on market terms. Partner C has guaranteed his friend's ₹90,000 dues to the company.

items.stem: What does clause 3(xi) actually require here?

options.text: Report both frauds with nature and amount — the clause covers any fraud on the company, noticed or reported, whoever committed it
options.why: CARO 2020 widened the clause to any fraud by the company or on the company noticed or reported during the year. The outsider's ₹1.2 crore is a fraud on the company, and its being reported to the police is exactly what makes it "reported". Nature and amount go into the report for each.

options.text: Report both, but omit amounts to avoid prejudicing the pending investigations
options.misconception: lets litigation caution trim a prescribed disclosure
options.why: The clause asks for nature and amount in terms. The auditor reports what was noticed; investigations run on their own track and are not compromised by a statutory report stating the figure involved.

options.text: Report only the stores officer — outsider frauds are police matters, not audit matters
options.misconception: carries the old officers-and-employees limit into the 2020 order
options.why: The 2016 order's wording was narrower; the 2020 clause dropped the limitation. An auditor answering the old question in the new report under-reports by ₹1.2 crore.

options.text: Report neither, since clause 3(xi) is triggered only by frauds the auditor discovers himself
options.misconception: reads "noticed or reported" as "noticed by the auditor"
options.why: Noticed or reported during the year — by anyone. Frauds surfacing through management, police complaints or whistle-blowers are squarely inside the words.

items.scenario: During the year, a company's stores officer was caught inflating supplier invoices for ₹40 lakh, and an outside gang defrauded the company of ₹1.2 crore through a fake vendor registration. Writing the CARO report, the audit senior drafts clause 3(xi) to cover only the stores officer, reasoning that CARO concerns frauds by the company's own people, and the vendor fraud was reported to the police, not to the auditor.

items.stem: Can the report be signed today?

options.text: No — for a listed entity the quality review must be completed before the report is dated
options.why: SQC 1 makes the engagement quality control review a gate, not a debrief: an objective look at the significant judgments and conclusions, finished before the report's date. A review conducted after signing can no longer change the one thing it exists to test.

options.text: Yes — the review is the firm's internal process and the report is the engagement's
options.misconception: files a signing condition under housekeeping
options.why: The review is internal in who performs it, not in what it protects. Its position before the report date is what gives the reviewer's objections any force.

options.text: Yes, provided the reviewer belongs to the engagement team and already knows the file
options.misconception: staffs the review with the people it is meant to check
options.why: The reviewer's value is distance — someone outside the team evaluating the team's judgments. A team member reviewing his own conclusions is the engagement grading itself.

options.text: No, unless the engagement partner documents that he considered the open issues himself
options.misconception: substitutes self-review for the second pair of eyes
options.why: The partner's own consideration is the thing under review. His memo cannot stand in for the objective evaluation SQC 1 assigns to another qualified person.

items.scenario: The audit of a listed company is nearly done. The engagement partner, under deadline pressure, proposes signing the report today and having the firm's quality control reviewer go through the significant judgments next week, arguing the review is an internal formality that does not concern the client.

items.stem: Is the clean audit a substitute for due diligence?

options.text: Yes for the financials, with diligence confined to legal and operational matters
options.misconception: carves financial diligence out on the audit's authority
options.why: Financial due diligence reads the same numbers with a buyer's eyes — quality of earnings, sustainability, normalisation. The audit did none of that, and a deal is priced on exactly that.

options.text: No, because audits performed by the target's own auditor are inherently unreliable
options.misconception: wins the right conclusion by slandering the wrong party
options.why: The reputed firm's work needs no doubting for the lawyer to be right. Even a flawless audit is a different exercise; the argument is scope, not competence.

options.text: Yes — a true and fair view certified by auditors is the highest assurance available
options.misconception: ranks assurance levels instead of matching scope to purpose
options.why: The opinion's assurance is high on the question it answered. A buyer's losses come overwhelmingly from matters outside that question — commitments, dependencies, liabilities that are disclosed correctly yet deadly.

options.text: No — the audit answered a different question for a different audience, and the rumour needs an investigation alongside the diligence, not instead of it
options.why: The audit opined that the statements fairly present the past under a framework — it never priced the business, tested contract terms, tax exposures or customer concentration, and it owed its opinion to shareholders, not to a buyer. Due diligence asks the buyer's questions. The promoter rumour is a specific suspicion — an investigation's job — and it runs beside the diligence with its own depth.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting

items.scenario: A client acquiring a rival says: "The target's accounts carry a clean audit opinion from a reputed firm, so due diligence would duplicate work already done. If anything, just investigate the promoter's rumoured side-dealings." His lawyer insists a full due diligence is still needed.

items.stem: What does propriety audit make of an unimpeachable file?

options.text: Nothing, unless a rule specifically caps renovation rates
options.misconception: demands a broken rule before any audit comment
options.why: Propriety supplies the standard where rules run out — that is its function. Waiting for a rate cap turns the auditor into a rule-checker for a class of loss rules cannot foresee.

options.text: The transaction fails — sanctioned extravagance in a relative's favour is exactly what propriety audit exists to catch
options.why: Regularity audit reads the file and finds every rule followed; propriety audit reads the bargain and asks whether a prudent person would pay triple his own money to a relative of the decision-maker. The standards of prudence, economy and no personal advantage condemn it however complete the sanctions.

options.text: The auditor may only report the relationship, not question the price
options.misconception: shrinks propriety to conflict disclosure
options.why: Economy is a propriety canon in its own right. Triple market rate fails it with or without the relative; the relationship adds the personal-advantage failure on top.

options.text: The transaction passes — audit tests compliance, and compliance is total
options.misconception: stops at the regularity rail
options.why: If sanction ended the enquiry, the surest waste would be waste with the best paperwork. Government audit added propriety precisely because public money can be lost lawfully.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings

items.scenario: A public sector company buys office renovation services at triple the market rate from a vendor who is the purchasing director's relative. Every step carried proper sanction: budget approval, tender committee sign-off, board ratification. Management tells the government auditor the file is unimpeachable.

items.stem: Do the objections hold?

options.text: Neither — the review tests the firm's systems on sample files, not the client's accounts, and access to attestation working papers is inherent in the framework
options.why: Nothing about the client reopens: the reviewer asks whether the firm's quality controls, documentation and standards compliance operated on that engagement. The confidentiality objection fails because the peer review framework itself provides for the reviewer's access with confidentiality obligations of his own — a member cannot plead the client against the profession's oversight of the member.

options.text: The confidentiality objection holds — client consent is needed for each file shown
options.misconception: puts a consent gate where the framework put an obligation
options.why: The reviewer stands under his own duty of confidentiality within the review's structure. Engagement-by-engagement client vetoes would let firms curate their own review.

options.text: Both — completed audits are closed files in every sense
options.misconception: confuses reviewing the auditor with reopening the audit
options.why: Closed for the client is not closed for the firm's own quality trail. The completed file is precisely the evidence of how the firm's systems behaved when it mattered.

options.text: Both fail, but only because peer review reports are never made public
options.misconception: right result hung on secrecy instead of scope
options.why: The objections fail on what review is — systems examination of the practice unit — not on who reads the outcome. Publicity is beside the point.

items.scenario: A peer reviewer examining an audit firm selects a completed statutory audit as a sample. The firm's managing partner objects on two grounds: the client's financial statements were approved long ago and cannot be reopened, and client confidentiality bars an outsider from the working papers.

items.stem: Who appoints the first auditor now?

options.text: The Registrar of Companies, on the company's application
options.misconception: imports a government-company style default into an ordinary company
options.why: The C&AG-then-Comptroller cascade belongs to government companies. For others the statute keeps the appointment inside the company — board, then members.

options.text: The board — statutory timelines for internal appointments are directory, not mandatory
options.misconception: keeps a lapsed power alive by calling the deadline soft
options.why: The section's structure is a handover: board first, members on the board's failure. Reading the deadline away erases the members' role the provision creates.

options.text: The members, in an extraordinary general meeting within ninety days
options.why: The board's thirty-day window from registration closed on 30 April; section 139(6) hands the power to the members, who appoint at an EGM within ninety days. The appointee serves until the first AGM concludes — the same tenure the board's appointee would have had.

options.text: No one — the company must wait for the first annual general meeting
options.misconception: leaves the company auditor-less for up to a year
options.why: The first auditor's whole purpose is covering the stretch before the first AGM. The ninety-day EGM route exists so the office never waits that long.

items.scenario: A private company incorporated on 1 April has a board that never appoints a first auditor. On 20 May the promoters realise the lapse. One director suggests the board can still appoint, being only a few days late; another says the power is gone and the Registrar now appoints; a third says the members must do it.

items.stem: What must change for the engagement to be forensic?

options.text: Nothing — audit methodology is the profession's standard for all engagements
options.misconception: stretches assurance methodology over investigation
options.why: Audit method is built for reasonable assurance about statements taken as a whole. Pointed at a suspected fraud, its materiality and reliance shortcuts are the hiding places.

options.text: Everything named — targeted procedures over materiality sampling, corroborated evidence over explanations, findings of fact over an opinion
options.why: A fraudster hides below sampling thresholds, so forensic scoping follows suspicion, red flags and data analytics across the whole population of interest. Management's word is a lead to verify, not evidence — the output may face a courtroom, where chain of custody and corroboration decide weight. And the deliverable reports what was found, quantified and attributed; assurance opinions belong to a different species of engagement.

options.text: The engagement should simply be declined — accountants cannot investigate
options.misconception: vacates a field the profession has standardised
options.why: ICAI issued the FAIS precisely because members do this work. The discipline is doing it under the right standards, not abstaining.

options.text: Only the sampling — deeper samples with the same reliance and opinion suffice
options.misconception: fixes coverage while keeping the wrong evidence bar and output
options.why: Full coverage of uncorroborated explanations proves nothing a tribunal will accept, and an opinion on fairness answers a question nobody in the fraud asked.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting

items.scenario: Engaged to investigate suspected procurement fraud, a forensic accountant is pressed by the audit-trained team to plan the work like a statutory audit: sample the vendors on materiality, accept management's explanations recorded in file notes, and conclude with an opinion that the procurement function presents fairly.

items.stem: Which of the colleague's two positions fail?

options.text: Both — regulatory requirements rise sharply up the layers, and the statutory auditor has direct reporting duties to RBI
options.why: Scale-based regulation is graduated by design: the upper layer carries prudential and governance requirements approaching a bank's, so the audit programme that fits a base-layer lender tests a fraction of what the housing financier must comply with. And the auditor's exception reporting to RBI is the auditor's own statutory duty — discharging it through management is not discharging it.

options.text: Only the reporting point — audit programmes standardise across any lender
options.misconception: concedes the rare duty and keeps the daily error
options.why: Programmes derive from what the entity must comply with. Two layers apart, the compliance universes differ in capital, concentration, governance and disclosure — the programmes cannot match.

options.text: Only the identical programmes — reporting to RBI is indeed management's channel
options.misconception: keeps the duty on the wrong desk
options.why: The exception-reporting framework names the statutory auditor. An auditor who found non-compliance and told only the client has kept the regulator blind exactly as the duty forbids.

options.text: Neither — NBFC prudential norms are uniform and reporting flows through the entity
options.misconception: audits the label instead of the layer
options.why: Uniformity is what the scale-based framework replaced. The audit scales with the regulation, and the direct reporting duty bypasses the entity deliberately.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies

items.scenario: You are auditing two NBFCs: a small base-layer lender, and an upper-layer housing financier that RBI's list places two layers higher. A colleague plans identical audit programmes for both, reasoning that an NBFC is an NBFC, and adds that any RBI Act non-compliance found is management's problem to report to the regulator.

items.stem: Can the two paragraphs go?

options.text: Yes — an unqualified opinion implies every subsidiary matter is satisfactory
options.misconception: folds express statutory answers into implication
options.why: Parliament asked for statements, not inferences. Readers — and regulators inspecting reports — check the answers as given, and an implied yes is a blank.

options.text: The books paragraph stays but the directors one goes — auditors cannot certify board matters
options.misconception: mistakes a written-representation-based statement for a certification
options.why: The auditor reports on 164(2) status on the strength of representations received from the directors, which is exactly how the section contemplates it. Difficulty of verification does not delete the duty.

options.text: Both go if the audit committee approves the shortened format
options.misconception: lets governance approve away statute
options.why: No committee controls the contents of a statutory report. The audit committee oversees the auditor's independence and work, not the statute's checklist.

options.text: No — each 143(3) matter is a statutory reporting duty answered expressly, clean opinion or not
options.why: The opinion answers true and fair; section 143(3) asks its own list of questions, and the report states the answer to each — proper books, information obtained, agreement of accounts with books, standards compliance, director disqualifications, and the rest. They are not commentary the drafter may trim; a missing answer is a non-compliant report however healthy the accounts.

items.scenario: Finalising a company audit report, the senior deletes two paragraphs as clutter: the statement on whether proper books of account were kept, since the opinion already covers the accounts; and the statement on directors' section 164(2) disqualification, since board matters are the secretary's field. The financial statements themselves are clean.

items.stem: Can the April test carry the year?

options.text: No — broken change management means the control tested in April may not be the control that ran in September
options.why: Reliance on an automated control across a period rests on general controls proving the application stayed as tested. Unapproved production changes and shared administrator access mean anyone could have altered or bypassed the match at any time, unlogged. The foundation failed, so the single test supports April at best — the auditor extends testing or goes substantive.

options.text: Yes for amounts below materiality, with manual testing above it
options.misconception: slices control reliance by transaction size
options.why: A compromised control is compromised for every rupee through it. Materiality shapes how much substantive work replaces the reliance, not a size-band where broken controls still count.

options.text: Yes — automated controls are consistent by nature, which is their audit advantage
options.misconception: quotes the benchmark while its condition lies broken
options.why: The consistency argument assumes the program is unchanged. That assumption is precisely what change management evidences, and here it evidences the opposite.

options.text: No, and the IT weaknesses also mean the financial statements must be qualified
options.misconception: jumps from control weakness to opinion modification
options.why: Control failure changes the audit approach — more substantive evidence — and earns a management letter, and IFC reporting where applicable. The opinion qualifies only if sufficient evidence cannot be obtained or misstatements stand.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit in an Automated Environment

items.scenario: An auditor tests the billing application's automated three-way match in April and finds it works perfectly, planning to rely on it for the whole year. Later he learns the IT team shares one administrator login, developers push changes straight to production without approval, and the change log for the year is unreliable.

items.stem: Which engagements does section 144 permit?

options.text: None — an auditor may render no other service of any kind
options.misconception: reads the prohibited list as a total ban
options.why: The section bars its listed services and routes the rest through approval. Tax audits, certifications and representations live lawfully beside statutory audits across the profession.

options.text: Only the tax representation — the spouse's bookkeeping is the auditor acting indirectly, and internal audit of the subsidiary is expressly barred
options.why: The prohibited list covers accounting and book keeping and internal audit, and it applies to the company, its holding company and its subsidiaries alike. "Directly or indirectly" was defined to reach exactly the spouse's-consultancy route. Tax representation is outside the prohibited list and stands with the audit committee's approval it received.

options.text: All three — only services to the audited company itself are restricted
options.misconception: stops the section at the company's own boundary
options.why: The section names the holding and subsidiary companies in the same breath. Auditing the parent while internally auditing the child is auditing one's own feeder work.

options.text: The bookkeeping and the tax work — a spouse's separate firm is a separate person
options.misconception: takes the corporate veil at face value against an anti-avoidance definition
options.why: The Explanation to section 144 defines indirect rendering through relatives and connected entities. The separate registration is the arrangement the definition was written to see through.

items.scenario: An audit firm holds a company's statutory audit. During the year: the partner's spouse's consultancy takes over the company's bookkeeping; the firm itself accepts the internal audit of the company's subsidiary; and the firm provides tax representation before the tribunal for the company, approved by the audit committee.

items.stem: What is missing from the audit of the claims liability?

options.text: The IBNR must be evaluated as an estimate built on an expert's work, and the data feeding the actuary tested — certification is not a substitute for either
options.why: Using an expert's work requires evaluating the expert's competence and objectivity, the reasonableness of methods and assumptions, and the relevance of the result — not re-performing actuarial science, but not outsourcing the opinion either. And the actuary's model eats the insurer's claims data: untested inputs make the finest model an amplifier of error. Reported claims alone are the visible half of the liability.

options.text: Nothing — a statutory appointee's certificate discharges the auditor on that item
options.misconception: lets one professional's certificate close another's duty
options.why: The opinion on the financial statements is the auditor's alone. Certificates are evidence to be evaluated, and the standards on estimates and experts say how.

options.text: The auditor should re-compute the IBNR with an independent actuarial model
options.misconception: replaces evaluation with re-performance
options.why: The auditor may engage an auditor's expert in a contested case, but the baseline duty is evaluation of methods, assumptions and data — a discipline the audit team itself must exercise, not a parallel actuarial department.

options.text: Only a larger sample of reported claims — IBNR is inherently unauditable
options.misconception: audits harder where it is easy and not at all where it matters
options.why: IBNR is an estimate, and estimates are audited through their method, data and assumptions every day. Declaring the uncertain unauditable concedes the riskiest number in the balance sheet.

items.scenario: Auditing a general insurer, the team verifies every reported outstanding claim against surveyor reports and calls the claims liability done. The IBNR figure — certified by the appointed actuary — is accepted without procedures, the senior reasoning that questioning an actuary is beyond an auditor's competence, and the claims data files sent to the actuary were never tested.

items.stem: What report does this engagement actually support?

options.text: No report at all — assurance-less engagements are not reportable
options.misconception: confuses no assurance with no deliverable
options.why: The factual findings report is the deliverable, and banks run covenant monitoring on such reports daily. It reports facts and disclaims assurance — both on purpose.

options.text: The positive opinion is fine, since the bank chose the procedures it trusts
options.misconception: lets the user's procedure list widen the practitioner's conclusion
options.why: The bank chose procedures, not an opinion. A conclusion beyond the work performed is unsupported whoever designed the work.

options.text: A limited assurance review conclusion in negative form
options.misconception: upgrades the engagement one rung instead of none
options.why: Even negative assurance needs the inquiry-and-analytics fabric of a review across the statements. Three covenant procedures support findings, not any form of assurance on the statements.

options.text: Factual findings of the specified procedures, no assurance expressed — the drafted opinion claims an audit nobody performed
options.why: Agreed-upon procedures deliver what was agreed: this ratio recomputed, that balance confirmed, findings stated, conclusions left to the bank. A true-and-fair opinion asserts reasonable assurance over the statements as a whole — evidence three procedures cannot carry. The generous-sounding report is the dangerous one: it promises the bank an audit's comfort at a procedures engagement's depth.

citation.ref: Ch. Review and Related Services (SRE 2400, SRS 4400)

items.scenario: A bank asks a CA firm to verify three specific covenant ratios in a borrower's quarterly figures using procedures the bank itself lists. The firm performs exactly those procedures and drafts a report concluding that "the quarterly statements present a true and fair view", reasoning that a positive conclusion serves the bank better than a dry list of findings.

items.stem: Is he exposed under the CA Act?

options.text: No, provided he declares the receipts in his income tax return
options.misconception: launders misconduct through tax compliance
options.why: Tax law asks whether income was declared; the conduct rule asks whether it should exist. A disclosed kickback is a documented one.

options.text: Yes, but only if the company proves it paid above-market fees
options.misconception: makes employer loss an ingredient
options.why: The clause requires acceptance of the share, nothing more. Loss aggravates; its absence does not absolve.

options.text: Yes — Part II of the First Schedule reaches members in service, and accepting a share of the employer's lawyer's fees is its named misconduct
options.why: The Part exists because the practice-only reading he relies on was too convenient: a member in employment who accepts any part of the fees of a lawyer, CA, broker or agent engaged by the employer commits professional misconduct in terms. Market-rate fees do not cure it — the kickback corrupts his judgment about whom to engage, which is the mischief whether or not the price moved.

options.text: No — the CA Act's schedules govern practice, and employment is outside them
options.misconception: the exact belief Part II was written to defeat
options.why: The Part is titled for members in service. Membership carries the discipline into employment; only the applicable clauses change.

items.scenario: A chartered accountant employed as a company's finance head engages a law firm for the company's litigation. The law firm, grateful for the steady work, credits him personally 10 per cent of its fees each quarter. He reasons that the conduct rules bind only members in practice, and that his employer suffers no loss since the legal fees are market rate.

items.stem: What should the forms actually be?

options.text: 3CB for both, as prepared — one uniform form simplifies compliance
options.misconception: chooses forms by convenience instead of by the other-law audit test
options.why: Rule 6G's split is the whole point of having two forms. A 3CB on a company asserts an opinion this engagement never formed, over an audit that already exists.

options.text: 3CD alone for both — the particulars are what the department reads
options.misconception: ships the annexure without its report
options.why: 3CD is a statement of particulars, certified by the report that covers it. Without 3CA or 3CB there is no auditor's report at all, and the filing is invalid.

options.text: 3CA with 3CD for the company; 3CB with 3CD for the proprietorship
options.why: The company's accounts already carry a Companies Act audit opinion, so the tax auditor reports in Form 3CA, referencing that audit and certifying the particulars in 3CD. The proprietorship has no other audit, so Form 3CB applies and this engagement itself opines on the accounts' true and fair view. "Fuller is safer" would have the tax auditor re-opining on statements another auditor signed.

options.text: 3CA for both, since a chartered accountant's involvement makes any audit statutory
options.misconception: reads "audited under any other law" as "audited by anyone"
options.why: The proprietorship's accounts are audited under no law but 44AB itself. With no other statutory audit to lean on, 3CA would reference an opinion that does not exist.

items.scenario: A CA accepts two tax audits: a private limited company whose statutory audit another firm completed last month, and a proprietorship trading firm with ₹4 crore turnover whose accounts nobody else audits. His article assistant prepares Form 3CB for both, reasoning that 3CB is the fuller form and fuller is safer, with Form 3CD attached to each.

items.stem: What does CARO 2020 require of the auditor here?

options.text: Nothing — CARO concerns the financial statements, and the books are correct
options.misconception: audits only the shareholder-facing set
options.why: The clause's subject is the bank-facing set. Correct books beside inflated bank statements is precisely the reportable condition, not a defence to it.

options.text: Report under clause 3(ii)(b) that the quarterly returns do not agree with the books, with details of the differences
options.why: Limits above five crore sanctioned against current assets put the company squarely in the clause, and its question is exactly this comparison. Padded stock statements inflate drawing power — borrowing against inventory that is not there — and the clause was inserted after bank frauds built on that habit. The explanation is the finding: management admits the two sets differ.

options.text: Qualify the audit opinion, since a 20 per cent difference is material
options.misconception: escalates a CARO disclosure into an opinion modification
options.why: The books — and so the financial statements — are right; the opinion has no misstatement to qualify. The CARO report carries the finding, and the banker reading it learns what the drawing power was built on.

options.text: Report only if the bank itself has complained of the difference
options.misconception: waits for the victim to notice
options.why: The clause asks the auditor to compare, not to await grievances. The banker's ignorance of the padding is the reason the auditor's comparison exists.

items.scenario: A company enjoys ₹40 crore of sanctioned working capital limits against stock and debtors. Comparing the quarterly stock statements filed with the bank against the books, the auditor finds the bank statements consistently report inventory 20 per cent higher. Management explains the bank figures are "estimates for drawing power" and the audited books are what matters.

items.stem: What does the performance audit examine that the department's defence does not touch?

options.text: Nothing — clean transactions at good prices exhaust an auditor's mandate
options.misconception: caps government audit at the voucher
options.why: That cap would grade every failed scheme by its bookkeeping. The C&AG's performance mandate asks what the public got, not only what the department spent.

options.text: Fraud — such waste must mean embezzlement to find
options.misconception: assumes failure implies theft
options.why: Programmes fail honestly through poor design and worse execution. Performance audit documents that failure and recommends redesign; investigation waits for indicators of dishonesty, absent here.

options.text: Efficiency and effectiveness — output per rupee and outcomes against the programme's purpose — where regular, economical spending can still fail
options.why: The defence covers regularity and one E, economy. Performance audit's other two Es are the ones bleeding: 30 per cent coverage measures poor efficiency of conversion from money to canals, and unchanged yields measure ineffectiveness against the objective the outlay was voted for. Cheap pipes to nowhere are the case the three-E framework exists to name.

options.text: The policy choice of irrigation itself, which the audit should condemn
options.misconception: audits the legislature's choice instead of the executive's delivery
options.why: Policy objectives belong to government; audit takes them as given and measures delivery against them. The line protects both the auditor's neutrality and the report's authority.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings

items.scenario: A state irrigation programme spent exactly its budget, every rupee sanctioned and vouched, buying pipes at good prices — but five years on, the canals reach 30 per cent of the intended farmland and crop yields in the command area are unchanged. A performance audit is criticised by the department: "every transaction was regular and economical; there is nothing left to audit."

items.stem: What does SRE 2410 require here?

options.text: Report the margin jump as a key audit matter in the review report
options.misconception: borrows the audit report's furniture for a review
options.why: KAMs belong to audit reports under SA 701. The review concludes in negative assurance — after the doubt is resolved — or carries a modification if it cannot be.

options.text: Resign the review and demand a full audit of the quarter
options.misconception: escalates past the standard's own answer
options.why: The standard's answer is extension, proportionate to the doubt. Most anomalies resolve in a day of targeted work; abandoning the engagement is for impasses, not first responses.

options.text: Extend procedures until the margin doubt resolves — a possible material misstatement suspends the lighter routine
options.why: Inquiry and analytics are the review's floor, not its ceiling. A fifteen-point margin jump is precisely the anomaly the analytics exist to surface, and once a possible material misstatement comes to the auditor's attention the standard requires additional procedures — corroborating the mix claim against sales data, testing cut-off, whatever the doubt demands. Timetables yield to unresolved doubts, or the conclusion does.

options.text: Accept the explanation — limited assurance means limited scepticism
options.misconception: scales scepticism down with the assurance level
options.why: The assurance level scales the planned procedures, never the auditor's duty to chase what those procedures find. Negative assurance over a known open doubt is a false statement in negative form.

items.scenario: During a quarterly limited review, analytical procedures show the quarter's gross margin jumping from 24 to 39 per cent with no price change the auditor knows of. The CFO's explanation is one line: "better product mix." The review timetable allows two days. The audit senior proposes accepting the explanation since limited reviews are built on inquiry, and confirmations would exceed the engagement's scope.
