options.text: Bring the net assets in at their ₹40 crore carrying amount from 1 October 2025 and leave the comparatives for the year ended 31 March 2025 exactly as published
options.misconception: treats a pooling as prospective from the scheme's effective date, missing the restatement in para 9
options.why: Getting the carrying amounts right is only half of pooling. Para 9 restates prior period information as if the combination had occurred from the beginning of the preceding period irrespective of the actual date, and the exception that limits restatement applies only where the entities came under common control after that date. P Ltd has controlled both since 2019, so the full restatement applies.

options.text: Apply the acquisition method — recognise the identifiable net assets at their ₹65 crore fair value and account for the difference against the consideration as goodwill or a bargain purchase
options.misconception: applies the acquisition method to the one class of combination Appendix C removes from it
options.why: The acquisition method is what Appendix C displaces. Because P Ltd controlled both companies before and after, and that control is not transitory, para 8 sends the transaction to pooling of interests, where para 9 expressly forbids adjusting to fair values or recognising new assets.

options.text: Bring the net assets in at their ₹40 crore carrying amount but recognise the ₹7 crore difference as a bargain purchase gain in other comprehensive income, accumulated in equity as capital reserve
options.misconception: imports Ind AS 103's Indian bargain purchase route into a pooling, where no gain arises at all
options.why: The other comprehensive income route for a bargain purchase belongs to the acquisition method, and it is the Indian departure from IFRS 3 that makes Ind AS 103 distinctive. It has no application in a pooling. Under para 12 the ₹7 crore is a direct transfer to capital reserve, never income of any kind.

citation.ref: Appendix C, para 8, para 9 and para 12

items.scenario: P Ltd has held every share of both A Ltd and B Ltd since 2019. Under a scheme approved on 1 October 2025, A Ltd absorbs B Ltd and issues equity shares of nominal value ₹15 crore to P Ltd. B Ltd's books show share capital of ₹22 crore, other reserves of ₹18 crore and net assets at a carrying amount of ₹40 crore; the fair value of those net assets is ₹65 crore. A Ltd is preparing its financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026, with comparatives for the year ended 31 March 2025.

items.stem: How does H Ltd account for the ₹30 crore increase in the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: Leave the liability at ₹40 crore, because contingent consideration is not remeasured after the acquisition date
options.misconception: applies para 58(a), the rule for equity-classified contingent consideration, to a cash-settled obligation
options.why: Only contingent consideration classified as equity escapes remeasurement, and its settlement is then accounted for within equity. This earn-out will be settled in cash, so it is a financial liability and para 58 sends it to fair value at every reporting date.

options.text: Increase goodwill by ₹30 crore, since the earn-out is part of the consideration transferred for the business
options.misconception: reads every later change in an earn-out as a measurement period adjustment to the acquisition accounting
options.why: The measurement period exists to finish incomplete acquisition-date accounting, not to track how the business performs afterwards. Para 45 lets goodwill absorb only what new information tells the acquirer about 1 July 2025. Here the facts at that date have not changed, only the outcome since.

options.text: Recognise nothing now and disclose the earn-out, bringing it into account when the contingency is settled in June 2027
options.misconception: treats an acquisition-date liability as an Ind AS 37 contingent liability awaiting crystallisation
options.why: Contingent consideration is recognised as a liability on the acquisition date under Ind AS 103 and measured under Ind AS 109 thereafter. It never sits in the Ind AS 37 contingent liability regime, so waiting for settlement understates both the liability and the year's charge.

options.text: Charge the ₹30 crore to profit or loss for the year and leave goodwill untouched
options.why: Para 58 splits contingent consideration by its acquisition-date classification. This one is a cash obligation within Ind AS 109's scope, so it is remeasured to fair value at each reporting date with the change in profit or loss. Goodwill would move only for a measurement period adjustment, and para 45 confines those to new information about facts that existed at the acquisition date. A rise driven by the acquiree trading ahead of plan is post-acquisition performance, so goodwill stays where it is.

items.scenario: H Ltd acquired S Ltd on 1 July 2025 for ₹500 crore cash plus an earn-out payable in cash on 30 June 2027 if S Ltd's revenue clears an agreed level. The earn-out was measured at a fair value of ₹40 crore at the acquisition date and is a financial liability within the scope of Ind AS 109. By 31 March 2026 S Ltd is trading well ahead of plan and the fair value of the earn-out has risen to ₹70 crore. Nothing new has come to light about facts that existed on 1 July 2025.

items.stem: What does P Ltd record in its consolidated financial statements?

options.text: Reduce the non-controlling interest by ₹60 crore and debit the remaining ₹35 crore directly to equity attributable to the owners of the parent
options.why: Para 23 makes a change in a parent's ownership interest that does not cost it control an equity transaction. Para B96 then adjusts the carrying amounts of the controlling and non-controlling interests for their new relative shares — half of the ₹120 crore non-controlling interest, being ₹60 crore, comes across — and recognises the ₹35 crore difference between that adjustment and the ₹95 crore paid directly in equity, attributed to the owners of the parent.

options.text: Recognise a loss of ₹35 crore in consolidated profit or loss for the year ended 31 March 2026
options.misconception: routes an equity transaction through profit or loss, as if part of a subsidiary had been bought at a bad price
options.why: Para B96 says the difference is recognised directly in equity. A transaction with owners in their capacity as owners cannot generate income or expense, which is why the ₹35 crore reduces equity without ever appearing in the year's result.

options.text: Remeasure S Ltd's identifiable net assets to fair value at 1 January 2026 and recognise the resulting adjustments in the consolidated financial statements
options.misconception: treats a step-up in an existing holding as a fresh business combination requiring identifiable net assets to be re-fair-valued
options.why: Fair valuing identifiable net assets happens on the date control is obtained. P Ltd already controlled S Ltd, so nothing about the subsidiary's assets changes; only the split of equity between the parent's owners and the minority moves.

options.text: Recognise additional goodwill of ₹35 crore, being the excess of the ₹95 crore paid over the ₹60 crore of net assets acquired
options.misconception: applies acquisition accounting to a purchase made after control was already held
options.why: Goodwill is measured once, when control is obtained. After that the parent is dealing with its own co-owners, not acquiring a business, so para 23 keeps the transaction inside equity. Creating goodwill here would recognise an asset for a transfer between shareholders.

items.scenario: P Ltd holds 80 per cent of S Ltd, which it has controlled for years. In P Ltd's consolidated financial statements the non-controlling interest in S Ltd is carried at ₹120 crore and the goodwill recognised on the original acquisition of S Ltd stands at ₹200 crore. On 1 January 2026 P Ltd buys a further 10 per cent of S Ltd from the minority shareholders for ₹95 crore in cash, taking its holding to 90 per cent.

items.stem: From what date, and on what basis, does the company measure the portfolio at fair value through profit or loss?

options.text: Never — the bonds stay at amortised cost, because a decision about one portfolio is a change of intention rather than a change of business model
options.misconception: mistakes the closure of an entire business line for a portfolio-level change of intention
options.why: A change in intention about particular assets is indeed not a change of business model, but that is not what happened. Ind AS 109's own examples of a qualifying change include an entity terminating a business line, which is exactly the closure of the treasury desk, so para 4.4.1 is engaged.

options.text: From 1 April 2025, restating the year's interest income and fair value movements as though the trading model had applied all year
options.misconception: applies a change of business model retrospectively, like a change in accounting policy
options.why: Para 5.6.1 is explicit that reclassification is prospective and that previously recognised interest, gains and losses are not restated. Treating it as a policy change under Ind AS 8 would rewrite a period during which the hold-to-collect model genuinely applied.

options.text: From 1 April 2026, applied prospectively, with amortised cost carried on unchanged until 31 March 2026 and no restatement of interest or gains already recognised
options.why: Shutting the whole desk is a change of business model, so para 4.4.1 requires reclassification. The date is not the board's, though. Appendix A defines the reclassification date as the first day of the first reporting period following the change, which for an annual reporter whose model changed in November 2025 is 1 April 2026. Para 5.6.1 then applies the reclassification prospectively from that date and bars restating previously recognised gains, losses or interest.

options.text: From 15 November 2025, the date the board approved the closure, with the difference recognised at that date
options.misconception: uses the date the business model actually changed instead of the reclassification date the Standard defines
options.why: The Standard deliberately separates the two dates. The change of model at 15 November 2025 is what triggers reclassification, but Appendix A fixes when it takes effect, and that is the first day of the next reporting period. Measuring from November would let the entity choose its own effective date.

citation.ref: para 5.6.1, with the Appendix A definition of reclassification date

items.scenario: A company's treasury desk holds a portfolio of corporate bonds measured at amortised cost under a business model of holding to collect contractual cash flows. On 15 November 2025 the board approves closing the treasury desk entirely and running the portfolio for short-term trading gains until it is sold down; the decision is announced and is demonstrable to outside parties. The company's reporting period is the year ending 31 March and it prepares no interim financial statements.

items.stem: How does the company account for the rescheduling?

options.text: Keep the loan at ₹500 crore and capitalise the ₹4 crore fee, amortising it over the extended term
options.misconception: treats a rescheduling as a mere change in the timing of cash flows, with the fee as a transaction cost of a continuing loan
options.why: A fee paid on renegotiation is not automatically a cost of a surviving loan. Para B3.3.6 brings the fee into the test itself, and once the test is failed the fee forms part of the consideration for extinguishing the old liability under para 3.3.3, not a deferred charge.

options.text: Treat the old loan as extinguished, recognise the new loan at its ₹470 crore fair value, and take the ₹26 crore difference after the ₹4 crore fee to profit or loss as a gain
options.why: Para B3.3.6 makes terms substantially different when the two present values, both taken at the original effective interest rate, are at least 10 per cent apart. Here ₹495 crore against ₹430 crore is a difference of about 13 per cent, so the test is failed and para 3.3.2 treats the modification as an extinguishment and the recognition of a new liability. Para 3.3.3 puts the difference between the ₹500 crore carrying amount and the consideration, being the ₹470 crore new liability plus the ₹4 crore fee, in profit or loss as a ₹26 crore gain.

options.text: Keep the original liability, recompute its carrying amount as the ₹430 crore present value of the revised cash flows at the original rate, and take the ₹65 crore difference to profit or loss
options.misconception: applies the non-substantial modification route after the 10 per cent test has already been failed
options.why: Recomputing at the original effective interest rate and adjusting the carrying amount is the treatment for a modification that is not substantial. The 10 per cent test is the gate that decides which route applies, and at roughly 13 per cent this rescheduling is through it, so the old liability goes and a new one takes its place.

options.text: Treat it as an extinguishment but present the ₹26 crore in other comprehensive income, as a gain arising from the entity's own credit standing
options.misconception: confuses the own credit risk presentation available for liabilities designated at fair value through profit or loss with a gain on extinguishment
options.why: The other comprehensive income presentation for own credit risk applies only to financial liabilities the entity has designated at fair value through profit or loss. This is an amortised cost loan being extinguished, and para 3.3.3 sends the difference to profit or loss.

citation.ref: para 3.3.2 and 3.3.3, with the 10 per cent test in para B3.3.6

items.scenario: A company carries a term loan at an amortised cost of ₹500 crore with an original effective interest rate of 12 per cent. On 1 October 2025 it agrees a rescheduling with the same lender that stretches the tenor and cuts the coupon, and pays the lender an arrangement fee of ₹4 crore. Discounted at the original 12 per cent, the cash flows under the new terms including that fee have a present value of ₹430 crore, against ₹495 crore for the remaining cash flows of the old loan. The fair value of the rescheduled loan on 1 October 2025 is ₹470 crore.

items.stem: How does the company account for the contract?

options.text: Recognise a contract liability and accrete interest, but reset the discount rate to the prevailing market rate at each reporting date
options.misconception: re-estimates the financing rate after inception, as if it were a floating obligation
options.why: Para 64 fixes the rate at contract inception, reflecting the credit characteristics of the party being financed, and states that the entity shall not update it for changes in interest rates or other circumstances afterwards.

options.text: Recognise revenue of ₹100 lakh on 1 April 2025, when the cash is received in full
options.misconception: treats receipt of the consideration as the point of revenue recognition rather than transfer of control
options.why: Payment and performance are separate questions under Ind AS 115. Control of the machinery passes only on delivery, so until then the cash received is a contract liability, and the time gap between the two is precisely what creates the financing component.

options.text: Recognise a contract liability of ₹100 lakh, accrete interest expense of ₹10 lakh in the year ended 31 March 2026 and ₹11 lakh in the year ended 31 March 2027, and recognise revenue of ₹121 lakh on delivery
options.why: A two-year advance gives the entity a significant benefit of financing, so para 60 requires the promised consideration to be adjusted for the time value of money. The contract liability is accreted at the rate para 64 fixes at inception, giving ₹10 lakh in the first year and ₹11 lakh on the grown balance in the second, and revenue equals the accreted balance of ₹121 lakh when control passes on 31 March 2027.

options.text: Recognise a contract liability of ₹100 lakh with no interest, and revenue of ₹100 lakh on delivery on 31 March 2027
options.misconception: reads the financing component as something only long credit creates, so an advance from the customer is ignored
options.why: Para 60 works in both directions and names the customer as well as the entity. The one-year practical expedient in para 63 would have removed the adjustment, but the gap here is two years, so the expedient is unavailable and the financing must be recognised.

items.scenario: On 1 April 2025 a company contracts to build and deliver custom machinery to a customer on 31 March 2027, control passing only on delivery. The customer pays the whole price of ₹100 lakh in advance on 1 April 2025. A separate financing transaction between these two parties at contract inception would carry a rate of 10 per cent a year.

items.stem: How does the lessee account for the modification?

options.text: Leave both the lease liability and the right-of-use asset as they are and simply charge the reduced rentals to profit or loss as they fall due
options.misconception: treats a renegotiated lease as a change in cash flows that needs no remeasurement
options.why: A modification changes the scope or the consideration of a lease that was not part of the original terms, and para 45 requires the liability to be remeasured at a revised discount rate. Running the new rentals through profit or loss would leave the balance sheet carrying an obligation for space the lessee no longer has.

options.text: Remeasure the lease liability at a revised discount rate and adjust the whole difference against the right-of-use asset, with no gain or loss
options.misconception: applies para 46(b), the route for all other modifications, to a modification that decreases scope
options.why: Para 46 splits into two. Sub-paragraph (b) absorbs the remeasurement into the right-of-use asset, but only for modifications that do not reduce scope. A reduction in scope falls under sub-paragraph (a) first, and a partial termination gain or loss has to be recognised before anything is adjusted against the asset.

options.text: Account for the change as a separate lease of the retained 3,000 square feet, leaving the original lease untouched
options.misconception: applies para 44 to a modification that reduces scope, when both of its conditions require an increase
options.why: Para 44 opens only when the modification adds the right to use one or more underlying assets and the consideration rises commensurately with the stand-alone price for that addition. Giving space back fails both limbs, so the existing lease is remeasured instead.

options.text: Cut the right-of-use asset by ₹24 lakh and the lease liability by ₹32 lakh for the 40 per cent partial termination, recognise the ₹8 lakh difference as a gain in profit or loss, then remeasure the remaining liability at a revised discount rate against the right-of-use asset
options.why: Para 44 is closed because the scope has fallen, not risen, so this is not a separate lease. Para 46(a) governs a modification that decreases scope — the right-of-use asset is first decreased to reflect the partial termination, which at 40 per cent of the space is ₹24 lakh against ₹60 lakh and ₹32 lakh against ₹80 lakh, and the ₹8 lakh difference goes to profit or loss. Para 45 then remeasures what is left at a revised discount rate, and that second adjustment goes to the right-of-use asset.

items.scenario: A lessee took 5,000 square feet of office space on a ten-year lease. At the start of year six it agrees with the lessor to give up 2,000 square feet, keeping 3,000 for the remaining five years, with the rent cut in proportion. Immediately before the change the lease liability stands at ₹80 lakh and the right-of-use asset at ₹60 lakh.

items.stem: What deferred tax does the parent recognise in its consolidated financial statements at 31 March 2026?

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹30 crore on the subsidiary and ₹8 crore on the associate, being 20 per cent of each amount
options.misconception: reads para 39 as an unconditional recognition rule and skips the two-part exception it carries
options.why: Para 39's exception is not optional where its conditions are met. Both limbs are satisfied for the subsidiary, so no liability is recognised on its ₹150 crore, however plainly the temporary difference exists.

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹8 crore on the associate, but only once the associate's dividend has actually been declared before the reporting date
options.misconception: makes recognition wait for the declaration rather than turning on whether reversal is expected in the foreseeable future
options.why: Para 39 turns on whether the investor can control the timing of the reversal and whether reversal is improbable in the foreseeable future, not on whether a dividend has been declared. An expected distribution is enough to close off the exception.

options.text: No deferred tax liability on the subsidiary's ₹150 crore, and a deferred tax liability of ₹8 crore on the associate's ₹40 crore
options.why: Para 39 requires a deferred tax liability on taxable temporary differences from investments in subsidiaries and associates unless both conditions are met. For the subsidiary they are — para 40 notes that a parent controlling the dividend policy controls the timing of the reversal, and the board's reinvestment resolution makes it probable there will be no reversal in the foreseeable future. For the associate the first condition fails, because a 30 per cent holder does not control the dividend policy, and a dividend is expected next year, so ₹40 crore at 20 per cent gives ₹8 crore.

options.text: No deferred tax on either, because undistributed profits consolidated into group reserves are not a temporary difference
options.misconception: denies that undistributed profits create a temporary difference on the investment at all
options.why: Para 38 names the existence of undistributed profits of subsidiaries, branches, associates and joint arrangements as a source of temporary differences, because the carrying amount of the investment in the consolidated financial statements moves with those profits while its tax base does not.

items.scenario: An Indian parent has two overseas investments. Its wholly owned subsidiary has undistributed post-acquisition profits of ₹150 crore at 31 March 2026, and the parent's board has resolved to reinvest those profits in the subsidiary's expansion with no dividend expected for many years. Its 30 per cent associate has undistributed post-acquisition profits attributable to the parent of ₹40 crore, and the associate's board is expected to declare a dividend next year. Distributions from either would be taxed in the parent's hands at 20 per cent.

items.stem: How is the ₹70 lakh impairment loss allocated?

options.text: Goodwill down to nil for ₹50 lakh, then the remaining ₹20 lakh pro rata — ₹4 lakh against the patent, ₹8 lakh against the plant and ₹8 lakh against the building
options.misconception: applies the pro rata step correctly but overlooks the floor para 105 puts under an individual asset
options.why: This gets the ordering right and then carries the patent to ₹26 lakh, below the ₹28 lakh a buyer would pay for it net of costs. Para 105 forbids that, caps the patent's share at ₹2 lakh, and pushes the ₹2 lakh released onto the remaining assets.

options.text: Goodwill down to nil for ₹50 lakh, the patent down to ₹28 lakh for ₹2 lakh, and the remaining ₹18 lakh split ₹9 lakh each against the plant and the building, leaving them at ₹51 lakh each
options.why: Para 104 runs the loss against goodwill first, taking ₹50 lakh and leaving ₹20 lakh. A pro rata allocation on carrying amounts would push the patent to ₹26 lakh, but para 105 bars writing any asset below the highest of its fair value less costs of disposal where measurable, its value in use and zero, so the patent stops at ₹28 lakh. Para 105 then reallocates what the floor blocked pro rata to the other assets, and the plant and building carry equal amounts at ₹60 lakh each, so they take ₹9 lakh each. The unit ends at ₹130 lakh.

options.text: The whole ₹70 lakh spread pro rata across all four assets on their carrying amounts, including goodwill
options.misconception: ignores the ordering in para 104 that makes goodwill absorb the loss before anything else
options.why: Para 104 is a sequence, not a formula. Goodwill is written down first and in full before any other asset in the unit is touched, precisely because goodwill has no measurable recoverable amount of its own.

options.text: Goodwill down to nil for ₹50 lakh, with the remaining ₹20 lakh charged wholly against the plant as the asset most likely to have lost value
options.misconception: allocates the residual by judgement about which asset caused the impairment instead of pro rata on carrying amounts
options.why: Para 104 allows no such judgement. Once goodwill is exhausted the balance is allocated pro rata on the carrying amount of each asset in the unit, and the only permitted departure is the para 105 floor, which protects an asset rather than singling one out.

items.scenario: A cash-generating unit carries goodwill of ₹50 lakh, a patent of ₹30 lakh, plant of ₹60 lakh and a building of ₹60 lakh, a total of ₹200 lakh. Its recoverable amount at the year end is ₹130 lakh, so an impairment loss of ₹70 lakh arises. The patent's fair value less costs of disposal can be measured reliably at ₹28 lakh. No other asset in the unit has a separately measurable fair value less costs of disposal or value in use.

items.stem: At what fair value does the company measure the holding?

options.text: ₹4,650 a tonne, or ₹4.65 crore in total — the Market X price less both transport and transaction costs, being what the company would actually realise
options.misconception: deducts transaction costs, treating fair value as a net realisable amount
options.why: Para 25 keeps transaction costs out. They are specific to how a particular entity enters a transaction rather than a characteristic of the asset, which is why two entities holding the same commodity in the same market measure the same fair value.

options.text: ₹4,800 a tonne, or ₹4.80 crore in total — the Market X price less transport, with transaction costs left out
options.why: Market X is the principal market, being the one with the greatest volume and level of activity that the company can access, so para 16 measures there. Para 18 keeps the measurement in that market even though Market Y would net ₹4,750 a tonne against Market X's ₹4,650. Para 25 refuses to adjust the price for transaction costs, and para 26 requires the ₹200 transport adjustment because location is a characteristic of the asset, leaving ₹4,800.

options.text: ₹5,000 a tonne, or ₹5.00 crore in total — the unadjusted quoted price in the principal market
options.misconception: leaves out the transport adjustment para 26 requires when location is a characteristic of the asset
options.why: Transport costs are not transaction costs. Para 26 says so expressly and requires the price to be adjusted for the cost of getting the asset from where it is to that market whenever location is one of its characteristics, as it is for a commodity.

options.text: ₹4,850 a tonne, or ₹4.85 crore in total — the Market Y price less transport, because Market Y leaves the company better off
options.misconception: goes to the most advantageous market when a principal market exists
options.why: The most advantageous market is a fallback, not a preference. Para 16 uses it only in the absence of a principal market, and para 18 says so directly, the price in the principal market is used even if a different market is potentially more advantageous.

items.scenario: A company holds 10,000 tonnes of a commodity and can access two markets for it. Market X has by far the greatest volume and level of activity for this commodity and is where the company normally transacts; its price is ₹5,000 a tonne, with transport of ₹200 and transaction costs of ₹150 a tonne. Market Y quotes ₹5,300 a tonne, with transport of ₹450 and transaction costs of ₹100 a tonne. Location is a characteristic of the commodity.

items.stem: How are the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026 presented?

options.text: Show the single ₹7 crore amount for the current year but leave the prior year's statement of profit and loss exactly as published, since the division was still a continuing operation then
options.misconception: treats discontinued operation presentation as prospective and ignores para 34
options.why: Para 34 requires the prior period disclosures to be re-presented so they relate to all operations discontinued by the end of the latest period presented. Without it the two years would not be comparable, which is the whole point of separating a discontinued operation.

options.text: Show a single net amount of ₹7 crore for the discontinued operation in the statement of profit and loss with the analysis in the notes, re-present the ₹30 crore in the prior year's profit or loss on the same basis, and leave the balance sheet at 31 March 2025 as published
options.why: Para 32 makes a separate major line of business that has been disposed of a discontinued operation. Para 33 collapses its post-tax result of minus ₹18 crore and the post-tax disposal gain of ₹25 crore into a single ₹7 crore amount on the face of the statement of profit and loss, with revenue, expenses, pre-tax result and tax analysed in the notes. Para 34 re-presents the prior period so the comparison is like for like, and para 40 expressly forbids doing the same to the balance sheets of prior periods.

options.text: Show the single ₹7 crore amount and re-present the balance sheet at 31 March 2025 to move the division's ₹90 crore of assets into a held for sale line
options.misconception: extends the re-presentation from the statement of profit and loss to the balance sheet
options.why: Para 34 re-presents only the para 33 disclosures, which are the profit or loss and cash flow figures. Para 40 is the direct answer for the balance sheet — amounts presented for assets and liabilities classified as held for sale are not reclassified or re-presented for prior periods.

options.text: Keep the division's revenue and expenses within continuing operations line by line for the year ended 31 March 2026 and disclose the ₹25 crore disposal gain as an exceptional item
options.misconception: treats a discontinued major line of business as an ordinary operation with a one-off gain attached
options.why: Once para 32 is met, para 33 requires the single amount presentation. Leaving the division's trading inside continuing operations tells the reader nothing about which part of the year's result will recur, which is exactly what the discontinued operation line is for.

items.scenario: A company sold its entire retail division, a separate major line of business, on 15 January 2026. For the year ended 31 March 2026 the division made a post-tax loss of ₹18 crore up to disposal, and the disposal itself produced a post-tax gain of ₹25 crore. In the year ended 31 March 2025 the division made a post-tax profit of ₹30 crore, shown line by line in that year's published statement of profit and loss, and its assets of ₹90 crore sat among the company's ordinary non-current assets in the balance sheet at 31 March 2025.

items.stem: How much of the ₹12 crore is recognised, where, and when?

options.text: Nothing until 30 November 2027, when the employees complete the two years and the improved benefit vests
options.misconception: makes recognition wait for vesting, which para 103 removed
options.why: Para 103 fixes recognition at the earlier of the plan amendment or curtailment and the recognition of related restructuring costs or termination benefits. Vesting is not one of those dates, so waiting for it leaves the obligation understated for two full years.

options.text: The whole ₹12 crore as an expense in profit or loss on 1 December 2025, when the plan amendment occurred
options.why: Para 102 makes the ₹12 crore past service cost, being the change in the present value of the obligation caused by a plan amendment. Para 103 recognises past service cost as an expense at the earlier of the date the amendment occurs and the date related restructuring costs or termination benefits are recognised, and there are none here. Para 120 puts service cost, past service cost included, in profit or loss.

options.text: ₹2 crore in the year ended 31 March 2026, being ₹12 crore spread on a straight-line basis over the two-year vesting period from 1 December 2025
options.misconception: applies the superseded treatment that amortised unvested past service cost over the period to vesting
options.why: Spreading unvested past service cost over the vesting period is the position Ind AS 19 removed. Para 103 recognises it in full at the amendment date, and it draws no distinction between benefits that have vested and benefits that have not.

options.text: The whole ₹12 crore in other comprehensive income, as a remeasurement of the net defined benefit liability
options.misconception: files past service cost with actuarial remeasurements instead of with service cost
options.why: Remeasurements are actuarial gains and losses, the return on plan assets beyond net interest, and asset ceiling movements, and para 120 keeps those in other comprehensive income. Past service cost is a component of service cost and goes to profit or loss.

items.scenario: On 1 December 2025 a company amends its gratuity plan to improve the benefit formula, and grants the improvement to all existing employees for their past service. The actuary measures the increase in the present value of the defined benefit obligation at ₹12 crore. Under the amendment an employee becomes entitled to the improved benefit only after completing a further two years of service. The finance team proposes to spread the ₹12 crore over those two years. The year ends 31 March 2026 and no restructuring or termination benefits are involved.

items.stem: How does P Ltd attribute the ₹40 crore loss, and where does that leave the non-controlling interests?

options.text: Charge the whole ₹40 crore against the owners of the parent, because the loss is larger than the ₹3 crore the non-controlling interests have at stake in S Ltd
options.misconception: treats the non-controlling interests as a limited-liability floor with the parent absorbing everything beyond it
options.why: Para B94 requires the entity to attribute profit or loss and each component of other comprehensive income to the owners of the parent and to the non-controlling interests, and it says in terms that the attribution of total comprehensive income continues even if it results in the non-controlling interests having a deficit balance. Nothing in Ind AS 110 moves the excess to the parent.

options.text: Charge ₹15 crore against the non-controlling interests for their equity share and credit them the ₹10 crore preference entitlement, a net ₹5 crore, leaving ₹35 crore with the owners of the parent and the non-controlling interests at a deficit balance of ₹2 crore
options.why: Para B95 computes the group's share of a subsidiary's result after adjusting for the dividends on cumulative preference shares classified as equity and held by non-controlling interests, whether or not those dividends have been declared. The ₹40 crore loss is therefore ₹50 crore attributable to the equity shares, of which the non-controlling interests' 30 per cent is ₹15 crore, against which their ₹10 crore preference entitlement is credited. Para B94 attributes profit or loss and total comprehensive income to the owners of the parent and to the non-controlling interests even if this results in the non-controlling interests having a deficit balance, so the ₹3 crore opening figure becomes a deficit of ₹2 crore rather than stopping at nil.

options.text: Charge ₹12 crore against the non-controlling interests and ₹28 crore against the owners of the parent, bringing the preference dividend into the attribution only in the year it is declared
options.misconception: waits for the preference dividend to be declared, when para B95 adjusts whether or not it has been declared
options.why: The whole point of para B95 is that a cumulative entitlement accumulates. Deferring the adjustment until declaration would let the group take 70 per cent of a result over which the preference shareholders have a prior claim, and would reverse itself in a later year with no economic event behind the reversal.

options.text: Charge ₹12 crore against the non-controlling interests, being 30 per cent of the ₹40 crore loss, and stop them at nil once the ₹3 crore opening balance is exhausted, the owners of the parent absorbing the rest
options.misconception: applies the equity method's nil floor for an associate's losses to a consolidated subsidiary's non-controlling interests
options.why: Two errors ride together here. The preference entitlement is ignored, and the losses are then stopped at zero as though the minority were an equity-accounted associate under Ind AS 28 para 38. Para B94 sets no floor at all — it attributes even where the result is the non-controlling interests having a deficit balance — and the nil floor belongs only to the equity method, where the investor has no obligation to fund further losses.

items.scenario: P Ltd holds 70 per cent of the equity shares of S Ltd. S Ltd also has 10 per cent cumulative preference shares of ₹100 crore, classified as equity, every one of them held outside the group. For the year ended 31 March 2026 S Ltd made a loss after tax of ₹40 crore and no preference dividend was declared. In P Ltd's consolidated balance sheet the non-controlling interests in respect of S Ltd's equity shares stood at ₹3 crore at 1 April 2025, and S Ltd had no other comprehensive income for the year.

items.stem: How are these holdings dealt with in V Ltd's and H Ltd's consolidated financial statements?

options.text: V Ltd measures the three portfolio companies at fair value through profit or loss, and H Ltd carries them at that same fair value because the measurement made by an investment entity subsidiary is preserved on consolidation upward
options.misconception: carries the investment entity's fair value measurement up to a parent that is not an investment entity, which para 33 refuses
options.why: Para 33 is explicit — a parent of an investment entity shall consolidate all entities that it controls, including those controlled through an investment entity subsidiary, unless the parent itself is an investment entity. H Ltd is an industrial group, so the fair value measurement stops at V Ltd and H Ltd consolidates the portfolio companies line by line.

options.text: V Ltd consolidates all four subsidiaries because it controls each of them, and H Ltd consolidates them in turn
options.misconception: reads control as always producing consolidation and misses the express exception in para 31
options.why: Control is the trigger for consolidation, and para 31 is a stated exception to it — an investment entity shall not consolidate its subsidiaries or apply Ind AS 103 when it obtains control of another entity. The exception is mandatory wherever the para 27 definition is met; it is not an accounting policy choice.

options.text: V Ltd measures the three portfolio companies at fair value through profit or loss and consolidates VS Ltd; H Ltd consolidates all four, the three portfolio companies included
options.why: Para 27 makes V Ltd an investment entity — it obtains funds from investors to provide them with investment management services, commits to invest solely for capital appreciation and investment income, and measures performance on a fair value basis. Para 31 then stops it consolidating its subsidiaries or applying Ind AS 103, and measures each investment in a subsidiary at fair value through profit or loss under Ind AS 109. Para 32 carves out a subsidiary providing services that relate to the investment entity's investment activities, so VS Ltd is consolidated. Para 33 makes a parent that is not itself an investment entity consolidate everything it controls, including what it controls through an investment entity subsidiary.
keywords: fair value through profit or loss

options.text: V Ltd measures all four subsidiaries at fair value through profit or loss, VS Ltd included, since the exception in para 31 admits of no exception of its own
options.misconception: overlooks the para 32 carve-out for a subsidiary providing investment-related services
options.why: Para 32 says, notwithstanding para 31, that where an investment entity has a subsidiary providing services that relate to the investment entity's investment activities, it shall consolidate that subsidiary and apply Ind AS 103 to its acquisition. VS Ltd exists to service V Ltd's own investing, so it is consolidated rather than fair valued.

items.scenario: V Ltd is a fund that raised money from forty unrelated investors, commits in its offering document to invest solely for capital appreciation and dividend income, and reports every holding to those investors at fair value. It controls three portfolio companies — a manufacturer, a software firm and a retailer — holding between 60 and 100 per cent of each. It also wholly owns VS Ltd, whose only business is providing investment advisory and administrative services to V Ltd itself. V Ltd is in turn wholly owned by H Ltd, a listed industrial group that is not an investment entity.

items.stem: What does A Ltd recognise for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: Leave A Ltd's own profit untouched, and recognise a share of the associate's profit of ₹222 lakh
options.misconception: treats a sale to an associate as a completed sale to an outsider, so no downstream elimination happens at all
options.why: Para 28 names downstream transactions — sales or contributions of assets from the investor to its associate — as one of the two cases it governs. A Ltd has an interest in the buyer, so 30 per cent of the ₹100 lakh has not been earned from anyone outside and is eliminated.

options.text: Reduce A Ltd's own profit by the whole ₹100 lakh, and recognise a share of the associate's profit of ₹222 lakh
options.misconception: eliminates a downstream unrealised profit in full, as if the associate were a consolidated subsidiary
options.why: Full elimination is the Ind AS 110 rule for a subsidiary, where the group owns the whole of the profit it is cancelling. An associate is not consolidated, and para 28 recognises the gain on a downstream sale to the extent of unrelated investors' interests — the other 70 per cent of B Ltd is owned by outsiders, so ₹70 lakh of A Ltd's profit is genuinely realised and only ₹30 lakh goes.

options.text: Reduce A Ltd's own profit by the whole ₹100 lakh, and recognise a share of the associate's profit of ₹180 lakh, being ₹240 lakh less the whole ₹60 lakh
options.misconception: applies Ind AS 110's full elimination of intragroup profits to an equity-accounted associate on both legs
options.why: This eliminates twice as much as the Standard asks on the downstream leg and more than three times as much on the upstream one. Para 28 caps both eliminations at the investor's own interest, so ₹30 lakh and ₹18 lakh, and the remaining unrealised profit belongs to unrelated investors in B Ltd.

options.text: Reduce A Ltd's own profit by ₹30 lakh for the downstream sale, and recognise a share of the associate's profit of ₹222 lakh, being ₹240 lakh less ₹18 lakh for the upstream sale
options.why: Para 28 recognises gains and losses from upstream and downstream transactions only to the extent of unrelated investors' interests in the associate, so 30 per cent of each unrealised profit is eliminated and no more. The downstream ₹100 lakh sits in A Ltd's own profit and loses ₹30 lakh there. The upstream ₹60 lakh sits inside B Ltd's ₹800 lakh, so A Ltd's ₹240 lakh share loses ₹18 lakh and becomes ₹222 lakh. The upstream leg gives the same ₹222 lakh whether the elimination is taken against the share or against the associate's result, which is why the downstream leg is where this question is decided.

items.scenario: A Ltd holds 30 per cent of B Ltd, an associate it equity accounts. During the year ended 31 March 2026 A Ltd sold goods to B Ltd for ₹500 lakh, making a profit of ₹100 lakh, and B Ltd still held the whole consignment at the year end. In the same year B Ltd sold goods to A Ltd for ₹300 lakh, making a profit of ₹60 lakh, and A Ltd still held all of those goods at the year end. B Ltd's profit for the year was ₹800 lakh. Neither transaction gives any evidence of a fall in net realisable value or of impairment.

items.stem: How does X Ltd account for the additional 20 per cent interest?

options.text: Apply the Ind AS 103 principles to the additional 20 per cent — its share of the identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value, goodwill for any excess, the ₹6 crore expensed — and leave the previously held 30 per cent at its ₹210 crore carrying amount
options.why: Para 21A applies all the Ind AS 103 business combinations principles that do not conflict with Ind AS 111 where the activity of a joint operation constitutes a business, and it says in terms that this covers additional interests as well as the initial one. Para B33A lists what comes across, including measuring identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value, recognising acquisition-related costs as expenses in the periods in which they are incurred, and recognising goodwill. Para B33C is the departure from a step acquisition — previously held interests in the joint operation are not remeasured if the joint operator retains joint control.

options.text: Apply the Ind AS 103 principles to the additional 20 per cent and also remeasure the previously held 30 per cent to its ₹360 crore fair value, taking the ₹150 crore gain to profit or loss
options.misconception: imports the step acquisition remeasurement of Ind AS 103 into a joint operation where joint control is retained
options.why: A step acquisition under Ind AS 103 remeasures a previously held equity interest because control is being obtained for the first time and the old stake is treated as sold and bought back. X Ltd had joint control before and has joint control after, so nothing crosses that line. Para B33C says previously held interests in the joint operation are not remeasured, and the ₹150 crore is never recognised.

options.text: Equity account the 50 per cent interest from 1 October 2025, since holding half of a joint arrangement makes it a joint venture rather than a joint operation
options.misconception: lets the size of the holding decide the classification, when Ind AS 111 turns on rights to assets and obligations for liabilities
options.why: The classification of a joint arrangement does not move with the percentage held. JO gives its parties rights to the assets and obligations for the liabilities, which makes it a joint operation whatever the split, and a joint operator records its share of each asset, liability, revenue and expense rather than equity accounting a net investment.

options.text: Capitalise the ₹6 crore of costs into the price of the additional interest and bring the identifiable assets and liabilities in at the seller's carrying amounts rather than at fair value
options.misconception: treats the purchase of an interest in a joint operation that is a business as the acquisition of a group of assets
options.why: Buying a group of assets is one thing and buying into a business is another. Para B33A brings the Ind AS 103 principles across for a joint operation whose activity is a business, and two of the items it lists are measuring identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value and recognising acquisition-related costs as expenses in the periods in which the costs are incurred.

items.scenario: X Ltd holds a 30 per cent interest in JO, a joint operation running a producing oilfield whose activity is a business as defined in Ind AS 103. The parties share joint control and X Ltd records its share of JO's assets and liabilities line by line. On 1 October 2025 X Ltd buys a further 20 per cent from another joint operator for ₹260 crore, taking it to 50 per cent and retaining joint control. The fair value of its existing 30 per cent interest at that date is ₹360 crore against a carrying amount of ₹210 crore. Legal and due diligence costs on the purchase were ₹6 crore.

items.stem: How is the subsidiary translated for the consolidated financial statements, and what exchange difference arises?

options.text: Assets and liabilities at the ₹88 closing rate and income and expenses at the ₹85 average rate, giving a translated profit of ₹1,700 lakh and an exchange difference of ₹560 lakh recognised in other comprehensive income
options.why: Para 39 translates assets and liabilities for each balance sheet presented at the closing rate at that date, income and expenses at the exchange rates at the dates of the transactions, and recognises all resulting exchange differences in other comprehensive income; para 40 accepts an average rate as an approximation where rates have not fluctuated significantly. Closing net assets of ₹10,560 lakh less opening net assets of ₹8,300 lakh less the ₹1,700 lakh translated profit leaves ₹560 lakh, which is exactly what para 41 describes — ₹500 lakh from retranslating the opening net assets at a closing rate that differs from the previous one, and ₹60 lakh from translating the profit at ₹85 while the closing balance sheet sits at ₹88.

options.text: Assets and liabilities at the ₹88 closing rate and income and expenses at the ₹85 average rate, with the ₹560 lakh exchange difference recognised in profit or loss
options.misconception: applies the para 23 treatment of an individual foreign currency monetary item to the translation of a whole foreign operation
options.why: Exchange differences on individual monetary items do go to profit or loss under para 23, and that is the rule the parent applies to its own dollar receivable. Translating a foreign operation is a different exercise. Para 39(c) sends all the resulting exchange differences to other comprehensive income, and para 41 keeps the cumulative amount in a separate component of equity until the foreign operation is disposed of.

options.text: Assets and liabilities at the ₹88 closing rate and income and expenses at the same ₹88 closing rate, giving a translated profit of ₹1,760 lakh and an exchange difference of ₹500 lakh in other comprehensive income
options.misconception: translates income and expenses at the closing rate, when para 39(b) uses the rates at the dates of the transactions
options.why: The balance sheet answer is right and the profit and loss answer is not. Para 39(b) uses the exchange rates at the dates of the transactions for income and expenses, which is why para 40 offers the average rate as the practical stand-in. Using the closing rate would value a year's trading at one day's rate and would hide the second source of exchange difference that para 41 identifies.

options.text: Non-monetary assets at the historical rates at which they were acquired and monetary items at the ₹88 closing rate, with the differences taken to profit or loss
options.misconception: applies the temporal method, translating a foreign operation item by item as though the rupee were its functional currency
options.why: Splitting monetary from non-monetary items is what an entity does inside its own books once its functional currency is settled. This subsidiary's functional currency is the US dollar, so para 39 translates its whole balance sheet at the closing rate, and the historical-rate approach would apply only if the rupee had been its functional currency in the first place.

items.scenario: An Indian parent presents in rupees and has a wholly owned United States subsidiary whose functional currency is the US dollar and whose economy is not hyperinflationary. The subsidiary's net assets were USD 100 lakh at 1 April 2025 and USD 120 lakh at 31 March 2026, and its profit for the year was USD 20 lakh, earned evenly through the year. No dividend was paid. The exchange rate was ₹83 to the dollar on 1 April 2025, ₹88 on 31 March 2026, and averaged ₹85 over the year, with no sharp swings inside it.

items.stem: What does the company recognise at 31 March 2026, and what becomes of the reserve when the purchase happens?

options.text: ₹110 lakh in other comprehensive income with nothing in profit or loss, because the reserve records the gain on the hedging instrument
options.misconception: takes the whole gain on the hedging instrument to the reserve instead of the lower of the two cumulative amounts
options.why: Para 6.5.11(a) is a lower-of test taken in absolute amounts, and the cumulative change in the hedged item at ₹100 lakh is the smaller of the two. An over-hedge is not effective merely because the instrument has moved, and para 6.5.11(c) sends the ₹10 lakh the hedged item cannot account for to profit or loss as hedge ineffectiveness.

options.text: ₹100 lakh in other comprehensive income building the cash flow hedge reserve and ₹10 lakh in profit or loss, with the ₹100 lakh later removed from the reserve and included in the initial cost of the inventory
options.why: Para 6.5.11(a) adjusts the cash flow hedge reserve to the lower, in absolute amounts, of the cumulative gain on the hedging instrument at ₹110 lakh and the cumulative change in the present value of the hedged expected future cash flows at ₹100 lakh, so the reserve carries ₹100 lakh. Para 6.5.11(b) puts that effective portion in other comprehensive income and para 6.5.11(c) sends the remaining ₹10 lakh to profit or loss as hedge ineffectiveness. Para 6.5.11(d)(i) then removes the accumulated amount from the reserve and includes it directly in the initial cost of the non-financial asset, which it states is not a reclassification adjustment.

options.text: ₹110 lakh in profit or loss, since a forward contract is a derivative measured at fair value through profit or loss
options.misconception: ignores the hedge designation and defaults to the measurement the derivative would carry without hedge accounting
options.why: A derivative is at fair value through profit or loss by default, and that default is precisely what hedge accounting displaces. The relationship meets the qualifying criteria in para 6.4.1, so para 6.5.11 governs, the effective portion goes to other comprehensive income and only the ineffective ₹10 lakh reaches profit or loss.

options.text: ₹100 lakh in other comprehensive income and ₹10 lakh in profit or loss, with the ₹100 lakh reclassified from the reserve to profit or loss when the inventory is eventually sold
options.misconception: applies para 6.5.11(d)(ii) to a forecast transaction that produces a non-financial asset, which para 6.5.11(d)(i) governs
options.why: The measurement at 31 March 2026 is right and what happens next is not. Para 6.5.11(d)(i) applies where the hedged forecast transaction results in the recognition of a non-financial asset, and it removes the accumulated amount from the reserve into the asset's initial cost as a basis adjustment. Reclassification to profit or loss when the hedged cash flows hit the result is para 6.5.11(d)(ii), which covers cash flow hedges other than those.

items.scenario: On 1 October 2025 a company designates a commodity forward contract as the hedging instrument in a cash flow hedge of a highly probable forecast purchase of raw material expected in June 2026. Every qualifying criterion in para 6.4.1 is met. At 31 March 2026 the cumulative gain on the forward contract since inception is ₹110 lakh, and the cumulative change in the present value of the hedged expected future cash flows since inception is ₹100 lakh. The forecast purchase is still expected to happen and will be recognised as inventory.

items.stem: What total loss allowance does the company carry at 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹2 lakh, ₹5 lakh and ₹1 lakh — ₹8 lakh in total, because none of the three borrowers has actually defaulted
options.misconception: waits for an actual default before moving an asset to lifetime expected credit losses
options.why: Para 5.5.9 compares the risk of a default occurring on the instrument at the reporting date with the risk of a default occurring at initial recognition, and it says the assessment uses the change in the risk of a default rather than the change in the amount of expected credit losses. A default is not the trigger. Loan B being more than 30 days past due raises the presumption in para 5.5.11 and moves it across.

options.text: ₹2 lakh, ₹22 lakh and ₹6 lakh — ₹30 lakh in total, treating Loan C's widened spread as a significant increase in credit risk
options.misconception: ignores the low credit risk simplification in para 5.5.10 and reads any deterioration as significant
options.why: Para 5.5.10 permits an entity to assume that credit risk has not increased significantly since initial recognition where the financial instrument is determined to have low credit risk at the reporting date. Loan C is investment grade at that date, so the simplification is available whatever the movement in its spread since purchase.

options.text: ₹2 lakh on Loan A, ₹22 lakh on Loan B and ₹1 lakh on Loan C — ₹25 lakh in total
options.why: Para 5.5.5 measures the allowance at 12-month expected credit losses where credit risk has not increased significantly since initial recognition, which is Loan A. Para 5.5.11 sets a rebuttable presumption that credit risk has increased significantly once contractual payments are more than 30 days past due, and the company has nothing with which to rebut it, so para 5.5.3 moves Loan B to lifetime expected credit losses. Para 5.5.10 lets an entity assume no significant increase where the instrument has low credit risk at the reporting date, so Loan C stays at 12-month expected credit losses.

options.text: ₹9 lakh, ₹22 lakh and ₹6 lakh — ₹37 lakh in total, lifetime expected credit losses on all three
options.misconception: applies the simplified approach to loan assets it does not cover
options.why: The simplified approach in para 5.5.15, which always measures at lifetime expected credit losses, is confined to trade receivables, contract assets and lease receivables. These are loans, so the general model in paras 5.5.3 and 5.5.5 applies and each asset is placed according to whether its credit risk has increased significantly since initial recognition.

items.scenario: A non-banking finance company holds three loan assets at amortised cost at 31 March 2026, none of them trade receivables, contract assets or lease receivables. Loan A's borrower carries the same credit rating as at origination and nothing is overdue; its 12-month expected credit losses are ₹2 lakh and lifetime ₹9 lakh. Loan B's contractual payments are 45 days past due, the company has nothing else suggesting the risk of default has changed, and no forward-looking information beyond past due status is available without undue cost or effort; its figures are ₹5 lakh and ₹22 lakh. Loan C is an investment-grade bond determined to have low credit risk at the reporting date although its spread has widened since purchase; its figures are ₹1 lakh and ₹6 lakh.

items.stem: What does the manufacturer recognise at 31 March 2026?

options.text: A warranty provision of ₹40 lakh, undiscounted, with the ₹15 lakh recovery disclosed rather than recognised
options.why: Para 36 makes the provision the best estimate of the expenditure required to settle the present obligation at the end of the reporting period, and para 39 reaches that estimate for a large population of items by weighting all possible outcomes by their associated probabilities — the expected value. Twenty per cent of ₹100 lakh plus five per cent of ₹400 lakh is ₹40 lakh. Para 45 requires present value only where the effect of the time value of money is material, which claims settled inside a year are not. Para 53 recognises a reimbursement when, and only when, it is virtually certain, so a probable recovery is disclosed instead.

options.text: No warranty provision at all, because 75 per cent of the products are expected to have no defect, so an outflow is not probable
options.misconception: applies the probable outflow test to each individual product rather than to the population of warranty obligations as a whole
options.why: Para 39 measures a large population of items by weighting all possible outcomes, which presupposes that the class is assessed together rather than product by product. Some of the products sold will certainly fail, so an outflow of resources is probable for the class, and the best estimate of it is the ₹40 lakh expected value.

options.text: A warranty provision of ₹400 lakh, being the cost of the most serious outcome the company could face
options.misconception: measures a provision at the worst case instead of at the best estimate
options.why: Para 36 asks for the best estimate of the expenditure required to settle the obligation, and para 39 reaches it for a large population by weighting all possible outcomes by their associated probabilities. Prudence is not a licence to provide the maximum, and the ₹400 lakh outcome carries a five per cent probability, so it enters the expected value at ₹20 lakh.

options.text: A warranty provision of ₹25 lakh, being the ₹40 lakh expected cost shown net of the ₹15 lakh expected reimbursement
options.misconception: nets a reimbursement against the provision on the balance sheet, when para 53 makes it a separate asset and only para 54 permits netting
options.why: Two things block this. Para 53 recognises a reimbursement only when it is virtually certain, and probable is the lower bar. Even had it been virtually certain, the reimbursement would be treated as a separate asset capped at the amount of the provision, with para 54 allowing the netting only in the statement of profit and loss and never on the balance sheet.

citation.ref: para 36, 39, 45 and 53, with the presentation in para 54

items.scenario: A manufacturer sells goods with a one-year warranty and has a long history to draw on. On the products sold in the year ended 31 March 2026, it expects 75 per cent to have no defect, 20 per cent to have minor defects that would cost ₹100 lakh in repairs if every product sold had them, and 5 per cent to have major defects that would cost ₹400 lakh on the same basis. All claims are expected to be settled within twelve months. The supplier of a component is expected to reimburse ₹15 lakh of the cost, and the company's lawyers say recovery is probable but not virtually certain.

items.stem: How does the company account for the repayment?

options.text: Charge the whole ₹60 lakh repayment to profit or loss at once, since there is no deferred income balance to absorb it
options.misconception: applies the para 32 route for a grant related to income to a grant related to an asset
options.why: Para 32 splits the two. Repayment of a grant related to income is applied first against any unamortised deferred credit with the excess to profit or loss. Repayment of a grant related to an asset is recognised by increasing the carrying amount of the asset or reducing the deferred income balance, and only the cumulative additional depreciation of ₹18 lakh reaches profit or loss.

options.text: Restate the financial statements for the three earlier years as a prior period error, correcting the depreciation charged in each of them
options.misconception: treats a repayment triggered by a later breach as an error in the earlier statements
options.why: Nothing was wrong when those statements were drawn up — the conditions were met then and the grant was properly recognised. Para 32 says a government grant that becomes repayable shall be accounted for as a change in accounting estimate under Ind AS 8, which works forward from the date of the change rather than by restating comparatives.

options.text: Increase the machine's carrying amount by ₹60 lakh and depreciate the whole of it over the seven remaining years, with nothing charged immediately
options.misconception: spreads the depreciation catch-up forward instead of recognising it at once as para 32 requires
options.why: Para 32 requires the cumulative additional depreciation that would have been recognised in profit or loss to date in the absence of the grant to be recognised immediately in profit or loss. Spreading it forward would carry the machine at ₹228 lakh, above the ₹210 lakh it would have stood at without the grant, and would leave three years of understated depreciation never made good.

options.text: Increase the machine's carrying amount by ₹60 lakh and charge ₹18 lakh of cumulative additional depreciation immediately to profit or loss, taking the machine from ₹168 lakh to ₹210 lakh, as a change in accounting estimate
options.why: Para 32 accounts for a government grant that becomes repayable as a change in accounting estimate, and recognises repayment of a grant related to an asset by increasing the carrying amount of the asset or reducing the deferred income balance by the amount repayable. This company deducted the grant, so the ₹60 lakh goes back onto the machine. Para 32 then recognises immediately in profit or loss the cumulative additional depreciation that would have been recognised in the absence of the grant — three years at ₹6 lakh, being ₹18 lakh — which leaves the machine at ₹210 lakh, exactly where it would have stood had the grant never been given.

items.scenario: On 1 April 2023 a company received a government grant of ₹60 lakh towards a machine costing ₹300 lakh, with a ten-year life, no residual value and straight-line depreciation. It presented the grant by deducting it in arriving at the carrying amount of the asset, so the machine went in at ₹240 lakh and has been depreciated at ₹24 lakh a year. On 1 April 2026, having taken three full years of that charge, the company breaches an employment condition attached to the grant and becomes liable to repay the whole ₹60 lakh.

items.stem: How much of the three grants reaches profit or loss for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹30 lakh for the sugarcane, nothing for the dairy herd and the whole ₹40 lakh for the buffaloes — ₹70 lakh in total
options.misconception: applies Ind AS 41's receivable test to a biological asset measured at cost, which para 37 hands to Ind AS 20
options.why: Para 37 is explicit that where a government grant relates to a biological asset measured at its cost less any accumulated depreciation and any accumulated impairment losses, Ind AS 20 is applied. The buffaloes are carried on exactly that basis under paragraph 30, so the ₹40 lakh is released over their remaining life rather than taken when receivable.

options.text: Nothing for the sugarcane because the cash has not been received, nothing for the dairy herd and ₹1 lakh for the buffaloes — ₹1 lakh in total
options.misconception: waits for receipt of the cash when para 34 turns on the grant becoming receivable
options.why: Para 34 fixes recognition at the point the government grant becomes receivable, not the point it is received. The sugarcane grant became receivable on 1 February 2026, so its ₹30 lakh belongs to the year ended 31 March 2026 with a receivable standing in the balance sheet.

options.text: ₹30 lakh for the sugarcane, ₹1.67 lakh for the dairy herd and ₹1 lakh for the buffaloes — ₹32.67 lakh in total
options.misconception: releases a conditional grant on a fair valued biological asset over the condition period, as Ind AS 20 would
options.why: Para 38 records that this Standard requires a different treatment from Ind AS 20 where the grant relates to a biological asset measured at its fair value less costs to sell. Para 35 recognises such a grant when, and only when, the conditions attaching to it are met, and para 36 allows recognition as time passes only where the terms let part of the grant be retained according to the time elapsed. These terms require the whole of it back, so nothing is recognised yet.

options.text: ₹30 lakh for the sugarcane, nothing for the dairy herd and ₹1 lakh for the buffaloes — ₹31 lakh in total
options.why: Para 34 recognises an unconditional government grant related to a biological asset measured at its fair value less costs to sell in profit or loss when, and only when, the grant becomes receivable, so the sugarcane's ₹30 lakh is taken in full although the cash has not arrived. Para 35 recognises a conditional grant only when the conditions are met, and para 36 says a grant returnable in full if the entity farms for less than five years is not recognised until those five years have passed, so the dairy grant gives nothing. Para 37 sends a grant on a biological asset carried at cost less accumulated depreciation to Ind AS 20, so the buffaloes' ₹40 lakh is released over ten years and three months of that is ₹1 lakh.
keywords: fair value less costs to sell

items.scenario: A plantation and dairy company has three government grants at 31 March 2026. First, an unconditional grant of ₹30 lakh on its standing sugarcane crop, a biological asset measured at fair value less costs to sell; it became receivable on 1 February 2026 and the cash will arrive in May 2026. Second, a grant of ₹50 lakh on its dairy herd, also measured at fair value less costs to sell, received on 1 March 2026 but returnable in full unless the company farms at the same location for five years. Third, a grant of ₹40 lakh received on 1 January 2026 towards a herd of breeding buffaloes whose fair value cannot be measured reliably and which is therefore carried under paragraph 30 at cost less accumulated depreciation over ten remaining years.

items.stem: How does the operator account for the road and for the ₹70 crore of borrowing costs under each version?

options.text: The road is never the operator's property, plant and equipment; version one gives a financial asset with the ₹70 crore expensed, version two gives an intangible asset with the ₹70 crore capitalised during construction
options.why: Para 11 of Appendix C keeps infrastructure within its scope out of the operator's property, plant and equipment, because the contractual service arrangement does not convey the right to control the use of the public service infrastructure to the operator. Para 16 gives a financial asset where the operator has an unconditional contractual right to receive cash from or at the direction of the grantor, which the guaranteed annual amount creates. Para 17 gives an intangible asset where the operator receives a right to charge users of the public service, since those amounts are contingent on the extent that the public uses the service. Para 22 then recognises borrowing costs as an expense unless the operator has a contractual right to an intangible asset, in which case they are capitalised during the construction phase.

options.text: The road is the operator's property, plant and equipment under both versions, depreciated over the twenty-year concession, with the ₹70 crore capitalised into its cost either way
options.misconception: reads physical possession and operation of the infrastructure as control of it
options.why: Para 11 answers this directly — infrastructure within the scope of the Appendix shall not be recognised as property, plant and equipment of the operator, because the arrangement does not convey the right to control its use. The operator has access to operate the road on behalf of the grantor on the contract's terms, which makes it a service provider rather than an owner.

options.text: A financial asset under both versions, since the operator will be paid for its construction services either way, with the ₹70 crore expensed under both
options.misconception: reads any expectation of cash as the unconditional contractual right para 16 requires
options.why: Para 17 answers version two — a right to charge users of the public service is not an unconditional right to receive cash, because the amounts are contingent on the extent that the public uses the service. Traffic risk sits with the operator there, so it holds an intangible asset, and para 22 then capitalises the borrowing costs during construction rather than expensing them.

options.text: An intangible asset under both versions, because the operator's real asset in either case is the twenty-year concession right, with the ₹70 crore capitalised under both
options.misconception: treats the concession licence as the asset regardless of who carries the demand risk
options.why: The Appendix classifies by the nature of the consideration the grantor gives, not by the label on the contract. Para 16 recognises a financial asset where the grantor contractually guarantees to pay specified or determinable amounts, which is version one, and para 22 then requires those borrowing costs to be recognised as an expense in the period in which they are incurred.

items.scenario: An operator builds a 60 km toll road for a state authority under a twenty-year concession, spending ₹900 crore and finishing on 31 March 2026, and must operate and maintain the road for the whole term. Two versions of the contract are under discussion. Under version one the authority contractually guarantees a specified annual amount whatever the traffic. Under version two the operator's only entitlement is to collect tolls from road users for twenty years, with no guarantee of any kind. The operator incurred ₹70 crore of borrowing costs during construction on loans raised for the project.

items.stem: How much borrowing cost does the company capitalise for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹65.04 crore — the same ₹47.04 crore on general borrowings, but ₹18 crore on the specific loan without deducting the ₹1.5 crore earned on the deposits
options.misconception: ignores para 12's deduction of investment income on the temporary investment of specific borrowings
options.why: Para 12 determines the amount eligible for capitalisation on a specific borrowing as the actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing during the period less any investment income on the temporary investment of those borrowings. The ₹1.5 crore earned on the idle ₹40 crore is not a separate windfall to be left out of the calculation; it reduces the cost carried into the asset.

options.text: ₹65.09 crore — a single 9.571 per cent rate, the weighted average of every borrowing including the specific loan, applied to the whole ₹680 crore of expenditure
options.misconception: builds the capitalisation rate from all borrowings, when para 14 excludes those made specifically for the asset
options.why: Para 14 defines the capitalisation rate as the weighted average of the borrowing costs applicable to the borrowings of the entity that are outstanding during the period, other than borrowings made specifically for the purpose of obtaining a qualifying asset. Folding the specific loan into the pool counts it twice, because para 12 has already dealt with that loan directly and at its own rate.

options.text: ₹63.54 crore — ₹16.5 crore on the specific loan and ₹47.04 crore from applying a 9.8 per cent capitalisation rate to the ₹480 crore of expenditure not met from it
options.why: Para 12 makes the amount eligible on funds borrowed specifically the actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing less any investment income on the temporary investment of those borrowings, so ₹18 crore less ₹1.5 crore is ₹16.5 crore. Para 14 applies a capitalisation rate to the expenditure met from general borrowings, the rate being the weighted average of the borrowing costs applicable to the entity's borrowings outstanding during the period other than those made specifically for a qualifying asset — ₹33 crore plus ₹16 crore over ₹500 crore, or 9.8 per cent — which on ₹480 crore gives ₹47.04 crore. The ₹63.54 crore total sits below the ₹67 crore actually incurred, so the para 14 ceiling does not bite.

options.text: ₹67 crore — the whole of the borrowing costs incurred during the year, since the plant is a qualifying asset and every borrowing helped to fund it
options.misconception: reads the para 14 cap as the amount to capitalise rather than as a ceiling on it
options.why: The sentence saying the amount an entity capitalises during a period shall not exceed the amount of borrowing costs it incurred during that period is a ceiling, not a measure. Para 14 measures the amount by applying the capitalisation rate to the expenditure on the asset, and ₹480 crore at 9.8 per cent plus ₹16.5 crore under para 12 gives ₹63.54 crore, comfortably inside the ceiling.

items.scenario: A company is constructing a plant, a qualifying asset, throughout the year ended 31 March 2026. It raised a ₹200 crore term loan specifically for the plant at 9 per cent, of which ₹40 crore sat in deposits for part of the year and earned ₹1.5 crore. Its general borrowings, outstanding all year, are ₹300 crore of debentures at 11 per cent and a ₹200 crore working capital loan at 8 per cent. Expenditure on the plant averaged ₹680 crore over the year, of which ₹200 crore was met from the specific loan.

items.stem: What basic earnings per share does the company report for the year ended 31 March 2026, and what happens to the comparative?

options.text: ₹13.80 for the year ended 31 March 2026, with the comparative restated from ₹12.50 to ₹10.00
options.misconception: treats the whole rights issue as a bonus issue, when only its bonus element is retrospective
options.why: Counting all 50,00,000 shares from the start of both years gives ₹13.80 and ₹10.00, and treats money that arrived on 1 October 2025 as though it had always been there. Appendix A para A2 isolates the gift from the fresh money through the factor of fair value per share immediately before the exercise of rights over the theoretical ex-rights fair value per share, and only that factor is retrospective.

options.text: ₹14.76 for the year ended 31 March 2026, with the comparative for the year ended 31 March 2025 restated from ₹12.50 to ₹11.50
options.why: Para 27(b) treats a rights issue priced below fair value as containing a bonus element. Appendix A para A2 multiplies the shares outstanding before the issue by the fair value per share immediately before the exercise of rights over the theoretical ex-rights fair value per share. That theoretical ex-rights price is ₹92 — ₹40,00,00,000 of existing value plus ₹6,00,00,000 of proceeds, over the 50,00,000 shares outstanding afterwards — so the factor is 100 over 92. The 40,00,000 shares of the first half year become 43,47,826 and weight to 21,73,913, the 50,00,000 of the second half weight to 25,00,000, and ₹6,90,00,000 over 46,73,913 shares is ₹14.76. The same factor restates the prior year to ₹11.50.

options.text: ₹14.76 for the year ended 31 March 2026, with the ₹12.50 comparative left as published because the rights issue happened after that year had ended
options.misconception: applies the adjustment factor to the current year only, when a bonus element is applied to every period presented
options.why: The current year is computed correctly and the comparative is not. Appendix A para A2 says the adjusted number of shares is used in calculating basic and diluted earnings per share for all periods before the rights issue, which is what moves the comparative from ₹12.50 to ₹11.50. Leaving it alone would show growth that is an artefact of the share count.
