The company secretary records Mr A in the register of significant beneficial owners and leaves Mrs B out, reasoning that Mr A's holding is the larger and that in any case section 90 speaks of twenty-five per cent, which neither of them reaches.

items.stem: What should the Tribunal do?

options.text: Reject the scheme — the meeting failed because approval by sixty per cent of those voting falls short of the three-fourths section 230(6) demands
options.misconception: applies the three-fourths test to the number of persons instead of to value
options.why: Section 230(6) needs a majority of the persons voting and three-fourths in value. Sixty per cent is a majority in number, and the three-fourths test is met by the eighty per cent in value.

options.text: Hear the four per cent shareholder's objection on its merits before deciding, since any member may object to a scheme that affects him
options.misconception: ignores the standing threshold the proviso to section 230(4) imposes on objectors
options.why: The proviso to section 230(4) was inserted to stop small holdings from stalling schemes. An objection may be made only by a holder of not less than ten per cent of the shareholding, or a creditor with not less than five per cent of total outstanding debt.

options.text: Sanction the scheme — the meeting has approved it and an auditor's certificate is good practice rather than a statutory precondition
options.misconception: treats the section 230(7) certificate as advisory
options.why: The proviso to section 230(7) says no compromise or arrangement shall be sanctioned unless the certificate has been filed with the Tribunal. It is a bar on the Tribunal's power, not a recommendation to the company.

options.text: Refuse to sanction until the auditor's certificate is filed — the meeting has cleared section 230(6), and the four per cent shareholder has no standing to object, but the proviso to section 230(7) bars sanction unless the company's auditor certifies that the scheme's accounting treatment conforms to the accounting standards prescribed under section 133
options.why: Section 230(6) needs a majority of the persons voting representing three-fourths in value — sixty per cent in number and eighty per cent in value clears both. The proviso to section 230(4) confines objections to a holder of not less than ten per cent of the shareholding or a creditor with not less than five per cent of the total outstanding debt, so four per cent has no standing. The certificate under the proviso to section 230(7) is a precondition to sanction and next year's audit report cannot stand in for it.

citation.ref: Sections 230(4) proviso, 230(6) and the proviso to section 230(7)

items.scenario: At a Tribunal-convened meeting of a company's equity shareholders on a scheme of arrangement, sixty per cent of those voting, holding eighty per cent in value of the shares voted, approve the scheme. A shareholder holding four per cent of the shareholding files an objection saying the scheme's accounting treatment writes goodwill straight off against reserves. The company files the petition for sanction without an auditor's certificate, on the view that the auditor will report on the treatment in the following year's audit anyway.

items.stem: Can the board do this?

options.text: Yes — a prior period error is corrected by the board under Ind AS 8, and re-filing the corrected statements is the mechanical consequence
options.misconception: treats an accounting standard as authority to withdraw and replace a filed statutory document
options.why: Ind AS 8 tells the company how to present the error in the current year's statements. It confers no power to withdraw a financial statement that has been adopted by members and filed with the Registrar; sections 130 and 131 govern that.

options.text: No — 2023-24 is beyond reach in any case, because a revision under section 131 may not go back more than one financial year
options.misconception: shortens the section 131 look-back period
options.why: Section 131(1) permits a revised financial statement or Board's report for any of the three preceding financial years. From 2026-27 that reaches 2023-24 comfortably.

options.text: No — replacing a filed financial statement needs the Tribunal's approval under section 131, which is available for any of the three preceding financial years, once in a financial year and confined to the non-compliance; Ind AS 8 governs a different remedy, restating the comparative figures in the 2026-27 financial statements, which needs nobody's approval
options.why: Section 131(1) is the directors' only route to revising a financial statement already adopted and filed, and it runs through the Tribunal. The 2023-24 year is within the three preceding financial years, so the route is open. Ind AS 8 answers a separate question — how the current year's statements present a prior period error — and restating comparatives there is ordinary accounting, not a revision of the earlier filing.

options.text: No — the company must apply under section 130 for an order re-opening its books, since that is the section dealing with correcting earlier years
options.misconception: reaches for section 130 where the company itself wants the change
options.why: Section 130 operates on an application by the Central Government, the income-tax authorities, the Securities and Exchange Board, another statutory regulatory body or a person concerned — it is not the company's own route. Section 131 is the voluntary route, and it is the one engaged here.

citation.ref: Sections 130(1) and 131(1), read with Ind AS 8

items.scenario: In November 2026, during the financial year 2026-27, a company discovers that revenue of ₹6 crore was recognised a year early in its financial statements for the year 2023-24, which were adopted at the annual general meeting and filed with the Registrar. The board passes a resolution to withdraw those filed financial statements, replace them with corrected ones and re-file them, without approaching anyone, saying that the correction of a prior period error is the board's own accounting decision under Ind AS 8.

items.stem: How should the two payments and the timetable be treated?

options.text: The ₹9 crore repayment falls inside the two-year look-back that section 43(4) applies to a related party and is a preference; the ₹4 crore payment is outside the one-year look-back for an unrelated party and cannot be a preference at all; and under section 26 the avoidance applications do not hold up the resolution process
options.why: Section 43(4) measures back from the insolvency commencement date and gives a related party a two-year look-back and everybody else one year. From 1 June 2026 the promoter's finance company is caught by the October 2024 repayment of an antecedent debt that put it ahead of where section 53 would have placed it, while the supplier's April 2025 payment sits more than one year clear and is beyond reach whatever its merits. Section 26 says in terms that filing an avoidance application shall not affect the proceedings of the corporate insolvency resolution process.

options.text: Both are preferences, and the resolution plan cannot be placed before the Tribunal until the avoidance applications have been decided
options.misconception: treats an avoidance application as a stay on the resolution process
options.why: Section 26 was written to prevent exactly that. An avoidance application runs on its own track and neither delays the resolution process nor dies when the plan is approved; the recovery, when it comes, goes to the corporate debtor's assets.

options.text: Neither payment is a preference, because both were made in the ordinary course of the corporate debtor's business and section 43(3)(a) excludes such transfers
options.misconception: reads the ordinary-course escape as covering only the corporate debtor's side
options.why: Repaying a promoter's finance company ahead of every other unsecured creditor is not the ordinary course of anybody's business. The Supreme Court in Anuj Jain held that the "or" in section 43(3)(a) must be read as "and", so the transfer has to be ordinary for the corporate debtor and the transferee before the escape applies.

options.text: Both payments are preferences, because the look-back under section 43 is two years for every counterparty and both fall inside it
options.misconception: applies the related-party look-back to an unrelated creditor
options.why: Section 43(4) draws a line between a related party, who gets a two-year window, and any other person, who gets one year. Collapsing the two into a single two-year period sweeps in ordinary trade payments the Code deliberately left alone.

items.scenario: A corporate insolvency resolution process commences on 1 June 2026. Two payments trouble the resolution professional. On 1 October 2024 the corporate debtor repaid ₹9 crore of an unsecured loan taken from a finance company wholly owned by its promoter, ahead of every other unsecured creditor. On 1 April 2025 it paid ₹4 crore to a raw-material supplier for goods delivered on ordinary sixty-day credit terms. The resolution professional wants to avoid both, and the committee of creditors asks whether filing the applications will stop the resolution plan being taken up.

items.stem: What is the correct analysis?

options.text: The correct route is section 339 of the Companies Act, 2013, since the Code's own provision applies only in liquidation and this company is in a resolution process
options.misconception: confines section 66 to liquidation and reaches for a section that still needs intent
options.why: Section 66(1) applies during a corporate insolvency resolution process or a liquidation process, and section 66(2) is expressly triggered on an application by the resolution professional during the resolution process. Section 339 of the Companies Act would in any case put the intent requirement back that section 66(2) removes.

options.text: The directors escape because the Explanation to section 66(2) protects anyone who acted on the auditor's report, and the auditor's going-concern paragraph was only a material uncertainty rather than an adverse conclusion
options.misconception: treats a going-concern paragraph as cover for the directors instead of evidence against them
options.why: The Explanation measures due diligence against a reasonably diligent person having the knowledge, skill and experience reasonably expected of a person carrying out the same functions. A material uncertainty paragraph is evidence of what the directors were told, and being told makes the standard harder to meet, not easier.

options.text: No order can be made, because section 66 requires the business to have been carried on with intent to defraud creditors and no such intent is shown
options.misconception: reads the section 66(1) fraud requirement into section 66(2)
options.why: Intent to defraud belongs to section 66(1), which reaches any persons knowingly parties to carrying on the business for a fraudulent purpose. Section 66(2) is a separate, self-contained provision aimed at directors who traded on when they should have stopped, and it asks nothing about dishonesty.

options.text: Section 66(2) applies to the directors without proof of dishonesty, because they knew or ought to have known before the insolvency commencement date that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding a corporate insolvency resolution process and did not exercise due diligence in minimising the loss to creditors; the contribution ordered goes to the corporate debtor's assets
options.why: Section 66(2) is wrongful trading, and it turns on knowledge and carelessness, not on intent to defraud. The board minutes of 10 May 2025 and the auditor's going-concern paragraph are the record that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding the process, and continuing to take ninety-day credit from new suppliers is the opposite of due diligence in minimising the potential loss to creditors. The order is a contribution to the assets of the corporate debtor, shared by all creditors, not a payment to the applicant.

citation.ref: Sections 66(1), 66(2) with its Explanation, and 67, read with SA 570

items.scenario: A company's board minutes of 10 May 2025 record that the bank had refused to renew the working capital limit, that no other funding was in sight and that the company could not meet its obligations as they fell due. The auditor's report for 2024-25 carried a material uncertainty related to going concern paragraph under SA 570. The directors nevertheless kept buying raw material on ninety-day credit from new suppliers until a corporate insolvency resolution process commenced on 1 March 2026, adding ₹22 crore of unpaid trade debt. There is no evidence that anyone intended to cheat anybody. The resolution professional applies under section 66.

items.stem: Where should the application have been filed, and what is the position of the civil suit?

options.text: The Debt Recovery Tribunal is correct, because a personal guarantor is an individual and Part III of the Code places individuals before that Tribunal in every case
options.misconception: applies the general Part III forum and misses the section 60(2) redirection
options.why: The Debt Recovery Tribunal is the adjudicating authority for individuals generally. Section 60(2) carves out the personal guarantor of a corporate debtor whose own process is already pending and sends him to the same National Company Law Tribunal, so that one forum sees the company and the guarantee together.

options.text: The forum is right or wrong as the case may be, but nothing is stayed until the Tribunal admits the application under section 100, so the civil suit continues meanwhile
options.misconception: starts the moratorium at admission instead of at the application
options.why: Section 96 begins the interim moratorium from the date of the application itself. It is the moratorium under section 101 that begins on admission and runs one hundred and eighty days; the interim one ends where that one starts.

options.text: The application is premature in any event, because the resolution professional must first report under section 99 and only then may a creditor apply under section 95
options.misconception: reverses the order of section 95 and section 99
options.why: The creditor's application under section 95 comes first. Section 97 then confirms or appoints the resolution professional, section 99 gives him ten days from his appointment to examine the application and report, and section 100 gives the Tribunal fourteen days from that report to admit or reject.

options.text: It should have been filed before the same National Company Law Tribunal at Mumbai under section 60(2), and an interim moratorium under section 96 began on 4 May 2026 — the date of the application, not of admission — so the civil suit filed on 20 May cannot proceed
options.why: Section 60(2) requires an application relating to the insolvency resolution or bankruptcy of a personal guarantor to be filed before, or transferred to, the National Company Law Tribunal where the corporate debtor's process is pending, and section 60(4) gives that Tribunal all the powers of the Debt Recovery Tribunal for the purpose. Section 96 starts an interim moratorium on the date of the application, staying any pending legal proceeding in respect of any debt and barring a fresh one, so the 20 May suit is caught.

items.scenario: A corporate insolvency resolution process against a corporate debtor is pending before the National Company Law Tribunal at Mumbai. Its managing director had given a personal guarantee to the lending bank. On 4 May 2026 the bank files an application through a resolution professional to initiate the insolvency resolution process of the guarantor before the Debt Recovery Tribunal, and starts a separate recovery suit against him in a civil court on 20 May 2026. The guarantor's counsel says nothing protects him until the application is admitted.

items.stem: What is wrong with this?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because voluntary liquidation is a members' decision and the creditors have no say where they are being paid in full
options.misconception: reads solvency as removing the creditors from the process entirely
options.why: Section 59(3)(c) requires the approval of creditors representing two-thirds in value of the debt whenever the corporate person owes any debt. Whether they will ultimately be paid in full is precisely what they are being asked to accept.

options.text: Three things — the declaration of solvency must be made by a majority of the directors and two of five is not a majority; the special resolution must be passed within four weeks of the declaration, and 20 May is beyond four weeks from 1 April; and creditors representing two-thirds in value of the debt must approve that resolution within seven days of it
options.why: Section 59(3)(a) requires a declaration of solvency from a majority of the directors, verified by affidavit and accompanied by the audited financial statements and the record of business operations for the previous two years. Section 59(3)(c) requires the special resolution within four weeks of that declaration, and where the corporate person owes any debt, approval by creditors representing two-thirds in value of the debt within seven days of the special resolution. Each of the three is a condition of the process being validly begun, not a formality.

options.text: The procedure is defective, but the liquidator is right that the order of payment is his to choose, because section 53 applies only to a liquidation ordered by the Tribunal
options.misconception: confines the waterfall to compulsory liquidation
options.why: Section 59(6) applies sections 35 to 53 to a voluntary liquidation. The waterfall governs the order of payment here as well; the only difference is that a solvent company reaches the bottom of it and the surplus goes to the members.

options.text: Only the creditors' approval is missing; a declaration signed by any two directors and a resolution passed at any time after it are both in order
options.misconception: treats the numbers in section 59(3) as directory rather than as conditions
options.why: Section 59(3) names a majority of the directors and a four-week window in the same breath as the creditors' approval. All three are conditions attached to a process that is open only to a corporate person that has committed no default, and the discipline is what keeps it out of the hands of the insolvent.

items.scenario: A profitable private company with five directors decides to shut down. It owes ₹3 crore to trade creditors and has assets comfortably worth ₹20 crore. Two of the five directors sign a declaration of solvency verified by affidavit on 1 April 2026, attaching audited financial statements for the previous two years. The members pass a special resolution to wind up voluntarily and appoint a liquidator on 20 May 2026. No approval is taken from the creditors, the company secretary reasoning that they will be paid in full anyway, and the liquidator proposes to pay the creditors in whatever order is convenient since there is enough for everybody.

items.stem: What is the position after 10 April 2026?

options.text: The immunity depends on the resolution plan saying so, and where the plan is silent the prosecution continues against the company as before
options.misconception: makes a statutory immunity depend on a term of the plan
options.why: Section 32A(1) operates on the approval of the plan and the change in management or control to a qualifying person. It is not a benefit the resolution applicant has to negotiate into the plan, and a silent plan does not lose it.

options.text: Nothing changes for the attachment, because an attachment under the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act is made under a special statute that the Code does not displace
options.misconception: leaves the property attached where section 32A(2) expressly releases it
options.why: Section 32A(2) says the property of the corporate debtor shall not be liable to attachment, seizure, retention or confiscation in relation to an offence covered by sub-section (1). It is on that provision that attachments made under the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act have been ordered released once a plan is approved.

options.text: Both the company and its erstwhile managing director are cleared, because section 32A gives the rescued business a complete clean slate for everything done before the process began
options.misconception: extends the corporate debtor's immunity to the individuals who ran it
options.why: The proviso to section 32A(1) says every person who was a designated partner, officer in default, or in any manner in charge of or responsible to the corporate debtor for the conduct of its business shall continue to be liable to prosecution and punishment. The immunity is the company's alone.

options.text: The company ceases to be prosecuted for the 2022 offence under section 32A(1) and the factory ceases to be liable to attachment under section 32A(2), but the erstwhile managing director continues to be liable under the proviso to section 32A(1), and section 32A(3) obliges the company to extend all assistance to the investigating authority
options.why: Section 32A(1) ends the corporate debtor's liability for a pre-commencement offence from the date the plan is approved, provided control passes to someone who was not a promoter, not in management or control, and not a related party of such a person. Section 32A(2) then protects the property from attachment, seizure, retention or confiscation for that offence. The proviso preserves the liability of every officer who was in charge of the business, and section 32A(3) requires the corporate debtor and such persons to extend all assistance and co-operation to the authority investigating it.

items.scenario: The Tribunal approves a resolution plan under section 31 on 10 April 2026. Control of the company passes to an unconnected industrial group that was never a promoter, is not a related party of any promoter, and against whom no investigating authority has reported any abetment. Before the process began, the Enforcement Directorate had attached the company's factory in connection with an offence committed in 2022, and criminal proceedings are running against the company and against its erstwhile managing director. The new management asks whether it must keep producing records to the investigating authority.

items.stem: Is the merchant banker right?

options.text: Wrong on the process but right on the price, because a resolution plan approved by the Tribunal binds all stakeholders under section 31 and a shareholder cannot complain about the rate he is offered
options.misconception: reads section 31's binding effect as removing the SEBI condition on the exit price
options.why: Section 31 makes the plan binding, but the exemption in Regulation 3(2)(b) is granted subject to its own provisos. A plan that pays public shareholders less than another shareholder does not qualify for the exemption in the first place.

options.text: Right on the price only — the exemption applies, but the exit price is fixed by the Regulations at the floor price computed under the reverse book building rules
options.misconception: keeps the delisting price-discovery rules alive inside an exemption that removes them
options.why: The exemption removes the Regulations, floor price and all. What replaces them is the comparative test in the first proviso: the public shareholders may not be paid less than any other shareholder given an exit under the same plan.

options.text: Yes on both — the Delisting Regulations apply to every delisting of a listed company, and insolvency changes nothing about the process or the pricing
options.misconception: ignores the carve-out in Regulation 3(2) for a section 31 resolution plan
options.why: Regulation 3(2)(b) exists precisely because the ordinary machinery cannot work for a company coming out of insolvency. Running a reverse book building would ask a resolution applicant to discover a price in a market that has already been told the company failed.

options.text: No on the process and no on the price — Regulation 3(2)(b) takes the Delisting Regulations off a delisting made pursuant to a plan approved under section 31, so no reverse book building is run, but the first proviso requires the public shareholders' exit price to be not less than the ₹5 given to the other shareholder, and the details with the justification for the exit price must reach the exchanges within one day of the approval
options.why: Regulation 3(2)(b) of the SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021 disapplies the Regulations, and with them the reverse book building machinery, where the resolution plan provides for delisting or for an exit to the existing public shareholders at a specified price. The first proviso is the protection that replaces it: the exit price shall not be less than the price at which a promoter, the promoter group or any other shareholder is given an exit under that plan. The second proviso requires disclosure to the recognised stock exchanges within one day of the approval of the resolution plan.

citation.ref: Regulation 3(2)(b) and its provisos, read with section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

items.scenario: A listed company emerges from a corporate insolvency resolution process. The resolution plan, approved by the Tribunal under section 31 on 3 August 2026, provides for the delisting of the equity shares and offers the existing public shareholders an exit at ₹2 per share, while a continuing non-promoter shareholder who is staying invested is bought out at ₹5 per share. The company's merchant banker advises that a reverse book building exercise with a ninety per cent acceptance threshold must be run before the shares can come off the exchange, and that the exit price is a commercial matter for the resolution applicant.

items.stem: What has the company secretary missed?

options.text: Nothing — a special resolution under section 62(1)(c) with a registered valuer's report fixes a lawful price, and SEBI does not second-guess a price the shareholders approved
options.misconception: treats company law approval as satisfying the ICDR floor price
options.why: Section 62(1)(c) requires the price to be determined by a valuation report; Chapter V of the ICDR Regulations imposes a separate statutory floor for a listed company. A special resolution cannot approve a price below that floor.

options.text: Only the lock-in — the pricing is right, because the floor for a frequently traded share is the volume weighted average price of the ten trading days preceding the relevant date
options.misconception: takes the shorter window alone instead of the higher of the two
options.why: Regulation 164 names both windows and requires the higher. Taking only the ten-trading-day price would let an issuer time a preferential allotment into a short dip.

options.text: Only the pricing — the floor is right, but the lock-in on a promoter allottee is three years, so eighteen months understates it
options.misconception: quotes the pre-2022 lock-in period
options.why: Three years was the position before the ICDR amendment of 2022, which reduced the promoter lock-in to eighteen months for an allotment up to twenty per cent of the post-issue paid-up capital and to six months for the excess.

options.text: Two things — Regulation 164 fixes the floor at the higher of the ninety-trading-day and the ten-trading-day volume weighted average price, so ₹340 is the minimum and ₹300 is below the floor; and Regulation 167 locks the promoter's shares in for eighteen months because the allotment is within twenty per cent of the post-issue paid-up capital
options.why: Regulation 164 of the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018 sets the floor price for frequently traded shares at the higher of the two volume weighted average prices, not the lower and not an average of them, so ₹340 governs. Regulation 167 locks in a preferential allotment to promoters for eighteen months up to twenty per cent of the post-issue paid-up capital and six months beyond that; the Companies Act machinery under sections 42 and 62(1)(c) runs alongside these conditions and does not replace them.

citation.source: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
citation.ref: Regulations 164 and 167, read with sections 42 and 62(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: A listed company whose shares are frequently traded proposes a preferential allotment to its promoter of shares equal to fifteen per cent of the post-issue paid-up capital. The volume weighted average price of the ninety trading days preceding the relevant date is ₹340 and that of the ten trading days preceding it is ₹300. The board fixes the issue price at ₹300. The company secretary records that a special resolution under section 62(1)(c), a valuation report and the private placement offer letter under section 42 complete the compliance, and that no lock-in arises because the Companies Act imposes none.

items.stem: What are the correct timelines and the correct accounting question?

options.text: Both within twelve hours, since twelve hours is the general timeline under Regulation 30(6) and a board decision is only one example of it
options.misconception: applies one timeline to events the regulation separates by origin
options.why: Regulation 30(6) sets three timelines, not one. The thirty-minute clock is specific to a decision taken in a board meeting, and the twelve-hour and twenty-four-hour clocks turn on whether the event emanated from within the listed entity.

options.text: The scheme goes to the exchanges within thirty minutes of the close of the board meeting, the award within twenty-four hours because it does not emanate from within the listed entity, and it is material because Regulation 30(4)(i) takes the lower of the three tests — separately, Ind AS 10 asks whether the award gives evidence of a condition existing at 31 March 2026
options.why: Regulation 30(6) gives thirty minutes from the closure of a board meeting for a decision taken in it, twelve hours for an event emanating from within the listed entity and twenty-four hours for one that does not; an award passed by an outside tribunal is in the last class. Regulation 30(4)(i) takes the lower of two per cent of turnover, two per cent of net worth and five per cent of the three-year average absolute profit after tax, so the one per cent of net worth figure governs and is crossed. Ind AS 10 is a separate question about whether the condition existed at the reporting date.

options.text: The scheme within thirty minutes, but the award is not material because the threshold is the higher of the three tests and three per cent of turnover does not reach it
options.misconception: takes the higher of the three materiality measures instead of the lower
options.why: Regulation 30(4)(i) takes the lower of the three, which makes the trigger easier to cross. Reading it as the higher would let a company with a large turnover keep quiet about an event that wipes out its net worth.

options.text: Both within twenty-four hours, and the finance head is right that an event after the reporting date never affects the financial statements for the year just ended
options.misconception: treats every post-balance-sheet event as non-adjusting
options.why: Ind AS 10 divides events after the reporting period into adjusting and non-adjusting. An arbitral award can be evidence of a condition — an obligation already in existence — that existed at the reporting date, in which case the amounts are adjusted rather than merely disclosed.

citation.ref: Regulations 30(4)(i) and 30(6), read with Schedule III Part A and Ind AS 10

items.scenario: A listed company's board meets on 5 May 2026 and, at 4:00 pm when the meeting closes, approves a scheme of amalgamation. At 6:00 pm the same day the company learns that a foreign arbitral tribunal has passed an award against it for an amount equal to three per cent of its consolidated turnover, one per cent of its net worth and eight per cent of the three-year average absolute profit after tax. The financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026 have not yet been approved. The company secretary proposes to disclose both items together within twelve hours, and the finance head says the award needs no accounting treatment because it arose after the year end.

items.stem: Is the firm right?

options.text: Wrong on the first point but right on the second — both bodies may proceed in parallel, since NFRA's power under section 132(4) is regulatory and the Institute's under section 21B is disciplinary
options.misconception: allows parallel proceedings the proviso to section 132(4) forbids
options.why: The proviso to section 132(4) says no other institute or body shall initiate or continue any proceedings in such matters of misconduct where NFRA has initiated an investigation. It is a bar on parallel action, whatever the two proceedings are called.

options.text: Wrong on both, and the penalty on the firm, if misconduct is proved, is not less than one lakh rupees extending to five times the fees received
options.misconception: applies the individual's penalty band to a firm
options.why: Section 132(4)(c) sets one lakh rupees to five times the fees received for an individual and five lakh rupees to ten times the fees received for a firm, with debarment for six months to ten years in either case.

options.text: No on both counts — Rule 3(1)(b) of the NFRA Rules, 2018 brings in an unlisted public company on turnover of not less than one thousand crore rupees as an alternative to the paid-up capital test, and the proviso to section 132(4) bars any other institute or body from initiating or continuing proceedings in the same matter of misconduct once NFRA has initiated an investigation
options.why: Rule 3(1)(b) lists paid-up capital of not less than five hundred crore rupees, annual turnover of not less than one thousand crore rupees, and outstanding loans, debentures and deposits of not less than five hundred crore rupees as alternatives; ₹1,300 crore of turnover brings the company in on its own. The proviso to section 132(4) then makes NFRA's jurisdiction exclusive for that matter once it has started, so the Institute's proceeding cannot be initiated or continued.

options.text: Right on the first point — the three tests in Rule 3(1)(b) are cumulative, so a company must cross all of them before NFRA has any jurisdiction over its auditor
options.misconception: reads alternative tests as cumulative
options.why: Rule 3(1)(b) joins the paid-up capital, turnover and borrowings tests as alternatives. Requiring all three would leave almost no unlisted public company inside NFRA's reach, which is the opposite of what the rule does.

citation.ref: Section 132(4) with its proviso and section 132(4)(c), read with Rule 3(1)(b) of the NFRA Rules, 2018

items.scenario: An unlisted public company has paid-up share capital of ₹120 crore, annual turnover of ₹1,300 crore and no outstanding loans or debentures. Its statutory auditor is a firm. The National Financial Reporting Authority opens an investigation into the firm's audit of that company for the year 2024-25. Two months later the Disciplinary Directorate of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India registers a case against the engagement partner on the same facts. The firm argues that the company is outside NFRA's reach because its paid-up capital is well below ₹500 crore, and that the Institute is the only proper forum.

items.stem: Where is the finance head wrong?

options.text: Only on the tax — the set-off is ₹30 lakh, since Rule 7(3) speaks of the excess amount spent and the source of the money is irrelevant
options.misconception: includes CSR surplus in the excess Rule 7(3) allows to be set off
options.why: Rule 7(3) says in terms that the excess amount available for set off shall not include the surplus arising out of the CSR activities. Money the CSR project itself generated was never the company's fresh contribution.

options.text: Only on the set-off — CSR expenditure that is otherwise allowable, such as the ₹15 lakh to a fund covered by section 80G, remains deductible under section 37(1)
options.misconception: keeps a section 37(1) deduction alive for CSR that qualifies elsewhere
options.why: Explanation 2 to section 37(1) removes CSR expenditure from section 37(1) altogether. Whether a particular payment qualifies under section 80G or section 35 is a separate question answered by those sections on their own terms.

options.text: Nowhere on the figures, but he has missed that no CSR Committee was needed here, since section 135(9) dispenses with it where the amount actually spent exceeds the obligation
options.misconception: reads the section 135(9) exemption off the amount spent instead of the amount required to be spent
options.why: Section 135(9) dispenses with the CSR Committee where the amount required to be spent does not exceed fifty lakh rupees. The obligation here is ₹80 lakh, so a Committee is required whatever the company chose to spend.

options.text: On all three — the set-off available under Rule 7(3) is ₹20 lakh, not ₹30 lakh, because the surplus arising out of CSR activities is excluded and a board resolution is required; Explanation 2 to section 37(1) puts the whole CSR spend outside business expenditure; and section 80G expressly denies the deduction for a CSR sum paid to the Clean Ganga Fund
options.why: Rule 7(3) of the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014 allows the excess to be set off against the obligation of up to the immediately succeeding three financial years, but the excess is computed after excluding the surplus arising out of the CSR activities, so ₹1.10 crore less ₹10 lakh less ₹80 lakh leaves ₹20 lakh, and the Board must resolve to claim it. Explanation 2 to section 37(1) says CSR expenditure is not deemed to be incurred for the purposes of the business. Section 80G allows a CSR donation in general but shuts out sums paid to the Swachh Bharat Kosh and the Clean Ganga Fund.

citation.ref: Rule 7(3) of the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014 and section 135(9), read with Explanation 2 to section 37(1) and section 80G of the Income-tax Act, 1961

items.scenario: For 2025-26 a company's obligation under section 135(5) is ₹80 lakh. It spends ₹1.10 crore on CSR, and ₹10 lakh of that ₹1.10 crore was funded by surplus generated by an earlier CSR project which it ploughed back. Of the total, ₹15 lakh went to the Clean Ganga Fund. The board has passed no resolution about the excess. The finance head proposes to carry ₹30 lakh forward as a set-off, to claim the whole ₹1.10 crore as business expenditure under section 37(1) and to claim section 80G on the ₹15 lakh.

items.stem: How many of the four propositions survive?

options.text: Three — everything is defective except the voting, since a shareholder who has put in thirty per cent of the capital is entitled to a proportionate vote in any company
options.misconception: applies ordinary share-proportionate voting to a producer company
options.why: Section 378D(1)(a) is the co-operative principle written into the Companies Act. Where the membership is all individual producers, every member has one vote irrespective of his shareholding or patronage, and a thirty per cent subscriber has exactly one.

options.text: One — only the director count is short, and adding a tenth subscriber of any kind would cure the formation defect
options.misconception: treats the tenth subscriber as fungible between an individual and an institution
options.why: Section 378C's third route requires a combination of ten or more individuals and producer institutions, so ten individuals plus the institution would work — but a tenth subscriber that is another institution would still leave only eight individuals, and the first two routes need ten individual producers or two or more producer institutions on their own.

options.text: Two — the formation and the director count are defective, but the two-hundred-member limit does apply and the auditor's duties are those of section 143 alone
options.misconception: carries the section 2(68) member cap into a producer company and drops section 378ZG
options.why: Section 378C says the limit of members shall not apply to a producer company even though it is registered as if it were a private limited company, and it can never become a public company. Section 378ZG then adds its own list of reporting matters to section 143.

options.text: None — section 378C admits only ten or more individual producers, two or more producer institutions, or a combination of ten or more individuals and producer institutions; section 378O requires at least five directors; section 378D(1)(a) gives a single vote to every member irrespective of shareholding; and section 378ZG adds matters to the auditor's report over and above section 143
options.why: Section 378C admits ten or more individuals each being a producer, two or more producer institutions, or a combination of ten or more individuals and producer institutions; eight individuals with one institution is nine in all and meets none of the three. Section 378O fixes the board at not less than five and not more than fifteen directors. Section 378D(1)(a) makes the vote a single vote for every member irrespective of his shareholding or patronage. Section 378ZG requires the auditor to report additionally on bad debts, the verification of cash balance and securities, the details of assets and liabilities, transactions contrary to the chapter, loans to directors, and donations or subscriptions given.

items.scenario: Eight individual farmers and one registered producer institution want to incorporate a producer company. They propose four directors, and one of the farmers, who will subscribe to thirty per cent of the share capital, insists on votes in proportion to his shareholding. The professional advising them says the entity can be registered as it stands, that it will be a private limited company subject to the two-hundred-member limit in section 2(68), and that its auditor will report only on what section 143 requires.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: Government approval is needed — the proviso to Rule 6(a) puts any investment by an entity of a land-border country on the Government route whatever the sector's own entry route, A Ltd's subscription is a downstream investment that counts as indirect foreign investment in B Ltd and must meet the same entry route and conditions as a direct investment, and Rule 23 forbids funding it out of money borrowed in the domestic market
options.why: The proviso to Rule 6(a) of the FEM (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 puts an investment by an entity of a country sharing a land border with India, or where the beneficial owner is situated in or is a citizen of such a country, on the Government route, and a sector whose own entry route is automatic does not override it. Rule 23 makes an investment by an Indian company owned or controlled by a non-resident into another Indian company a downstream investment, treated as indirect foreign investment subject to the same entry route, sectoral caps and pricing, and requires the funds to be brought in from abroad rather than borrowed in the domestic market.

options.text: No approval and no reporting are needed, because an investment by one Indian company in another Indian company is a domestic transaction outside the FEM (Non-debt Instruments) Rules altogether
options.misconception: ignores that ownership and control by a non-resident make the investment indirect foreign investment
options.why: Rule 23 exists for exactly this transaction. Where the investing Indian company is owned or controlled by a person resident outside India, its investment downstream is indirect foreign investment and carries the conditions that would have applied had the money come directly from abroad.

options.text: Government approval is needed, but the rupee term loan is unobjectionable because the restriction on borrowed funds applies only to a foreign investor remitting money into India
options.misconception: reads the funding restriction as applying to the offshore leg rather than to the downstream leg
options.why: Rule 23 requires the funds for a downstream investment to be brought in from abroad and not leveraged from funds borrowed in the domestic market. The restriction attaches to the Indian company making the downstream investment, which is A Ltd here.

options.text: No approval is needed, because the sector permits one hundred per cent foreign direct investment on the automatic route and the entry route is a sectoral question
options.misconception: lets the sectoral entry route override the land-border proviso
options.why: The land-border proviso to Rule 6(a) is about who the investor is, not what the sector is. It applies on top of the sectoral route, so an automatic-route sector still needs Government approval for such an investor.

citation.ref: Proviso to Rule 6(a) and Rule 23 of the FEM (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019

items.scenario: An Indian company, A Ltd, is owned and controlled by a company incorporated in a country that shares a land border with India. A Ltd proposes to subscribe to sixty per cent of the equity of B Ltd, an Indian company in a sector where one hundred per cent foreign direct investment is permitted on the automatic route, and to fund the subscription out of a rupee term loan from an Indian bank. A Ltd's adviser says that because the money is Indian and the sector is automatic, no approval is needed and nothing has to be reported.

items.stem: What should the consultant have said?

options.text: The entry tests for a liaison office are met — a three-year profit record and a net worth of not less than USD 50,000 — but the proposed activity is not, because a liaison office may not undertake commercial activity or earn income in India and must meet its expenses wholly through inward remittances; negotiating and signing contracts creates a business connection under section 9(1)(i) and a permanent establishment, and a branch office is out of reach at a net worth of USD 70,000
options.why: FEMA 22(R) requires a profit-making track record in the immediately preceding three financial years and a net worth of not less than USD 50,000 for a liaison office, both of which this company clears, against five years and USD 100,000 for a branch office, which it does not. But a liaison office is a communication channel only: it may not undertake any commercial, trading or industrial activity and must meet its expenses through inward remittances of foreign exchange. Concluding contracts and billing Indian buyers is business, and it creates a business connection under section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and a permanent establishment under the treaty, making the profits attributable to it taxable in India.

options.text: The proposal is fine, because a liaison office that merely recovers its costs from Indian buyers earns no profit and therefore has nothing to be taxed on
options.misconception: equates no profit margin with no taxable presence
options.why: Taxability turns on whether there is a business connection or permanent establishment, not on whether the office kept a margin. Once the office concludes contracts, profits are attributed to it under section 9(1)(i) whatever it charged for its own costs.

options.text: The activity is permitted, and the only consequence is that the Annual Activity Certificate must be filed with the authorised dealer bank by 30 September each year
options.misconception: treats a reporting requirement as the answer to a prohibited activity
options.why: The Annual Activity Certificate from a chartered accountant is filed by 30 September with the authorised dealer bank and the Director General of Income-tax (International Taxation), and it is the document in which a prohibited activity is usually discovered. Filing it does not make the activity permissible.

options.text: The liaison office is not permitted at all, because a liaison office needs a net worth of not less than USD 100,000 and a profit record of five financial years
options.misconception: applies the branch office entry test to a liaison office
options.why: USD 100,000 and a five-year profit record are the branch office conditions. A liaison office needs a profit-making track record for the immediately preceding three financial years and a net worth of not less than USD 50,000.

citation.ref: FEM (Establishment in India of a Branch Office or a Liaison Office or a Project Office or any other place of business) Regulations, 2016, read with section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

items.scenario: A United States company with a net worth of USD 70,000 and profits in each of the last four financial years wants a presence in India. It proposes a liaison office whose staff will negotiate prices with Indian buyers, sign supply contracts on the head office's behalf and recover a service fee from those buyers to cover local costs. Its Indian consultant says the liaison office route is the easy one and that a liaison office is never taxable in India.

items.stem: Where is the banker wrong?

options.text: Only on the rate for the share purchase — five per cent is right for the education remittance because five per cent is the education rate whatever the source of funds
options.misconception: keeps the five per cent education rate where the loan exemption applies
options.why: Five per cent is the education and medical rate for a remittance not financed by a qualifying loan. Where the remittance for education is made out of a loan from a financial institution referred to in section 80E, no tax is collected at all.

options.text: On all three — no tax is collected on an education remittance financed by a loan from a financial institution referred to in section 80E, the twenty per cent applies only to so much of the ₹60 lakh as exceeds the ₹10 lakh threshold, and tax collected is creditable against his own tax liability under section 206C(4)
options.why: The Finance Act, 2025 removed the collection altogether where a remittance for education is made out of a loan obtained from a financial institution referred to in section 80E, with effect from 1 April 2025, and it raised the section 206C(1G) threshold from seven lakh rupees to ten lakh rupees. The rate of twenty per cent bites on the amount exceeding that threshold, not on the whole remittance. Section 206C(4) treats the amount collected as a payment of tax on his behalf, creditable against his liability.

options.text: Only on the education remittance — the twenty per cent does apply to the whole ₹60 lakh once the threshold is crossed, and the collection is final
options.misconception: applies the rate to the entire remittance instead of to the excess over the threshold
options.why: Section 206C(1G) applies the rate to so much of the amount as exceeds the threshold. Tax collected is also never final for the remitter — section 206C(4) gives him credit for it against his own liability.

options.text: Nowhere on the tax, but he has missed that the ₹60 lakh share purchase is not permissible under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme at all, which covers only current account transactions
options.misconception: reads the Scheme as a current account facility only
options.why: The Scheme covers any permissible current or capital account transaction or a combination of both, up to USD 250,000 in a financial year. It is the route through which a resident individual makes overseas portfolio investment under the FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022.

citation.ref: Schedule III to the FEM (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000, read with sections 206C(1G) and 206C(4) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 as amended by the Finance Act, 2025

items.scenario: During 2025-26 a resident individual remits ₹18 lakh for his son's university fees abroad, funded entirely by an education loan from a scheduled bank that is a financial institution referred to in section 80E, and separately remits ₹60 lakh to buy listed shares on a foreign exchange. The two together are well inside the annual ceiling. His banker tells him that tax collected at source at five per cent applies to the education remittance because it exceeds ₹10 lakh, that twenty per cent applies to the whole ₹60 lakh, and that the tax collected is a final levy he cannot recover.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: No notice was required, because section 5 tests a combination only on the assets and turnover of the enterprises and their group, and the target is below those figures
options.misconception: reads section 5 as containing only the asset and turnover tests
options.why: Clauses (a) to (c) of section 5 do work on assets and turnover. Clause (d) was added precisely for the target that holds few assets and earns little revenue here while having substantial business operations in India.

options.text: Notice was required and the standstill was breached, but no penalty follows because section 43A applies only where a party fails to give notice at all
options.misconception: confines the gun-jumping penalty to a failure to notify
options.why: Section 43A reaches a failure to give notice under section 6(2) and consummation in contravention of the standstill, and the penalty may extend to one per cent of the total turnover or assets or the value of the transaction referred to in clause (d) of section 5, whichever is higher.

options.text: Notice was required, but closing at day forty-five is lawful because the parties may act once thirty days have passed from the notice without an order
options.misconception: substitutes a thirty-day waiting period for the statutory standstill
options.why: There is no thirty-day right to close. Section 6(2A) fixes the standstill at one hundred and fifty days from the notice, or an order of the Commission, whichever comes first.

options.text: It is a combination under section 5(d) because the value of the transaction exceeds two thousand crore rupees and the target has substantial business operations in India, and closing at day forty-five breaches the standstill in section 6(2A), which forbids the combination taking effect until one hundred and fifty days have passed or the Commission has ordered, whichever is earlier
options.why: Section 5(d), inserted by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023, makes a transaction a combination on its value alone once that value exceeds two thousand crore rupees and the target has substantial business operations in India, so an asset and turnover analysis showing nothing is only half the answer. Section 6(2A) then bars the combination from coming into effect until one hundred and fifty days have passed from the notice or the Commission has passed an order under section 31, whichever is earlier.

citation.ref: Sections 5(d), 6(2), 6(2A) and 43A, as amended by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023

items.scenario: An acquirer agrees to buy the whole of a technology target for ₹2,400 crore. The target owns Indian assets of ₹200 crore and earns Indian turnover of ₹400 crore, but a substantial share of its users and one of its two engineering centres are in India. The parties file a notice with the Competition Commission of India and, having heard nothing for forty-five days, close the transaction. Their counsel says the asset and turnover figures are too small for section 5 to be engaged at all, and that in any case silence for thirty days is approval.

items.stem: What is the correct assessment of the two activities?

options.text: Registration is needed for the newsletter and that is the whole of it — once SEBI grants a certificate, the Institute has nothing further to say about the activity
options.misconception: treats a SEBI registration as substituting for the Council's permission
options.why: The two permissions answer different questions. Clause 11 of Part I of the First Schedule asks whether a member in practice may engage in an occupation other than accountancy at all, and only the Council can answer it; a certificate from SEBI does not.

options.text: The tax-planning advice is incidental to his professional service and is covered by the exemption in Regulation 4, but the subscription newsletter is investment advice carried on as an activity for consideration and needs registration under Regulation 3(1) — and it is also an occupation other than accountancy needing the Council's general or specific permission under Clause 11
options.why: Regulation 4 of the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013 exempts a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India who gives investment advice incidental to his professional service, which is what advising a tax client on an equity linked savings scheme during tax planning is. A separately marketed, separately charged newsletter to people who are not his clients is not incidental to anything, so Regulation 3(1) bites. Clause 11 of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 separately requires the general or specific permission of the Council before a member in practice engages in any other business or occupation.

options.text: Both need registration, because any advice on securities given by any person for any reason is investment advice within Regulation 3(1)
options.misconception: ignores the incidental-advice exemption altogether
options.why: Regulation 4 exists so that a professional does not have to register to answer a question that arises inside the work he was engaged for. SEBI's own guidance gives tax planning leading to an equity linked savings scheme recommendation as the example that qualifies.

options.text: Neither needs registration, because a member of the Institute is exempt from the Investment Advisers Regulations by virtue of his membership
options.misconception: reads the exemption as attaching to the person rather than to the nature of the advice
options.why: The exemption in Regulation 4 is conditional on the advice being incidental to the member's professional service. A member who provides investment advisory services as an activity or business, not incidental to his main activity, is required to register.

citation.ref: Regulations 3(1) and 4, read with Clause 11 of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

items.scenario: A chartered accountant in practice does two things. As part of the tax planning he does for a long-standing tax client, he advises the client to put ₹1.5 lakh into a particular equity linked savings scheme; he charges nothing extra for that advice. Separately he launches a monthly subscription newsletter recommending specific shares, charging ₹2,000 a month to two hundred subscribers, none of whom is a client of his practice. He has taken no permission from the Council of the Institute and holds no registration from SEBI.

items.stem: As auditor, what do you require before the report is signed?

options.text: A written representation from the CFO that the banks have been informed separately
options.misconception: routes a reporting defect into a representation
options.why: Whom the bankers heard from privately has no bearing on what the statements must say to every reader. And a representation is never sufficient evidence on its own, least of all about a disclosure that is visibly missing.

options.text: Disclosure of the material uncertainty in the notes to the financial statements themselves
options.why: Ind AS 1 puts the disclosure duty on the financial statements when management is aware of material uncertainties over going concern. The directors' report is not audited to the same standard and is not where SA 570's dedicated section can point. Without the note the statements are misstated, and the opinion — not just a paragraph — is what changes.

options.text: Nothing further, since the auditor's own going concern section will inform readers
options.misconception: uses the auditor's report to carry management's disclosure duty
options.why: The auditor's section draws attention to the note; it does not replace it. Where the note is absent, the statements are wrong and the response is a modified opinion, not a louder auditor's paragraph.

options.text: A more detailed description in the directors' report, cross-referenced from the audit report
options.misconception: accepts other-information disclosure as a substitute for the note
options.why: The directors' report is other information. A cross-reference from the audit report cannot cure an omission inside the statements — it would advertise the very gap it papers over.

items.scenario: A company has defaulted on its term loans and its net current liabilities are ₹80 crore. The CFO agrees a material uncertainty exists but proposes to describe it in the directors' report only, keeping the financial statements clean "so the bankers do not panic". The audit is in final review.

items.stem: What does section 188 require for this contract?

options.text: No approval, because buying fabric is the company's ordinary course of business
options.misconception: applies half the exemption and drops the arm's length half
options.why: The exemption needs both limbs: ordinary course and arm's length. An 8 per cent premium concedes the second limb, and one failed limb brings the section fully into play.

options.text: Only disclosure in the board's report, since the amount is below ₹50 crore
options.misconception: substitutes a disclosure threshold for the approval requirement
options.why: Thresholds decide when shareholders must approve on top of the board — they never reduce the requirement to disclosure alone. The board resolution is the floor, not the ceiling.

options.text: Approval of the Registrar of Companies before execution
options.misconception: sends a governance decision to the regulator
options.why: Section 188 keeps the decision inside the company — board, and shareholders where thresholds require. The Registrar receives filings; he does not approve contracts.

options.text: Board approval by resolution, with the interested director not participating
options.why: The counterparty is a related party and the pricing is not arm's length, so the ordinary- course-and-arm's-length exemption is unavailable. Section 188 then requires a board resolution — with shareholder approval as well if the prescribed thresholds are crossed — and the interested director stays out of the discussion and the vote.

items.scenario: A public company proposes to buy fabric worth ₹12 crore annually from a partnership in which a director's son is a partner, at prices about 8 per cent above the market, citing assured quality. The purchase committee asks what approvals the contract needs.

items.stem: Can the auditor accept this fee arrangement?

options.text: Yes, because fee structure is a private contract between auditor and client
options.misconception: places the engagement contract above the professional schedules
options.why: The Chartered Accountants Act sits over every engagement letter a member signs. A contract cannot authorise what the First Schedule defines as misconduct.

options.text: Yes, if the arrangement is disclosed to shareholders in the general meeting
options.misconception: treats disclosure as curing a prohibited arrangement
options.why: Disclosure cures conflicts that are permissible to hold. This one is prohibited outright; telling the shareholders about it only documents the misconduct.

options.text: No — fees contingent on results or based on a percentage of profits are prohibited
options.why: An auditor paid a share of the profit he certifies holds a stake in the number under audit. The First Schedule makes such fees professional misconduct, outside the narrow exceptions the Council has prescribed for specific engagements — statutory audit is not among them.

options.text: No, unless the percentage is capped at a maximum absolute amount
options.misconception: believes a ceiling converts a contingent fee into a fixed one
options.why: A capped percentage still rises and falls with the profits below the cap — the stake in the certified number remains. The defect is the linkage, not the size.

items.scenario: A client offers its statutory auditor a fee of 2 per cent of audited net profits, arguing it aligns the auditor's diligence with the company's success and is common for consultants.

items.stem: What does section 143(12) require of you?

options.text: Qualify the audit opinion and treat that as the report
options.misconception: treats the audit report to members as the fraud report to the Government
options.why: The opinion speaks to the financial statements; the 143(12) report is a separate filing to a different addressee with its own form and timeline. One cannot stand in for the other.

options.text: Report to the Central Government, routing it through the board or audit committee for their reply within the prescribed time
options.why: The fraud is by an employee against the company and crosses the one crore threshold, so the report goes to the Central Government in the prescribed manner — the board or audit committee gets the prescribed window to respond, and their comments travel with the report. Handling it quietly is not among the options the section leaves open.

options.text: Resign from the engagement to avoid association with the fraud
options.misconception: substitutes exit for the statutory duty
options.why: Resignation does not discharge section 143(12), and a resigning auditor still carries reporting duties. The Act wants the fraud reported, not the auditor gone.

options.text: Report it to the audit committee only, since internal fraud is a governance matter
options.misconception: applies the below-threshold route to an above-threshold fraud
options.why: Audit-committee-only reporting is the route for frauds under one crore. At ₹1.8 crore the section escalates the duty to the Central Government, and the committee cannot absorb it.

items.scenario: During the audit of a listed company you find that a purchase manager, colluding with a vendor, has siphoned ₹1.8 crore through inflated invoices over two years. Management asks you to note it internally and let the audit committee handle it quietly.

items.stem: Does section 135 apply?

options.text: Yes — the thresholds are alternatives, and the profit test is crossed
options.why: Any one of the three gates opens the section, and ₹6.2 crore of net profit is past the ₹5 crore gate. The committee, the policy and the 2 per cent of three-year average net profits all follow, however modest the balance sheet looks beside the other thresholds.

options.text: No, because CSR obligations attach only to listed companies
options.misconception: confuses CSR applicability with listing status
options.why: Section 135 never mentions listing. A private limited company past any threshold is as bound as a listed one.

options.text: Yes, but spending is optional so long as the board explains the shortfall
options.misconception: carries the old comply-or-explain regime past its amendment
options.why: Explain-only died with the 2021 amendments. Unspent money now transfers to an ongoing project account or a specified fund on a statutory clock, with penalties behind it.

options.text: No, because two of the three thresholds are not met
options.misconception: reads the alternative thresholds as cumulative
options.why: Requiring all three would confine CSR to giants. The section says net worth OR turnover OR profit, and one is enough.

items.scenario: A company has net worth ₹120 crore and turnover ₹800 crore, but its net profit for the immediately preceding year was ₹6.2 crore. The CFO argues CSR does not apply because the company is nowhere near the net worth or turnover thresholds.

items.stem: How do the two opinions in your report come out?

options.text: Unmodified on the financial statements; adverse on internal financial controls
options.why: Section 143(3)(i) makes controls a separate opinion answering a separate question. A material weakness draws an adverse controls opinion even where extended substantive work let the statements themselves be proved true and fair.

options.text: Unmodified on both, because the statements were ultimately proved right
options.misconception: lets the financial statement outcome absolve the controls
options.why: The controls opinion reports the state of the controls, not the state of the numbers. A material weakness that existed at the year end is reported whether or not it did damage.

options.text: The control failures go only in a management letter, not the audit report
options.misconception: demotes a statutory reporting duty to a private communication
options.why: The management letter supplements; it cannot substitute. Section 143(3)(i) puts the controls opinion in the report to members by force of statute.

options.text: Both must be qualified, since a control failure infects the statements
options.misconception: chains the two opinions together
options.why: The opinions can and do diverge. Broken controls raise the risk of misstatement; they do not prove one occurred, and here the substantive work proved otherwise.

items.scenario: Finalising a listed company's audit, you conclude the financial statements are true and fair, but testing showed the purchase-to-pay controls failed repeatedly and a material weakness exists at the year end.

items.stem: Which of the four falls foul of Clause 6?

options.text: The tender response, because concurrent audit was never offered to this firm personally
options.misconception: treats responding to an open invitation as uninvited approach
options.why: A tender is an invitation to everyone qualified. Answering an invitation is the opposite of soliciting; the mischief is approaching those who never asked.

options.text: The letter to the other firm, since work must come from clients directly
options.misconception: bars the one channel the clause expressly keeps open
options.why: Securing work from another chartered accountant in practice is a stated exception — professional sub-engagement is how overflow and specialisation have always moved.

options.text: All four, since each is an attempt to obtain professional work
options.misconception: reads the bar as covering every pursuit of work
options.why: The clause was never a vow of passivity. Its carve-outs exist precisely so that open, invited competition — tenders, empanelment, professional-to-professional requests — stays lawful.

options.text: Only the brochure mailing to the two hundred companies
options.why: Unsolicited circulars to prospective clients are the textbook form of solicitation the clause bars. The other three are its stated exceptions — responding to tenders, applying against announced empanelments, and seeking work from another chartered accountant in practice.

items.scenario: A firm of chartered accountants does four things in one quarter — mails brochures about its audit expertise to two hundred companies chosen from the registrar's records, responds to a public tender floated by a state bank for concurrent audit, applies against a public empanelment notice of a government corporation, and writes to another CA firm offering to take its overflow tax work.

items.stem: Does the proposed committee comply?

options.text: Yes, provided the committee's recommendations are ratified by the full board
options.misconception: cures defective composition with board ratification
options.why: Ratification cannot rebuild the committee. The statute regulates who deliberates, not just what emerges; a wrongly composed committee stays wrongly composed however its output is later blessed.

options.text: No, because the CFO's relative can never sit on any board committee
options.misconception: invents a blanket relative disqualification
options.why: Relationship to an officer affects independence classification, not committee membership as such. The defect is arithmetic — the independents lack a majority — not the presence of one related non-executive.

options.text: Yes — four exceeds the minimum of three, and independents are represented
options.misconception: checks the headcount and skips the majority condition
options.why: Representation is not the test; majority is. The minimum of three and the independent majority are separate conditions, and the second one fails here.

options.text: No — independent directors must form the majority, and two of four is not one
options.why: Section 177 requires a minimum of three directors with independents in the majority. Two of four fails the majority test, and a committee chaired by the managing director invites exactly the management dominance the composition rules exist to prevent.

items.scenario: A listed company proposes an audit committee of four directors — two independent, the managing director, and the CFO's brother as a non-executive director, chaired by the managing director. The company secretary certifies the composition complies with section 177.

items.stem: Does CARO 2020 apply to this company's audit?

options.text: No, since two of the three financial limits are within bounds
options.misconception: reads the cumulative exemption conditions as majority-satisfied
options.why: The exemption is conjunctive. Meeting two limits while breaking the third is simply breaking the conditions — the order does not average them.

options.text: Yes, but only the fraud and statutory dues clauses apply to private companies
options.misconception: invents a partial CARO for private companies
options.why: CARO has no reduced edition. Once applicable, the whole order applies; applicability is the only company-level question.

options.text: Yes — the revenue of ₹14 crore crosses the ten crore limit, and one breach is enough
options.why: The private-company exemption needs every limit honoured together — capital and reserves, borrowings, and revenue. Revenue at ₹14 crore breaks the ten crore ceiling, so the order applies with all its reporting clauses, whatever the other two figures say.

options.text: No, because CARO never applies to private companies
options.misconception: turns a conditional exemption into a blanket one
options.why: Private companies are exempt only inside the size limits. Beyond them, a private company answers every CARO clause a public one does.

items.scenario: A private limited company, not a holding or subsidiary of a public company, has paid-up capital and reserves of ₹80 lakh, bank borrowings that peaked at ₹95 lakh during the year, and revenue of ₹14 crore. Its auditor treats CARO 2020 as inapplicable since capital and borrowings are within a crore each.

items.stem: What is the most the company can distribute from current profits?

options.text: ₹28 crore, by adding the securities premium to distributable profit
options.misconception: treats securities premium as a free reserve
options.why: Premium is shareholders' capital contribution, usable only for the purposes section 52 lists. Distribution as dividend is not among them.

options.text: ₹3 crore — after depreciation and after setting off the carried-forward loss
options.why: Section 123 charges depreciation first (₹10 minus ₹3) and then requires previous losses and unabsorbed depreciation to be set off (₹7 minus ₹4), leaving ₹3 crore of distributable profit. The premium and revaluation balances watch from the sidelines.

options.text: ₹7 crore — depreciation must be provided, but old losses concern the balance sheet, not dividends
options.misconception: provides depreciation and skips the loss set-off
options.why: The set-off is a statutory pre-condition, not a presentation nicety. Paying dividends across an unabsorbed loss distributes capital dressed as income.

options.text: ₹18 crore, by drawing on the revaluation surplus
options.misconception: distributes an unrealised book write-up
options.why: A revaluation surplus is an accounting remeasurement, not realised profit. Dividending it hands out money the company never earned and may never see.

items.scenario: A company has current-year profit of ₹10 crore before providing ₹3 crore of depreciation, a brought-forward business loss of ₹4 crore, a securities premium of ₹25 crore, and a revaluation surplus of ₹15 crore. The board wants the largest lawful dividend.

items.stem: Can either proposal stand?

options.text: Neither — the cooling-off blocks any reappointment for five years, and the partner-linked firm is equally barred
options.why: Ten years is the ceiling, and the five-year cooling-off admits no short extensions — two years inside a barred window is barred. The fallback fails on the same section's own words: a firm with common partners as at the appointment date stands in the retiring firm's shoes.

options.text: The linked firm works, because it is a distinct legal entity
options.misconception: hides continuity behind a fresh registration
options.why: The statute anticipated the manoeuvre and named it: common partners carry the disqualification across the entity line.

options.text: The two-year extension works, since it is shorter than a term
options.misconception: reads the bar as prohibiting only full terms
options.why: The section bars appointment as auditor during the cooling-off, for any length. Slicing the term thin does not slip it through.

options.text: Both work if the audit committee certifies the firm's independence
options.misconception: lets a committee certify around a statutory bar
options.why: Independence certification supplements eligibility; it cannot manufacture it. A candidate the statute disqualifies stays disqualified with the finest certificate attached.

items.scenario: An audit firm completes its second five-year term at a listed company. The shareholders, pleased with its work, propose reappointing it for two more years only, arguing a short extension is not a fresh five-year term. As fallback they suggest a different firm in which three partners of the retiring firm hold a majority.

items.stem: Which of the CFO's three grounds survives section 138?

options.text: The first — private companies are outside internal audit requirements
options.misconception: reads section 138 as a public-company provision
options.why: The rule names private companies with their own thresholds. Two hundred crore of turnover is one of them, and this company is past it.

options.text: The third — the internal auditor must be a practising chartered accountant
options.misconception: narrows the section's deliberately wide eligibility
options.why: The provision expressly allows a cost accountant or such other professional as the board decides, and the rule adds that the appointee may be an employee. Parliament left the choice to the board.

options.text: None — the turnover line is crossed, in-house review is not internal audit, and the board may appoint a qualified employee
options.why: A private company past two hundred crore of turnover is squarely covered. A management team reviewing its own controls is self-review, not the independent function the section contemplates — but the section is generous on who: a chartered accountant, cost accountant or other professional, employee included, as the board decides.

options.text: The second — a documented monthly management review satisfies the requirement
options.misconception: accepts self-review as the audit of self
