options.why: The reviewers report to the very management whose controls they review. Internal audit exists to stand outside that loop, reporting toward the audit committee.

items.scenario: A private company had turnover of ₹230 crore in the preceding year and no borrowings. The CFO resists appointing an internal auditor on three grounds — the company is private, its own accounts team reviews controls monthly, and in any case only chartered accountants can be internal auditors, which would mean hiring outside.

items.stem: Is the company covered, and can unspent CSR sit in the balance sheet?

options.text: Covered — the profit test alone triggers section 135 — and unspent amounts must move to the statutory accounts, not sit in the balance sheet
options.why: The three thresholds are alternatives; net profit of ₹9 crore against the five-crore line is enough on its own. Since the 2019 amendments, unspent money has mandated destinations — an unspent-CSR account within thirty days for ongoing projects, a Schedule VII fund within six months otherwise. A general reserve is neither.

options.text: Covered, but spending remains comply-or-explain, so unspent amounts need only a board explanation
options.misconception: states the pre-2019 regime as current law
options.why: Explanation alone was the original design. The amendments kept the explanation and added teeth — mandatory transfer of unspent amounts on a statutory clock, with penalties behind it.

options.text: Not covered — CSR needs at least two of the three thresholds crossed
options.misconception: reads "or" as "and"
options.why: The section strings its thresholds with "or". One gate open is enough, and the profit gate is open by four crore.

options.text: Covered, and the obligation is two per cent of the preceding year's ₹9 crore profit
options.misconception: computes on one year instead of the three-year average
options.why: Eligibility reads one year; the spend reads three. Two per cent applies to the average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years, which smooths a lumpy profit like this one.

items.scenario: A company with turnover of ₹800 crore and net worth of ₹300 crore earned net profit of ₹9 crore in the immediately preceding year. Its CFO argues CSR does not apply since neither the net worth nor the turnover threshold is crossed. The board separately proposes that if CSR does apply, any unspent amount can be carried in the general balance sheet for later use.

items.stem: Which alternatives does section 149 permit?

options.text: The third — a gap of any length resets the two-term count
options.misconception: reads the cooling-off as a courtesy interval rather than a three-year statutory bar
options.why: The reset needs the full three years. A shorter gap leaves him inside the exclusion period, and any association during it is itself prohibited.

options.text: The first, with shareholders' special resolution blessing the third term
options.misconception: lets a resolution extend a statutory maximum
options.why: The special resolution is how a second term is granted. No resolution reaches past two consecutive terms; the statute's ceiling binds the shareholders too.

options.text: None of the three — ten years is the ceiling, and the three-year cooling-off bars any association, consultancy included
options.why: Two consecutive terms exhaust the independent-director route, and section 149(11)'s cooling-off is not merely a pause before reappointment — during those three years he may not be appointed in or associated with the company in any other capacity. The consultancy and the one-year gap both walk into that bar.

options.text: The second — the consultancy is a different capacity outside section 149
options.misconception: routes around the bar through a side door the section explicitly closed
options.why: The subsection's words reach appointment in the company "in any other capacity". A paid consultancy is also precisely the pecuniary relationship that destroyed independence while he served.

items.scenario: A listed company's independent director completes two consecutive five-year terms. The board, valuing his experience, proposes three alternatives: reappoint him for a third term as independent director; appoint him immediately as a paid consultant to the company; or bring him back as an independent director after one year's gap.

items.stem: How many section 186 requirements does the proposal break?

options.text: Three — the limit needs a special resolution, board approval must be unanimous, and the rate is below the statutory floor
options.why: ₹140 crore exceeds both limbs of the limit — sixty per cent of ₹200 crore is ₹120 crore — so shareholders must pass a special resolution first. The board sanction must carry the consent of all directors present, which two dissents defeat. And no loan may be priced below the government-security yield for the matching tenor; a group discount is exactly what the floor exists to stop.

options.text: One — only the shareholder resolution is missing; boards act by majority and price freely
options.misconception: applies ordinary board-majority rules to a section that demands unanimity
options.why: Section 186(5) requires the consent of all directors present at the meeting for these decisions — a deliberate departure from majority rule — and subsection (7) fixes the interest floor.

options.text: Two — resolution and unanimity fail, but interest is a commercial matter for the board
options.misconception: concedes the process points while missing the pricing floor
options.why: Subsection (7) writes the minimum into the statute: not lower than the prevailing yield on government securities closest to the loan's tenor. Commercial freedom starts above that line, not below it.

options.text: None — lending to a group company is exempt from section 186
options.misconception: stretches the wholly-owned-subsidiary carve-outs over the whole group
options.why: The exemptions cover specific cases such as loans to wholly owned subsidiaries. A group company generally is just another body corporate, and every limb of the section applies.

items.scenario: A company with paid-up capital plus free reserves of ₹200 crore (free reserves portion ₹90 crore) has existing inter-corporate loans of ₹100 crore. The board wants to lend a further ₹40 crore to a group company at an interest rate below the prevailing government-security yield, approving it by majority vote at a board meeting with two directors dissenting.

items.stem: Which advances can lawfully be made?

options.text: All three, if shareholders approve each by special resolution
options.misconception: reads the whole section as resolution-curable
options.why: The special resolution route exists only for the entities in which directors are interested. For the director personally, the prohibition has no key — that is the section's core.

options.text: The first and third — loans to individuals are personnel matters outside company law
options.misconception: exempts exactly the person the section names first
options.why: "Any loan to any of its directors" is the opening prohibition. The individual director is not the exception; he is the addressee.

options.text: The second with a special resolution, and the third under the employee-scheme exception — never the first
options.why: The direct loan to a director sits in section 185's absolute bar; no resolution reaches it. The interested private company is in the conditional ring — special resolution plus use in the borrower's principal business activities. The managing director's housing loan rides the exception for schemes extended to all employees.

options.text: None — section 185 bans anything that benefits a director directly or indirectly
options.misconception: inflates the bar over the section's own exceptions
options.why: The 2017 rewrite deliberately split the section into a bar, a conditional window and exceptions. Reading it as a wall outlaws employee welfare schemes Parliament expressly saved.

items.scenario: A public company's board considers three advances: ₹50 lakh to a director to buy a house; ₹2 crore to a private company in which the same director holds 40 per cent, for that company's working capital; and ₹30 lakh to the managing director under a housing-loan scheme the company extends to all employees.

items.stem: What happens to the section 9 application?

options.text: It fails — the rejection letter is a pre-existing dispute, and section 9 cannot decide whose case is right
options.why: The dispute predates the demand notice by six months in writing, which is exactly what the dispute defence requires. The adjudicating authority only asks whether a plausible dispute existed before the notice — not who would win it — because the Code rescues failing companies rather than collecting contested bills. The supplier's forum is a civil suit or arbitration.

options.text: It succeeds — the undisputed two-thirds alone exceeds the threshold
options.misconception: severs the debt to salvage the application
options.why: A genuine dispute touching the claimed operational debt bars the application; the tribunal does not carve the invoice into clean and contested slices to keep the petition alive.

options.text: It succeeds if the supplier proves the goods were not defective
options.misconception: turns the admission stage into the trial
options.why: Proof of quality is a trial, with evidence and cross-examination — everything the summary admission under the Code is built not to be. Plausibility of the dispute ends the enquiry.

options.text: It fails only if the buyer had also filed a suit before the notice
options.misconception: demands litigation where the Code asks only for a dispute
options.why: The definition covers a dispute including a suit or arbitration — the correspondence raising a real quality claim is enough. Requiring a filed suit would reward the fastest court fee, not the true state of accounts.

items.scenario: A supplier is owed ₹3 crore for goods delivered. Six months before any insolvency step, the buyer had written rejecting a third of the goods as defective and withholding payment. The supplier now serves a section 8 demand notice and, on non-payment, files under section 9, arguing the defect claim is an afterthought to dodge insolvency.

items.stem: Which section 203 breaches are running?

options.text: None — the search is genuine and the CEO's roles are both disclosed
options.misconception: substitutes good faith and disclosure for statutory limits
options.why: The six-month line and the one-company rule are bright lines. Diligent interviewing past the deadline is still a default, disclosed dual office still a dual office.

options.text: Only the CFO vacancy — CEOs are not key managerial personnel
options.misconception: drops the CEO from the definition
options.why: Section 2(51) lists the chief executive officer among KMP expressly. The whole-time restrictions ride on that definition.

options.text: Two — the CFO vacancy passed its six-month limit in July, and a whole-time KMP cannot hold office in an unrelated company
options.why: The board's window to fill a KMP vacancy is six months from the date it arose; September is past it, and an informal stand-in is not an appointment. The one-company rule for whole-time KMP allows only a subsidiary as the second seat — an unrelated company fails it, and part-time labels do not undo the office.

options.text: Only the CEO's dual role — vacancies may stay open until the right candidate appears
options.misconception: reads the six-month limit as aspirational
options.why: The section commands the board to fill the vacancy within six months, with penalties behind it. Candidate quality is why the window is six months, not why it is open-ended.

items.scenario: A listed company's CFO resigns in January. In September, the board is still interviewing, with the finance controller handling the work informally. Meanwhile the company's CEO also serves as CEO of an unrelated private company, describing both as part-time engagements.

items.stem: Is the group barred?

options.text: No — any single shareholder may always petition against oppression
options.misconception: erases the standing requirement altogether
options.why: Open standing would hand every disgruntled member a Tribunal lever against the company. The thresholds filter; the waiver handles the exceptions.

options.text: Yes — thresholds are jurisdictional and the Tribunal cannot relax them
options.misconception: reads the section without its waiver proviso
options.why: The proviso to section 244(1) exists precisely so a meritorious minority is not silenced by arithmetic. Waiver is discretionary, but the power is in the text.

options.text: Not necessarily — the tests are alternatives with a waiver besides; 80 falls short of each, but the Tribunal can waive on merits
options.why: Section 244 offers the least demanding of its routes: one hundred members, one-tenth of members (600 here), or one-tenth of capital. The group misses all three — but the proviso lets the Tribunal waive the requirement for a case worth hearing, and adding 20 consenting members would cure standing outright. The objection opens a door; it does not close the case.

options.text: Yes, unless the group first acquires two more per cent of capital
options.misconception: fixes on the capital route as if it were the only one
options.why: Ten per cent of capital is one of three alternative routes, and the cheapest fix here is twenty more consenting members — or persuading the Tribunal to waive numbers entirely.

items.scenario: A company has 6,000 members. A group of 80 members holding 8 per cent of the issued capital wants to petition against the promoters for oppression. The promoters' counsel objects: fewer than one hundred members, less than ten per cent of capital — no standing, end of matter.

items.stem: What stops the proposal?

options.text: Nothing — the amount is within the board's ten per cent power
options.misconception: clears the quantum test and stops reading
options.why: Section 68 stacks its conditions; each stands independently. The cooling period exists so buy-backs are considered capital events, not a running price-support tool.

options.text: The absence of a special resolution, required for every buy-back
options.misconception: erases the board-only route
options.why: Up to ten per cent of paid-up equity plus free reserves, the board's resolution suffices — that carve-out is the provision's whole convenience. The defect here is timing, not authority.

options.text: The size — buy-backs are capped at ten per cent of paid-up capital alone
options.misconception: shrinks the base to bare capital
options.why: Both the ten and twenty-five per cent ceilings measure against capital plus free reserves. On ₹400 crore, the board route alone reaches ₹40 crore.

options.text: The one-year cooling period since the last buy-back — the arithmetic is within the board's limit, but the calendar is not
options.why: Ten per cent of ₹400 crore is ₹40 crore, so ₹38 crore sits inside the board-resolution route. What the proposal cannot survive is the bar on a fresh buy-back within one year of the preceding one's completion — a limit that applies whichever organ approves. Wait four months, and the same resolution works.

items.scenario: A company with paid-up equity of ₹100 crore and free reserves of ₹300 crore completed a buy-back eight months ago. The board now proposes, by board resolution alone, a fresh buy-back of ₹38 crore, noting it is under ten per cent of capital plus reserves and therefore within the board's own power.

items.stem: How many section 42 violations are running, and which is the gravest?

options.text: Three besides the lapsed timeline — and the forum post is gravest, converting the issue into a deemed public offer
options.why: The 180 identified offerees are fine; everything after is not. Cash application money breaks the banking-channel mandate; spending before allotment and filing breaks the separate-account discipline; week ten has passed the sixty-day allotment-or-refund line. The forum post outranks them all — public solicitation makes the placement a deemed public offer, importing prospectus and penalty consequences wholesale.

options.text: The spending alone, since money once received belongs to the company
options.misconception: mistakes custody for entitlement
options.why: Application money is the applicants' until allotment and the return's filing. That is why it must sit in its own account — spending it early is using other people's money.

options.text: Only the cash collection, curable by depositing it into the separate account now
options.misconception: picks the most fixable breach and forgets the fatal one
options.why: Banking the cash cures nothing already broken, and the deemed-public-offer consequence of the forum post cannot be deposited away.

options.text: None — private companies raising from under two hundred persons are outside section 42's formalities
options.misconception: reads the headcount as the section's only rule
options.why: Two hundred is one gate of several. The banking channel, the escrow discipline, the sixty days and the no-advertisement bar each bind independently of the count.

items.scenario: A private company raising ₹15 crore emails its offer letter to 180 hand-picked investors, posts the "opportunity" on a public investor forum "for wider reach", collects some application money in cash for convenience, and starts spending receipts while allotment paperwork is still pending in week ten.

items.stem: Where does the bank stand?

options.text: The loan itself is void and the bank recovers nothing at all
options.misconception: extends the charge's fate to the debt
options.why: Only the security fails. The money remains owed — indeed it becomes immediately payable — and the bank proves for it as an unsecured creditor.

options.text: Unsecured in the liquidation — the unregistered charge is void against the liquidator, and the bank could have filed the charge itself
options.why: Section 77 makes an unregistered charge void against the liquidator and creditors, which is precisely when security earns its keep. The deed binds the company while it lives; in liquidation the bank stands in the unsecured queue for its surviving debt. The sting is self-inflicted — section 78 let the charge-holder register on the company's default, and the bank held the papers for two years.

options.text: Secured — a valid mortgage deed cannot be defeated by a missing form
options.misconception: treats registration as clerical rather than constitutive against third parties
options.why: The register exists so later lenders and the liquidator can see what is already pledged. A secret mortgage defeats that purpose, so the statute defeats the secret mortgage.

options.text: Secured, because the liquidator had actual notice of the mortgage from the company's own records
options.misconception: substitutes notice for registration
options.why: The section voids the unregistered charge against the liquidator without a notice exception. Actual knowledge does not repair a statutory invalidity.

items.scenario: A bank lends ₹50 crore against a factory mortgage. The company never files the charge with the Registrar, and the bank, holding its own copy of the mortgage deed, does not press. Two years later the company enters liquidation, and the liquidator treats the bank as an unsecured creditor. The bank protests that the mortgage deed is valid between the parties and the loan documentation impeccable.

items.stem: What is wrong with the two proposals?

options.text: Nothing — annexed reports need no response, and any qualified professional may sign
options.misconception: reads the annexure as the end of the board's duty
options.why: The response requirement exists so shareholders see the board answer the criticism. The signature requirement exists because compliance auditing was assigned to the secretarial profession deliberately.

options.text: Only the response point — auditors can hold both offices with member approval
options.misconception: makes eligibility a matter of resolution
options.why: No resolution converts a chartered accountant into a company secretary in practice. The statute names the profession, and approval processes choose within it, not around it.

options.text: The board must explain every qualification in its report, and secretarial audit belongs to a practising company secretary, not the statutory auditor
options.why: Section 204(3) obliges the board to explain in full any qualification or observation in the secretarial audit report — silence is itself a default. And the section reserves the engagement to a company secretary in practice: the statutory auditor holds a different office under a different section, and consolidation would put one professional's certificate where the law demands another's.

options.text: Only the auditor point — boards respond to financial qualifications alone
options.misconception: limits the response duty to the financial audit
options.why: Section 204 carries its own explanation obligation, parallel to the one for the financial auditor's qualifications. Both reports get answered.

items.scenario: A large listed company receives a secretarial audit report qualified on delayed stock exchange intimations and a related party approval taken ex post facto. The board proposes to file the report without comment, reasoning that qualifications in an annexure speak for themselves; the CFO separately suggests next year's secretarial audit be given to the statutory auditors to consolidate work.

items.stem: What is the company's true position?

options.text: The plan is fine, and the Registrar can add three months if needed
options.misconception: extends the inextensible first AGM
options.why: The extension proviso carves out the first AGM in terms. Planning that leans on an unavailable extension is planning to default.

options.text: The company defaulted by holding no AGM in 2025 — a meeting is required in every calendar year
options.misconception: applies the old calendar-year rule to the first AGM's own window
options.why: The first AGM clock runs from the first financial year's close, not the calendar. A January 2025 company with a March 2026 year-end lawfully holds its first AGM late in 2026.

options.text: 15 November is lawful — the first AGM window runs nine months from 31 March 2026, but no Registrar extension exists for a first AGM
options.why: A company may take its first financial year to the 31 March following incorporation, and the first AGM is due within nine months of that year-end — by 31 December 2026, with no meeting needed in the incorporation year at all. The comfort the second director seeks is not available: the Registrar's three-month extension power expressly excludes the first AGM. December is a wall.

options.text: The AGM was due by 30 September 2026 — six months from the year-end
options.misconception: applies the subsequent-AGM deadline to the first
options.why: Six months governs later years; the first AGM gets nine. The two windows differ precisely because a new company's first close carries first-time burdens.

items.scenario: A company incorporated on 1 January 2025 closes its first financial year on 31 March 2026. The directors plan the first AGM for 15 November 2026, and one director worries they have already defaulted since no AGM happened in calendar 2025. Another proposes seeking the Registrar's extension "as a safety margin" in case preparations slip past December.

items.stem: Can the creditor get the company restored, and did the debt die?

options.text: Yes — a creditor's restoration application runs for twenty years, and liabilities survive striking off as if the company continued
options.why: The three-year clock the ex-directors quote belongs to the aggrieved person's appeal; section 252 separately lets the company, any member, creditor or workman apply within twenty years of the notice. And section 248's own scheme preserves every liability of the company, its directors and members despite the dissolution — the warehouse can answer the decree once the register revives the debtor.

options.text: No — dissolution extinguishes the company and everything it owed
options.misconception: gives an administrative housecleaning the effect of insolvency discharge
options.why: Strike off clears dead names from the register; it is no scheme of creditor settlement. The statute says liabilities continue precisely so debtors cannot die their way out of decrees.

options.text: No — all restoration routes closed three years after the strike off
options.misconception: reads the short window and misses the long one
options.why: Two routes, two clocks. The twenty-year application exists for exactly this discovery-years-later creditor.

options.text: Yes, but only the Registrar can seek restoration once struck off
options.misconception: hands the remedy to the striker alone
options.why: Section 252 names the company, members, creditors and workmen as applicants. The creditor petitions the Tribunal in his own right.

items.scenario: A company is struck off by the Registrar for two years' inactivity. Four years later a creditor with an unpaid ₹1 crore decree discovers the striking off and wants the company back on the register to execute against its still-existing warehouse; the ex-directors respond that the company's death extinguished its debts and, in any case, all remedies lapsed three years after the strike off.

items.stem: How many defects does the arrangement carry?

options.text: Only the reappointment — an adjourned AGM genuinely extends every director's tenure
options.misconception: gives the adjournment the effect the section pre-empted
options.why: The "date by which the AGM should have been held" language exists precisely for this manoeuvre. Statutory AGM deadlines, not the board's calendar, end the seat.

options.text: Two — a candidate rejected in general meeting is barred from the additional route, and the office ends when the AGM should have been held, adjournment or not
options.why: Section 161(1) closes both doors in its own words. The proviso bars appointing as additional director a person who fails to get appointed at a general meeting — the board cannot overrule the shareholders it answers to. And tenure runs to the AGM or the last date by which it should have been held, whichever is earlier: postponing the meeting postpones nothing for this seat.

options.text: Only the adjournment trick — a fresh board appointment cures a general meeting rejection
options.misconception: lets the appointing organs outrank each other in the wrong order
options.why: The proviso's whole purpose is that a shareholder verdict cannot be reversed in the boardroom. The appointment was void at inception, before the adjournment added the second defect.

options.text: None — the board's power to appoint additional directors is unfettered where the articles allow
options.misconception: reads the power without its proviso and its clock
options.why: The articles enable the power; the statute conditions it. Both conditions here are in the section's text, not in implication.

items.scenario: Shareholders reject a promoter's nominee at the AGM. A month later the board appoints the same person as an additional director, and when the next AGM approaches with the shareholders still hostile, the board adjourns the meeting indefinitely so the seat continues. The articles authorise additional directors.

items.stem: Can it claim the small company privileges?

options.text: Yes for accounts, no for meetings — privileges are severable by choice
options.misconception: lets a non-qualifying company pick privileges à la carte
options.why: Status is the gate and it is closed. A company is small or it is not; the privileges flow together from the definition, never individually by preference.

options.text: Yes — the thresholds are the definition, and both are met
options.misconception: reads the limits without the exclusions
options.why: The proviso is half the definition. Size measures the company alone; the exclusions measure what stands behind it, and a listed parent stands behind this one.

options.text: No — a subsidiary is excluded from the definition whatever its size, so every skipped compliance is a default
options.why: The numbers fit — capital under four crore, turnover under forty — but section 2(85)'s proviso excludes holding and subsidiary companies from small company status outright. Group membership means group-scale resources and group-scale stakes, so the concessions for genuinely small standalone businesses are withdrawn: the cash flow statement, the four board meetings and the rotation discipline all apply in full.

options.text: No, but only because turnover must be measured on the consolidated group
options.misconception: fixes the outcome with an invented consolidation test
options.why: The definition tests the company's own figures; the group enters through the subsidiary exclusion, not through aggregation. The right answer needs the right reason — the proviso, not arithmetic.

items.scenario: A private company with paid-up capital of ₹3 crore and turnover of ₹35 crore claims small company status: it skips the cash flow statement, holds two board meetings, and keeps its auditor indefinitely. It happens to be the wholly owned subsidiary of a large listed manufacturer.

items.stem: Which two corrections does the plan need?

options.text: The plan works as drafted — 75 per cent of a well-attended meeting suffices
options.misconception: imports the NCLT route's majority into the no-NCLT route
options.why: Three-fourths of those present and voting is section 230's standard, purchased with judicial oversight. The fast track's price is near-unanimity measured on the whole capital.

options.text: Correct thresholds, but once on the fast track no authority can derail the scheme
options.misconception: mistakes no-court-by-default for no-court-ever
options.why: The Regional Director's power to refer objectionable schemes to the Tribunal is the route's safety valve. Fast track means presumption of speed, not immunity from scrutiny.

options.text: The fast track is unavailable — listed companies must always go to the Tribunal
options.misconception: adds a listing bar the section does not contain
options.why: The classes are defined by relationship and size, and holding-WOS is one of them regardless of listing. Securities law adds disclosures, not a different route.

options.text: Holding-WOS mergers qualify, but approval needs ninety per cent of TOTAL shares — not 75 per cent of those voting — and objections can still push the scheme to the Tribunal
options.why: The route fits: holding company with wholly owned subsidiary is a named fast-track class whatever the listing status. But section 233's thresholds are stricter than section 230's — ninety per cent of the total number of shares, and ninety per cent in value of creditors — precisely because no judge scrutinises the scheme. And the safeguard the director asks about exists: Registrar or Official Liquidator objections with substance send the scheme to the Tribunal after all.

items.scenario: A listed company wants to absorb its wholly owned subsidiary and its lawyers propose the section 233 fast track, obtaining approval from 75 per cent of members in a meeting with strong turnout — the threshold they know from ordinary schemes of arrangement. A director asks whether skipping the Tribunal means creditors and regulators simply have no say.

items.stem: Which of the two positions survives section 212?

options.text: The Registrar may finish; only fresh investigations are barred
options.misconception: saves pending work from a transfer provision that names it
options.why: The subsection transfers pending proceedings expressly. Completion by the old agency would produce the dual findings the exclusivity exists to prevent.

options.text: The arrest stands, but SFIO's report needs a police FIR to prosecute
options.misconception: adds a police layer the section removed
options.why: The investigation report is treated as a report filed by a police officer for framing charges. Requiring a second agency to re-investigate would waste the first's statutory design.

options.text: Both — administrative inquiries can run in parallel, and arrests need police
options.misconception: keeps the fragmented pre-SFIO world
options.why: Fragmented parallel investigations tripping over each other were the failure the exclusive-assignment rule fixed. And the arrest power is in the section's own text, exercised routinely in major fraud cases.

options.text: Neither — the assignment ousts every parallel Companies Act investigation, files and all, and SFIO's arrest power for section 447 fraud is statutory
options.why: Section 212(2) is written to prevent exactly the parallel track proposed: on assignment, no other Companies Act agency proceeds, and pending investigations transfer to SFIO with their documents — the work is not wasted, it is handed over. On the promoters' side, the section arms designated SFIO officers with arrest powers for the section 447 offence, which the Act makes cognizable for this purpose; serious corporate fraud stopped being a purely civil affair when that section was enacted.

items.scenario: After a listed company's books collapse in scandal, the Registrar's inspectors are mid-inquiry when the Central Government assigns the case to SFIO. The Registrar's team proposes finishing its almost-complete inquiry in parallel "to avoid wasting work"; the promoters, arrested by SFIO officers, argue the arrest is illegal since company law violations are civil matters and only police can arrest.

items.stem: Which raisings are lawful?

options.text: None — private companies cannot accept deposits at all
options.misconception: erases the members' route
options.why: Members' deposits under section 73(2) are available to private companies, with relaxations for many. The prohibition aims at the public's money, not the members'.

options.text: The first two — member deposits with the section 73 conditions, and director money excluded from "deposit" by the declaration; the public raising is barred outright
options.why: Members' deposits are open to any company that walks section 73(2)'s path — resolution, circular, the conditions. Directors' own funds with the written declaration sit in the deposit definition's exclusions. Public deposits belong only to eligible companies — public companies clearing the hundred-crore net worth or five-hundred-crore turnover line — and a ₹40 crore private company fails every element of that description; its FD advertisements solicit what it cannot lawfully accept.

options.text: Only the first — any money from directors is a deposit like any other
options.misconception: reads the definition without its exclusions
options.why: The definition's exclusion for directors' declared own funds is standing law. The declaration is the safeguard: borrowed money relabelled through a director stays a deposit.

options.text: All three — money freely offered may be freely taken
options.misconception: treats deposit-taking as ordinary borrowing
options.why: Public deposit-taking is a licensed privilege ringed with rating, reserve and repayment rules, because the depositors are the least able to assess the company. The bar on the ineligible is the core of the chapter.

items.scenario: A private company with net worth ₹40 crore raises money three ways: ₹5 crore from its members after a general meeting resolution and the prescribed circular; ₹2 crore from its directors, each declaring in writing the money is their own and not borrowed; and ₹8 crore from the general public through attractive fixed-deposit advertisements.

items.stem: How many composition defects does the committee carry?

options.text: None — boards structure committees as they see fit
options.misconception: treats a statutory committee as an internal working group
options.why: The section prescribes the composition in terms. A committee of the management, for the management, defeats the accountability it implements.

options.text: Only the chairing — the MD may be a member but not preside
options.misconception: halves the exclusion
options.why: Non-executive directors "only" is the membership rule; the MD fails it as a member, not merely as chair.

options.text: Only the CFO's seat — directors of any kind may fill the rest
options.misconception: catches the obvious outsider and misses the executive bar
options.why: The CFO's seat is the loudest defect but the MD's is the more dangerous one — it puts the paid at the table where pay is set.

options.text: Three — an executive member and chair, a non-director member, and independent directors short of half
options.why: Section 178 builds the committee from non-executive directors only, so the managing director cannot sit on it, let alone chair it. The CFO is not a director at all. And with at least half required independent, one of three fails the fraction even before the other defects. The self-approved policy shows why the composition rules exist: the committee prices the very executives it must exclude.

items.scenario: A listed company constitutes its nomination and remuneration committee: the executive chairman-cum-managing director as its chairperson "for continuity", one independent director, and the CFO as the third member. The committee's first act is approving a remuneration policy drafted by the chairman for himself.

items.stem: What is wrong across the two companies?

options.text: The subsidiary's borrowings put it inside the requirement, and the parent's transfer plus HR-only routing defeat the two safeguards the section names
options.why: Fifty crore of bank borrowings is the trigger that reaches unlisted companies, so the subsidiary owes a mechanism now. The parent has one in form and neither of its substance: adequate safeguards against victimisation — a retaliatory transfer is the textbook case to investigate — and direct access to the audit committee chairperson in appropriate cases, which an HR-only funnel forecloses by design.

options.text: Both companies comply if their board reports disclose the policies
options.misconception: substitutes disclosure for operation
options.why: Disclosure reports the mechanism; the duty is running one that works. Reporting a funnel that punishes users discloses the breach, not compliance.

options.text: Nothing at the subsidiary; the parent's transfer is an ordinary staffing matter
options.misconception: reads the trigger narrowly and the retaliation charitably
options.why: The borrowing trigger is in the rule's text, and a transfer days after a fraud report is the pattern victimisation safeguards exist to catch — it must at least be examined as such.

options.text: The subsidiary is exempt as unlisted; the parent's only defect is the routing
options.misconception: forgets the deposits-and-borrowings limb
options.why: Listing is one of three triggers. The ₹50 crore borrowing line was drawn precisely for companies like this subsidiary.

items.scenario: An unlisted public company with ₹80 crore of bank borrowings says vigil mechanisms are a listed-company luxury it need not run. Meanwhile, at its listed parent, an employee who reported inventory fraud through the mechanism is transferred to a remote branch the following week, and the whistle-blower policy routes all complaints exclusively through the HR head with no other channel.

items.stem: Is the CFO's eleven-per-cent comfort enough?

options.text: No — the inner limits bind too; the MD's ₹12 crore breaches his five per cent (₹10 crore) and the NEDs' ₹3 crore breaches their one per cent (₹2 crore), each needing a special resolution
options.why: Section 197 nests its ceilings: eleven per cent overall, but five per cent for a single managing director and one per cent for non-executives where an MD exists. Both inner lines are crossed, and since 2018 the cure is a special resolution of the shareholders — not government approval, and not the ordinary resolutions on file. Unauthorised excess is held in trust for the company and must be refunded unless the shareholders waive it by special resolution.

options.text: No, and the excess amounts are irrecoverably forfeit to the government
options.misconception: invents a confiscation the section does not contain
options.why: The excess is held in trust for the company — recovered from the director, or waived by special resolution. The State takes nothing under this section.

options.text: Yes, provided Central Government approval is applied for
options.misconception: routes the cure through an approval abolished in 2018
options.why: The 2018 amendments moved the say entirely to shareholders by special resolution. Applications to the Centre for excess pay belong to history.

options.text: Yes — one aggregate cap governs and ₹15 crore is inside it
options.misconception: reads the outer ceiling as the only ceiling
options.why: The sub-limits allocate the eleven per cent among classes precisely so one well-placed executive cannot absorb the whole pool. Aggregate comfort answers the wrong question twice here.

items.scenario: A public company's net profits computed under section 198 are ₹200 crore. Its managing director drew ₹12 crore and its three non-executive directors ₹3 crore in aggregate, with only ordinary resolutions in place. The CFO sees no issue: total managerial pay of ₹15 crore is well inside eleven per cent of profits, which is ₹22 crore.

items.stem: How must the ISD distribute the credit on this invoice?

options.text: Entirely to the Delhi branch, since the invoice was addressed to the head office there
options.misconception: treats the billing address as the distribution rule rather than the recipients who benefit
options.why: The campaign benefits three branches. Section 20 apportions by turnover of the actual recipient units, not by where the supplier happened to send the bill.

options.text: The head office keeps the credit and sets it off against its own output tax
options.misconception: treats an ISD as an ordinary taxable person entitled to use credit itself
options.why: An ISD distributes; it does not consume. With no outward taxable supply of its own, the head office has no output liability to use this credit against.

options.text: Pro rata to the turnover of the three branches in the relevant period, by issuing ISD invoices
options.why: Section 20 requires distribution in the ratio of each recipient unit's turnover during the relevant period, carried out through an ISD invoice — not by head-office discretion over who gets how much.

options.text: Equally, one-third to each branch regardless of their size
options.misconception: assumes an equal split rather than a turnover-proportionate one
options.why: An equal split ignores the turnover ratio the section requires — a large branch and a small one do not receive identical shares by law.

items.scenario: A company's head office in Delhi receives an invoice for a pan-India advertising campaign benefiting its Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru branches, each separately registered. The head office itself is registered as an Input Service Distributor and makes no outward taxable supply of its own.

items.stem: What does the law require of this credit?

options.text: Reverse it only if exempt turnover exceeds fifty per cent of total turnover
options.misconception: invents a threshold that the reversal mechanism does not contain
options.why: The Rule 42 ratio applies at whatever level exempt turnover sits — there is no fifty per cent gate before reversal begins.

options.text: Reverse the portion of the common credit attributable to exempt turnover, computed by Rule 42's formula
options.why: Rule 42 apportions common credit that cannot be directly attributed, using the ratio of exempt to total turnover, reversed monthly and trued up annually against the actual figures.

options.text: Nothing — credit taken on a valid tax invoice for common expenses stands as taken
options.misconception: treats invoice validity as the whole test, ignoring the use-based restriction
options.why: Section 17(2) denies credit attributable to exempt supplies regardless of invoice validity; Rule 42 is the mechanism that carves that portion back out.

options.text: Reverse the entire common credit, since it partly serves exempt supplies
options.misconception: reverses the whole amount instead of only the exempt-attributable share
options.why: Rule 42 apportions rather than disallowing wholesale — the taxable-turnover share of the common credit stays available to the trader.

items.scenario: A trader deals in both taxable goods and exempt goods from the same warehouse, using common input services such as rent and security for both lines. He takes full credit on these common services in the month they are billed.

items.stem: How much must the company pay on this sale under section 18(6)?

options.text: Nothing — the credit was validly taken and fully utilised when the machine was bought
options.misconception: treats a valid original credit as immune to any later event
options.why: A valid intake credit does not insulate a later disposal. Section 18(6) treats supply of capital goods as its own taxable event carrying its own payment rule.

options.text: ₹6 lakh — the full original credit, since disposal reverses it entirely
options.misconception: ignores the prescribed reduction for the period the asset was actually used
options.why: The clawback tapers with use. Paying back the full original credit is the outcome only for a near-immediate resale, not after two years of legitimate business use.

options.text: ₹80,000 — GST on the transaction value, exactly as for any other supply
options.misconception: treats a capital-goods disposal like an ordinary supply and skips the comparison
options.why: Section 18(6) is not satisfied by ordinary output tax alone; it demands the higher of that figure and the reduced original credit.

options.text: ₹4.2 lakh — the higher of the reduced credit and the tax on transaction value
options.why: Section 18(6) requires payment of whichever figure is higher. ₹4.2 lakh, the reduced credit, exceeds the ₹80,000 transaction-value tax, so ₹4.2 lakh is what falls due.

items.scenario: A company took ₹6 lakh input tax credit on a machine bought two years ago and now sells it as scrap for a transaction value on which GST works out to ₹80,000. Reducing the ₹6 lakh credit by the prescribed percentage points for the two years of use leaves ₹4.2 lakh.

items.stem: What lets him achieve this under the scheme?

options.text: He cannot — QRMP filers report invoices only once a quarter, and recipients must wait for the quarterly return
options.misconception: misses the Invoice Furnishing Facility built into the scheme for exactly this gap
options.why: The Facility exists for the first two months of the quarter so quarterly filing does not stall recipients' credit that long. Details furnished through it are not repeated in the quarterly GSTR-1.

options.text: He must exit QRMP for that quarter and file monthly instead
options.misconception: assumes the scheme offers no half-way option and forces an exit
options.why: Wanting faster recipient visibility does not force an exit — the Invoice Furnishing Facility is the scheme's own accommodation for it. Exit is compulsory only when aggregate turnover crosses ₹5 crore during a quarter, and then from the next quarter.

options.text: He must pay tax quarterly along with the return, since QRMP means quarterly for everything
options.misconception: assumes QRMP makes payment quarterly too, not only the return
options.why: QRMP keeps monthly payment even while return filing turns quarterly — tax for each of the first two months goes in Form GST PMT-06 by the 25th of the following month. The scheme's split name is the clue.

options.text: Uploading that invoice through the Invoice Furnishing Facility between the 1st and the 13th of the following month, while still paying tax monthly in Form GST PMT-06 and filing GSTR-3B quarterly
options.why: The scheme pairs quarterly return filing with monthly tax payment, and Rule 59(2) gives an optional Invoice Furnishing Facility for the first two months of the quarter — up to ₹50 lakh a month, filed between the 1st and the 13th of the succeeding month — precisely so a recipient is not stuck waiting a full quarter for the credit to show in his GSTR-2B.

citation.ref: Rule 61A (manner of opting) and Rule 59(2) (Invoice Furnishing Facility), read with Notification No. 84/2020-Central Tax dated 10.11.2020 issued under the proviso to section 39(1), and CBIC Circular No. 143/13/2020-GST dated 10.11.2020

items.scenario: A registered dealer whose aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year was ₹3 crore — inside the ₹5 crore QRMP limit — has opted into the scheme. In the first month of the new quarter he raises a ₹18 lakh invoice on a large corporate buyer, who wants to see the credit promptly rather than waiting for the quarterly GSTR-3B.

items.stem: What is the due date, under section 44?

options.text: 31 July 2026, four months after the financial year ends, as with an income tax return
options.misconception: imports an income-tax filing rhythm into GST
options.why: The GST annual return runs on its own section 44 timeline, unconnected to the Income-tax Act's due dates.

options.text: There is no fixed due date — it may be filed whenever the department asks for it
options.misconception: treats a statutory deadline as discretionary
options.why: Section 44 sets a hard date, and late filing draws its own late fee under the Act — it is not left to the department's convenience.

options.text: 30 November 2026, the same date that governs the last date for taking credit
options.misconception: confuses the section 16(4) credit cut-off with the annual return's own due date
options.why: The two dates belong to different provisions with different purposes. The annual return's due date runs a month later than the credit cut-off.

options.text: 31 December 2026, unless extended by the Government
options.why: Section 44 fixes the annual return's due date at the thirty-first of December following the end of the financial year — here 2025-26, so 31 December 2026.

items.scenario: A regular registered taxpayer files monthly GSTR-3B and GSTR-1 throughout 2025-26. Its accountant is unsure by when the annual return for that year is due.

items.stem: Which provision governs this demand, and what follows from that choice?

options.text: Section 74 — because tax was short-paid, and that alone is enough to invoke it
options.misconception: assumes any shortfall automatically reaches the fraud provision
options.why: Fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression is an ingredient to be shown, not an inference from a shortfall — and for FY 2025-26 section 74 is out of time in any case. Under section 74A that ingredient no longer decides which section applies; it decides only whether the penalty is ten per cent of the tax or the whole of it.

options.text: Neither — a clerical error is corrected only by revising the return, with no demand possible
options.misconception: assumes a revised-return mechanism exists that removes the demand power
options.why: GST has no revised-return concept. A shortfall found after filing is recovered under section 74A for FY 2024-25 onwards, or under section 73 or 74 for periods up to FY 2023-24, whichever the facts fit.

options.text: Section 73 — the shortfall is bona fide, and section 73 is the non-fraud provision
options.misconception: applies the old 73 vs 74 split to a period past the FY 2024-25 cut-off
options.why: Right instinct on the facts, wrong section for the period. Section 73's own sub-section (12), inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, stops it at FY 2023-24. For FY 2025-26 the same non-fraud outcome is reached inside section 74A instead.

options.text: Section 74A — the single demand provision for FY 2024-25 onwards, under which the absence of fraud shows up in the penalty, ten per cent of the tax or ₹10,000 whichever is higher
options.why: Sections 73(12) and 74(12) confine those two sections to determination of tax pertaining to periods up to FY 2023-24. FY 2025-26 falls inside section 74A, whose heading says it governs demands "pertaining to Financial Year 2024-25 onward". Honesty still counts, but now only in the consequences: section 74A(5)(i) sets the non-fraud penalty at ten per cent of the tax or ₹10,000, whichever is higher, and section 74A(8)(ii) closes the proceedings with no penalty at all if the tax and interest are paid within sixty days of the notice.

citation.ref: Section 74A(5)(i) and 74A(8)(ii) (inserted by section 138 of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, in force 01.11.2024 by Notification No. 17/2024-Central Tax dated 27.09.2024), read with sections 73(12) and 74(12)

items.scenario: A department audit of a company's FY 2025-26 returns finds that taxable value was under-reported on genuine invoices because of a bona fide clerical error in its accounting software, resulting in short payment of ₹6 lakh of tax, with no evidence of any intent to evade. The company's consultant reaches for section 73, as he always has.

items.stem: What must he pay to have the appeal entertained?

options.text: Nothing — filing the appeal itself automatically stays the entire demand
options.misconception: assumes the appeal alone stays recovery without any payment
options.why: The stay on the disputed balance is conditional on the pre-deposit being paid; an unpaid appeal does not stay recovery.

options.text: ₹10 lakh admitted tax in full, plus ten per cent of the ₹40 lakh disputed — ₹14 lakh in total
options.why: Section 107(6) makes payment of the full admitted amount, plus ten per cent of the disputed amount, a precondition to the appeal being entertained at all — not merely to a stay.

options.text: The full ₹50 lakh, with a refund to follow if the appeal succeeds
options.misconception: treats the pre-deposit as full payment rather than the statutory fraction
options.why: The ten per cent pre-deposit exists precisely so the appellant is not forced to pay the entire disputed sum up front while the dispute is pending.

options.text: Ten per cent of the full ₹50 lakh, with the admitted ₹10 lakh deferred to the appeal's outcome
options.misconception: extends the ten per cent concession to the admitted portion too
options.why: The admitted amount carries no discount and must be paid in full; only the disputed remainder gets the ten per cent treatment.

items.scenario: A taxpayer disputes a demand order raising ₹50 lakh tax, of which he admits ₹10 lakh is correctly due. He wants to file a first appeal contesting the remaining ₹40 lakh, and asks his consultant how much he must pay before the appeal can even be filed.

items.stem: From when does interest run on the additional tax found due at finalisation?

options.text: From the date of the final assessment order, since no shortfall existed before then
options.misconception: treats the shortfall as arising only at finalisation rather than always having existed
options.why: The shortfall existed from the original due date — finalisation only quantifies it; interest compensates for the entire period of underpayment.

options.text: From the original due date for payment of tax on that supply, not from the date of the final order
options.why: Section 60 treats the provisional payment as an estimate; interest on any shortfall found at finalisation runs from when the tax was originally due, so the length of time finalisation took does not buy an interest-free period.

options.text: No interest is payable, since the delay in finalisation was the department's, not the taxpayer's
options.misconception: assigns fault for the delay and lets that decide interest liability
options.why: Section 60's interest rule does not turn on whose delay it was — it simply follows the shortfall from its original due date.

options.text: From six months after the provisional order, since that is when finalisation was due
options.misconception: anchors interest to the statutory finalisation deadline rather than the tax due date
options.why: The six-month period is a deadline for the officer to finalise, not the interest clock's starting point.

items.scenario: An importer-cum-trader cannot fix the correct valuation of a new product line pending a technical classification opinion and requests provisional assessment. The final order, issued eight months later, fixes a higher value and demands additional tax.

items.stem: Must the company destroy the records once the seventy-two months run out?

options.text: Yes — seventy-two months is an absolute outer limit regardless of any pending matter
options.misconception: reads the seventy-two months as a hard ceiling rather than a floor the proviso can extend
options.why: The proviso exists precisely to stop records disappearing while they are still live evidence in an unresolved dispute.

options.text: No, but only if the company itself applies to the department for an extension
options.misconception: makes the extension conditional on an application, when the statute grants it automatically
options.why: The extension operates by the section's own terms once a proceeding is pending — no separate request is needed to trigger it.

options.text: Yes, because the retention obligation concerns only the department's audit rights, not appeal proceedings
options.misconception: narrows section 36's proviso to audits alone
options.why: The proviso names appeal, revision, any other proceeding, and investigation together — an appeal is squarely inside it.

options.text: No — records tied to a pending proceeding are kept a year beyond its final disposal, or to the seventy-two-month mark, whichever is later
options.why: Section 36's proviso extends retention specifically for records relevant to a pending appeal, revision or investigation, overriding the plain seventy-two-month clock until a year after the matter is finally closed.

items.scenario: A company's records for 2020-21 are due to complete their seventy-two-month retention period in early 2027. In late 2026 a demand appeal concerning that very year is still pending before the Tribunal.

items.stem: What is the consequence of that delay?

options.text: Nothing is due yet — the ninety-day interest-free window is counted from the end of the one-year warehousing period, so interest could not start before fifteen months
options.misconception: starts the ninety days at the close of the warehousing period instead of at the section 60(1) order
options.why: Both clocks start at the same point. Section 61(1)(c) gives one year from the section 60(1) order, and section 61(2) counts its ninety days from that same order — not from the end of the year. Interest is the earlier of the two by a wide margin, which is why goods can be well inside the warehousing period and still bearing interest, as here.

options.text: The rate of duty is frozen at the rate on the date of warehousing, so the delay costs nothing extra
options.misconception: assumes the into-bond date fixes the rate, when the ex-bond clearance date does
options.why: Section 15(1)(b) takes the rate of duty and tariff value on the date the ex-bond bill of entry is presented under section 68, so a delay can move the rate itself as well as drawing interest. Note the split: it is the rate that moves to the ex-bond date, while the value of the goods stays as assessed on the into-bond bill of entry.

options.text: The goods are automatically confiscated the moment the interest-free period expires
options.misconception: escalates a delay straight to confiscation, skipping the interest mechanism
options.why: Overstaying ninety days triggers interest, nothing more. Confiscation attaches to specific defaults such as improper removal, and it is only on overstaying the warehousing period itself that section 72 treats the goods as improperly removed.

options.text: Interest runs on the duty from the ninety-first day after the section 60(1) order until the duty is paid, on top of the duty itself
options.why: Section 61(2) charges interest once clause (c) goods sit in the warehouse beyond ninety days from the date of the section 60(1) order, at the rate fixed under section 47, on the duty payable at clearance, for the stretch from the ninety-first day to the day the duty is paid. Bonding defers duty; it does not make the delay free.

citation.ref: Sections 61(1)(c) and 61(2) (ninety days from the order under section 60(1)), read with sections 68 and 15(1)(b)

items.scenario: An importer warehouses machinery in a licensed public bonded warehouse. The proper officer's order under section 60(1) permitting the deposit is made on 1 June. The importer files the ex-bond bill of entry for home consumption on 1 February the following year — eight months later, so still inside the one-year warehousing period, but long past ninety days.

items.stem: How do the Baggage Rules treat the worn clothing and the used laptop, compared with the new gift item?

options.text: Only the laptop is free, under the laptop allowance in rule 5, and the worn clothing counts against the General Free Allowance
options.misconception: reaches for the new-laptop allowance for a laptop that is already free as a used personal effect
options.why: Rule 5's laptop allowance is for one new laptop or notepad, for a passenger of eighteen or above who is not a crew member. It is not needed here: a two-year-old laptop is already free under rule 3 as a used personal effect, and so is the worn clothing.

options.text: All three are added together and tested against the same General Free Allowance ceiling
options.misconception: folds used personal effects into the value-capped allowance meant for other articles
options.why: Used personal effects sit outside the value test entirely under rule 3. Lumping them in would let routine luggage — worn clothes, a used laptop — eat into an allowance meant for purchases.

options.text: The worn clothing and used laptop clear under rule 3 with no value ceiling at all; only the ₹60,000 gift is tested against the General Free Allowance, and at ₹75,000 the allowance covers it
options.why: Rule 3 of the Baggage Rules, 2026 clears used personal effects required for satisfying daily necessities of life, and travel souvenirs, free of duty without any value limit, other than Annexure-I articles. The General Free Allowance in rule 5 is a separate, value-capped allowance for other articles — ₹75,000 for a resident arriving other than by land — and the newly bought gift is exactly the kind of thing it is meant to cover.

options.text: The used effects are free, but the allowance for the gift is ₹50,000, so duty is payable on the ₹10,000 excess
options.misconception: applies the General Free Allowance figure from the superseded Baggage Rules, 2016
options.why: ₹50,000 was the figure under rule 3 of the Baggage Rules, 2016. Those rules were superseded by the Baggage Rules, 2026 with effect from 2 February 2026, and rule 5 now sets the allowance at ₹75,000 for a resident arriving other than by land. A ₹60,000 gift is inside it, so nothing is payable.

citation.ref: Rules 3 and 5 of the Baggage Rules, 2026 (Notification No. 14/2026-Customs (N.T.) dated 01.02.2026, in force 02.02.2026), read with CBIC Master Circular No. 4/2026-Customs dated 01.02.2026

items.scenario: A resident flies home from the United States in June 2026 carrying his own worn clothing and a laptop he has used for two years, plus one new gift item worth ₹60,000 bought at the airport duty-free shop. Nothing he carries appears in Annexure-I.

items.stem: What is this deposit, and when is registration ordinarily due to expire without extension?

options.text: A refundable security deposit unrelated to tax liability, with registration valid for a year like an ordinary taxpayer
options.misconception: treats the payment as a generic security deposit and imports the ordinary annual renewal cycle
options.why: The payment is specifically advance tax pegged to estimated liability, and a casual taxable person's registration is deliberately short-lived, not annual.

options.text: Advance tax as described, but registration lasts exactly thirty days, extendable only once
options.misconception: substitutes an invented thirty-day figure for the statutory ninety-day validity
options.why: The default outer limit is ninety days from the effective date, not thirty, before any extension is even considered.

options.text: Advance tax equal to his estimated liability for the period, and registration expires on the earlier of the specified period or ninety days from the effective date
options.why: Section 27 conditions a casual taxable person's registration on an advance deposit of estimated tax, and caps validity at ninety days from the effective date unless the applicant asked for a shorter specific period.

options.text: No deposit is required, since the fair lasts only ten days, well under any threshold
options.misconception: assumes a short event escapes the advance-tax condition
options.why: The advance-tax requirement is not scaled by event length; it attaches to casual-taxable-person registration regardless of how brief the activity is.

items.scenario: A trader from Pune registers as a casual taxable person to sell goods at a ten-day trade fair in Jaipur, where he has no fixed place of business. Before approving his application, the department asks him to deposit an amount.

items.stem: What is the place of supply, and which tax does the Mumbai firm charge?

options.text: Maharashtra, because the service was actually performed there — so the firm charges CGST and SGST
options.misconception: applies a performance test to a service the general rule governs by recipient location
options.why: Where the service was performed decides the place of supply only for the specific services listed in sections 12(3) to 12(14). Consultancy is not among them, so the general rule and the recipient's location govern.

options.text: Gujarat, the location of the registered recipient — so the firm charges IGST
options.why: Section 12(2)(a) fixes the place of supply for a registered recipient at that recipient's location. The supplier sits in Maharashtra and the place of supply is Gujarat, so the supply is inter-State and carries IGST.

options.text: Gujarat, but the firm charges CGST and SGST because both parties are inside India
options.misconception: gets the place of supply right and then misreads what makes a supply inter-State
options.why: A supply is inter-State when the supplier's location and the place of supply are in different States, whether or not both are in India. Maharashtra against Gujarat makes it inter-State, so IGST applies.

options.text: Maharashtra, because the supplier is located there — so the firm charges CGST and SGST
options.misconception: falls back to the supplier's location, which applies only when no address is on record for an unregistered recipient
options.why: The supplier's location is the last resort under section 12(2)(b), reached only for an unregistered recipient with no address on record. A registered recipient's own location governs.

items.scenario: A management consultancy firm registered in Mumbai is engaged by a manufacturing company registered in Gujarat. Every meeting and workshop is held at the firm's own Mumbai office, and the report is delivered there. Consultancy is not one of the services listed in sections 12(3) to 12(14).

items.stem: What are the two places of supply?

options.text: Goa for organising the conference, and Delhi for the festival admission
options.misconception: inverts the two rules, swapping the venue test and the recipient test
options.why: This reverses both provisions. Organisation follows the registered recipient's location and admission follows the venue, not the other way round.

options.text: Delhi for organising the conference, and Goa for the festival admission
options.why: Section 12(7) puts organisation of an event at the location of a registered recipient, so the conference is supplied in Delhi. Section 12(6) puts admission at the place the event is actually held, so the tickets are supplied in Goa whoever buys them.

options.text: Goa for both, since both the conference and the festival physically take place there
options.misconception: applies the venue rule to organisation as well, missing that section 12(7) looks at a registered recipient
options.why: The venue governs admission under section 12(6), and governs organisation only where the recipient is unregistered. Here the recipient is registered, so the conference follows Delhi.

options.text: Delhi for both, since the recipient is registered in Delhi in each case
options.misconception: applies the recipient-location rule to admission, which section 12(6) decides by venue alone
options.why: Section 12(6) makes no distinction between a registered and an unregistered ticket buyer. The place the event is held governs admission regardless.

items.scenario: An event management company registered in Goa is hired to organise a three-day dealer conference at a Goa resort for a company registered in Delhi. Separately, the same Goa company sells admission tickets to a music festival it holds in Goa, and a Delhi-registered firm buys a block of those tickets for its staff.

items.stem: Where is the repair service supplied?

options.text: Chennai, because the place of supply of any service performed on goods physically present in India is where the goods are
options.misconception: converts the remote-supply proviso, which is about electronic delivery, into a general goods-location rule
options.why: The location of the goods governs only where the service is rendered from a remote location by electronic means. A physical repair on site is not that, and the temporary-import proviso controls instead.

options.text: Outside India, at the recipient's location in Germany, because the second proviso to section 13(3)(a) takes this case out of that clause and back to section 13(2)
options.why: Goods temporarily imported for repairs or any other treatment or process, and exported after it without being put to use in India, are expressly carved out of section 13(3)(a). The general rule in section 13(2) then applies and the place of supply is the recipient's location, so the repair can qualify as an export of services.

options.text: Outside India, but only because payment was received in convertible foreign exchange
options.misconception: confuses a condition of export of services under section 2(6) with the rule that fixes the place of supply
options.why: Foreign exchange is one of the five conditions in section 2(6) for a supply to be an export. It has nothing to do with fixing the place of supply, which section 13 alone decides.

options.text: Chennai, because the service was actually performed there on goods made physically available to the supplier
options.misconception: applies section 13(3)(a) without reading its second proviso, the exact trap the proviso exists to close
options.why: Section 13(3)(a) would give Chennai, which is why the proviso was written. Temporary import for repair followed by export is precisely the fact pattern it removes from that clause.

citation.ref: Section 13(3)(a), second proviso, read with Section 13(2)

items.scenario: A German company ships a specialised machine to a workshop in Chennai for repair. The machine is temporarily imported, repaired at the Chennai workshop, and exported back to Germany without being put to any use in India other than what the repair itself needed. Payment comes in convertible foreign exchange, and the two companies are separate legal persons.

items.stem: What is the time of supply for this reverse-charge service?

options.text: 5 May 2026 — the date of the advocate's invoice
options.misconception: carries the forward-charge habit of taking the invoice date across to reverse charge
options.why: The invoice date fixes time of supply under forward charge. Under reverse charge the invoice only starts the sixty-day count; it is not itself the time of supply.

options.text: 20 August 2026 — the date the company paid the advocate and entered it in its books
options.misconception: treats the date of payment as the whole rule and ignores the sixty-day outer limit
options.why: Payment is only one of the two limbs, and section 13(3) takes whichever comes earlier. Delaying payment past sixty days cannot push the liability out with it.

options.text: 5 July 2026 — the day immediately following sixty days from the invoice date
options.why: Section 13(3) takes the earlier of the date of payment and the day immediately following sixty days from the invoice. Sixty days from 5 May 2026 ends on 4 July 2026, so the second limb gives 5 July 2026 — earlier than the 20 August payment.

options.text: 5 June 2026 — the day immediately following thirty days from the invoice date
options.misconception: applies the thirty-day limit for goods to a supply of services
options.why: Thirty days is the section 12(3) limit for goods under reverse charge. Services run on sixty days under section 13(3).

items.scenario: A registered company receives legal services from an advocate — a supply on which the company itself must pay tax under reverse charge. The advocate finishes the work on 30 April 2026 and issues his invoice on 5 May 2026. The company makes payment on 20 August 2026 and records it in its books that day.

items.stem: What is the trader's liability under section 9(4) as it stands?

options.text: Reverse charge, but only if the trader's aggregate turnover crosses the registration threshold
options.misconception: invents a turnover gate that section 9(4) does not contain
options.why: The current sub-section turns on being a notified class of person receiving a notified supply, not on turnover. Turnover decides registration, not this liability.

options.text: Reverse charge on the full ₹90,000, since every registered person pays tax on inward supplies from unregistered persons
options.misconception: states the pre-2019 rule as if it were still the law
options.why: That was the position under the original sub-section, which was suspended and then replaced. The current sub-section applies only to notified classes.

options.text: Nothing — section 9(4) now reaches only a notified class of registered persons on notified supplies, and this trader is not in it
options.why: Section 9(4) was substituted with effect from 1 February 2019. It no longer applies to purchases from unregistered persons generally; it bites only where the Government has notified both the class of registered person and the supply. An ordinary trader buying cartons is outside it.

options.text: Reverse charge on the amount by which the day's purchases from unregistered suppliers exceed ₹5,000
options.misconception: applies the exemption limit that went with the original version of section 9(4), long since gone
options.why: That daily limit belonged to an exemption notification under the original section 9(4). Both the original sub-section and its exemption are gone; the trader is not liable at all, so no limit needs testing.

citation.ref: Section 9(4), as substituted with effect from 1 February 2019

items.scenario: A registered trader in Nagpur buys packing cartons worth ₹90,000 during June 2026 from a small local supplier who is not registered under GST. The trader is not a promoter and the cartons have nothing to do with any construction project.

items.stem: What is the position on input tax credit for the contractor's works contract service and the materials?

options.text: Only the portion of the cost not capitalised is blocked, so the whole credit is available here
options.misconception: reads the capitalisation clause as a relief when it is what extends the block to repairs and renovation
options.why: The reference to capitalisation widens construction to take in renovation, alteration and repairs to the extent they are capitalised. It does not release capitalised construction cost, which is squarely inside the block.

options.text: Both are allowed, because the office block will be used in the course or furtherance of the company's taxable business
options.misconception: treats business use as sufficient, when clause (d) blocks the credit even where the property is used in business
options.why: Clause (d) says in terms that the block applies even where the goods or services are used in the course or furtherance of business. Business use is the very argument the words shut out.

options.text: Both are allowed, because the Supreme Court in Safari Retreats read "plant or machinery" in clause (d) widely enough to cover such a building
options.misconception: relies on a judicial reading that a retrospective amendment has since displaced
options.why: Section 124 of the Finance Act (No. 7) of 2025 substituted the words to read plant and machinery, and that substitution is deemed to have been made from 1 July 2017 — the day GST began. The same section added Explanation 2 to clause (d) from 1 October 2025, directing that any reference to plant or machinery be construed, and always be deemed to have been construed, as plant and machinery, notwithstanding any judgment, decree or order of any court. The wide reading no longer stands for any period.

options.text: Both are blocked — the works contract service under clause (c) and the materials under clause (d), because an office block is a building and so outside plant and machinery
options.why: Clause (c) blocks works contract services for construction of immovable property, and clause (d) blocks goods and services received for construction on one's own account. The explanation to section 17 keeps land, buildings and other civil structures out of plant and machinery, so the carve-out does not rescue an office block.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(c) and (d) with Explanations 1 and 2 and the explanation to section 17, clause (d) as substituted by section 124 of the Finance Act (No. 7) of 2025

items.scenario: A manufacturing company constructs a new administrative office block on its own land, engaging a contractor for the civil work and buying cement and steel itself. The whole cost is capitalised. The block will be used entirely for the company's own taxable business.

items.stem: How much input tax credit may the bank take for the month?

options.text: ₹45 lakh — fifty per cent of the ₹90 lakh, with the same-PAN credit excluded altogether
options.misconception: reads the proviso as removing the same-PAN credit rather than exempting it from the fifty per cent cut
options.why: The proviso protects that credit; it does not disallow it. The ₹10 lakh is added in full, not struck out.

options.text: ₹50 lakh — fifty per cent of the whole ₹100 lakh
options.misconception: applies the fifty per cent cut to everything and misses the same-PAN proviso
options.why: The proviso exists precisely so that a bank's internal cross-charges between its own State registrations are not halved. Applying the cut to all ₹100 lakh ignores it.

options.text: ₹55 lakh — the ₹10 lakh from its own same-PAN registration in full, plus fifty per cent of the remaining ₹90 lakh
