options.why: The proviso to section 17(4) keeps the fifty per cent restriction off tax paid on supplies from another registered person having the same PAN. That ₹10 lakh comes in whole, and the fifty per cent cut applies only to the other ₹90 lakh, giving ₹45 lakh — ₹55 lakh in all.

options.text: ₹100 lakh — the whole eligible credit, since the bank can switch back to proportionate reversal for this month
options.misconception: treats the section 17(4) option as changeable month to month
options.why: The option once exercised cannot be withdrawn during the remaining part of the financial year. Having chosen the fifty per cent route, the bank is on it for the year.

items.scenario: A banking company has opted for the fifty per cent route under section 17(4) for the year. For June 2026 its eligible input tax credit is ₹100 lakh in total, of which ₹10 lakh is tax on services received from its own branch registered in another State under the same PAN.

items.stem: What is the consequence under section 19?

options.text: The one year ran from 10 June 2026, the date the job worker received the steel, so the despatch is deemed a supply by the principal to the job worker on the day the inputs were sent out
options.why: The proviso to section 19(3) counts the one year from the date of receipt by the job worker where inputs go directly to him. That year ended in June 2027, the goods came back in August 2027, and the deemed supply falls on the day the inputs were sent out.

options.text: No credit was available in the first place, because the steel never reached the principal's premises
options.misconception: assumes physical receipt by the principal is a condition of credit on job work inputs
options.why: Section 19(2) allows the principal the credit even where inputs are sent directly to the job worker. Direct despatch is expressly permitted, not a bar.

options.text: Nothing is due, because capital goods and inputs sent for job work both carry a three-year window
options.misconception: applies the three-year limit for capital goods to inputs
options.why: Three years is the limit for capital goods. Inputs run on one year, and this despatch missed it by more than two months.

options.text: The one year ran from the date the principal took the credit in his return, so the window was still open in August 2027
options.misconception: anchors the period to the credit entry instead of to the sending out or the job worker's receipt
options.why: Section 19(3) counts from the date of sending out, and its proviso from the date of receipt by the job worker where the goods went directly. The date credit was claimed does not enter the computation.

items.scenario: A principal in Pune buys steel and instructs the supplier to deliver it straight to a job worker in Nashik, where it arrives on 10 June 2026. The steel never enters the principal's own premises. The finished components come back to Pune on 20 August 2027.

items.stem: For how many days is the e-way bill valid?

options.text: Five days — one for the first 200 kilometres and one more for each further 200 kilometres or part thereof
options.why: The first 200 kilometres give one day. The remaining 610 kilometres are three full stretches of 200 plus a part stretch, and a part counts as whole, so four more days. Five days in total.

options.text: Nine days — one day for every 100 kilometres or part thereof
options.misconception: uses the earlier 100-kilometre scale that the current rule 138(10) replaced
options.why: Rule 138(10) once ran at one day per 100 kilometres. It now runs at 200, so a validity worked out on the old scale comes out roughly twice as long as the law allows.

options.text: Four days — 810 kilometres divided by 200, taking the whole number
options.misconception: drops the "or part thereof", which turns the leftover 10 kilometres into a full extra day
options.why: The rule counts every 200 kilometres or part thereof. The leftover 10 kilometres is a part stretch and earns a day of its own.

options.text: Forty-one days — one day for the first 20 kilometres and one more for every 20 kilometres or part
options.misconception: applies the over dimensional cargo scale to ordinary cargo
options.why: The 20-kilometre scale is for over dimensional cargo, or a multimodal shipment with a leg by ship. This consignment is ordinary road cargo and runs on the 200-kilometre scale.

items.scenario: A consignment of ordinary cargo — not over dimensional, and moving entirely by road — has to travel 810 kilometres. The transporter enters the vehicle details in Part B of the e-way bill at 4 p.m. on 3 June 2026.

items.stem: What can the exporter expect ahead of final sanction?

options.text: ₹40 lakh in full, since a low-risk exporter's claim is sanctioned outright
options.misconception: treats a clean risk score as replacing the ninety per cent provisional split
options.why: The risk evaluation decides whether the provisional route is taken, not how much it releases. The provisional figure stays at ninety per cent, with the remaining tenth on final sanction.

options.text: Nothing until the officer completes his detailed verification and passes a final refund order
options.misconception: ignores the provisional refund route altogether, treating final sanction as the only payment
options.why: The whole point of section 54(6) is to release most of the money ahead of verification. Waiting for the final order describes the position for claims that do not qualify for the provisional route.

options.text: ₹36 lakh sanctioned provisionally, within seven days of the acknowledgement, with the balance to follow on final sanction
options.why: Section 54(6) allows ninety per cent of the amount claimed to be sanctioned on a provisional basis for a refund arising from zero-rated supplies, and rule 91 gives seven days from the acknowledgement. Ninety per cent of ₹40 lakh is ₹36 lakh.

options.text: ₹36 lakh, but only after the officer completes his detailed examination of the claim
options.misconception: collapses the provisional sanction into the final one and drops the seven-day timeline
options.why: Provisional sanction comes before detailed examination, not after — rule 91 runs its seven days from acknowledgement. An officer who wants to examine first must record his reasons in writing for declining the provisional route.

citation.ref: Section 54(6) with Rule 91(2) of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: An exporter supplying goods under a letter of undertaking, without payment of tax, claims a refund of ₹40 lakh of unutilised input tax credit. The application is acknowledged on 12 May 2026 and the system's risk evaluation flags nothing against him.

items.stem: What is the value of this supply under rule 28?

options.text: Nil — services between a head office and its own branch are not a supply, being within one legal entity
options.misconception: forgets that distinct persons under section 25 supply to each other even without consideration
options.why: Schedule I treats supplies between distinct persons in the course of business as a supply even without consideration. The transaction is taxable; only its value is in question.

options.text: ₹1,00,000 — the invoice value, which the second proviso deems to be the open market value where the recipient is eligible for full credit
options.why: Head office and branch are distinct persons under section 25, so rule 28 governs. Its second proviso says that where the recipient is eligible for full input tax credit, the value declared in the invoice is deemed to be the open market value — so ₹1,00,000 stands.

options.text: ₹4,50,000 — ninety per cent of the open market value
options.misconception: applies the first proviso, which is only for goods the recipient will supply onward as such
options.why: The ninety per cent option is confined to goods intended for further supply as such by the recipient, and it is the supplier's option at that. It has no application to a support service consumed by the branch.

options.text: ₹5,00,000 — the open market value, since rule 28 opens with open market value as the first measure
options.misconception: applies the main rule and stops before the proviso that governs a full-credit recipient
options.why: Open market value is the opening measure, but the second proviso displaces it entirely where the recipient can take full credit. The exercise would be revenue-neutral anyway.

items.scenario: A company's head office in Mumbai provides accounting and payroll support to its own branch in Chennai, separately registered under the same PAN. An independent firm would charge ₹5,00,000 for the same work. The head office raises an invoice for ₹1,00,000. The Chennai branch makes only taxable supplies and is eligible for full input tax credit.

items.stem: By when must the company issue its own invoice for this supply?

options.text: By 2 May 2026 — within sixty days, matching the outer limit for time of supply under reverse charge
options.misconception: borrows the sixty-day cap from section 13(3) and treats it as the invoicing deadline
options.why: Sixty days is the outer limit for fixing the time of supply of services under reverse charge. The self-invoice runs on rule 47A's thirty days, a different provision with a different clock.

options.text: By 2 April 2026 — within thirty days of receiving the supply, under rule 47A
options.why: Section 31(3)(f) requires a recipient paying under reverse charge to issue an invoice where his supplier is unregistered, and rule 47A, in force from 1 November 2024, fixes that at thirty days from the date of receipt of the supply. Thirty days from 3 March 2026 is 2 April 2026.

options.text: No invoice is needed from the company — the foreign supplier's own invoice is the document for the supply
options.misconception: assumes a supplier's document discharges the recipient's separate obligation under section 31(3)(f)
options.why: Section 31(3)(f) puts the obligation on the recipient precisely because an unregistered supplier issues no GST tax invoice. The company must raise its own.

options.text: By 17 April 2026 — within forty-five days, the period allowed for financial services
options.misconception: applies the extended period meant for an insurer, bank or non-banking financial company to an ordinary recipient
options.why: Forty-five days under rule 47 is for an insurer, a banking company, a financial institution or an NBFC issuing invoices for its own outward services. It does not extend a recipient's self-invoice deadline.

citation.ref: Rule 47A, read with Section 31(3)(f) of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A registered Indian company receives consultancy services from a supplier located outside India on 3 March 2026. The supply is an import of services on which the company must pay tax under reverse charge, and the foreign supplier is not registered in India.

items.stem: What is the value for customs purposes before duty is applied?

options.text: ₹24,22,500 — FOB plus freight at twenty per cent of FOB plus insurance at 1.125 per cent of FOB
options.misconception: uses the twenty per cent fallback for freight even though the actual cost is documented
options.why: Twenty per cent of FOB is a fallback for when the cost of transport cannot be ascertained. Here it can be, and the documented ₹1,00,000 is what goes in.

options.text: ₹21,43,725 — ₹21,22,500 plus a landing charge of one per cent
options.misconception: still adds the flat one per cent landing charge that was removed in September 2017
options.why: The one per cent notional loading was deleted from rule 10(2) with effect from 26 September 2017. Adding it applies a rule that no longer exists.

options.text: ₹21,00,000 — FOB plus the actual freight, with insurance left out because it cannot be ascertained
options.misconception: treats an unascertainable cost as an absent one rather than applying the prescribed rate
options.why: Rule 10(2) supplies a figure precisely so that an unascertainable insurance cost is never simply dropped. It is taken at 1.125 per cent of the FOB value.

options.text: ₹21,22,500 — FOB plus the actual freight of ₹1,00,000 plus insurance at 1.125 per cent of FOB
options.why: An actual, documented freight figure is used as it stands. Only insurance falls back to the rule 10(2) rate of 1.125 per cent of the FOB value, which is ₹22,500 on ₹20,00,000. The total is ₹21,22,500, with no landing charge added.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007

items.scenario: Goods are imported by sea at a free on board value of ₹20,00,000. The importer has documentary evidence of ocean freight actually paid of ₹1,00,000. No insurance document is available and the cost of insurance cannot be ascertained.

items.stem: What route is open to him, and within what time?

options.text: Claim drawback under section 74 instead, which refunds up to ninety-eight per cent of the duty paid
options.misconception: reaches for the re-export drawback when the goods were manufactured and exported, not re-exported as they came
options.why: Section 74 refunds duty on imported goods re-exported as the same identifiable goods. Duty on inputs consumed in manufacturing an exported product is section 75, and the two never apply to one claim.

options.text: Nothing — an All Industry Rate once notified is final, and an exporter takes it as it comes
options.misconception: treats the notified rate as conclusive and misses the special brand rate remedy entirely
options.why: The rules provide a remedy precisely because a rate fixed for a whole class can sit well below one exporter's actual incidence. Rule 7 is that remedy.

options.text: Apply under rule 6 for a brand rate, since the notified rate does not reflect his own duty incidence
options.misconception: confuses rule 6, which is for where no rate has been determined at all, with rule 7
options.why: Rule 6 applies where no amount or rate of drawback has been determined for the goods. Here one has been determined; it is merely low, which is rule 7's ground.

options.text: Apply under rule 7 for a special brand rate, because the All Industry Rate is less than eighty per cent of the duties actually paid, within three months of the relevant date
options.why: Rule 7 of the Drawback Rules, 2017 is for exactly this — an All Industry Rate exists but recovers less than eighty per cent of the duties paid on the materials. The application runs to three months from the relevant date, extendable on payment of the prescribed fee.

citation.ref: Section 75, with Rules 6 and 7 of the Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017

items.scenario: An exporter manufactures and exports a product for which the Government has notified an All Industry Rate of drawback. On working it out, the rate gives him back roughly sixty per cent of the customs duty he actually paid on the imported materials that went into the goods.

items.stem: Which officer of Central Tax is the proper officer to issue the notice and pass the order?

options.text: The Deputy or Assistant Commissioner
options.why: Where a notice covers more than one tax, Circular No. 254/11/2025-GST fixes the officer on the combined amount of central tax, integrated tax and cess — here ₹26 lakh — tested against the integrated tax steps of ₹20 lakh and ₹2 crore. ₹26 lakh sits above ₹20 lakh and well below ₹2 crore, which is the Deputy or Assistant Commissioner's slab.

options.text: The Superintendent, because the central tax involved is only ₹6 lakh, inside his ₹10 lakh limit
options.misconception: tests each tax against its own column instead of adding them, which the circular requires where one notice covers several
options.why: The ₹10 lakh ceiling applies where central tax is all that is in issue. This notice carries integrated tax and cess as well, so the combined amount governs and the central tax figure read alone decides nothing.

options.text: The Superintendent, because the largest single component, integrated tax of ₹18 lakh, is inside his ₹20 lakh limit
options.misconception: takes the biggest component as the test and drops the cess out of the reckoning altogether
options.why: The circular adds central tax, integrated tax and cess together; it does not pick the largest. Leaving the ₹2 lakh of cess and the ₹6 lakh of central tax out is what makes this answer come out one rank too low.

options.text: The Commissioner, because section 74A carries no monetary limits — only sections 73 and 74 have them, under the 2018 circular
options.misconception: treats Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST as the whole law and leaves section 74A unassigned
options.why: Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST did cover only sections 73 and 74, and that gap is exactly what Circular No. 254/11/2025-GST closed on 27 October 2025 by extending the same three-tier scheme to section 74A.

citation.ref: Section 74A, read with Table II of Circular No. 254/11/2025-GST dated 27 October 2025

items.scenario: A show cause notice under section 74A is to be issued to a taxpayer for FY 2025-26. The shortfall proposed is central tax ₹6 lakh, integrated tax ₹18 lakh and compensation cess ₹2 lakh, all arising from the same set of transactions and all to go into one notice.

items.stem: Is he eligible for rule 14A, and what decides it?

options.text: No — the two figures add to ₹3 lakh a month, which is above the ₹2,50,000 ceiling
options.misconception: pulls business-to-consumer output tax into a test rule 14A confines to supplies made to registered persons
options.why: The ₹1.2 lakh on supplies to unregistered customers does not enter the calculation. The rule counts output tax on supplies made to registered persons and nothing else.

options.text: Yes, and being low risk under rule 9A he gets registration in three working days without needing Aadhaar authentication
options.misconception: drops the Aadhaar condition, which rule 14A makes compulsory even though rule 9A works on the system's risk data alone
options.why: Rule 9A grants registration on data analysis and risk parameters. Rule 14A is a separate, opted-into scheme and makes Aadhaar authentication of the primary authorised signatory and at least one promoter or partner a condition of entry.

options.text: No — his aggregate turnover of ₹60 lakh is above the ₹40 lakh limit, so he must take ordinary registration
options.misconception: reads the ₹2,50,000 as a turnover gate and imports the section 22 threshold, which decides whether to register rather than how
options.why: Aggregate turnover under section 22 decides whether a person must register at all. Rule 14A decides the route by which an applicant is registered, and its test is a monthly output tax figure, not turnover.

options.text: Yes — the test is the monthly output tax on supplies made to registered persons, ₹1.8 lakh here, against the ₹2,50,000 ceiling
options.why: Rule 14A measures the total output tax liability on supplies made to registered persons and asks whether it exceeds ₹2,50,000 a month. His figure on that base is ₹1.8 lakh, so he qualifies, provided Aadhaar is authenticated for the primary authorised signatory and at least one promoter or partner.

citation.ref: Rule 14A, inserted by Notification No. 18/2025-Central Tax dated 31 October 2025

items.scenario: A trader in Indore applies for registration in June 2026. His aggregate turnover for the year will be about ₹60 lakh. His monthly output tax on supplies made to registered dealers works out at roughly ₹1.8 lakh, and on supplies to unregistered walk-in customers at roughly ₹1.2 lakh. He wants the three-working-day route under rule 14A.

items.stem: How is the appeal to be heard?

options.text: By a bench of two Members, because the amount is read across the whole order
options.why: Section 109(8) lets a single Member hear an appeal only where the amount involved does not exceed ₹50 lakh and no question of law arises. The figure is read cumulatively across every issue and tax period in the order, so ₹22 lakh, ₹19 lakh and ₹16 lakh add to ₹57 lakh and the ceiling is crossed.

options.text: By a bench of two Members, because a single Member Bench may only hear appeals about a penalty and never about tax
options.misconception: invents a subject-matter bar that section 109(8) does not contain
options.why: Section 109(8) speaks of the tax or input tax credit involved and of the fine, fee or penalty determined, treating them alike. The subject matter is not what decides; the amount and the question of law are.

options.text: By a single Member, because no one tax period in the order carries more than ₹50 lakh
options.misconception: tests the ceiling period by period rather than on the order as a whole
options.why: Splitting the order into its periods is what makes this answer look right. The ₹50 lakh is read cumulatively across all the issues and tax periods the order covers, and the total is ₹57 lakh.

options.text: By a single Member, because the appeal raises no question of law and that is what section 109(8) turns on
options.misconception: takes the question-of-law condition as sufficient and drops the monetary ceiling, which must be satisfied as well
options.why: Both conditions must hold together. Absence of a question of law is necessary but not enough; the amount involved must also stay within ₹50 lakh, and here it does not.

citation.ref: Section 109(8), read with Rule 110A of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: One order of the Appellate Authority disposes of three tax periods together, confirming tax of ₹22 lakh, ₹19 lakh and ₹16 lakh respectively. The taxpayer appeals to the Appellate Tribunal against the whole order. Nobody suggests the appeal raises a question of law.

items.stem: By when must the proper officer finalise the assessment?

options.text: By 10 May 2026, two years from the date of the provisional assessment
options.misconception: counts from the original assessment and misses the transitional rule for assessments pending on 29 March 2025
options.why: Two years is the right period, but not the right starting point for this case. Where the provisional assessment was pending on 29 March 2025, the clock is reset to that date.

options.text: Within six months, extendable by the Commissioner
options.misconception: carries the GST provisional assessment clock in section 60 of the CGST Act across into customs
options.why: Six months is the ordinary period for finalising a provisional assessment under section 60 of the CGST Act. Customs runs on section 18(1B) and its two years.

options.text: There is no outer date; a provisional assessment stands open until the officer chooses to finalise it
options.misconception: states the position before the Finance Act, 2025, which is exactly what section 18(1B) was inserted to end
options.why: That was the law until the Finance Act, 2025 inserted section 18(1B). A provisional assessment now carries a statutory deadline and the officer must record why he cannot meet it.

options.text: By 29 March 2027, extendable by one further year
options.why: Section 18(1B) allows two years, and for an assessment already pending on 29 March 2025 the two years are reckoned from that date rather than from the original provisional assessment. The first proviso lets the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner extend by one further year on sufficient cause recorded in writing.

citation.ref: Section 18(1B) with its first proviso, read with the Customs (Finalisation of Provisional Assessment) Regulations, 2025, Notification No. 55/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 12 September 2025

items.scenario: A consignment was assessed provisionally under section 18(1) of the Customs Act on 10 May 2024 because the declared value was under enquiry. The assessment was still open on 29 March 2025 and remains open today. No stay, no Board direction and no foreign enquiry is in the way.

items.stem: Which statement is correct?

options.text: He may transfer ₹2,00,000 of the scrip and keep the balance, since duty credit is divisible like any other credit
options.misconception: assumes a scrip can be split, which regulation 7 expressly forbids
options.why: Regulation 7 allows the duty credit in an e-scrip to be transferred at a time for the entire amount in that scrip, and says a part transfer is not permitted.

options.text: The scrip lapses one year from creation, so any balance must be used by 31 May 2027
options.misconception: uses the original one-year validity, which the 2022 amendment raised to two years
options.why: The Electronic Duty Credit Ledger Regulations, 2021 first gave one year. Notification No. 79/2022-Customs (N.T.) dated 15 September 2022 substituted two years, and a transfer does not restart that period.

options.text: The credit pays basic customs duty only, a scrip transfers whole or not at all, and it runs for two years from creation
options.why: The duty credit in an e-scrip pays only the duties specified in the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, that is basic customs duty. Regulation 7 transfers the entire amount of a scrip at a time and permits no part transfer, and regulation 6 gives it two years from creation in the ledger, after which anything unused lapses.

options.text: The credit may be set against basic customs duty and against the integrated tax on the import, since both fall due at the same moment
options.misconception: treats everything collected at import as payable from the ledger, when the credit reaches only the First Schedule duties
options.why: Integrated tax and compensation cess are collected at import under the Customs Tariff Act's own charging provisions, not as duties in the First Schedule. The ledger cannot pay them.

citation.ref: Section 51B, read with regulations 6 and 7 of the Electronic Duty Credit Ledger Regulations, 2021, as amended by Notification No. 79/2022-Customs (N.T.) dated 15 September 2022

items.scenario: An exporter's RoDTEP claim is credited as an e-scrip of ₹5,00,000 created in his electronic duty credit ledger on 1 June 2026. He plans to use ₹3,00,000 of it against an import, transfer the remaining ₹2,00,000 to a supplier who holds an Importer-Exporter Code, and treat the scrip as good until 31 May 2027.

items.stem: How is each of the three treated under GST?

options.text: Both policies are exempt but the reinsurance is taxable, because reinsurance is a separate service between two insurers
options.misconception: exempts the group policy and taxes the reinsurance, which is the reverse of what entries 36D and 36E say
options.why: Entry 36E was inserted precisely so that reinsurance of an exempt individual policy is itself exempt. The group policy, on the other hand, was never brought inside 36D.

options.text: The individual policy is exempt, the group policy is taxable at eighteen per cent, and the reinsurance is exempt
options.why: Entry 36D exempts health insurance business provided to an insured who is not a group, which covers an individual and his family. A group policy falls outside those words and stays taxable at eighteen per cent. Entry 36E then exempts reinsurance of a service covered by 36C or 36D, so the cession follows the policy it reinsures.

options.text: All three are exempt, since the exemption covers health insurance business as a class
options.misconception: reads entries 36C and 36D as class exemptions and misses the words that keep a group out
options.why: Neither entry exempts health insurance business at large. Each is confined to an insured who is not a group, so an employer's cover for its staff is outside and remains taxable.

options.text: The individual policy and the reinsurance are zero-rated, so the insurer keeps full input tax credit on them
options.misconception: confuses exemption with zero rating, and so keeps a credit chain that exemption breaks
options.why: Only exports and supplies to a special economic zone are zero-rated. These entries grant an exemption, which breaks the insurer's input tax credit on those supplies rather than preserving it.

citation.ref: Serial numbers 36C, 36D and 36E, inserted by Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 with effect from 22 September 2025

items.scenario: In June 2026 an insurer issues three things: a health insurance policy to an individual covering him and his family; a group health policy to a company covering its employees; and it cedes part of the risk on the individual policy to a reinsurer, who charges reinsurance premium.

items.stem: What is his composition tax for the quarter?

options.text: ₹1,44,000, being six per cent of ₹24,00,000
options.misconception: applies the section 10(2A) rate for service providers to a supplier of goods
options.why: Six per cent belongs to the section 10(2A) scheme for a supplier of services whose preceding year's aggregate turnover stayed within fifty lakh rupees. It has nothing to do with a trader in goods under section 10(1).

options.text: ₹24,000, being one per cent of the whole ₹24,00,000
options.misconception: applies the manufacturer's base, turnover in State, to a trader whose rule 7 entry says turnover of taxable supplies
options.why: Turnover in State, exempt supplies included, is the base for a manufacturer. For any other eligible supplier rule 7 shifts the base to the turnover of taxable supplies, and that difference is the whole reason the two entries are separate.

A trader falls in the residual entry of rule 7 and pays one per cent of the turnover of taxable supplies of goods and services in State. That base is ₹18,00,000, since the ₹6,00,000 of exempt goods is left out, and one per cent of it is ₹18,000.

options.text: ₹1,20,000, being five per cent of ₹24,00,000
options.misconception: uses the restaurant rate for a trader
options.why: Five per cent is the rate for a supplier making restaurant supplies without alcohol. A trader pays one per cent, and on the narrower base at that.

citation.ref: Rule 7, read with section 10(1) of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A registered trader in Jaipur is under the composition levy. For the quarter ended 30 June 2026 his turnover in the State is ₹24,00,000, of which ₹18,00,000 is taxable goods and ₹6,00,000 is goods that are exempt. He is not a manufacturer and runs no restaurant.

items.stem: What does section 122B add?

options.text: ₹1,00,000, the fixed penalty section 122B prescribes
options.misconception: takes the fixed figure as the whole rule and drops the comparison the section requires
options.why: ₹1,00,000 is only the floor. The section takes whichever is higher of that figure and ten per cent of the tax payable on the goods, and here the percentage wins.

options.text: Nothing, because section 148A is an enabling provision and carries no penalty of its own
options.misconception: looks only at section 148A and misses the separate penalty section that gives it teeth
options.why: Section 148A does indeed impose no penalty; that is why the Finance Act, 2025 also inserted section 122B, in force from 1 October 2025, to punish a contravention of it.

options.text: ₹1,50,000, on top of the ₹50,000 under section 122
options.why: Section 122B sets the penalty at ₹1,00,000 or ten per cent of the tax payable on the goods, whichever is higher. Ten per cent of ₹15,00,000 is ₹1,50,000, which is higher, and the section says the amount is in addition to any other penalty, so the ₹50,000 stands as well.

options.text: ₹1,50,000, and the ₹50,000 under section 122 is absorbed into it, since one act cannot be penalised twice
options.misconception: reads section 122B as a substitute penalty when its own words make it an addition
options.why: Section 122B says the penalty is in addition to any penalty under Chapter XV or under the penalty chapter. The two run together rather than one swallowing the other.

items.scenario: The Government has notified a class of goods and the persons dealing in them under section 148A, requiring a unique identification marking. A dealer moves a consignment of those goods without affixing the marking. The tax payable on the consignment is ₹15,00,000. He is separately liable to a penalty of ₹50,000 under section 122 for the same consignment.

items.stem: What is his position under section 18A of the Customs Act?

options.text: He may file an electronic revised entry at the port where the duty was paid and pay the ₹4,00,000 with interest, without penalty
options.why: Section 18A lets an importer voluntarily revise an entry after clearance, and the revised entry is treated as a self-assessment. Where it shows duty short paid he pays it with interest; no penalty attaches and no notice under section 28 issues. The application is filed electronically at the port where the duty was paid, with a fee of ₹1,000.

options.text: He must wait for the department, since only the proper officer can reopen a completed assessment, by a notice under section 28
options.misconception: states the position before the Finance Act, 2025, which section 18A was inserted to change
options.why: That was the position until section 18A came in. The importer no longer has to wait for a notice under section 28 to correct his own error.

options.text: He should apply under section 149 to amend the bill of entry, which is the only route for correcting a document after clearance
options.misconception: confuses amendment of a document under section 149 with revision of the entry and its assessment under section 18A
options.why: Section 149 amends a document. Section 18A revises the entry and with it the self-assessment, and it is the provision that deals with duty short paid or paid in excess on that revision.

options.text: He may revise, but the short payment carries a penalty as it would on a section 28 demand, because the error was his own
options.misconception: carries the section 28 penalty into a route whose whole purpose is that voluntary correction costs interest and nothing more
options.why: The absence of a penalty is what makes the route worth using. Voluntary revision under section 18A attracts the duty and interest alone.

citation.ref: Section 18A, read with the Customs (Voluntary Revision of Entries Post Clearance) Regulations, 2025, Notification No. 70/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 30 October 2025

items.scenario: An importer's own review in June 2026 finds that a bill of entry cleared in March 2026 classified the goods under the wrong heading and that ₹4,00,000 of duty was short paid. No audit, search, seizure or investigation has been started against him, and the entry has not been reassessed.

items.stem: Can he file it?

options.text: No — the three years from the due date ran out on 20 August 2025 and section 39(11) bars the return
options.why: Section 39(11) forbids a return being furnished after three years from the due date of furnishing it. That due date was 20 August 2022, so the door closed on 20 August 2025. Willingness to pay does not reopen it.

options.text: Yes, because the three years runs from the due date of the annual return for FY 2022-23
options.misconception: borrows the annual return's due date, which anchors the section 74A limitation rather than this one
options.why: The annual return's due date is the anchor for the section 74A limitation on demands. The three-year bar in section 39(11) runs from the due date of the very return being furnished.

options.text: Yes, on paying the late fee and interest, since the Act sets no outer date for filing a return
options.misconception: states the position before the Finance Act, 2023 sub-sections were brought into force
options.why: That was true until 1 October 2023, when the sub-sections inserted by the Finance Act, 2023 came into force under Notification No. 28/2023-Central Tax. Late fee buys lateness, not a barred return.

options.text: No, and nothing can ever revive it — the bar admits of no exception
options.misconception: misses the proviso letting the Government, on the Council's recommendation, allow a barred return on notified conditions
options.why: Each of the four sub-sections carries a proviso under which the Government may, on the recommendations of the Council, notify conditions on which a barred return may still be furnished. The bar is hard but not beyond relief.

citation.ref: Section 39(11), inserted by the Finance Act, 2023 and brought into force with effect from 1 October 2023 by Notification No. 28/2023-Central Tax dated 31 July 2023

items.scenario: A registered person never filed his return in FORM GSTR-3B for the month of July 2022, which was due on 20 August 2022. In June 2026 he wants to file it, and is willing to pay the late fee and the interest.

items.stem: What must he do in the return for the tax period following those 180 days?

options.text: Add the whole ₹1,80,000, since the invoice was not paid in full within 180 days
options.misconception: reverses everything, which was the position before rule 37 was substituted with effect from 1 October 2022
options.why: Rule 37 as substituted with effect from 1 October 2022 makes the reversal proportionate to the unpaid amount. Full reversal on a part payment overstates the liability by ₹90,000.

options.text: Add ₹90,000 to his output tax liability, with interest
options.why: Rule 37 makes the reversal proportionate to the amount left unpaid. Half the invoice value with tax is unpaid, so half the credit — ₹90,000 — is added to his output tax liability in the return for the period immediately following the 180 days, with interest under section 50.

options.text: Nothing — the credit stands, and only interest is payable on the unpaid portion
options.misconception: treats the consequence as interest alone, when the proviso adds the credit itself back to output tax liability
options.why: The second proviso to section 16(2) adds an amount equal to the credit availed to his output tax liability. Interest is on top of that, not instead of it.

options.text: Add ₹90,000, and treat that credit as lost for good, because section 16(4) has since closed for a April 2026 invoice
options.misconception: applies the section 16(4) time limit to re-availment, which rule 37(4) expressly frees from it
options.why: Rule 37(4) lets him take the credit back when he pays the supplier, and says the section 16(4) time limit does not apply to that re-availment. The credit is suspended, not destroyed.

citation.ref: Second proviso to section 16(2), read with rule 37 of the CGST Rules, 2017 as substituted with effect from 1 October 2022

items.scenario: A registered person receives a supply on an invoice dated 5 April 2026 for ₹10,00,000 plus GST of ₹1,80,000, and takes the full credit of ₹1,80,000. By the 180th day from the invoice he has paid the supplier ₹5,90,000, exactly half of the ₹11,80,000 due, and nothing more. The supply is not one on which tax is payable under reverse charge.

items.stem: What is the outcome?

options.text: The appeal is admitted, and because the members differ it is deemed that no advance ruling can be issued on that point
options.why: Section 100(2) gives thirty days from communication of the ruling, and its proviso allows a further thirty days where the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause, so day forty-seven is within reach. Section 101(3) then says that where the members differ on any point, it is deemed that no advance ruling can be issued on that point.

options.text: The appeal is admitted, and the difference between the members is referred to the Appellate Tribunal for a ruling
options.misconception: assumes an appeal upward exists, when the advance ruling machinery stops at the Appellate Authority
options.why: The advance ruling route ends at the Appellate Authority. Nothing goes on to the Appellate Tribunal, and a difference between the members leaves the applicant where he started.

options.text: The appeal is admitted, and where the members differ the presiding member's casting vote settles the point
options.misconception: imports a casting vote that section 101(3) does not provide
options.why: There is no casting vote in the Appellate Authority. A difference between the two members produces no ruling at all on the point they differ on.

options.text: The appeal is time barred, because the thirty days in section 100(2) cannot be extended
options.misconception: reads the thirty days as absolute and misses the proviso allowing a further thirty
options.why: The proviso to section 100(2) allows a further period of thirty days where the Appellate Authority is satisfied that sufficient cause prevented the appellant from filing in time. Illness proved to its satisfaction is such a cause.

citation.ref: Section 100(2) with its proviso, read with section 101(3)

items.scenario: An advance ruling is communicated to the applicant on 4 May 2026. He files his appeal before the Appellate Authority for Advance Ruling on 20 June 2026 — the forty-seventh day — and satisfies the Authority that illness prevented him from filing sooner. The Authority hears the appeal, and its two members then take opposite views on the only point in issue.

items.stem: Until when does the exemption hold?

options.text: Indefinitely, until the Government rescinds it, since section 25(4A) governs only a special order under section 25(2)
options.misconception: puts the sunset on the wrong sub-section; section 25(2) special orders are a different power altogether
options.why: Section 25(4A) applies to a conditional exemption granted by notification under section 25(1). A special order under section 25(2), for goods of a strategic or secret nature or for a charitable purpose, is made case by case and is a separate power.

options.text: Up to 31 March 2029
options.why: Section 25(4A) ends a conditional exemption on the 31st day of March falling immediately after two years from the date it was granted. Two years from 15 July 2026 runs to 15 July 2028, and the 31 March next after that is 31 March 2029.

options.text: Up to 31 March 2027, the end of the financial year in which it was issued
options.misconception: reads the sunset as an annual expiry at each financial year end rather than a two-year run followed by the next 31 March
options.why: There is no annual expiry in section 25(4A). The date is found by running two years from the grant and then taking the 31 March immediately after.

options.text: Up to 14 July 2028, being exactly two years from the date it was granted
options.misconception: stops at the two years and misses that the sunset then falls on the following 31 March
options.why: The two years is only the first step. Section 25(4A) then carries the expiry forward to the 31st day of March falling immediately after that point.

items.scenario: The Central Government issues a notification under section 25(1) of the Customs Act on 15 July 2026 exempting a class of imported goods from basic customs duty, subject to the importer using them for a specified purpose. The notification says nothing about how long it will last, and the exemption is not one that flows from any trade agreement or international obligation.

items.stem: What must the exporter do?

options.text: Pay the integrated tax with interest by 25 April 2027, and the LUT facility stays withdrawn until he does
options.why: Rule 96A(1)(b) makes the tax payable within fifteen days after one year from the date of the export invoice where payment has not been received in convertible foreign exchange. One year from 10 April 2026 ends on 10 April 2027, so the fifteen days run to 25 April 2027. Until the amount is paid the Letter of Undertaking facility is withdrawn, and it is restored on payment.

options.text: Pay by 25 July 2026 — fifteen days after three months from the invoice
options.misconception: applies the goods clock in rule 96A(1)(a) to an export of services
options.why: Three months is the period for goods, and it measures whether the goods left India. For services rule 96A(1)(b) gives one year and measures receipt of payment instead.

options.text: Pay the tax with interest, but the LUT continues, since it is withdrawn only where fraud is found
options.misconception: misses that the facility is withdrawn on the default itself and restored only when the amount is paid
options.why: No finding of fraud is needed. The export facility under bond or Letter of Undertaking is withdrawn the moment the exporter fails to pay the amount due, and is restored once he pays.

options.text: Nothing is payable, because for services the undertaking is tested by whether the service was performed, not by payment
options.misconception: transplants the goods test onto services, where the rule turns on receipt in convertible foreign exchange
options.why: Performance is not the test for services. Rule 96A(1)(b) asks whether payment has been received in convertible foreign exchange, and non-receipt within the year makes the tax fall due.

citation.ref: Rule 96A(1)(b), read with section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A registered exporter of consultancy services holds a Letter of Undertaking and exports without payment of integrated tax. He issues an export invoice on 10 April 2026. By 10 April 2027 the client has still not paid, no money has come in convertible foreign exchange, and the exporter has asked the Commissioner for no extension.

items.stem: Where does he stand?

options.text: Within time — he has until 19 May 2027 to put the goods to the intended purpose
options.why: Notification No. 07/2025-Customs (N.T.) substituted one year for six months in the IGCR Rules, 2022 with effect from 2 February 2025, so the period for putting the goods to the intended purpose runs a full year from import. Goods cleared on 20 May 2026 are within time until 19 May 2027.

options.text: Out of time, and the concessional rate is void from the date of import, so the full duty and a penalty are payable
options.misconception: treats a failed end-use condition as voiding the assessment, when the rules simply make the differential duty payable
options.why: Failing the condition does not undo the import or the assessment. The consequence the rules prescribe is that the differential duty becomes payable, with interest.

options.text: Within time, and he need file no statement at all until the goods are actually consumed
options.misconception: drops the periodic reporting, which runs on its own regardless of whether the goods have been used
options.why: The statement in Form IGCR-3 is due quarterly, a quarter being three consecutive calendar months ending in March, June, September or December. It does not wait on consumption.

options.text: Out of time — the six months ran out on 19 November 2026, and the differential duty is now payable with interest
options.misconception: uses the six-month period that Notification No. 07/2025-Customs (N.T.) replaced with one year
options.why: Six months was the period until 1 February 2025. The amendment substituted one year in both the end-use rule and the rule on re-export of unutilised or defective goods.

citation.ref: Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty or for Specified End Use) Rules, 2022, rules 6, 7 and 10, as amended by Notification No. 07/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 1 February 2025

items.scenario: An importer clears goods on 20 May 2026 at a concessional rate of duty conditional on their use in manufacture, following the IGCR Rules, 2022. On 1 December 2026 a part of the consignment is still lying unused in his factory.

items.stem: What must the head office do?

options.text: Nothing — the credit belongs to whoever the invoice names, so the head office may simply keep it
options.misconception: lets the head office retain credit on services its branches consume, which is what the ISD mechanism exists to prevent
options.why: The head office makes no outward supply of its own against which to use that credit. The Input Service Distributor mechanism exists precisely so the credit reaches the registrations that consumed the service.

options.text: Take an ISD registration and distribute both credits, paying the tax on the legal service first under its own ordinary registration
options.why: From 1 April 2025 section 20 says an office receiving invoices for input services on behalf of distinct persons shall distribute the credit through the Input Service Distributor mechanism, and section 24(viii) makes that registration compulsory. Section 2(61) now takes in invoices for services taxable under section 9(3) or 9(4), so the reverse charge legal service goes through the ISD too — the tax is paid under the ordinary registration and the credit is then distributed.

options.text: Cross-charge both services to the branches by raising a tax invoice on them as distinct persons, as it did before
options.misconception: keeps the pre-April 2025 choice, which the substitution of section 20 removed
options.why: Cross-charge was one of two permitted routes until 31 March 2025. The substituted section 20 changed may to shall, so distribution of common input services through an Input Service Distributor registration is now compulsory.

options.text: Take an ISD registration for the software subscription, but keep the legal service out, since the ISD mechanism covers only forward-charge invoices
options.misconception: applies the old definition of Input Service Distributor, which said nothing about invoices taxable under section 9(3) or 9(4)
options.why: The substituted section 2(61) expressly brings in invoices for services on which tax is payable by the recipient under section 9(3) or section 9(4). Reverse charge input services received for a branch now run through the ISD as well.

citation.ref: Sections 2(61) and 20 as substituted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 April 2025, read with section 24(viii)

items.scenario: A company's head office in Bengaluru receives two invoices in FY 2026-27. One is for a pan-India software subscription used by all three of its branches, each separately registered. The other is for legal services from an advocate, taxable in the company's hands under reverse charge, and availed entirely for the Mumbai branch.

items.stem: Can the company take the ₹7.2 lakh input tax credit?

options.text: No, and the goods must also be returned to the supplier
options.misconception: attaches a consequence to the goods when the defect is in the tax chain
options.why: The purchase itself is untouched — the goods are the company's. What fails is the credit; the company's remedy against the supplier is contractual, not a return of goods.

options.text: Yes — a valid invoice and receipt of goods complete the recipient's obligations
options.misconception: treats the recipient-side conditions as the whole test
options.why: That was the intuition under the old regime and it is the specific thing section 16(2)(c) rejects. The credit is of tax paid, and no tax was paid.

options.text: No — payment of the tax to the Government by the supplier is itself a condition
options.why: Section 16(2)(c) makes the supplier's actual payment a condition of the recipient's credit. Invoice, receipt and GSTR-2B appearance satisfy three conditions of five; all of them must hold together, and the missing one defeats the claim.

options.text: Yes, provisionally, reversible if the supplier stays in default for six months
options.misconception: recalls the provisional-credit mechanism that no longer exists
options.why: Provisional credit was removed from the law. Credit now follows GSTR-2B and the satisfied conditions, with no provisional window to occupy.

items.scenario: A company buys raw material worth ₹40 lakh plus ₹7.2 lakh GST, holds a valid tax invoice, has received the goods, and the invoice appears in its GSTR-2B. It then learns the supplier collected the tax but never deposited it with the Government.

items.stem: What is the GST position on these fees?

options.text: The company pays under reverse charge by debiting its input tax credit
options.misconception: discharges a reverse-charge liability through the credit ledger
options.why: Reverse charge must be paid through the cash ledger. The credit ledger can pay output tax on the company's own supplies, not the tax it owes as a recipient.

options.text: The company pays the GST under reverse charge, in cash
options.why: Legal services from an advocate to a business entity are notified under section 9(3), so the liability sits on the recipient. Reverse charge liability is discharged in cash — the company may then take credit of it, but cannot pay it out of credit.

options.text: The advocate should have charged GST on the bill
options.misconception: applies forward charge to a notified reverse-charge supply
options.why: For notified services the supplier neither charges nor collects. A bill without GST is the correct bill here; the tax travels on the company's own liability.

options.text: No GST arises, because legal services are exempt
options.misconception: stretches the small-recipient exemption to every recipient
options.why: The exemption covers advocates serving individuals and small business entities below the registration threshold. A ₹300 crore company is squarely outside it.

items.scenario: A manufacturing company with ₹300 crore turnover engages a senior advocate for a High Court matter and pays fees of ₹5 lakh. The advocate's bill shows no GST.

items.stem: Is registration required?

options.text: Yes, because every supplier of services must register from the first rupee
options.misconception: erases the threshold entirely for services
options.why: First-rupee registration applies to specific cases — inter-State taxable supply, e-commerce, reverse-charge recipients — not to services as a class.

options.text: No, not until turnover reaches ₹1.5 crore
options.misconception: mistakes the composition ceiling for the registration threshold
options.why: ₹1.5 crore is the composition scheme's eligibility ceiling — a choice available after registration, not a limit before it.

options.text: No, not until turnover reaches ₹40 lakh
options.misconception: applies the goods-only threshold to a service provider
options.why: The ₹40 lakh limit belongs to suppliers exclusively of goods in eligible States. One rupee of service supply keeps the ₹20 lakh limit in charge.

options.text: Yes — the services threshold of ₹20 lakh is crossed
options.why: A supplier of services takes the ₹20 lakh aggregate turnover limit, and ₹25 lakh is past it. Registration follows, with tax on supplies from the effective date.

items.scenario: A management consultant in Madhya Pradesh, supplying only services within the State, reaches aggregate turnover of ₹25 lakh during the year and asks whether registration is now compulsory.

items.stem: Can he make this supply while remaining in the scheme?

options.text: Yes, because his turnover is within the ₹1.5 crore ceiling
options.misconception: treats the turnover ceiling as the only eligibility condition
options.why: The ceiling is one condition of several. The inter-State bar is separate, and breaching it disqualifies regardless of how modest the turnover is.

options.text: No — inter-State outward supply ends composition eligibility
options.why: Section 10(2) bars a composition taxpayer from inter-State outward supplies. Shipping to Maharashtra means leaving the scheme and paying tax as a regular taxpayer, with the compliance that follows.

options.text: Yes, paying IGST on this order at the composition rate
options.misconception: extends the composition rate across State lines
options.why: There is no composition IGST. The scheme is a local-trade bargain, and the levy it charges exists only for intra-State supply.

options.text: Yes, if the Maharashtra buyer arranges his own transport from Indore
options.misconception: locates the supply by who carries the goods
options.why: Place of supply follows the movement's termination for delivery, not who pays the transporter. Goods bound for Maharashtra make an inter-State supply either way.

items.scenario: A composition dealer in Indore, selling hardware with turnover of ₹90 lakh, receives a large order from a buyer in Maharashtra and intends to supply it under the composition scheme.

items.stem: Which of these amounts is not added in arriving at the assessable value?

options.text: The selling commission of $2,000
options.misconception: excludes all commissions instead of only the buying commission
options.why: Selling commission is paid for the seller's benefit and is expressly added. The carve-out is for buying commission alone.

options.text: None of them — all payments connected with the import are added
options.misconception: adds everything rather than testing each payment against the rule
options.why: The rule works addition by addition, and buying commission is its stated exception. Adding everything overstates the value and the duty with it.

options.text: The buying commission of $1,500
options.why: Rule 10(1)(a) adds commissions and brokerage except buying commission. The importer's own agent works for the buyer, and paying him is part of the cost of buying, not part of the price of the goods.

options.text: The freight of $3,000
options.misconception: leaves transport out of a value that is built to the place of importation
options.why: Cost of transport to the place of importation is a Rule 10(2) addition. Assessable value is the landed value, and freight is part of landing the goods.

items.scenario: An importer's invoice shows goods at $50,000, selling commission of $2,000 paid to the exporter's agent, buying commission of $1,500 paid to the importer's own agent abroad, and freight of $3,000 to the Indian port.

items.stem: Can the credit still be taken?

options.text: No, because credit must be taken in the same month as the invoice
options.misconception: shrinks the statutory window to the invoice month
options.why: The law allows credit any time up to the section 16(4) date — often twenty months from an early-year invoice. The failure here is missing a generous window, not a same-month rule.

options.text: Yes, because the annual return for 2025-26 has not yet been filed
options.misconception: reads the two limbs as alternatives that each keep the window open
options.why: The section takes the EARLIER of the two dates. An unfiled annual return cannot extend the November cut-off; it can only close the window sooner.

options.text: No — the window closed on 30 November 2026
options.why: The invoice belongs to financial year 2025-26, so section 16(4) shuts the credit at the thirtieth of November following that year's end. Discovery in December is discovery too late, however eligible the credit was on its merits.

options.text: Yes, at any time within four years, as with other indirect tax refunds
options.misconception: imports a limitation period from refund law into the credit provision
options.why: Refund limitation under section 54 is a different clock for a different claim. Credit has its own guillotine in section 16(4), and it is measured in months, not years.

items.scenario: During a December 2026 review, a company discovers an unclaimed input tax credit of ₹6 lakh on a supplier invoice dated 14 February 2026. All section 16(2) conditions are satisfied and the annual return for 2025-26 has not yet been filed.

items.stem: What is the place of supply, and which tax applies?

options.text: Madhya Pradesh, because the buyer arranged the transport himself
options.misconception: lets who carries the goods decide the place of supply
options.why: Movement "whether by the supplier or the recipient" is within the same rule. The statute cares about the destination of the movement, not about whose truck it is.

options.text: Madhya Pradesh — an intra-State supply, since delivery was taken at the factory gate
options.misconception: fixes the place of supply where possession changed hands rather than where movement ends
options.why: Handing over at the gate is how the movement begins, not where it terminates. The section looks at where the goods are going for delivery to the recipient, which is Ahmedabad.

options.text: Gujarat, but as an intra-State supply of Gujarat attracting CGST and SGST
options.misconception: gets the place right and then misreads what inter-State means
options.why: Inter-State or intra-State compares the supplier's location with the place of supply. Supplier in Madhya Pradesh, place of supply Gujarat — that is inter-State, and IGST is the levy.

options.text: Gujarat — an inter-State supply attracting IGST
options.why: The supply involves movement of goods, and the movement terminates for delivery at the Ahmedabad plant. Section 10(1)(a) fixes the place of supply there, and Madhya Pradesh to Gujarat is inter-State, so IGST applies.

items.scenario: A dealer in Bhopal sells machinery to a buyer registered in Gujarat. The buyer sends its own truck, takes delivery at the Bhopal factory gate, and carries the machinery to its Ahmedabad plant.

items.stem: Who pays GST in March on the advance?

options.text: Neither, because no invoice has been issued by either
options.misconception: makes the invoice the sole trigger for both goods and services
options.why: For services the payment reaches back as a trigger on its own. The software company's liability arises in March with or without an invoice.

options.text: Both, since money received against a taxable supply is taxable when received
options.misconception: applies the services rule across the goods-services line
options.why: That was the position for goods only briefly. The notification removed advances on goods from the net after the compliance burden proved unworkable, and the asymmetry is now the tested point.

options.text: Only the manufacturer, since goods are tangible and the machine is identifiable
options.misconception: reverses the asymmetry
options.why: The rule runs the other way. Tangibility has nothing to do with it — the notification names goods as the excused side.

options.text: Only the software company — advances for services are taxable on receipt; for goods they are not
options.why: Time of supply for services reaches the earlier of invoice and payment, catching the advance in March. For goods, Notification 66/2017 confined the liability to invoice issue, so the manufacturer pays in May with the invoice.

items.scenario: On 20 March a machine manufacturer receives a ₹10 lakh advance against a machine to be delivered in May, and a software company receives a ₹10 lakh advance against an implementation project starting in May. Both are regular taxpayers.

items.stem: Which discount reduces the value of supply for GST?

options.text: The 2 per cent scheme discount, provided the dealer reverses the proportionate credit
options.why: It was agreed before the supplies, is linkable to specific invoices, and the recipient's credit reversal completes section 15(3)(b). The tax follows the price the parties had genuinely agreed all along.

options.text: Both, since both are genuine discounts actually passed on
options.misconception: treats commercial genuineness as the statutory test
options.why: Genuineness is necessary but the section demands prior agreement and invoice linkage. The goodwill discount was born after the supplies and fails at the first condition.

options.text: Neither, because post-supply discounts never reduce taxable value
options.misconception: reads the pre-supply agreement condition as banning all later discounts
options.why: The section exists precisely to allow post-supply discounts that were pre-agreed. What it shuts out is the discount invented after the event.

options.text: The goodwill discount, since it is unconditional and unilateral
options.misconception: rewards the discount with fewer strings as the cleaner deduction
options.why: Unconditional generosity is exactly what the section will not net off. The strings — prior agreement, linkage, reversal — are the qualification, not the disqualification.

items.scenario: A distributor agreement signed in April promises a 2 per cent year-end discount on all purchases if the dealer crosses ₹5 crore. The dealer crosses it, and the distributor issues a credit note for ₹10 lakh plus tax, linked invoice-wise. Separately, the distributor gives another dealer an unplanned ₹4 lakh goodwill discount for staying loyal in a hard year.

items.stem: On what amount does the section 50 interest run?

options.text: On the full ₹20 lakh of the liability
options.misconception: charges interest on the gross liability the way the section originally read
options.why: Gross-liability interest was the original position, litigated hard and then rewritten retrospectively. Answers citing the old position are answering a repealed law.

options.text: On nothing, since the liability was fully discharged at filing
options.misconception: treats the eventual payment as erasing the delay
options.why: The tax was due with the period's return, not four months later. Discharge ends the clock; it does not unwind it.

options.text: On the ₹14 lakh met from credit, since credit was applied late
options.misconception: inverts the proviso and charges the credit portion
options.why: The proviso protects exactly that portion. Credit sitting in the ledger was already tax paid once; charging interest on it would tax the delay twice.

options.text: On the ₹6 lakh paid through the cash ledger
options.why: The proviso to section 50(1) confines interest, where the return is filed late, to the portion discharged through the electronic cash ledger. The ₹14 lakh met by credit was the Government's money in the system all along, and Parliament amended the section retrospectively to say so.

items.scenario: A taxpayer files a GSTR-3B four months late. The tax liability of ₹20 lakh for the period was covered ₹14 lakh by input tax credit and ₹6 lakh by cash, both applied on the day of the late filing.

items.stem: What is the position in August 2026?

options.text: Neither, because goods sent for job work are not supplies at all
options.misconception: remembers the concession and forgets its condition
options.why: The tax-free movement is conditional on timely return. Break the condition and the law rewrites history — the despatch becomes a taxable supply from day one.

options.text: The fabric is deemed supplied in June 2026, when the year expired
options.misconception: dates the deemed supply at the breach instead of the despatch
options.why: The deeming is retrospective to the date the goods went out. That is what makes the interest bite — fourteen months of it here, not two.

options.text: The fabric is deemed supplied on 1 June 2025, with tax and interest; the dies have time until June 2028
options.why: Inputs get one year, and the fabric's year ran out in June 2026 — the deeming reaches back to the day of despatch, so interest runs from 2025, not from the breach. Capital goods get three years, so the dies are safely out until 2028.

options.text: Both are deemed supplied, since neither returned within one year
options.misconception: applies the inputs window to capital goods
options.why: The section keeps two clocks. Dies are capital goods on a three-year clock, and treating them on the one-year clock manufactures a liability that does not exist.

items.scenario: A manufacturer sent dies worth ₹30 lakh (capital goods) and fabric worth ₹12 lakh (inputs) to a job worker on 1 June 2025 without payment of tax. The fabric is still with the job worker in August 2026; the dies are expected back in 2027.

items.stem: Is the colleague right?

options.text: Yes, unless the exporter pays IGST on exports first and reclaims it
options.misconception: makes the pay-and-refund route the only lawful one
options.why: Paying IGST and claiming it back is one of two routes. The LUT route reaches the same destination without routing ₹18 lakh through the Government and back.

options.text: Partly — credit survives but can only offset future domestic output tax, never refund
options.misconception: allows the credit but denies the refund that makes exporting viable
options.why: An exporter with no domestic sales would accumulate credit forever. Refund of unutilised credit on zero-rated supplies is the section's whole mechanism.

options.text: No — zero-rating keeps the credit alive, and the unutilised ₹18 lakh is refundable
options.why: Zero-rated is a different legal creature from exempt. Section 16 of the IGST Act preserves credit on inputs feeding zero-rated supplies, and the LUT route exists precisely so the exporter can skip charging tax yet recover the input side as a refund.

options.text: Yes — supplies on which no tax is charged are exempt, and exempt supplies block credit
options.misconception: collapses zero-rated into exempt
options.why: For exempt supplies the credit dies; for zero-rated it survives by express provision. The zero on the invoice looks identical and works oppositely, which is why the paper tests it.

items.scenario: An exporter of garments buys inputs carrying ₹18 lakh of GST and exports the entire output under a letter of undertaking, charging no tax on the export invoices. A colleague warns that selling without charging tax makes the supplies exempt, killing the input credit.

items.stem: Was an e-way bill required?

options.text: Yes — the bill attaches to movement of goods above fifty thousand rupees, sale or no sale
options.why: Rule 138 is triggered by causing movement of a consignment worth more than ₹50,000, and a branch transfer moves goods as surely as a sale does. The delivery challan takes the place of the invoice; the e-way bill is needed either way.

options.text: No, because both godowns belong to the same legal entity
options.misconception: treats intra-entity movement as outside the rule
options.why: The rule asks what is moving and how much it is worth, not who owns each end of the journey. Same-entity transfers above the limit are squarely inside it.

options.text: Yes, but only if the goods cross the State border
options.misconception: confines the requirement to inter-State movement
options.why: Intra-State movement carries the requirement too, though States may set higher limits for it. Indore to Bhopal is within one State and still within the rule.

options.text: No, because an e-way bill accompanies a tax invoice, and none exists here
options.misconception: ties the bill to the invoice instead of the movement
options.why: Movements without invoices travel on delivery challans, and the rule expressly covers reasons other than supply. The paperwork changes; the bill does not.

items.scenario: A registered dealer sends goods worth ₹3.2 lakh from its Indore godown to its own Bhopal branch, a stock transfer with no sale and no payment. The despatch clerk skips the e-way bill on the ground that nothing has been sold.

items.stem: What does release under section 129 cost him?

options.text: Nothing beyond a ₹10,000 general penalty, since no tax was evaded
options.misconception: imports the no-evasion leniency into a strict transit provision
options.why: Section 129 is deliberately indifferent to intent. The absent e-way bill is the offence, and courts have upheld the harshness because transit checks are where evasion hides.

options.text: A bond for the goods' value, with the penalty argued later in adjudication
options.misconception: offers the security route available to a non-owner as the owner's escape
options.why: Security in lieu is a route the section provides, but the release price stays the same penalty. The bond defers payment; it does not reduce what unlocks the truck.

options.text: A penalty of ₹3.6 lakh — two hundred per cent of the tax payable
options.why: Where the owner comes forward, section 129(1)(a) prices release at 200 per cent of the tax payable on the goods. The invoice showing tax charged does not soften it — the section punishes the movement's non-compliance, not evasion of the levy.

options.text: The ₹1.8 lakh tax plus a modest general penalty
options.misconception: applies the pre-amendment tax-plus-penalty formula
options.why: The section was rewritten to a pure penalty of 200 per cent. Answers built on the old tax-plus-100-per-cent split describe a provision that no longer exists.

items.scenario: A truck carrying taxable goods worth ₹10 lakh (tax ₹1.8 lakh) is intercepted without a valid e-way bill. The consignor owns up, produces the invoice showing tax fully charged, and argues that since the tax is on the invoice and will be paid with the return, only a token fine can apply.

items.stem: What is the GST position on the two transactions?

options.text: Neither is taxable, since GST requires consideration
options.misconception: treats consideration as indispensable to supply
options.why: Consideration is the general rule and Schedule I is the list of exceptions to it. The van is the textbook case — credit was enjoyed on the way in, so the way out is taxed.

options.text: The van is a deemed supply and taxable; the hampers stay outside as gifts within fifty thousand
options.why: Permanent disposal of a business asset that carried credit is Schedule I's first entry — consideration is irrelevant once the credit was taken. Employee gifts have their own carve-out and ₹4,000 sits well inside the fifty-thousand-per-employee-per-year line.

options.text: The van escapes because it went to a charity; the hampers are taxable perquisites
options.misconception: imports an income-tax charity instinct and a perquisite label into GST
options.why: GST has no donee-based relief here — the recipient's character does not undo Schedule I. And perquisite is an income-tax word; for GST the hampers are simply gifts under the fifty-thousand line.

options.text: Both are taxable, since both are supplies without consideration by a business
options.misconception: sweeps the employee-gift carve-out into the deeming
options.why: Gifts up to fifty thousand rupees a year per employee are expressly kept out. Taxing the hampers taxes what the proviso protects.

items.scenario: A company gives away an old delivery van, on which it had claimed input tax credit, free to a charitable school. The accountant books no GST since nothing was received in return. The same month, the company gifts each of its forty employees a festival hamper worth ₹4,000.

items.stem: How do these two sales sit under GST?

options.text: The building is taxable because it was sold by a developer in the course of business
options.misconception: lets the seller's trade override the completion certificate
options.why: Business character brings a transaction into GST only if it is a supply. A completed building with its certificate is out by schedule, developer or not — the tax belongs to under-construction sales.

options.text: Both are exempt supplies, and count toward aggregate turnover
options.misconception: confuses non-supplies with exempt supplies
options.why: Exempt supplies are supplies that a notification relieves; Schedule III transactions never become supplies in the first place. The difference shows up exactly where the accountant worried — turnover computations.

options.text: The land escapes but the building attracts GST at the works contract rate
options.misconception: taxes a completed sale as if construction services were still being supplied
options.why: Works contract rates belong to construction underway for a buyer. After completion and certification there is no service left to tax; what changes hands is immovable property.

options.text: Neither is a supply at all — Schedule III keeps land and completed buildings outside GST
options.why: Sale of land, and of a building after its completion certificate, are Schedule III entries — treated as neither goods nor services. They are not exempt supplies; they are non-supplies, which is why they also stay out of aggregate turnover.

items.scenario: A developer sells a completed office building with its occupancy certificate in hand for ₹48 crore, and separately sells a plot of land for ₹12 crore. His new accountant worries that these sales, being high-value, will attract GST and swell aggregate turnover past every threshold.

items.stem: Is the refund claim within time?

options.text: Yes — where tax was paid under a demand later set aside, the relevant date is the judgment's date
options.why: Section 54's two years run from the relevant date, and the definition assigns judgment-driven refunds the date of the judgment. The clock the department is reading — the payment date — belongs to a different ground of claim.

options.text: No — two years from payment is absolute, and equity cannot extend limitation
options.misconception: reads one relevant date as the only relevant date
options.why: The rigour of the limitation is real, but the statute itself moves the starting line by ground of claim. No equity is needed; the definition does the work.

options.text: Yes, because limitation never applies to tax collected without authority
options.misconception: right result, lawless route
options.why: Even unconstitutional levies travel through the refund machinery with its windows. The claim succeeds here because the statutory clock starts at the judgment, not because clocks stop for good causes.

options.text: No, unless the company had paid the tax under protest in 2024
options.misconception: imports the old excise protest requirement into GST
options.why: Payment under protest shaped refunds under the old law. Section 54's relevant-date definition replaced that scaffolding; the judgment date governs with or without a protest letter.

items.scenario: In August 2026 a company wins its writ petition: tax of ₹40 lakh it paid in March 2024 under a demand is held to have been collected without authority. The department resists the refund, arguing the two-year window from the March 2024 payment closed in March 2026.

items.stem: Is the adviser right?

options.text: No — the consultancy can use the ordinary one per cent traders' rate instead
options.misconception: puts the right taxpayer into the wrong scheme
options.why: The ordinary scheme's rates belong to manufacturers, traders and restaurants. A pure service provider enters through 10(2A) and pays that scheme's six per cent, not the traders' one.

options.text: Yes for this year, since eligibility needs current-year turnover below fifty lakh first
options.misconception: tests eligibility on the running year instead of the preceding one
options.why: The gate reads the preceding financial year — ₹42 lakh, inside the line. The current year's growth ends the scheme prospectively when it crosses, never retrospectively.

options.text: Yes — composition remains closed to every service except restaurants
options.misconception: states the pre-2019 law as current
options.why: True until section 10(2A) arrived, and stale ever since. The scheme the adviser denies is sitting in the section he cited.

options.text: No — section 10(2A) gives pure service providers their own scheme at six per cent within fifty lakh
options.why: The adviser's rule described the original section 10. The 2019 insertion built a parallel scheme for exactly this taxpayer — services, preceding-year turnover within fifty lakh, six per cent on turnover, with the same stay-local discipline.

items.scenario: An interior design consultancy with preceding-year turnover of ₹42 lakh wants a simple flat levy instead of regular GST compliance. Its adviser rules out composition entirely, saying the scheme is for traders and restaurants, never for service providers.

items.stem: On which vehicles is the credit good?

options.text: All three — each vehicle is used in the course of business
options.misconception: lets section 16's general test override section 17's specific block
